title: 5 Los Angeles Rams to watch vs. the Buffalo Bills
summary: The Buffalo Bills and the Los Angeles Rams entered the 2026 season as a popular pick for a Super Bowl matchup in February. Despite how we feel about Buffalo’s 29-26 defeat at the hands of the New England Patriots, the odds still seem to be in favor of said matchup, as the Bills sit at […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills and the Los Angeles Rams entered the 2026 season as a popular pick for a Super Bowl matchup in February. Despite how we feel about Buffalo’s 29-26 defeat at the hands of the New England Patriots, the odds still seem to be in favor of said matchup, as the Bills sit at +750. That trails only the Rams, whose odds remain great at +650 even with their 2-2 start to the season. This might be a great time for all of us to release our inner Han Solo—“never tell me the odds!”—because those odds may exist, but they mean little in practical terms. The games still need to be played, and on Monday, these two teams will face off in what is one of the NFL’s marquee games this season. Los Angeles is as complete a football team as Buffalo will face this season, and while their offense grabs most of the headlines, the Rams’ defense is incredible, as well. Currently, L.A. is No. 9 in points against and No. 2 in yards against this season, which is significantly better than Buffalo’s rankings. The Bills find themselves at No. 25 in points against and No. 27 in yards against. Our five players to watch, then, could easily discuss plenty of defensive standouts. Aaron Donald, for example, has the ability to wreck the entire offensive gameplan if he suits up. Byron Young and his 3.5 sacks have made the loss of Myles Garrett, who still hasn’t played since Week One thanks to a knee injury, a bit more palatable. Thanks to the depth of this roster, though, we’re acknowledging that there are going to be some players that we “miss” here. And, given how poorly Buffalo has played on defense this season, I argue that the unit under the most pressure to succeed on Monday night is not the Buffalo offense. So, with all of that in mind, here is our offensive-heavy edition of Five (Rams) Players to Watch this week. _____________________________________________________________________________ QB Matthew Stafford Buffalo just allowed Drake Maye to carve them up last week. As if it wasn’t bad enough that the 2025 NFL MVP runner-up looked as good as he did, now Buffalo has to contend with the 2025 NFL MVP. Stafford can still sling it at age 38, and if the Bills give him time, he will have a field day. Buffalo’s corners have struggled to cover even average receivers, and the Rams’ pass-catching group is well above that mark. Defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard is going to have to dial up a pass rush that can move Stafford off his platform and keep him uncomfortable all night. That’s the only hope this week for a better result on defense: Whereas Maye used his legs to evade danger, Stafford doesn’t do much running, so he isn’t going to beat you with his legs. He needs clean pockets and to stay upright. If Buffalo can pound on him early, they can speed his internal clock, which could force him into some mistakes. Stafford has six interceptions this season after throwing just eight picks all last season. The pass rush is going to need to impact this game for Buffalo to win it. RB Kyren Williams L.A.’s one-two punch of Williams and Blake Corum is outstanding, but it’s Williams who makes me the most wary. He can beat a team as a runner and as a receiver, as he’s totaled 294 yards and three touchdowns rushing to go with 21 receptions for 173 yards and a touchdown receiving. Buffalo has contained opposing running backs, and they’re going to need to continue that trend. Opening up Stafford’s game to play-action shots after Williams gashes them for big runs is a recipe for disaster, so Buffalo will need to keep Williams in check. The Rams love to use their big personnel to create mismatches, but honestly, I think that grouping might help the Bills this week. I feel much more confident in the front seven than I do anyone in the secondary right now, so if the Rams continue to utilize their “13” personnel grouping, it could help Buffalo put their stronger base defenders on the field in positions to succeed. That could be a factor in limiting Williams, as well. WR Davante Adams Who is going to cover the veteran? Adams may not be a top-three receiver in the league anymore, but he’s still plenty good at age 34. He leads Los Angeles in targets (38), receptions (22), receiving yards (390), and receiving touchdowns (2). Christian Benford has returned to practice for the Bills, but while he may be able to play through his toe injury, which kept him out of last week’s loss, he may still be limited by it. If he can’t go, it will likely be Maxwell Hairston, who was abysmal last week, or Davison Igbinosun, who had his moments but is still a rookie. This is not a great matchup for Buffalo, but someone needs to step up and make a play this week. WR Puka Nacua If Buffalo finds a way to slow Adams down, they’ll still have to contend with Nacua, who can operate from multiple alignments to create chaos in a banged-up Buffalo secondary. Dee Alford is dealing with an ankle injury, and his backup, practice squad player Te’Cory Couch, hurt his hamstring last week. During the game, Jim Leonhard’s answer to those injuries was to play either Damar Hamlin or Cole Bishop in the slot, which didn’t work. He might not have a choice again this week, though, and that could mean that Nacua has a huge game. Buffalo needs to figure out some way to limit him, and my hope is that they finally activate rookie Jalon Kilgore for a game. Yes, he’s just a rookie, but he at least has the athleticism to compete with Nacua. He also has experience playing as a slot defender, and he could not only help on Nacua, but he could also help against the Rams’ tight ends thanks to his size (6’1” 210 lbs.). Sticking with Hamlin, who is a heady player but a limited athlete, seems like the wrong move. CB Jaylen Watson Trent McDuffie is elite, and he’s somehow been even better so far this season than he was in Kansas City. McDuffie has seen 21 targets, according to Pro Football Reference , and he’s allowed just seven completions, 42 yards, and 22.5 quarterback rating against. He’s an eraser, and while Watson isn’t a bum, he’s not McDuffie. Buffalo has plenty of experience going against this duo from their time as teammates with the Kansas City Chiefs, so they’re intimately acquainted with what they can do. The Bills and quarterback Josh Allen can’t ignore McDuffie’s side altogether, but they’re going to want to find where No. 35 is and throw to that side more often.
author: Sean Murphy

title: Buffalo Bills vs. Los Angeles Rams: A history of memorable games
summary: The Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams don’t have the kind of rivalry that comes from playing twice a season, but their occasional meetings have produced some pretty memorable moments. There have been last-second touchdowns, Hall of Fame milestones, a Super Bowl celebration spoiled, and a six-touchdown performance that somehow wasn’t enough to win.  The two franchises have met […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams don’t have the kind of rivalry that comes from playing twice a season, but their occasional meetings have produced some pretty memorable moments. There have been last-second touchdowns, Hall of Fame milestones, a Super Bowl celebration spoiled, and a six-touchdown performance that somehow wasn’t enough to win. The two franchises have met 15 times since 1970, with Buffalo holding a 9–6 advantage. The Bills have won five of the last six, although the Rams claimed the most recent meeting in a game that might still give Buffalo fans a headache. With the Bills headed to Los Angeles for Monday Night Football, it’s time to open the Time Capsule and revisit some of the history between these two teams. ____________________________________________________________________________ The early years: Los Angeles gets the better of Buffalo The Bills and Rams first crossed paths on September 27, 1970, during the NFL’s first season following the AFL-NFL merger. Buffalo had spent the previous decade in the AFL, winning back-to-back championships in 1964 and 1965, while Los Angeles had been part of the NFL since 1937. The Rams weren’t especially welcoming. They traveled to Buffalo and handed the Bills a 19–0 shutout, beginning a stretch in which Los Angeles won three of the first four meetings between the franchises. Buffalo’s first win didn’t come until December 7, 1980, when the Bills earned a 10–7 win at home. It was hardly an offensive showcase, but it finally put Buffalo in the win column against a team that had reached the Super Bowl the previous season. The Rams responded with a 41–17 victory in 1983, leaving Buffalo trailing the series 3–1. It would be another six years before the two teams met again, and by then the Bills were building a roster that would eventually lead them to four consecutive Super Bowls. ____________________________________________________________________________ The Super Bowl years: Reich, Thomas, and a little Monday night magic The Rams had gotten the better of Buffalo through the first four meetings, but that changed in 1989. The Bills would win the next three matchups, including a Monday night thriller and a blowout that put a future Hall of Famer into the NFL record books. On October 16, 1989, an undefeated Rams team arrived at Rich Stadium for Monday Night Football. Jim Kelly was sidelined with a shoulder injury, leaving backup Frank Reich to make his first NFL start. For most of the evening, Reich did enough to keep Buffalo competitive. A fourth-quarter touchdown pass to Thurman Thomas gave the Bills a 16–13 lead, and when Buffalo recovered possession late in the game, it appeared the outcome was settled. Then Thomas fumbled. Los Angeles recovered, and Jim Everett connected with Flipper Anderson for a 78-yard touchdown. Suddenly, the Rams led 20–16 with just 1:22 remaining. Reich, who had never started an NFL game before that evening, responded by completing seven consecutive passes. The final one went eight yards to Andre Reed for the winning touchdown with 16 seconds left on the clock. Buffalo won 23–20, handing Los Angeles its first defeat of the season. It wasn’t the comeback that would eventually make Reich famous, but it was an early demonstration of what the Bills had waiting behind Kelly on the depth chart. Three years later, the Rams returned to Buffalo for the 1992 season opener. This time, there would be no need for a dramatic finish. The Bills rolled to a 40–7 win, the largest margin in the history of the series. Thomas scored four touchdowns, three on the ground and one through the air, while Buffalo’s defense intercepted Rams quarterback Jim Everett four times. But the afternoon wasn’t entirely about the scoreboard. Veteran receiver James Lofton, already one of the NFL’s most accomplished pass catchers, surpassed Steve Largent to become the league’s all-time leader in career receiving yards that day. Lofton finished the afternoon with six catches for 56 yards, adding an NFL record to a game that also marked the beginning of Buffalo’s third consecutive Super Bowl run. The Bills would add another win over the Rams in 1995, winning 45–27 in the franchises’ first meeting after the Rams relocated to St. Louis. ____________________________________________________________________________ The St. Louis years: Buffalo maintains the upper hand The Rams moved to St. Louis in 1995, where they would eventually become the Greatest Show on Turf, win a Super Bowl with Kurt Warner, and spend 21 seasons before returning to Los Angeles. Interestingly, the Bills never faced that championship team. The franchises met five times while the Rams called St. Louis home, with Buffalo winning three of those matchups. The Bills took the first meeting in 1995 with a 45–27 win, but the Rams squeaked out a 34–33 victory in 1998. Buffalo responded with wins in 2004 and 2008 before St. Louis got the last word in 2012, winning 15–12 in what would be the teams’ final meeting before the Rams returned to Los Angeles. ____________________________________________________________________________ The Josh Allen era: Big wins, bigger numbers, and one painful loss By the time the Bills and Rams met again in September 2020, Buffalo had a new franchise quarterback and was beginning to establish itself as an AFC contender. The first meeting of the Allen era almost became a disaster. Buffalo built a 28–3 lead in the third quarter at Bills Stadium, only to watch Jared Goff and the Rams score 29 unanswered points. Los Angeles led 32–28 with less than five minutes remaining, leaving Allen to rescue a game that he had seemed to have had comfortably in hand. The quarterback directed a 75-yard touchdown drive, aided by a controversial fourth-down pass interference call, and found Tyler Kroft in the end zone with 15 seconds remaining. Buffalo escaped with a 35–32 victory and a 3–0 start to the season. Two years later, the Bills returned to face the Rams under considerably brighter lights. Los Angeles was coming off its victory in Super Bowl LVI, and the NFL had selected Buffalo as the opponent for the league’s traditional Thursday night season opener. The Rams were raising a championship banner at SoFi Stadium, but the Bills had no intention of contributing to the celebration. The teams went into halftime tied at 10, despite Buffalo turning the ball over three times in the first two quarters. The second half was a completely different game. Allen threw three touchdown passes and added another score on the ground, while the Buffalo defense intercepted Matthew Stafford three times and sacked him seven times. The Bills scored 21 unanswered second-half points and left Los Angeles with a convincing 31–10 victory. The Bills returned to Los Angeles two years later, and Allen had an even bigger game. Unfortunately for Buffalo, the Rams had a pretty good day, too. On December 8, 2024, the Bills returned to SoFi Stadium riding a seven-game winning streak. Allen was in the middle of what would become his first NFL MVP season, and he delivered one of the most remarkable individual performances in league history. He threw for 342 yards and three touchdowns. He rushed for 82 yards and three more scores. In doing so, he became the first player in NFL history to throw three touchdown passes and rush for three touchdowns in the same game. Six touchdowns. No turnovers. And a loss. Stafford threw for 320 yards and two touchdowns, while Puka Nacua caught 12 passes for 162 yards and scored twice, once receiving and once rushing. The Rams built a 38–21 lead entering the fourth quarter, forcing Buffalo into another desperate comeback attempt. Allen nearly pulled it off. His third rushing touchdown brought the Bills within two points in the final minute, but Los Angeles recovered the ensuing onside kick and held on for the 44–42 win. The teams combined for 86 points and more than 900 yards of offense. Buffalo scored more points than any losing team in…
author: Rachel Auberger

title: Buffalo Bills record book watch: Josh Allen, James Cook, Greg Rousseau, and Dawson Knox
summary: We got to break out the permanent marker last week as Josh Allen moved past Andre Reed and Thurman Thomas to take over the top spot on the Buffalo Bills’ all-time touchdown list. That one’s officially in the books, and we can put the pencil away.  But don’t put the office supplies back in the drawer just yet. James […]
full_text: We got to break out the permanent marker last week as Josh Allen moved past Andre Reed and Thurman Thomas to take over the top spot on the Buffalo Bills’ all-time touchdown list. That one’s officially in the books, and we can put the pencil away. But don’t put the office supplies back in the drawer just yet. James Cook is closing in on another milestone, Greg Rousseau is looking to climb the franchise leaderboard, and Dawson Knox has a couple of opportunities to make us do some rewriting. And Allen? Well, he’s still got plenty of names to chase. We’ve got our usual four chapters — S ure Things, A Good Bet, Not Impossible , and Superhuman — and a fresh batch of numbers to play with. Let’s see what Monday night might do to the record book. _____________________________________________________________________________ Chapter 1: Sure Things James Cook: 4,700 career rushing yards James Cook needs just 20 rushing yards against the Los Angeles Rams to reach 4,700 for his career. Considering he hasn’t finished a game with fewer than 75 rushing yards this season, this one seems like a pretty safe bet. We’re tempted to go ahead and write this one in ink, but we’ll give Cook a chance to actually earn those 20 yards first. _____________________________________________________________________________ Chapter 2: A Good Bet Josh Allen: Climbing the NFL rushing touchdown list Josh Allen has 86 career rushing touchdowns, putting him in a tie with Priest Holmes for 16th place in NFL history. One more against the Rams would give Allen sole possession of that spot. And with Allen’s history of running the ball into the end zone, one touchdown seems like a pretty good bet. But why stop at one? Allen started the season with back-to-back-to-back two-touchdown games, and if he can get back to that pace, things could get interesting in a hurry. Two rushing touchdowns against Los Angeles and another two next week would put him at 90 for his career, tied with Eric Dickerson and Curtis Martin. We’re not asking for much here. Just four touchdowns in two games. Dawson Knox: Passing James Lofton Dawson Knox is just 13 receiving yards away from passing James Lofton on Buffalo’s all-time receiving yards list. Knox has 2,724 yards. Lofton has 2,736. One decent catch could be enough to move Knox into 16th place in franchise history. Now, Knox is averaging just 7.5 receiving yards per game this season, which doesn’t exactly scream Sure Thing . But we’re talking about 13 yards here. One catch could take care of the whole thing, and that’s not asking too much. Greg Rousseau: Climbing Buffalo’s sack leaderboard Greg Rousseau has 38 career sacks, putting him just half a sack behind Darryl Talley on Buffalo’s all-time list. One sack against the Rams would move Groot past Spider-Man and into eighth place in franchise history. Who knew the Bills record book had its own Marvel cinematic universe? _____________________________________________________________________________ Chapter 3: Not Impossible We’re getting a little more ambitious now. Neither of these would be a huge shock, but we’re going to need a little more than business as usual to make them happen. Dawson Knox: Catching Jerry Butler Dawson Knox has 28 career receiving touchdowns, putting him just one behind Jerry Butler on Buffalo’s all-time list. One touchdown catch against the Rams would pull Knox into a tie with Butler at 29. Of course, the Bills have several options when they get close to the goal line, and Allen has a habit of keeping the football for himself. Knox might have to convince his quarterback to share. Greg Rousseau: Two sacks? How about three? We already have Rousseau chasing Darryl Talley in A Good Bet , but let’s see how far we can push this. Two sacks against the Rams would give Rousseau 40 for his career and bring him to eight this season, tying his personal best. And if he manages three? That would give him nine sacks on the season and a new career high. We’re getting greedy, sure, but that’s what this chapter is for. _____________________________________________________________________________ Chapter 4: Superhuman James Cook — The quarterback is still in the way Remember when we started tracking whether Cook could pass Allen on Buffalo’s all-time rushing list? What began as a ridiculous single-game possibility is slowly becoming a little less ridiculous. Cook rushed for 75 yards against New England, while Allen managed just four. That 71-yard difference cut the gap between them from 230 yards to 159. The two currently sit fourth and fifth on Buffalo’s all-time rushing list, and if they swap places, Cook can start setting his sights on Fred Jackson, O.J. Simpson, and Thurman Thomas. To make that happen against the Rams, Cook would need to outgain Allen by at least 160 yards. That’s still a pretty tall order for one game, but considering Cook has already produced a 154-yard rushing performance this season, we’re not throwing away our scratch paper just yet. We may have to move this one out of the Superhuman chapter before long. _____________________________________________________________________________ We’ve got Cook chasing his quarterback, Groot taking on Spider-Man in the Buffalo-verse, and Knox hoping Allen remembers he’s allowed to throw touchdowns, too. Not a bad little to-do list for Monday night. We’ll keep the pencils handy, just in case the Bills give us a reason to do some rewriting.
author: Rachel Auberger

title: Has Aaron Donald made the Rams more dangerous?
summary: The Los Angeles Rams have been known to go all in whenever they can and this season they pulled off a surprising move. They managed to convince Aaron Donald to end his retirement and return to the gridiron. A defensive tackle who really needs little to no introduction, Donald’s name is one quarterbacks have come […]
full_text: The Los Angeles Rams have been known to go all in whenever they can and this season they pulled off a surprising move. They managed to convince Aaron Donald to end his retirement and return to the gridiron. A defensive tackle who really needs little to no introduction, Donald’s name is one quarterbacks have come to fear. Is that still true? Has there been a tangible benefit since his return in Week 3? Let’s find out! The Stats First and foremost, if Aaron Donald’s presence is having an impact it’s not showing up on his personal stat sheet. Aaron Donald has four combined tackles (one solo), is credited with one tackle for loss, one QBhit… and zero sacks. The Rams are 22nd in the league with sack rate, though it’s only four games into the season. What do the Donald vs. No Donald splits tell us? In the two weeks with No Donald; the Rams had four sacks, nine QB hits, and five TFLs. With Donald, that line goes to; three sacks, eleven QB hits, and five TFLs. On the surface, it seems like Aaron Donald hasn’t really helped. They’ve had more QB hits with him on the field, but only by one. Of those hits, one less resulted in a sack as well. We could get into score, and that might be illuminating. In the No Donald games, they’ve allowed 27 points to San Francisco 49ers and 20 to the Philadelphia Eagles for a total of 47 points allowed. With Donald on the field, it’s been six points to the New York Giants, and 30 to the Denver Broncos for a total of 36. That’s a good improvement on the surface, but it should be noted the 30 allowed is the current highest for the Rams this year. Total yards allowed was 379 and 172 without Donald for 551 yards. With Donald it’s 182 and 257 or 439 total. trends similarly with 379, 182, 257, and 172 in that order. I could break that down further and further, but with the small sample size and fluctuations between opponent quality a bit, it’s hard to draw a perfect conclusion though most indicators do suggest some impact from having Donald on the field. Being candid though, that in and of itself is a solid conclusion. Aaron Donald has historically been a game changer. You’d expect then, that he would have changed the game for the Rams and so far that just hasn’t been conclusive. Let’s look in one more spot… The Film pic.twitter.com/78vxjruhof — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) October 9, 2026 I’ve already made you read a lot so let’s cut this short (and you can watch what I think are representative samples right up above). At age 35, the obvious conclusion is that Aaron Donald’s best days are behind him. That said, he seems to have good days ahead still. Having done film study before on Donald, at his peak he was preposterous. It’s rare to see physical dominance between players at this level, but Donald was able to ragdoll very large humans on the offensive line. I don’t see the ragdoll capability any longer, but he’s plenty strong. In Play 1 above, the offensive lineman sets up well against Donald and is still shoved into the running lane. It’s not a ragdoll moment, but you still have to respect the man’s strength. On Play 7, a good guess is the lineman wanted him to push that direction, but I can’t imagine the entire distance covered was intended. Donald cleared a lot of room for the blitz. One of the hallmarks of a truly elite player is the combination of physical capability and skill. In Play 2, Aaron Donald times his sidestep into the running lane exceedingly well. Not so early that the running back doesn’t commit to the gap, but early enough to be a major force in making the tackle. The spin move in Play 3, the slap to the shoulder in Play 4 and many more I could have recorded are a testament to the man’s dedication to the craft. I know I highlighted two mediocre reps for Aaron Donald in the clip and I’ll come back to that in a second, but Donald’s experience and technique have me of the opinion he can be a major threat for awhile yet. Back to the mediocre plays, no person in the history of the league has won or lost every snap they played. It’s all about the frequency of wins and losses. I focused on Week 3 of this season, the most recent contest and game closest to “back soreness.” I don’t know if Donald is fully healthy, but in this game I saw that Father Time will always be undefeated. Donald is a threat, but not like he used to be. You need to know where he is, just not triple team worthy snap in and snap out.

title: Buffalo Bills rooting interests: Who needs to win in Week 5
summary: Well, that wasn’t a fun week. Let’s try again.  The Buffalo Bills suffered their first loss of the season Sunday night, and losing to the New England Patriots made it hurt a little more. Buffalo is still 3-1 and still very much in control of where this season goes, but the loss did change the rooting-interest game a bit.  For […]
full_text: Well, that wasn’t a fun week. Let’s try again. The Buffalo Bills suffered their first loss of the season Sunday night, and losing to the New England Patriots made it hurt a little more. Buffalo is still 3-1 and still very much in control of where this season goes, but the loss did change the rooting-interest game a bit. For starters, the division tiebreaker no longer belongs to Buffalo. Hopefully, that is temporary. The Bills also dropped from the top spot in the AFC, with Kansas City moving into the No. 1 seed, Jacksonville sitting at No. 2, and Buffalo falling all the way to No. 3. None of that is particularly concerning five games into a 17-game season, and all of it is reversible. But we have reached the point where simply rooting against the AFC East isn’t enough. Now we need some help knocking down division leaders and thinning out the teams hanging around the AFC playoff picture. So, the rules are getting a little more complicated. Buffalo wins. The rest of the AFC East loses. AFC division leaders lose, and when two of them meet, we root against the team holding the better seed. Wild-card contenders lose, unless Buffalo needs them to strengthen its schedule — and the AFC East rule always wins that argument. After that, we’ll happily give some wins to the teams hanging around the bottom of the AFC and let them move a little farther away from the top of the draft. And then there’s the NFC, where things are a little simpler. Buffalo opponents can win for strength of schedule — unless, of course, they’re playing the Bills. We’d also like to knock the NFC division leaders down a little when we can, while letting the teams at the bottom stay there and keep those premium draft picks on the other side of the league. Got all that? Good. Let’s find Buffalo some help. _____________________________________________________________________________ AFC EAST Buffalo Bills (3-1) at Los Angeles Rams (2-2) Root for: BILLS We don’t need to overthink this one. There’s only ever one right answer here, but in case you need a reason, here you go: Buffalo has to take care of its own business before any of the help elsewhere really matters. The Bills get the Monday night stage this week, and a win gets them right back on track after last week’s loss. Go Bills! Las Vegas Raiders (3-1) at New England Patriots (2-2) Root for: RAIDERS Remember when we said the AFC East rule trumps everything else? Here is our first test. Buffalo plays Las Vegas next week, so a Raiders win would give the Bills a little strength-of-schedule boost. More importantly, though, New England just handed Buffalo its first loss and owns the head-to-head tiebreaker. We don’t need the Patriots stacking wins while they have that in their pocket, so this one gives us double the benefit: Go Raiders. Cleveland Browns (3-1) at New York Jets (1-3) Root for: BROWNS This one breaks another rule. Cleveland is sitting at the top of the AFC North, which would normally make the Browns exactly the kind of team we want knocked down. But the Jets are the Jets, they live in the AFC East, and the division rule comes first. We’ll deal with Cleveland later. For now, give New York another loss — although at this rate, it won’t be long before the Jets aren’t a factor (I know, I know, but for now we have to let the math do its work), and we will be trying to get them out of draft position. But not quite yet. Cincinnati Bengals (2-2) at Miami Dolphins (0-4) Root for: BENGALS Cincinnati is hanging around the AFC playoff picture, while Miami is still looking for its first win. Normally that would make the Dolphins useful — give a basement team a win, hurt a potential wild-card contender, and call it a day. Nope. Miami is still in the AFC East, and we’re not volunteering to help anybody in the division. Let the Dolphins stay winless for another week. _____________________________________________________________________________ REST OF THE AFC Philadelphia Eagles (2-2) at Jacksonville Jaguars (3-1) Root for: EAGLES Here’s the big one. Jacksonville has jumped Buffalo in the AFC standings and currently owns the No. 2 seed, so knocking the Jaguars back down is exactly the kind of help we’re looking for now. This one doesn’t require any complicated tiebreaker math or competing rules. We need Jacksonville to lose. Fly Eagles, Fly. Baltimore Ravens (3-1) at Atlanta Falcons (3-1) Root for: FALCONS Baltimore isn’t leading the AFC North right now, but the Ravens are sitting in a wild-card spot at 3-1 and are very much part of the AFC race. Buffalo will get its own shot at Baltimore later this season, but for now we can let an NFC team do some work for us. A Falcons win puts another loss on an AFC contender without giving anything to another AFC team. Yes, there’s the whole strength-of-schedule thing since Buffalo plays Baltimore later, but at some point we have to stop helping good AFC teams win games just because they’re on the Bills’ schedule. Indianapolis Colts (2-2) at Pittsburgh Steelers (2-2) Root for: STEELERS Now we get into the games where somebody in the AFC has to win. Neither team currently holds a playoff spot, but Indianapolis is in the AFC South chasing Jacksonville, while Pittsburgh is trying to keep pace in the North. Buffalo already beat Pittsburgh, so if one of these teams has to move to 3-2, we might as well make it the one that helps the Bills’ strength of victory. Denver Broncos (2-2) at Los Angeles Chargers (0-4) Root for: BRONCOS Normally we’d be all aboard the 0-4 Chargers finally winning one and moving themselves away from the top of the draft. But Denver is on Buffalo’s schedule, which gives us a reason to keep building the Broncos’ record before the Bills see them later this season. Strength of schedule wins this argument. Go Broncos. Houston Texans (0-4) at Tennessee Titans (0-4) Root for: TEXANS We have been begging Houston to do something for weeks, so how about starting here? The Bills already have a win over the Texans, which means every Houston win from here makes that victory a little more valuable for strength of victory. The fact that it would also pull the Texans away from the top of the draft is just a bonus. Come on, Houston. Surely you can beat somebody. _____________________________________________________________________________ NFC Detroit Lions (2-2) at Arizona Cardinals (1-3) Root for: LIONS Buffalo already has a win over Detroit, so every Lions win from here makes that victory a little more valuable. That’s enough to make this an easy choice. The Cardinals can keep doing their thing at the bottom of the NFC while Detroit gives Buffalo a little strength-of-victory help. Chicago Bears (3-1) at Green Bay Packers (2-2) Root for: BEARS Chicago is on Buffalo’s schedule later this season, so we’re sticking with the Bears here. Sure, they’re 3-1 and hanging around near the top of the NFC North, but that doesn’t matter nearly as much to Buffalo as a stronger schedule could when the AFC playoff tiebreakers start coming into play. We’ll worry about where Chicago sits in the NFC another time. For now, Bear Down. San Francisco 49ers (4-0) at Seattle Seahawks (3-1) Root for: SEAHAWKS This is exactly what our new NFC rules were made for. San Francisco is undefeated and sitting atop the NFC West, so let’s knock the 49ers down a little. Seattle isn’t exactly a basement dweller at 3-1, but somebody has to win this thing. Give the division leader a loss and tighten up the NFC West. Minnesota Vikings (4-0) at New Orleans Saints (1-3) Root for: SAINTS Here’s where two of our NFC rules run into each other. We’d be perfectly happy leaving New Orleans near the bottom and keeping premium draft picks in the NFC, but Minnesota is 4-0 and leading the NFC North. Knocking down the division leader wins out. Give the Vikings their first loss, and we’ll worry about the Saints’ draft position another week. BONUS HINT: Keeping NFC division leaders’ records below their AFC counterparts also helps keep the better draft picks…

title: Buffalo Bills will get Dome Josh Allen vs. Los Angeles Rams on Monday Night Football in Week 5
summary: Josh Allen is a superstar in any weather. And starting right around November, at home, he plays in plenty of windy, snowy games in Orchard Park. For as much as Allen has embraced the elements as Buffalo’s starting quarterback and played a myriad of outstanding games when the weather has been far from ideal, the […]
full_text: Josh Allen is a superstar in any weather. And starting right around November, at home, he plays in plenty of windy, snowy games in Orchard Park. For as much as Allen has embraced the elements as Buffalo’s starting quarterback and played a myriad of outstanding games when the weather has been far from ideal, the best Josh Allen is Dome Josh Allen. Here are Allen’s career stats in his nine games when playing in a dome: Completion rate: 68.8% Yards per attempt: 8.81 TD & INT: 19 & 6 Passer rating: 110.1 Rushing yards & rushing TDs per game: 43 & 1.33 To put that 110.1 rating into perspective, to date, Allen’s best season-long rate came in 2020, and it was 107.4. It was 101.4 when he won MVP in 2024 and 102.2 a season ago. And of course, SoFi Stadium is a dome, where the Bills will take on the Rams on Monday Night Football in Week 5. We all remember Allen’s outrageous performance against the Rams back in 2024, when he went 22-of-37 for 342 yards with three passing touchdowns, no interceptions, and toted the rock 10 times for 82 yards and three more scores. Pro Football Reference makes a distinction between dome and retractable roof stadium, the latter of which would include Houston’s Reliant Stadium. Allen did some rough outings in that building but did go bonkers on the Texans defense inside in Week 1. Yet in a classic dome, Allen has been spectacular both as a passer and a runner.

title: Panthers Transactions – Week 5
summary: The Carolina Panthers front office is busy throughout the season with transactions, roster moves, and injury updates. Here’s what’s happening at Mint Street this week. Transactions Signed CB Marco Wilson to the practice squad While few practice squad signings end up having a significant impact on the 53-man roster, the addition of Marco Wilson is […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - AUGUST 11: Marco Wilson #20 of the Arizona Cardinals looks on during pregame warmups prior to an NFL preseason football game against the Denver Broncos at State Farm Stadium on August 11, 2023 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Ryan Kang/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Carolina Panthers front office is busy throughout the season with transactions, roster moves, and injury updates. Here’s what’s happening at Mint Street this week. Transactions Signed CB Marco Wilson to the practice squad While few practice squad signings end up having a significant impact on the 53-man roster, the addition of Marco Wilson is one to watch. This is a guy who has started 37 of 64 career games with 179 tackles, three interceptions, and 20 passes defended in his career. Wilson was a fourth round pick in 2021 by the Arizona Cardinals. He won the starting corner job as a rookie and over the next three seasons with the Cardinals he started 37 of 43 games. But he was released near the end of his 2023 season, signed with the New England Patriots, and has bounced around since then. He spent 2025 with the Cincinnati Bengals appearing in four games with three tackles before hitting the injured reserve with a hamstring injury. Now, I’m not saying Marco Wilson is the immediate answer to fill in for Jaycee Horn or Mike Jackson. However, the Panthers did well to kick the tires on a 27-year-old corner with 37 career starts. There’s no downside. If he doesn’t work out, then fine. But if he ends up providing some situational depth on the 53-man roster down the road, then this could end up being a very shrewd signing. Signed OLB Nick Hampton to the practice squad Hampton was a fifth-round pick by the Los Angeles Rams in the 2023 draft. In three seasons with the Rams he appeared in 36 games with 17 total tackles. He recorded three playoff tackles last year for the Rams. During his time in Los Angeles he played 188 defensive snaps and 510 on special teams, giving the 26-year-old a decent amount of seasoning. He originally signed with the Panthers in March 2026, got waived during the preseason, and is now back on the practice squad. Waived RB/KR Tre Tyus then re-signed him to the practice squad Tre Tyus continues to be the Panthers ping pong ball this year. He was signed to a futures contract in January 2026, was waived in August during final roster cuts, and has then bounced around between being waived, signed to the practice squad, or elevated to the 53-man roster at any given time. Tyus has appeared in two games for the Panthers this year, playing two offensive snaps and 32 on special teams. He has returned five kickoffs for the Panthers this season with a solid 25.4 yard average per return. Released OLB Jeremiah Moon, CB Robert Rochell, and OL Isaia Glass from the practice squad Jeremiah Moon seems to get waived, re-signed, or elevated to the 53-man roster on a near weekly basis. In two games with the Panthers this year he has played 41 defensive snaps and 19 on special teams with seven tackles and a pass defended. Robert Rochell, a six-year NFL veteran, played in four games for the Panthers last year and has one appearance in 2026 with one tackle. He’s another yo-yo player who regularly gets released and re-signed to the practice squad. Isaia Glass was one of the Panthers undrafted rookie free agents this year and is also living the unstable life of getting repeatedly released from then re-signed to the practice squad.

Walker Clement: How much of Bryce Young’s resurgence (surgence?) is attributable to unpublished and probably spurious reports of him hiring Brenton Bersin as his life coach? I would say about 50%. I’m sure Nick Scott being there to mentor him as the uncrowned captain of the defense also helps. Both Brenton and Nick know all about excelling despite catching the vitriol of the fan base. So this era of Sunshine in Carolina can definitely be attributed to the devoted disciples of House Bersin. TXPanther: Is this the worst hypothetical trade scenario you’ve ever seen? It’s at least top 5. My proposed trade idea: Pittsburgh receives: WR Jalen Coker, a 2027 3rd and a 2028 5th or 6th. Carolina receives: Alex Highsmith. — Jared Kane (@BaddestBearJew) October 5, 2026 Yes. This is a reminder that fans of NFL teams can be very dumb. I would imagine a lot of non-Panthers fans don’t realize the Panthers just gave Jalen Coker a nice extension. A sick trade for an EDGE might get made, but Jalen Coker will not be a part of it. Brice Guild: I am starting to see posts here and have seen talking heads from many national sports shows say, ” Bryce Youngs has increased his arm strength this year” . What say you? Is that really a thing? Or could it be he is confident and more assertive with his throwing motion, or a better pocket to step up into or has BY actually increased his actual power and speed of his passes? ? I’m sure Bryce Young has gotten objectively stronger since being drafted as part of an NFL training program. But I do think the zip and accuracy on his passes comes more from being more confident in the system and mechanically cleaning some things up. He’s still making some pretty crazy throws without having his mechanics in proper structure, so I attribute most of the change to just being decisive and trusting his reads. He’s been making a lot of checks at the line presnap as well so he’s clearly settled in to the snap to snap flow that a good quarterback in the league has to. schrodingersblackcat: Say the stars align. Bryce emerges as a consistent QB1 this season with a few more flashes of Drew Brees 2.0, injuries don’t derail us any further, our offense becomes a major NFL storyline with Tet and Coker becoming household names. Maybe we even somehow end up winning a playoff game. What does Brad Idzik’s future look like? Its an interesting situation, Brad Idzik is basically a direct extension of Dave Canales but if the offensive production continues as it has, I would imagine he’s interviewing at least for head coaching positions this off-season and likely gone following the 2027 season to a head coaching job. The NFL head coaching group is constantly churning and many organizations like to pair an offensive leaning head coach with a shiny young quarterback. I would love for him to stick around for as long as possible if the offense and Bryce Young continues on this pace, but I do believe Dave Canales is already developing his successor. Remember, Dave has made a point to give some of his positional coaches reps to call plays in the preseason, that is definitely by design for long term development. DannyLimes: given the state of our injuries, the bucs falling apart and the saints wild inconsistency… are the falcons suddenly favourites for the NFC behind a currently health Mike Penix and Bijan Robinson? I could definitely see the Falcons being a head of the Panthers at some point in the season, their defense has been very good minus the Panthers week 2 game, which mostly was a blowout because of the Falcons offense and a 3rd string QB. The NFC South playoff picture will likely be messy once again this season. The Bucs just won last night and that puts them only a game or two outside of the top of the division right now. JakeNCVA: We are four games into the season. There are three undefeated teams, eight at 3-1, twelve at 2-2, four at 1-3, and five at 0-4 — so only 11 of 32 have winning records (I know its early!). The only team I have not seen play are the 49’ers — but everyone else looks beatable — including the 4-0 Minnesota Vikings. The Panthers remaining schedule all of the sudden looks easier than it did a few weeks ago — both because of how the rest of the league is playing and how well the Panthers are playing – even with 2 losses they look to be trending way up from the past. What is your revised look at the W-L record? We only have Minn, Baltimore and Seattle left that are above 500 – at the moment. Do you think the teams have settled into their “personalities” for the season yet, or are they still working things out, and we may still see hot risers and plummeting disappointments. I’m still sitting at around 9-10 wins. I expect the Panthers offense to come down to Earth against some of the better defenses on the schedule and the injury bug has already hit them very hard. Don’t get me wrong, 12 wins wouldn’t necessarily surprise me, but I expect the Panthers to be in more close games than blow outs, so the margin for error is much smaller there. TXPanther: Since you miss food questions, what are your: Favorite dessert orders at The Cheesecake Factory? Top 3 fast food spots and favorite order at each one? In no particular order Wawa: Honey Smoked Turkey hoagie with all the usual sub fixin’s and spicy mustard. Or the Gobbler Bowl around Thanksgiving time. Popeye’s: Spicy Chicken Sandwich White Castle: Crave Case, easily. The restaurants are spread thin but I’ve found a way to them many times on a long road trip. SmoothC: If panthers made 1 trade for a decent to good player, but only 1, would you get a pass rusher, CB or OL? I’d probably go with a cornerback. EDGE rushers are always expensive to trade for and I think the Panthers have enough talent on the shelf that should be returning on the offensive line. They will likely just try to weather that storm, but it seems they’ll have some reinforcements coming after the bye. WanderingJanusz: Which game(s) are you watching this Sunday and why Chargers vs Broncos because I apparently hate myself and loaded up on Chargers in Dynasty fantasy with Justin Herbert (traded Javonte Williams for him, L) and I drafted Omarion Hampton 2nd overall in the rookie draft last year, and I drafted RJ Harvey in the first round of that same draft. So watching just to hate my dynasty squad. And I’ll probably have the Jets/Browns game on because I ALSO drafted Quinshon Judkins in the first round of that same rookie draft. I always enjoy the catch of the day when I am travelling overseas, sushi is one of my favorite things, and you just can’t beat some good old BBQ from the south. So I would assume he’s not going to be available for week 6. The Panthers are “hopeful” Jalen Coker will be available following the bye week. Canales also said that the injuries to both Monroe Freeling and Jaelan Phillips aren’t believed to be serious and they…

title: Has Bryce Young done enough to earn your confidence?
summary: Opinions on Bryce Young have been mixed pretty much since the moment he had his name announced as the first overall pick in the 2023 NFL Draft. Some, including a lot of people in draft circles in the draft media ecosystem, lauded Young for his processing speed and decision makers. Others were adamant that his […]
full_text: Opinions on Bryce Young have been mixed pretty much since the moment he had his name announced as the first overall pick in the 2023 NFL Draft. Some, including a lot of people in draft circles in the draft media ecosystem, lauded Young for his processing speed and decision makers. Others were adamant that his physical limitations would be too much to overcome. The latter seemed to be winning out for the first couple years of his career. He followed a discouraging rookie year with an early season benching in year two. However, he bounced back from the objectively bad start to his career to firmly entrench himself in a place no one wants their quarterback to be—purgatory. The tail end of Young’s second season and the majority of his third season was a Rorschach test of quarterback evaluation. Conversations about his play were basically an exercise in confirmation bias. Those in his corner saw a quarterback being shackled by conservative play calling and suboptimal weaponry. Those in the opposite corner saw a hesitant shot caller that did not have the physical tools to overcome his inconsistent decision making. Seldom is there a quarterback who is so commonly viewed as a surefire franchise guy while also being commonly seen as the team’s weak link. And then the first four weeks of this season happened. This is not the Bryce Young we had gotten for the first three years of his career. He’s been letting it rip all season. He currently leads the NFL in passing yards, is tied for third in passing touchdowns, and is fifth in QBR. He’s objectively been one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL for four weeks. Now the discussion part. Do you trust that Bryce Young can sustain this level of play? My answer: Yes, but with some minor reservations. I had been a Bryce Young detractor for most of his last two seasons, and it’s hard for me to shake the concerns I had for the last few years. That said, other than the Browns game, he’s looked so composed and confident despite the offensive line not giving him the cleanest situations to work out of. I think it’s more likely than not that he continues on some sort of upward trajectory, even if it isn’t the MVP-caliber play he’s put forth through four games. I won’t be shocked if he regresses back to his old self, but I’m not expecting it to happen. He’ll get tested as the season goes on. The Panthers schedule gets progressively more difficult for the offense as we get to the later parts of the season. If he can sustain anything close to this level of play through the end of the season, I think the Panthers should be comfortable planning on a long term contract for Young.

title: Wild swings and championship rings: the complete history of the Bears-Packers rivalry

full_text: AUTHOR’S NOTE, Oct. 9, 2026: The original version of this story was published Sep. 28, 2017, before the first Bears-Packers game of that season. It has been updated to include all games through the 2025 seaso n. (Please also note that because I have updated this every year since 2017, it’s possible there are references in this that I wrote in another year and didn’t fix. Feel free to comment and let me know.) Thank you for reading, and in the words of our main man Thomas Jones, who went 4-2 against the Packers as a member of the beloved, Bear TF Down! Justin Fields, your table is ready. And you’ve got your work cut out for you. Let me explain. With three minutes remaining in their — WAIT. Wait a second. That was the lead to this story in 2022. Let’s get this puppy updated. Caleb Williams, your table is ready. Much better. I’ll tell you something I’ve learned since writing this story in 2017: history is hard to frame while you’re living it. When I first broke the Bears-Packers rivalry into eras, I had an era that ended in 2016 and started fresh with the Trubisky era. That didn’t work, and I had to create an era called “2017-2020: Money Mitch and Matt falter where others also faltered.“ Then I started a new era called “2021-present: Justin Fields rides to the rescue (we hope).” And now here I am in 2026 and I’ve had to make 2017 to 2023 an era, in hopes that Caleb and Ben Johnson can create a lasting success. We’ll need it, because 2017 is when the Packers overtook the all-time series lead and proceeded to put the ongoing rivalry belt out of reach for perhaps a decade. So let’s take a trip back 93 years, incredibly, to the previous time that the Green Bay Packers owned the all-time series lead. The day was Sept. 24, 1933, and the Packers led the defending champion Chicago Bears 7-0 when Bears star and future Hall of Famer Bill Hewitt struck with one of the most magnificent sequences to close a game in franchise history. First, with about five minutes to play, Hewitt blocked a Packers field goal that would have put the game out of reach at 10-0. Back on offense, he took a handoff on an end-around, slowed down, and heaved a touchdown pass 46 yards to Luke Johnsos. The Bears converted the extra point and tied the game at 7. Green Bay tried to drive but was stuffed three times, and instead set up to punt with less than a minute to go. That’s when Hewitt struck again. As reported by the Chicago Daily Tribune : Once again Hewitt flashed in front left end and this time the ball bounced laterally from Bill’s chest. Hewitt followed its bounding course, picked it up in front of a teammate who watched to protect him from any opponent, and finished his sprint behind the goal line. With less than a minute remaining, the Packers got the ball back, “but their long pass, the final play of the game, was batted down.” The Bears won the game, 14-7. The Tribune wrote about the majesty of Hewitt. It wrote about the implications the win might have for the NFL’s Western division race. It also made mention of the impact the game had on the all-time series: The Bears’ victory this afternoon was the 11th in the series in 27 games. The Packers have won 12 times and four have ended in ties. However, one of those Packers wins was a 1924 preseason game, so the Bears win actually tied the all-time series 11-11-4. We beat the Packers twice more that season, meaning Hewitt’s clutch plays ended Green Bay’s brief run as the series’ all-time leader in wins. For 84 seasons, from 1933 to 2016, the Bears led the series, sometimes by as much as 24 games, sometimes only by one. In 2016, Green Bay swept both games to tie the series at 94-94-6 , while its sweep in 2017 gave them a two-game lead. The second of those two losses launched what we all hoped would be the new, sustained era in the rivalry, when Mitch Trubisky started his first game of the series. The Packers made short work of the Trubisky era, winning seven of eight games. Our only win was the thrilling division clinching victory in 2018, capped off by Leonard Floyd’s rag doll sack on Aaron Rodgers . I truly thought that signified our disposal of Rodgers once and for all. It was but a mere blip, as we now trail the all-time series 95-107-6 , a 12-game deficit and the largest lead Green Bay has ever held in the rivalry. Their previous largest lead? Two games, in 1932. We need much more than a Bill Hewitt blocked punt and touchdown and Leonard Floyd toss-sack to get back in front. For the third time since I wrote the first version of this story, our beloved Bears have a new savior at quarterback. Among the many problems is that for the third time since 1992, the Packers do too. Green Bay drafted Jordan Love in the first round of 2020 and already has a playoff win under his belt. So now we have a young gun battle for NFC North supremacy. The Bears and Packers haven’t had Pro Bowl quarterbacks in the same season since 1956 , but before we get ahead of ourselves, Bears fans are simply hoping that Caleb becomes the first Bears QB as a non-alternate Pro Bowler since 1985. In doing so, he can get us back in the win column not just against the Packers, but overall ahead of the Packers, who in 2022 snatched the one remaining feather in our rivalry cap, surpassing us as the winningest team in NFL history (which they now lead 805-797), despite the Bears having played two seasons-worth of games more than the Packers . So congratulations, my fellow Bears fans: we are living through the unequivocally worst era of the Bears-Packers rivalry. By every measure other than members of the Pro Football Hall of Fame, Green Bay has us beat. Fortunately, I believe Caleb is the man to get us back ahead. Like trailing the 2006 Cardinals 20-0 at halftime, if they can run up a crazy lead, we can take it right back, starting this weekend at Lambeau Field. In the meantime, let’s explore how momentum has swung in the greatest rivalry in sports. 1921-1927: The dawn of the rivalry Dominant team: Bears, 7-1-2 All-time series: Bears, 7-1-2 Streak: Bears win the first three games of the series Biggest win: 21-0 Bears, Nov. 22, 1925 Championship count in the era: Bears 1 (1921), Packers 0 Championship count overall: Bears 1, Packers 0 The first game of the series didn’t even technically include the Bears. The Chicago Staleys, as they were known in 1921, beat the Packers 20-0 at Cubs Park to launch the historic series. The Staleys were 6-1, coming off a 7-6 loss to the Buffalo All-Americans in what would be their only loss of the season. Head coach, two-way star and NFL founder George Halas scheduled the game in hopes of adding enough wins to give the Staleys the league championship, which was then determined by a vote of the owners after the season, dictated by team winning percentage. Halas would forever stew about that system, in his view, costing the Staleys the league championship in 1920, and since teams made their own schedules, and there were no rules about game limits, Halas sought to add games to the back-end of the schedule in 1921 to stack wins and, he hoped, win the ‘21 title. Here’s Packers historian Cliff Christl with the story: The first Bears-Packers game on Nov. 27, 1921, was the result of the then-Chicago Staleys needing an easy win to stack more victories for a looming owners’ vote for the 1921 title. George Halas had learned his lesson. Here is Packers historian Cliff Christl telling the story: pic.twitter.com/FPBSFax1fL — Jack M Silverstein 🇺🇸 (@readjack) December 4, 2022 The gambit worked. The Staleys blanked the Packers 20-0 and eventually received the owners’ vote for the 1921 championship. In that first game of the rivalry, three men scored for the future-Bears : Pete Stinchomb in the 2nd quarter on a 45-yard run, Pard Pearce ran in what seems from the reporting to have been a QB sneak, and Halas caught a 10-yard touchdown from Chic Harley. The Tribune ’s headline that day, buried toward the bottom of an inside page, read: “Staleys Whale Green…

title: Bears-Packers Franchise Connections
summary: It’s no secret that the Bears and Packers have one of the most heated rivalries in the NFL. When you have two blue-blood franchises that are located nearby and have been at each other’s throats since the 1920s, you’re naturally going to have plenty of hype when the two teams match up. Each week going […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - OCTOBER 26: Jonathan Ford #96 of the Chicago Bears looks on during an NFL football game against the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium on October 26, 2025 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s no secret that the Bears and Packers have one of the most heated rivalries in the NFL. When you have two blue-blood franchises that are located nearby and have been at each other’s throats since the 1920s, you’re naturally going to have plenty of hype when the two teams match up. Each week going forward, we’re going to highlight some of the connections that the Bears’ coaching staff and roster each have with their opponent, as well as their opponent’s ties to Chicago. This week, we’re looking at the overlap between the Bears and the Packers. Usually, there’s a decent amount of overlap from a roster perspective between the Bears and the Packers. We’ve seen players like Jimmy Graham, Julius Peppers, Adrian Amos, Ha Ha Clinton-Dix, and Marcedes Lewis suit up for both teams in recent years. Going into 2026, though, there aren’t as many roster connections as usual. The only player on the Packers who has played for the Bears before is defensive tackle Jonathan Ford, who spent the 2024 and 2025 seasons in Chicago. He played in 12 games for the Bears across his tenure, combining for 13 tackles and one tackle for loss. He was originally a seventh-round pick by Green Bay in the 2022 NFL Draft and spent three seasons there, though he never played in a game before the Bears claimed him off the Packers’ practice squad in December of 2024. Ford rejoined Green Bay late in 2025 and has played in all four games for them so far in 2026. He currently ranks No. 101 out of 118 qualified defensive tackles with a 70.4 PFN DT Impact grade, which generally places him as a mediocre backup option. Nobody on the Bears’ active roster has played for the Packers before. However, practice squad defensive back Anthony Johnson Jr. was originally drafted by Green Bay in the seventh round of the 2023 NFL Draft. He played in 12 games for the team in 2023, starting in four. In that time, he tallied 24 tackles, an interception, and three pass deflections. The Packers released him during roster cuts before 2024, and he spent some time with the Giants before signing with the Bears this May. There’s a good amount of overlap between the two teams’ coaching staffs, though. On Green Bay’s side, their quarterbacks coach and assistant head coach is Luke Getsy, who was the Bears’ offensive coordinator in 2022 and 2023. Tight ends coach John Dunn was a football assistant and a offensive assistant for the Bears in 2016 and 2017, while offensive line coach Luke Butkus was previously an offensive assistant and assistant offensive line coach for Chicago between 2007 and 2009. It’s worth noting that Butkus had a tryout with the Bears as a player in 2002, and as the name suggests, he is the nephew of Hall of Fame linebacker Dick Butkus. No current Bears coaches have coached for the Packers before, but two of them have played for Green Bay. The most notable of which is Al Harris, Chicago’s defensive backs coach and defensive passing game coordinator. He spent seven seasons as a cornerback for the Packers, making the Pro Bowl twice and earning a second-team All-Pro nomination in 2007. He was enshrined in the Green Bay Packers Hall of Fame after his playing career and received a Super Bowl ring with them in the 2010 season, though he was injured and eventually released that year. The Bears’ safeties coach and assistant defensive backs coach, Matt Giordano, also played for the Packers, albeit in a much shorter stint. He spent 2009 with Green Bay and played in five games there as a safety, notching two tackles. The team signed him a few weeks into the season, though he was inactive for most of its games. There’s no confirmation on whether Giordano has any relation to the family that owns the Chicago deep dish pizza chain.
author: Jacob Infante

title: Chicago Bears-Green Bay Packers: Keys for a Chicago victory
summary: The Chicago Bears are heading up north to face the Green Bay Packers. It feels like this game is the rivalry teetering on an edge, with the last 34 years of Packers dominance on one side and a slide back in Chicago’s favor on the other. At least, that seems to be how Chicago media […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - SEPTEMBER 24: Christian Watson #9 of the Green Bay Packers looks on from the sideline during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Atlanta Falcons at Lambeau Field on September 24, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears are heading up north to face the Green Bay Packers. It feels like this game is the rivalry teetering on an edge, with the last 34 years of Packers dominance on one side and a slide back in Chicago’s favor on the other. At least, that seems to be how Chicago media is framing this game. But fans know that isn’t that easy. Nothing’s been easy for the Bears against the Packers since all those years ago when the first Hall of Famer took over for the green and gold. The Packers, no matter how vulnerable they seem, will always give the Bears a fight. I don’t think it’s a coincidence that two of the years the Bears were able to take it to Green Bay, those seasons ended with a coaching change up north. However, the Packers have a lot more questions than the Bears this week. And on paper, the Bears look like they should be deserving road favorites. So what’s it going to take for the Bears to win? Let our crew explain. Sam: The Bears want to kill their opponents every which way. By a thousand cuts in the ground game or by dropping big explosive plays over the defense’s head, or by throwing blitzes and disguises at you on defense that the offense gives it away. But with a backup QB, Ben Johnson is going to want to establish a stranglehold on Green Bay, dominate both lines of scrimmage and impose the Bears’ physical will on the Packers. Lester: On Monday, Bears wideout Luther Burden said, “We just want to beat them real bad and make them quit.” Which seems like the only key I want to highlight this week. Chicago has the NFL’s best rushing offense, and the Packers are allowing 140 rushing yards per game. Give me 50 rushing attempts and pummel them into submission. ECD: Offense: Limit the turnovers — looking at you, Agent Bagent — and maintain ball possession much like you did against the Jets. Defense: Force the Packers to maintain long drives into the red zone, and challenge them on third downs. Then make Jordan Love’s life hell behind the league’s worst OL. They have the 6th most “3-and-outs” in the league. Special Teams: Set up big returns on kickoffs and pin the Packers deep in their own territory. Bonus: Get under Matt LaFleur’s skin. He crumbles when pressed into a corner. Josh: he Bears need to relentlessly attack the ground game until they break the defense’s will. It’s an injured unit that already has to be feeling thinned out, so just make them exhaust themselves. On the flip side, they need to keep the ball in front of them and limit explosive plays by just refusing to let scheme beat them. Gary: Feels like beating a dead horse but pound the rock!! Packers run defense is near the bottom of the league and we field the best rushing attack in the NFL. Wear down their defense, take advantage of them overcommitting to the box with play action, and control the game like we saw against the Jets. This is a Packers team reeling right now; marching into Lambeau and punching them in the gut might be a deathblow for their season. On defense, it’s simple: pressure Love and what little offensive success the Packers can commit to falls apart. He’s had a horrible time with pressure this year, and early pressure in a game only compounds that, causing inaccuracy issues down the stretch of four quarters, in both situations with and without pressure. Sarah: Bears offense needs to start hot. In the matchups against Green Bay last season, they didn’t get going until the second half. They also need to capitalize in the red zone, as that’s been a struggle for them these past few weeks. The Packers defense has struggled in the red zone. Our run game will be a huge advantage to us since the Packers have a poor run defense and a terrible run game. Additionally, Bagent needs to do a better job of protecting the ball. On defense, put pressure on Love and take advantage of their bad offensive line. Donald: Is it strange I think the key to the game against the Packers is just – don’t hand them anything? The Bears have the best rushing attack in the NFL and the Pack is one of the worst teams at stopping the run. And I haven’t even mentioned their historically bad pass rush win rate for their offensive line. So the key here – for Bagent (as he has been named starter by Ben) – just don’t screw it up, man. Don’t throw bad, underthrown, passes over the middle that are easily picked off. Stay within yourself, let the run game carry the Bears, and you’ll walk your way into a victory. For the Defense – it is pin your ears back time, boys. Go get Love, because the Pack doesn’t have the horses on the offensive line to turn you back. I’m expecting multiple pressures and sacks as the Bears disrupt the Packers’ passing attack, and their run fails because they don’t have the line or the backs to challenge in the run game. Follow that path and it is not just a Bears win – it is a Bears rout. What are your keys to the game? Let us know in the comments.
author: Donald Gooch

title: Bears at Packers: 3 Props to Play
summary: After a bumpy 2-week stretch where we went 1-5, we bounced back last week with a 3-0 performance to even our record at 6-6 on the year. Far more respectable than the heinous 3-6 record we were sitting at heading into the Jets game. The Chicago Bears head north of the border to face the […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 04: Luther Burden III #10 of the Chicago Bears runs the ball during the first quarter against the New York Jets at Soldier Field on October 04, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Jessie Alcheh/Getty Images) | Getty Images After a bumpy 2-week stretch where we went 1-5, we bounced back last week with a 3-0 performance to even our record at 6-6 on the year. Far more respectable than the heinous 3-6 record we were sitting at heading into the Jets game. The Chicago Bears head north of the border to face the Green Bay Packers this week in the first matchup of the year between these two rival franchises. How will we fare this week? Here are the three props we like this week. As always, lines courtesy of FanDuel. D’Andre Swift OVER 82.5 Rushing Yards -114 This is quite a big number for Swift, but I think he has another 100+ yard day on the ground. Kyle Monangai is going to miss this game, and I think it sets up for the Chicago Bears to want to establish their will on another team and dominate the run game, and Swift should see north of 20 carries this week. Yes, Roschon Johnson will see a handful of carries, but I don’t think Ben Johnson will play on using him for 15 carries like he would Monangai. I think Swift is out to prove that the fumble issue is behind him, and he will run hard and run for a big day. Marshawn Lloyd UNDER 27.5 Rushing Yards -114 The Packers’ offensive line is a mess, and it’s made their running game nonexistent. The Bears have shown that they will give up some rushing yards, but it’s been trending in a direction that Kaleb Johnson is the far more effective back and Lloyd, well, just isn’t. Lloyd has averaged 2.8, 3.3, 2.8, and 1.9 rushing yards in each of his 4 games and hasn’t gone above 20 yards since week 1. Johnson will get the carries; Lloyd will see 5 to 10 carries and won’t average more than about 3 yards per carry. This number should go under. Luther Burden OVER 46.5 Receiving Yards -114 Burden has gone over 60 yards in three of his four games this season. The only game he was under 60 yards was the slop fest in Minnesota. This number feels off. Last week with Bagent, he had 63 yards and was targeted 6 times. With a struggling Packers defense, I think Burden finds room to run and finds a couple of explosive plays as well. I don’t think he pushes for 100 yards or anything, but another 60- to 70-yard output seems pretty inevitable.

title: Bears vs. Packers Injury Report: Kyle Monangai Out, Caleb Williams Questionable
summary: The Chicago Bears and Green Bay Packers meet on Sunday, and the injury reports are in. Bears running back Kyle Monangai has been ruled out with a thumb and toe injury, and he’s in a walking boot for the turf toe. Head coach Ben Johnson said he’s week-to-week and that injured reserve isn’t an option […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 18: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears high fives Kyle Monangai #25 after throwing a touchdown pass during the fourth quarter against the Los Angeles Rams in the NFC Divisional Playoffs at Soldier Field on January 18, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears and Green Bay Packers meet on Sunday, and the injury reports are in. Bears running back Kyle Monangai has been ruled out with a thumb and toe injury, and he’s in a walking boot for the turf toe. Head coach Ben Johnson said he’s week-to-week and that injured reserve isn’t an option right now. That’s good news, as they presumably expect him back sooner than the 4-game minimum he’d miss on IR. Also out for the Bears is rookie linebacker Keyshaun Elliott with a quad injury. The Bears list four players as questionable, including quarterback Caleb Williams, who is progressing from his hamstring injury. Before today’s practice, Johnson said Williams has been throwing after practice this week, and the team has been slowly ramping up his running. He must have felt good after working out on Wednesday and Thursday, because he was limited at practice today, which opens the door — albeit just a crack — for him to dress on Sunday. Tyson Bagent is still in line to start. Here’s video of Caleb Williams back at practice Friday. On Monday, Ben Johnson said that Williams is “not going to be there for us this week” against Green Bay and said Tyson Bagent “will be the guy.” Now Williams is listed as QUESTIONABLE for Week 5 against the Packers. pic.twitter.com/Ic4xv8oI8e — Courtney Cronin (@CourtneyRCronin) October 9, 2026 Also questionable for the Bears are the three players in the 21-day practice window coming back from the PUP list: defensive back Kyler Gordon (calf), linebacker Noah Sewell (Achilles), and defensive lineman Shemar Turner (knee). Johnson said they’ll likely activate one of their three players currently on the PUP list. That roster move would come on Saturday, and since the 53-man roster is currently at 52, a corresponding move wouldn’t be needed. All three of those players practiced in full. Every other Bear who popped up on the list earlier this week was a full participant and have no injury designation. The Packers have ruled two players out: running back Chris Brooks (ankle) and wide receiver Savion Williams (ankle). Starting guards Aaron Banks (knee/toe) and Jacob Monk (quadricep) are both doubtful after they returned to practice in a limited capacity on Friday. The Packers signed 36-year-old guard Kevin Zeitler last week, and he got some work with the first team over the last couple of days, but they are noncommittal about him playing. Green Bay lists defensive tackles Javon Hargrave (toe) and Anthony Campbell (ankle), and center/guard Jager Burton (back) as questionable. Hargrave’s injury popped up today, and all three players were limited.
author: Lester A. Wiltfong Jr.

title: Who should the Chicago Bears avoid at the trade deadline?
summary: The 3-1 Bears have been linked to the trade market, with fans and pundits speculating that they might make a move to solidify a defense that is showing what some might call a surprising ability to shut down offenses. However, not all moves are created equal. In our last installment, we asked what trade we […]
full_text: The 3-1 Bears have been linked to the trade market, with fans and pundits speculating that they might make a move to solidify a defense that is showing what some might call a surprising ability to shut down offenses. However, not all moves are created equal. In our last installment, we asked what trade we would like Ryan Poles to pursue. Now, we’re looking at the other side of the equation and asking what trade targets we hope Chicago stays away from. What “reasonable target” do you hope Chicago doesn’t pursue in the trade market? Lester Wiltfong: As much as I’d be excited by it, I don’t think targeting a high-priced player like Vita Vea or Maxx Crosby makes sense for the Bears. Besides the cap hit, I don’t want to see them unload day one and two picks. Bryan Orenchuk: I hope they do not pursue another WR, even though they may come super cheap. Marvin Harrison Jr., Brian Thomas Jr., and Jerry Jeudy are all quality players in their own right, but we don’t need their services on this roster. Erik Duerrwaechter: There’s been some buzz around the Chargers being sellers at the deadline. A player who wouldn’t cost much, but wouldn’t be a great fit for the Bears, is Teair Tart. The 5-tech DE is an O-K run stuffer who doesn’t add too much into the pass rush. It would make me ask the question, “why trade Gervon Dexter Sr away if this is your replacement plan?” Donald Gooch: Daron Payne’s name has been bandied about and, sure, he might help our run defense a bit up the middle. But Payne is a shadow of himself, and I’d rather not give up draft capital for a player who doesn’t significantly change our defensive line’s profile. Mongo Peanut: Maxx Crosby. I understand the appeal given his consistent dominance, but his failed physical and his consistent media presence give me concern. I think he likely fetches a similar or higher price than Simmons given the Raiders are still in the hunt. Josh Sunderbruch : Anyone who costs a first-round pick or more is out of the question for me. I would hesitate to move for Simmons unless the Titans settle for a 2nd-rounder or a package of offsetting picks. So what about you? Let us know below who you hope the Bears stay away from in the trade market. Do you want them to avoid trades entirely?
