title: 2 very important Cowboys players suffered injury vs Bucs
summary: We are going to add a little injury to insult. Obviously the insult is the Dallas Cowboys losing to the formerly winless Tampa Bay Buccaneers. At home. Against a rookie UDFA replacement quarterback. I probably didn’t need to remind you of that. The injury is what happened to two very important Cowboys players – CeeDee […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Kevin Jairaj-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect We are going to add a little injury to insult. Obviously the insult is the Dallas Cowboys losing to the formerly winless Tampa Bay Buccaneers. At home. Against a rookie UDFA replacement quarterback. I probably didn’t need to remind you of that. The injury is what happened to two very important Cowboys players – CeeDee Lamb and Tyler Guyton. Fortunately, it doesn’t sound too serious in either case. Lamb was hit on his quad and missed the latter part of the game for the most part. It was a very quiet game for Lamb after absolutely torching the Houston Texans last week. He finished with two catches for nine yards. Brian Schottenheimer said that Lamb got hit in the quad muscle at the same spot he got hit last week, aggravating that injury. The fact that Lamb was able to actually go out there on some plays after the injury points to nothing very serious. Tyler Guyton has been re-born this season and has made Cowboys fans forget about supposed issues at left tackle. He came out of the game with a back injury late in the fourth quarter. Schottenheimer said that initial x-rays looked good but that they would have to run more tests. Fortunately the Cowboys have a few extra days to heal up before they travel to play the Green Bay Packers in Week 6 on Sunday night.
author: David Halprin

title: Cowboys defense’s inability to do basic things emblematic of problems
summary: The futility of the Dallas Cowboys offense on Thursday night against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers was a surprise. Dak Prescott not being able to handle a lot of blitzing is out of character. He’s known as one of the best against the blitz in the league. Once the All-22 comes out maybe we can dig […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Kevin Jairaj-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The futility of the Dallas Cowboys offense on Thursday night against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers was a surprise. Dak Prescott not being able to handle a lot of blitzing is out of character. He’s known as one of the best against the blitz in the league. Once the All-22 comes out maybe we can dig a little deeper into that problem. The futility of the Cowboys defense, on the other hand, is no surprise. Christian Parker has had his struggles early getting the players accustomed to his new scheme. That was expected to some extent. The blizzard of injuries also adds to the problem, especially with the cluster of missed games in the secondary. Dallas couldn’t even get their new weapon, Joey Porter Jr., on the field because of illness. Sometimes you start to think the team is cursed on that side of the ball. You think maybe Parker is asking too much, or the scheme is flawed. All kinds of theories are floated about changes to the scheme. We get caught up in strategy and scheme, in alignments and run fits. Then you see something like the picture below and all that just goes out the window. This is just basic football. This is not scheme, this is not assignment, this is five Cowboys players surrounding Bucky Irving, only to watch him escape for a 72-yard run. How in the world is that not a short gain? The Cowboys defense missed 12 tackles during the game. That number actually feels low. Multiple times they had running backs bottled up for short gains only for them to break through and pick up significant yards. They surrounded quarterback Jalon Daniels on plenty of dropbacks, but only came away with one sack. The Bucs explosive plays were not just on a banged up secondary. They weren’t just on busted assignments or mental lapses. They exposed a Dallas defense that doesn’t even do the most fundamental things right. Gang tackling should have been a given on that Irving run. It most certainly wasn’t. The Cowboys defense has so far to go, and the schedule only has so many games left.
author: David Halprin

title: Cowboys hopes for ‘26 season cannonball after loss to Bucs
summary: The Dallas Cowboys simply refuse to perform under pressure, be it mental or whatever as they had no answers for from the Tampa Bay Buccaneers defense on Thursday night. Any type of pressure is too much for this team, and 2026 is looking no different after a 24-16 loss that sinks the Cowboys to 2-3 […]
full_text: Photo by Ron Jenkins/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys simply refuse to perform under pressure, be it mental or whatever as they had no answers for from the Tampa Bay Buccaneers defense on Thursday night. Any type of pressure is too much for this team, and 2026 is looking no different after a 24-16 loss that sinks the Cowboys to 2-3 with alternating wins and losses through five weeks. The Bucs came in on a short week and managed to get themselves into another one-score game, their fifth straight to start the year, and rallied to beat the Cowboys with QB Jalon Daniels looking like a seasoned vet. On the other hand, the Cowboys did not learn their lesson about the dangers of starting slow against a winless team from their game in Houston, in fact starting even slower. Their second-half comeback fell short, and arguably makes this loss feel even worse in hindsight. All it did was shine a brighter light on the things this football team is supposed to prioritize doing well, but isn’t right now. Just hours before kickoff, we took our routine weekly look at what the Cowboys needed to do to win this game , and what they couldn’t let happen to avoid being upset. Giving Dak Prescott time to throw was the top priority, and although he wasn’t sacked, the Cowboys did not achieve this. Not letting Bucky Irving beat them was the key to avoiding a loss, and they certainly did not achieve this either. The Cowboys ended this game with the highest percentage of passes compared to runs in their run/pass split of any game under Brian Schottenheimer so far, and conceding 165 yards to Bucky Irving and always chasing this game as a result was the reason why. The Cowboys are now 4-6-1 in one score games under Brian Schottenheimer. With that, let’s get to some notes on Thursday’s action. Turned on it’s head Back at home for the first time since week two, the Cowboys went right down the field for an opening drive touchdown and immediate 7-0 lead. Instead of following this with a three and out on defense, the Cowboys gave up a methodical drive to let the Bucs tie the game. Jalon Daniels and the Tampa offense picked up a pair of third-down conversions before the rookie passer was sacked on the ensuing third down, but a DaRon Bland holding penalty bailed them out. Bland would give up yet another third down in the red zone, and when it looked like Christian Parker’s defense had a chance to dig in and at come up with a red zone stop, Rashan Gary was drawn offsides. This turned a 2nd-and-10 into second and manageable, creating a layup throw from Daniels to Irving for his first touchdown of the night. Daniels went eight for eight passing on this drive. The only possible positive thing to take away from the Cowboys defense at this moment in the game was they kept a lid on the Bucs offense and didn’t allow a play longer than 14 yards on this scoring drive. In theory only, this is a bit of how the Parker scheme that’s derived from Vic Fangio’s should play, and the Cowboys are built to invite teams to take such a long way down the field if they choose, knowing their offense is built to score quickly, and consistently. From this point on though, none of these things happened. A Cowboys offense that came into this game having not punted more than twice in an entire game at any point in their last ten games punted three straight times after their opening touchdown. They possessed the ball for only a combined 4:51 over these three drives, the last one being a 37 second three and out. The Cowboys basically never punt. Ten consecutive games with either 1 or 2 punts… never more than 2. It's the longest streak in the Super Bowl era. And yet they're 4-6 in that stretch. Elite offense + very not elite defense. Rinse, repeat. pic.twitter.com/VOIrlzQEkc — Mike Leslie (@MikeLeslieWFAA) October 8, 2026 Amazingly, the defense forced three punts of their own in response to this. What the Bucs did do in this stretch was hold onto the ball for over eight minutes, nearly double the amount of time it took the Cowboys to get the same three drive endings. The seed was planted for the Buccaneers to play this game on their terms by absolutely dominating time of possession. The Cowboys lost time of possession in this game 39:21 to 20:39, a differential of minus 18:42. It is the worst differential Dallas has had in this stat since Week 9 of 2021, that infamous 30-16 home loss to the Denver Broncos. Denver held the ball for 24:41 more than Dallas did in that game. The breaking points came on both sides of the ball. Schottenheimer said going into the locker room at halftime that everything going wrong in this game was about him “calling better plays”. Christian Parker must not have gotten this message to start the second half either, as the Cowboys suddenly couldn’t limit big plays. They gave up a two-play touchdown drive to start the third quarter, also allowed a Tez Johnson 64-yard catch and a 3rd-and-21 conversion, and allowed Irving to run out the clock and end the game on 2nd-and-12 with a 22-yard blast up the middle. Always behind the trend Another truth about the NFL is that it is a copycat league, and perhaps more accurately, there are trends every year that winning teams take to, and those that can’t follow along simply don’t win come the stretch run and playoffs. One of the things being heavily discussed this year as making a difference in wins and losses is which quarterbacks (and play callers) can best attack the middle of the field. There are good offenses that don’t major in doing so, but the separation point to great offenses that stress defenses the most are the ones that aren’t afraid to really open up the whole field. It took until the Cowboys were literally within a few blades of grass of having no hope at all in this game, about to go down 31-10, for the offense to unlock this part of the pass game consistently. With 99 yards to go in a hurry down two scores, the Cowboys went into Madden mode and spammed the slant route to get downfield in three minutes and change for a George Pickens acrobatic touchdown. Three straight passes went for at least 13 yards to ignite the drive, to three different receivers in Ryan Flournoy, KaVontae Turpin, and Pickens. A heavy, heavy focus by the Buccaneers defensively in this game was to play outside leverage against the Cowboys receivers and force them back over the middle into more coverage. The touchdown drive was the highlight of how the Cowboys took advantage of this, but there were too many lowlights in this area that cost them the game as well. A few plays before Prescott’s first interception, he hit Pickens for a 27-yard slant on third down out of the condensed formation that Dallas needs to use more often, but isn’t. On the next third down, in the exact same down and distance, they spread it out more, targeted Flournoy in traffic instead, and the pass was intercepted. Jake Ferguson is another player holding the Cowboys back from being on the right side of another winning trend around football right now. Not only are tight ends supposed to have a significant role in the middle of the field passing game, but being a reliable checkdown option against pressure looks is valuable as well. Ferguson is neither of these things right now. The Cowboys proved they can get the easy yards that the best offenses are getting with ease right now by simply scheming touches for their most dynamic skill players in this game, but also that they just won’t do so consistently enough to be taken seriously, or avoid the game-losing plays in between the positive ones even against bad opponents. No Schott? With the Cowboys having an extended period of time off before their next game, coming out of a stretch of three games in 12 days, now is as good a time as ever to check in on how well this team is taking to the identity of how Brian Schottenheimer very publicly told the world he wants his team to look and feel. Winning the line of scrimmage was supposed to be…
author: Sean Martin

title: 5 plays that cost the Cowboys vs. the Buccaneers
summary: Why? Just why? Why do the Dallas Cowboys keep disappointing this badly? You’re at home on a short week, playing a winless team that is starting an undrafted free agent at quarterback. You would have never noticed with how poorly the defense looked. Once again, they failed to limit explosive plays. If the Tampa Bay […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Kevin Jairaj-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Why? Just why? Why do the Dallas Cowboys keep disappointing this badly? You’re at home on a short week, playing a winless team that is starting an undrafted free agent at quarterback. You would have never noticed with how poorly the defense looked. Once again, they failed to limit explosive plays. If the Tampa Bay Buccaneers wanted to gash them on the ground, they could. If they wanted to exploit them through the passing game, no problemo. This defense is a rudderless ship that cannot get out of its own way. As for the offense that was tabbed the Greatest Offense There Is (GOTI), not so fast either. The offense led by Dak Prescott was lifeless in the first half. Prescott was far from his normal self, and the offense paid dearly for it. When you lose this badly, and in this embarrassing way, there’s no shortage of identifying where it all went so sour. We’re going to sit on this loss for a while. Here are the key plays that cost the Cowboys. The drive that started it all, 1st QTR, 9:33, 3rd-and-4 The Cowboys were off to a fast start. After the receiving the opening kick, the Cowboys took a quick 7-0 lead and immediately put the pressure on Jalon Daniels and the offense to answer back. Facing an early 3rd-and-4, the Dallas defense does a good job in coverage, blanketing Tampa Bay’s available receivers. However, Rashan Gary doesn’t keep containment on his side, and Daniels is able to escape the pocket to his right as he manages to get the first down running. This wiped away a 3-and-out opportunity. More than once, Gary failed to maintain the edge or make a tackle in space, and the Buccaneers benefited from it. On Tampa Bay’s opening drive, the Buccaneers held the ball for 10:58 of game clock. During the drive, DaRon Bland drew a holding penalty. That nullified a sack and further kept the drive alive. That one play would have knocked the Buccaneers out of field goal range and ended an excruciating drive much sooner. The Buccaneers more than doubled the time of possession in the first half versus the Cowboys. However, you can point back to Daniels getting out of the pocket initially to keep the chains moving and the Cowboys off the field, which foreshadowed a maddening evening. Dak misses a big shot to CeeDee Lamb, 2nd QTR 9:29, 3rd-and-10 If we know anything about Todd Bowles, he’s going to bring to bring pressure and overwhelm your offensive lineman with extra numbers in the face of the quarterback. Historically, Dak Prescott is very good against the blitz, but something wasn’t quite right with Prescott for much of the evening. After a Bryan Anger punt that landed inside the Tampa Bay 5-yard line and a rare 3-and-out from the defense, the offense had prime real estate. The Cowboys had the chance to take back the lead and the momentum from the Buccaneers. Facing a critical third down, Prescott breaks away from a sure sack and, once he bails the pocket, has a clear shot down the field at CeeDee Lamb. If Prescott lays the ball out and puts some air under it, Lamb likely makes the catch and waltzes into the end zone. Instead, Prescott throws it short, and it is very nearly intercepted. Had Prescott hit that throw deep, it likely changes the way Bowles attacks the Dallas offense the remainder of the night. Prescott has been terrific all season, but that was one he had to have. There was a lid on the Cowboys offense for far too long on the evening and that moment they needed to have to get out of that funk. Bucky breaks free 3rd QTR 14:54, 1st-and-10 Take your pick of which explosive play allowed by the defense upset you the most. Was it the defense allowing a 3rd-and-21 to be converted after bailing out into a soft zone defense with easy access to Emeka Egbuka? Or was it DaRon Bland falling as Tez Johnson was wide open in the secondary and took it 64 yards? Let’s settle on Bucky Irving’s 72-yard run to open the half. The Cowboys decided to aggressively blitz the run to stop Irving. For a moment, it looked to be successful. However, the defense didn’t show enough effort to rally to the ball to make the tackle. It looks like Jaishawn Barham did a solid job redirecting Irving in the backfield, but instead Irving leaks out of the pile of bodies to set up Tampa Bay deep in Dallas territory. Still shell-shocked from what happened, the defense looks like they don’t know what hit them. On the very next play, Emeka Egbuka trots in for the score to give the Buccaneers the lead. It’s an abysmal pattern, but this defense hemorrhages big plays at the worst possible time. Bland drops the ball, 4QTR 3:58, 3rd-and-8 DaRon Bland had a rough night. Multiple times he was on the receiving end of huge plays that went against his team. He hasn’t been playing very well for quite a long time, but all could have been forgiven if he just made one play that slipped through his fingers. At this point in the game, the Cowboys should be disappointed with how they had played against Jalon Daniels. They hadn’t been able to get him to the ground regularly; they were unable to cover his receivers, and they had allowed him to overcome repeated penalties by his offense. Yet, with the Cowboys needing to score a touchdown and a two-point conversion, Daniels threw a pass right to Bland that he should’ve intercepted for a touchdown. This is the same player that has the NFL record for most interceptions returned for a touchdown in a given season. If there was any indicator that Bland isn’t the player he once was and probably wont ever be again, its that moment right there. There are few play calls by Christian Parker where you feel he got the better of the opposing offensive coordinator. Dallas missed his call of the night. Parker dialed up a blitz to ensure that Daniels would be forced to get the ball out quickly, and Bland also knew it and was in perfect position. That play call was worth six points, and Bland couldn’t deliver. Ferguson completes the hat trick 4th QTR 1:22 The Cowboys turned the ball over three times on Thursday night; two of them were because of balls that hit the intended receiver in the hands. Jake Ferguson’s mishandling of Dak Prescott’s pass resulted in effectively the game-sealing turnover, which left fans in attendance stunned. For the second week in a row, Dak Prescott was engineering a late fourth-quarter drive. It looked as if he was going to get his sputtering offense in the end zone once again. At that point, the personnel was falling apart. Tyler Guyton had left the game; CeeDee Lamb was also on the sideline with a quad injury. For as poorly as he had been playing, Prescott was doing his best to drag his offense to a tie. That is, until Jake Ferguson let the ball slip through his hands, off his helmet, and into the arms of Alex Anzalone. In the last few weeks, Ferguson has mishandled the football several times. From a fumble in Brazil to a drop during the two-minute offense before the break, Ferguson had to come up with that catch at the end of regulation. It’s a shame that the game was ultimately decided by a simple pitch-and-catch that was poorly executed.
author: LP Cruz

title: 10 thoughts on the Cowboys loss to the Buccaneers
summary: Watching the Dallas Cowboys find new ways to lose games has started to become really annoying. On Thursday night, they were supposed to easily handle the winless Tampa Bay Buccaneers, but it didn’t go down like that. Instead, it was the Bucs that took it to Dallas in a convincing 24-16 road win. Insert sadface […]
full_text: Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images | Getty Images Watching the Dallas Cowboys find new ways to lose games has started to become really annoying. On Thursday night, they were supposed to easily handle the winless Tampa Bay Buccaneers, but it didn’t go down like that. Instead, it was the Bucs that took it to Dallas in a convincing 24-16 road win. Insert sadface emoji. This latest loss serves as a stark reminder that this team has a ways to go. We know about the defensive problems, but what happens when the offense is having a rough go too? Well, that’s what we found out on Thursday in this very unpleasant primetime affair. Here are 10 thoughts on the Cowboys’ very upsetting defeat to the Bucs. 1. A slow death After the Cowboys opened the game with a quick four-minute drive that went 70 yards for a touchdown, things were looking good. This is what we came for. But then something awful happened. The Bucs answered with a touchdown drive of their own, only it wasn’t just any touchdown drive. The Tampa offense held the ball for 11 minutes as we watched the Cowboys’ defense commit penalties and repeatedly couldn’t make stops on third down. They did a good thing here and there, but it wasn’t enough to get off the field, and just like that, it was already the second quarter and the game was tied 7-7. 2. A quick death If you don’t care for the slow burn of a long, time-consuming drive that the Bucs employed to start the game, don’t fret. The Cowboys’ defense made adjustments to start the second half. Instead of a slow death, they allowed the Bucs to pull off a two-play, 86-yard drive that took just one minute. In the blink of an eye, the Bucs jumped ahead 14-10. Slow or fast, the defense is destined to play poorly regardless of the pace. 3. Bad bounces When the Bucs struck quickly to take their first lead of the game, the Cowboys’ offense needed to answer back. And it looked like they would, as they immediately drove down the field into Tampa territory. Sadly, a Prescott pass was deflected and volleyed around before landing into the arms of the Bucs. 4. Momentum killed Not only did the Bucs turn that deflected interception into points to go up 21-10, but on the ensuing kickoff, KaVontae Turpin put the ball on the turf. Did the Cowboys recover it? Nope. It was Tampa ball again with a chance to break this game wide open. 5. 3rd-and-21 The Cowboys didn’t die, at least not yet. After the Turpin fumble, the defense showed up with two great plays, both by rookie edge Malachi Lawrence. First with a sack, then by deflecting the ball, setting up a third-and-21. Finally, a stop! Not quite. In true Cowboys’ defense form, they allowed the Bucs to convert, setting them up for a field goal and a 24-10 lead. The defense did a decent job putting the Bucs’ offense in third-and-long situations, but they were equally atrocious at stopping them in those moments. It was tough to watch. 6. Huge coaching mistake When you’re an 0-4 team, things can seem bleak, so it’s understandable why Todd Bowles wanted to put a resounding stamp on this game by making it a 21-point game and putting a dagger through the heart of the Cowboys. But when your team struggles to win, how about just securing the win? Making it a three-score game wouldn’t have been enough of a stamp for him, but a failed fourth-down play allowed the Cowboys to have life, and based on what happened next, Bowles must have felt a little regretful about his decision. 7. One last chance Despite all the madness, the Cowboys still had a chance to win the game. After the failed fourth-down play at the goal line, the Cowboys drove 99 yards to make it a one-score game. Then, the defense forced a well-timed, quick three-and-out to give the Cowboys the ball back, keeping the comeback alive. Unfortunately, the drive ended when a Prescott pass went off the face of Jake Ferguson and into the arms of a Bucs linebacker, and it was game over. 8. Going for two When the Cowboys scored in the fourth quarter, Brian Schottenheimer opted to go for a two-point conversion. The analytics supported his decision as it gave the team a chance to win the game with another touchdown, and if they didn’t convert, they would still have another shot to convert if they scored that second touchdown. Had the Cowboys scored again and come up short on the two-point conversion, the fans would have come at Schotty with torches, but regardless, it was the smart choice. 9. The unsavory Bland It feels weird to single out one player when the entire defense was bad, but can anyone tell us what has happened to DaRon Bland? He continues to have a tough time. He has been a liability all year, and this game might be his worst. He could not stay with his man, arrived late at times, fell down, and did everything but make a play. He had a chance to redeem himself when he stepped in front of an out route late in the fourth quarter, but of course, he couldn’t make the play. One of his patented pick-sixes would have been huge there. Oh well. 10. Late casualties Not only did the Cowboys lose this game, but they also suffered some casualties late in the fourth quarter. Both CeeDee Lamb (quad)and Tyler Guyton (back) had to come out of the game. The severity of these injuries is unclear, but at least the Cowboys now have 10 days before their next game, so hopefully, these guys can heal up soon.
author: Dan Rogers

title: Cowboys news: Dallas loses in embarrassing fashion to formerly winless Bucs
summary: Bucs take down Cowboys, 24-16, in Thursday night showdown at AT&T Stadium – CBS News The Cowboys were a lock to win this football game by most media and betting outlets. Instead they fall to 2-3 with plenty of tough games coming up on their schedule. Bucky Irving ran for a career-high 165 yards, including […]
full_text: Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images | Getty Images Bucs take down Cowboys, 24-16, in Thursday night showdown at AT&T Stadium – CBS News The Cowboys were a lock to win this football game by most media and betting outlets. Instead they fall to 2-3 with plenty of tough games coming up on their schedule. Bucky Irving ran for a career-high 165 yards, including a 72-yard run to set up the touchdown that put Tampa Bay ahead for good while scoring twice himself, and the Buccaneers beat the Dallas Cowboys 24-16 on Thursday night for their first win of the season. Jalon Daniels threw a TD pass to Irving in the first half while directing a turnover-free offense amid several Dallas miscues in just the second start for the undrafted rookie. CeeDee Lamb injury update as Cowboys star WR exits vs. Buccaneers – Jacob Camenker, USA Today Not only did the Cowboys drop one of the games circled as a win, they also could be without CeeDee Lamb. Lamb left the game in the fourth quarter with an injury and attempted to return to the game for the Cowboys failed two-point conversion attempt to cut the score to 6. All eyes will be on Lamb’s injury status over the next 10 days. The Dallas Cowboys may have lost one of their top pass-catching weapons in their Week 5 game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers . CeeDee Lamb is dealing with a quad injury. He was deemed “questionable” to return to the game, according to Amazon’s sideline reporter Kaylee Hartung, when Dallas began a drive with 8:32 remaining in regulation. Lamb briefly returned to the field for a play after Hartung’s report. However, he was seen hobbling off the field shortly after the play. Cowboys vs Buccaneers recap: Dallas drops a game they had no business losing – Dave Halprin, Blogging the Boys Good teams win these types of football games. Right now, the Cowboys are not a good team. There are a lot of questions to be answered over the Cowboys mini-bye week before the Cowboys take on the Green Bay Packers in week six. The Dallas Cowboys just did what almost no one thought they would do. They were an 8.5-point favorite going against a winless team, a team playing without its starting QB, instead playing an undrafted rookie at QB in his second-ever start. They lost to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 24-16. Going into a mini-bye, the Cowboys needed this game for momentum, stacking wins, and putting a turbulent early season behind them. The Cowboys failed to intercept Daniels, who had thrown four picks in his first two NFL games, extending their streak of interception-free defense to eight games, dating to last season. It is the longest streak without an interception in team history. The Cowboys are also the 15th team since the NFL-AFL merger to go without an interception through the first five games of a season. Dak Prescott’s batted pass turned into an interception, and five plays later the Bucs scored another touchdown. KaVontae Turpin then fumbled the ensuing kickoff, and the Bucs turned that into a field goal. title: Scouting the Enemy: Los Angeles Chargers
summary: The Denver Broncos take on the Los Angeles Chargers on this Sunday. At 2-2, the Broncos are looking to rebound after their Week 4 loss to the San Francisco 49ers. The Chargers are winless on the season, depleted by injuries, and have major issues on offense and defense. Here is a deeper look at Denver’s […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - OCTOBER 04: Justin Herbert #10 of the Los Angeles Chargers passes against the Seattle Seahawks during the fourth quarter at Lumen Field on October 04, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Olivia Vanni/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos take on the Los Angeles Chargers on this Sunday. At 2-2, the Broncos are looking to rebound after their Week 4 loss to the San Francisco 49ers. The Chargers are winless on the season, depleted by injuries, and have major issues on offense and defense. Here is a deeper look at Denver’s Week 5 opponent. 2025 Los Angeles Chargers Season Review The Chargers finished their 2025 regular season with an 11-6 record earning second place in the AFC West. They lost to the New England Patriots in the AFC Wildcard Round. 2026 Los Angeles Chargers Offseason Additions and Departures The Chargers made several big additions this offseason. Unfortunately, a handful of those players haven’t been able to stay healthy. Tyler Biadasz was their big addition to bolster their pivot of their offensive line, but he suffered a knee injury during the offseason and is out for the entire year. They also added two tight ends in David Njoku and Charlie Kolar. Njoku’s season is already over after suffering a broken leg, while Kolar fractured his forearm and is questionable to play against Denver on Sunday. They opted to re-up the contracts of several key players on defense including edge rusher Khalil Mack, safety Tony Jefferson, as well as versatile interior defensive lineman Teair Tart. Their most notable departure was edge rusher Odafe Oweh who signed a lucrative 4-year, $96 million contract with the Washington Commanders. Los Angeles had eight selections in the 2026 NFL Draft. Miami standout Akheem Mesidor was their first-round pick to bolster their pass rush, while they continued to fortify their offensive line by drafting Florida center Jake Slaughter in the second round. Fourth-round pick Genesis Smith, a versatile defensive back, has two interceptions on the season and has already earned half of their defense’s snaps thus far. Offensive X-Factor: Quarterback Justin Herbert Justin Herbert is having a rough start to his 2026 season. The seventh-year signal caller is posting career lows across the board. His completion percentage is under 60-percent. Not only that, but Herbert has also been sacked 12 times and sports more interceptions (6) compared to touchdowns (4). It’s not all Herbert’s fault. His offensive line is tremendously banged up, and the lack of quality protection up front is a big reason why the Chargers are struggling on offense. Even with his issues thus far, I’m still dubbing him as their X-Factor on offense. We’ve seen him play big games against the Broncos in the past. Denver can’t afford to let him and the winless Chargers find a way to earn an upset victory. Patrick Surtain II will be out for Sunday’s matchup and there is a good chance Riley Moss will be too. That means Jahdae Barron and Kris Abrams-Draine will be starting on the boundary. To help the secondary out, this is a game where the pass rush has to kick into high gear. The Chargers could be without three starters up front. All things considered, this should be an advantageous matchup for Denver to get back on track sacking opposing quarterbacks. Defensive X-Factor: Edge Rusher Tuli Tuipulotu Like their offense, the Chargers’ defense isn’t firing on all cylinders. There has been a significant dropoff in their cohesiveness compared to last season where they were a top ten unit in the NFL. As of now, they rank middle of the pack in scoring defense and are below league-average when it comes to defending the run and pass. However, one particular player is still playing quite well. That’s Tuli Tuipulotu. The fourth-year edge rusher is coming off a great 2025 gridiron campaign. He posted 45 tackles, 22 tackles for loss, 13 sacks and 61 quarterback pressures. That production earned him the first Pro Bowl honor of his promising career. Through four games, Tuipulotu has 18 tackles, 5 tackles for loss, 1 forced fumble, two sacks, and 13 pressures. There has been a slight decrease in his hurry and pressure rate, but they are still quite good for the position overall. He’s a quality pass rusher who can also wreck an opposing run game. The Broncos offensive line will need to be prepared for his well-rounded game and play at a high level to keep him at bay. How the Broncos can secure a victory over the Chargers ICYMI: Yesterday, I gave three things the Broncos must accomplish to earn their third victory of the season. Even though the Chargers are winless on the year, Denver has to treat Sunday’s matchup like a must-win game. They have a lot to prove and have yet to play a complete game in all three phases. All things considered, I think they’ll find a way to defeat their division rival and get their third victory of the season. Hart’s Prediction: Broncos 27, Chargers 17.

title: Sean Payton explains why he’s taking back Broncos play-calling
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country! What’s old is new again. By now, you’ve heard that Sean Payton is taking back play-calling duties for the Denver Broncos offense. Through the first four weeks, the Broncos have been inept offensively. That’s not all on the new offensive coordinator, Davis Webb, who was calling plays in the first four […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - JANUARY 04: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos and Head coach Sean Payton of the Denver Broncos speak in the second quarter against the Los Angeles Chargers at Empower Field At Mile High on January 04, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by C. Morgan Engel/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country! What’s old is new again. By now, you’ve heard that Sean Payton is taking back play-calling duties for the Denver Broncos offense. Through the first four weeks, the Broncos have been inept offensively. That’s not all on the new offensive coordinator, Davis Webb, who was calling plays in the first four games. As Payton said to the media on Thursday after practice, it’s a collective. In the end, the Broncos offense has not been good enough, and Payton felt the time was right for the change. Denver heads on the road to face the hapless and winless Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday. As Payton said on Thursday: “We’ll make a change offensively. I’ll call the plays. I understand the questions at the start of the week. I want to say this first, and I said it to Davis the other day, talking to him. I’ve done this long enough where I know when I have a future head coach, and he’s going to be one. All the things that it’s hard to find will happen. In fact, the same thing to some degree — a little bit different — happened to myself early in my career. I met with the offense. “As the head coach, no different than evaluating your right tackle, your slot receiver, your running backs, something to change it up. Ultimately, I used that word the ‘collective’ yesterday. It’s the group. So when I met with the offense, it’s about buttoning up all of the little things that keep you from sustaining drives. Davis is all-in with the game plan, just like we’ve been operating. He’ll be down on the field with me.” When Payton was asked why he made the change now rather than waiting, he said there were too many to list. “We know we have to improve our balance in running the football,” he said to the media. “There’s a handful of things. Then the hard thing when you are not the head coach is certainly there are things you want to feel like are cleared, where when you’re calling them as the head coach, you’re in your mind prepared to say, ‘I don’t have to run it by anyone.’ So it’s changing things up and really trying to reduce some of the calories to get back to getting some things really well. That’s going to be the focus.” If it’s any solace to Webb, Payton had the play-calling duties taken away from him in 2002 when he was with the New York Giants. So Payton is using that experience now in Denver. “We’ll do what’s best for the team." HC Sean Payton to reassume play-calling responsibilities ahead of #DENvsLAC » https://t.co/hpkLHNtgWd pic.twitter.com/F9XQefRqLl — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) October 8, 2026 “It was tough,” Payton said when asked how he handled getting the play-calling taken from him. “Davis, he’s going to respond well. It was different. I’d just lost my mother during the bye week. We got imbalanced a little bit. I just remember the professional setback, if you will. We had gone to the Super Bowl in (2000) so this was a couple years into it. It wasn’t until a couple years later that you’re like, ‘Man, you really didn’t mourn the loss of your mom because you were so out of whack with your career.’ And the team did better. “Very quickly, it’s still about the team, and we went to the playoffs. There are certain things that I learned that maybe I needed to. Then shortly thereafter, I’m in Dallas, and then three years later, I get that opportunity (in New Orleans). He’s been fantastic. A much different situation, if you will.” As for this Sunday, Payton will be the voice in Bo Nix’s helmet. Payton also said he and the Broncos are focused on this week. As the head coach, Payton felt the time was right to make the move for the team. He saw something that needed correcting, and this was the course of action to fix it. “Everyone’s a little disappointed because you feel like you let one of your teammates down,” Payton said when asked if Nix had any reaction. “That’s the human part of it. That’s our game a little bit in this league. I’m going to go back to what I said earlier relative to (Webb’s) talent. It’s rare. He’s gifted. It’s all ahead of him.” Broncos links

title: Discussion: What can the Lions defense do vs. Cardinals to earn faith?
summary: One of the more interesting questions from Dan Campbell’s Friday press conference was about how he can regain confidence in the Detroit Lions defense. In short, what did he need to see in Sunday’s game against the Arizona Cardinals to make him feel better about the direction of the defense. Campbell’s answer was basically three-fold: […]
full_text: Dec. 16, 2012; Glendale, AZ, USA; The Detroit Lions defensive line faces off against the Arizona Cardinals offense during the first half at University of Phoenix Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Matt Kartozian-USA TODAY Sports | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect One of the more interesting questions from Dan Campbell’s Friday press conference was about how he can regain confidence in the Detroit Lions defense. In short, what did he need to see in Sunday’s game against the Arizona Cardinals to make him feel better about the direction of the defense. Campbell’s answer was basically three-fold : force turnovers, get to the quarterback, and cut down significantly on the missed assignment and missed executions. It’s a fair answer, but probably not one that makes Lions fans feel good enough about the state of the defense. So for today’s Question of the Day, I’m going to ask you the exact same question Campbell was asked: What would make you feel good about the direction of the defense going into the bye? What benchmarks do you want to see? My answer: First of all, I want y’all to put your thinking caps on. I know I’m probably going to get at least 50 “Fire Sheppard” answers here, but let’s dig a little deeper. Before we do, I think it’s at least exploring if there’s anything Detroit can do on Sunday to build faith in the defense. We have to recognize that the Cardinals are not a very good offense right now, and that any “improvement” we see from the Lions could also just be interpreted as facing a poor offense. That said, I just need to see this team be assignment sound. If Trey McBride and Michael Wilson just win their 1-on-1s, I can live with that as long as Detroit doesn’t have any glaring mental mistakes. If there are terrible run fits, wide open spaces in zones, and failed communications in the secondary, then Detroit can produce as many takeaways as they want—I won’t feel good about this defense making any progress. If you want to shorten that to one statistical benchmark: no rushes of over 15 yards allowed vs. the Cardinals. The explosive-prone run defense needs to stop or this team has no hope. Still, I don’t think there’s a ton Detroit can do to make me believe the defense will turn things around based on a single performance against a subpar offense. But they can certainly show progress and lead me to believe they can at least string together some acceptable games of defense. title: Dan Campbell takeaways: 3 things he needs to see from Detroit Lions defense
summary: Dan Campbell wrapped up the week of media sessions on Friday before the team heads to Arizona to take on the Cardinals in Week 5. He said that they are not likely to active Brian Branch (PUP, achilles) or Cade Mays (IR, wrist) this week, but there were a few other takeaways from his press […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 04: Head coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions looks on during the game against the Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Dan Campbell wrapped up the week of media sessions on Friday before the team heads to Arizona to take on the Cardinals in Week 5. He said that they are not likely to active Brian Branch (PUP, achilles) or Cade Mays (IR, wrist) this week, but there were a few other takeaways from his press conference, as well. Here’s what you need to know. Remembering Mike Ditka News broke less than an hour before Campbell’s press conference that legendary Chicago Bears coach Mike Ditka had passed away at the age of 86. A reporter actually broke the news to Campbell. “No! I didn’t know that! Oh my gosh. Wow,” Campbell reacted in real time. He almost immediately jumped into a story about meeting Ditka. Campbell was coming out of college at the NFL Combine, and he had heard that Ditka—then the head coach of the New Orleans Saints—wanted to meet with him. I’ll let him fill in the rest. “I know he’ll be in there, but it’s going to be a little bit—no, no, no. I go in and there’s one little light on. It’s like a little lamp in the corner. It’s at the train station and there’s nothing in there. There’s no couches. The room is totally cleaned out and there’s one little table and the room is full of smoke. I mean, you can’t hardly even see him. You just see this image off in the corner of this little lamp and smoke everywhere and he’s got that big fat cigar. It was one of the best times of my life and most intimidating times of my life sitting across from Mike Ditka. It was awesome though. Just him asking questions about where you grew up, how you think, how you’re wired, the game, what you see. It was awesome. And so, thoughts and prayers go out to his family. He’s a legend.” What Campbell needs to see from the defense Campbell received a very good question, asking what he needs to see from the defense against the Cardinals to feel good about the direction that unit is going before the bye week. His answer consisted of three things. Turnovers: “I think I’m always going to ask for multiple takeaways. We’ve got to have multiple takeaways and certainly we need to see punch outs on the tape. Numerous punch outs, not just one or two. We need to come out of there and say, ‘Man, we saw six, seven, eight of these punch outs.’ You’re trying to get them out.” Quarterback pressure: “I want to see disruption on the quarterback. (We’ve) been pretty good. Got to continue that.” Elimination of mental mistakes: “I want to eliminate the MAs [missed assignments] and dumb penalties. Let’s cut those in half. The MEs, missed execution, or MAs, and the penalties that are just neutral zone infractions or jumping offsides or it dealt with technique. ‘I got myself in a bind because I didn’t use my help.’ Those are inexcusable.” Stopping Cardinals’ outside zone runs I pointed it out in my Cardinals/Giants recap post . Erik Schlitt listed it in his keys to the game . But a potential area of weakness for the Lions this week is against Arizona’s outside zone running scheme, which has been very successful outside the tackles. Meanwhile, that’s exactly where the Lions have struggled in defending the run. I asked Campbell how they plan to attack that potential mismatch this week, and he focused his answer on being disciplined in their run fits, despite the eye candy Arizona will throw at them. “It really is all about fitting your gap. And let’s say you have a post safety, and the other nine guys fit it right and we have one guy that is not where he’s supposed to be. It destroys your run defense. It absolutely destroys it. So, they’re going to give you eye candy. They’re going to do movement. They’re trying to make you to move just a little bit to where you get off. We do the same thing on offense ourselves. You’re just trying to get dirty eyes and somebody not to fit it right, and that’s all it takes. Cardinals first-round pick Jeremiyah Love has been dealing with an ankle injury, and Arizona has limited his playing time while he continues to try and get 100%. Campbell fully expects Love to play this week, has noticed him getting better every week, and knows they have their hands full on Sunday. “He’s an explosive dynamic runner. He’s got vision, explosiveness, speed, and he’s really good out of the backfield,” Campbell said. “And they’ve just scratched the surface of that. That hadn’t even opened it up yet. That’s coming.” Love’s workload continues to fluctuate, but is mostly trending up, as he splits time with veteran Tyler Allgeier. Week 1: 11 carries, 41 yards, TD; 2 catches, 9 yards Week 2: 9 carries, 29 yards; 3 catches, 16 yards Week 3 : 21 carries, 90 yards; 5 catches, 19 yards Week 4: 14 carries, 63 yards; 1 catch, -8 yards

title: Lions vs. Cardinals preview: 3 key matchups
summary: The Detroit Lions will have an opportunity to be great when they hit the road to take on the Arizona Cardinals in Week 5. Why do I phrase it like that? An opportunity to be great. Because that is what we all expect now from this organization. It’s no longer a hope. It’s the floor. […]
full_text: Detroit Lions wide receiver Jameson Williams (1) celebrates a first down against Carolina Panthersm during the first half at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte on Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions will have an opportunity to be great when they hit the road to take on the Arizona Cardinals in Week 5. Why do I phrase it like that? An opportunity to be great . Because that is what we all expect now from this organization. It’s no longer a hope. It’s the floor. “Man, if you want be great. They should want to score 35 points a game at a minimum,” said Dan Campbell when discussing his offense . “That’s what greatness is. That’s what they’re charged with. We’ve got plenty of weapons on offense, and if we’re going to accept mediocrity, then no. Then yeah, we can make all of the excuses in the world. But if we want to spit and sputter and be average, that’s one thing. We’re not going to be average. We’re going to raise the floor on these guys. Man, we’re going to push them.” That is what this game at Arizona is about. While the focus has been on what Kelvin Sheppard said at his press conference and who deserves the blame for the defensive miscues, the truth is that the ceiling for this team rests with the offense. I don’t need to lay the foundation to prove it. If you’re reading this, you’re acutely aware of the Lions’ offensive success in the Dan Campbell era. The 2026 version of that offense has been very good through four weeks, boasting the fourth-highest scoring offense at 29.8 points per game. Yet, the it still feels like the offense has not come close to putting together a game that exemplifies its potential. The matchup keys I have picked out are the critical elements that are necessary to go from being average to being great. Discipline vs. self-inflicted mistakes Above all else, if the offense is going to live up to the standard of greatness, it needs to eliminate the elementary self-inflicted mistakes. A clear indicator of this so far has been the uncharacteristically high rate of presnap penalties through the first four weeks. In 2026, the Lions are outside the top 20 in both pre-snap penalties per game (3.25) and pre-snap penalties per play (1.929) . This is entirely an unacceptable rate and dramatically different that what a Dan Campbell-led program is known for. In 2025, the pre-snap penalty rate was top 12 at 2.42 per game, 1.454 per play, and top-five in both 2024 at 1.56 per game, 1.003 per play and in 2023 at 1.6 per game, 1.026 per play. Correcting these simple mental errors will go a long way in taking this offense to the next level fulfilling the potential that they clearly have evidenced by all of the talent on that side of the ball. This is a great opportunity to return to greatness. Jameson Williams vs. Wydett Williams Jr. Our own Erik Schlitt tagged Jameson Williams as being the catalyst for the offense’s success in his weekly Honolulu Blueprint . Erik discusses all of the key attributes and growth of the Lions star receiver as reasons for this success. (Seriously, go check it out). I’m going to take it another layer deeper. The Cardinals are likely going to be without their starting free safety Andrew Wingard (more on him later), and will be starting undrafted free agent Wydett Williams Jr. Still no S Andrew Wingard (knee) or Edge Jordan Burch (personal) at Cardinals practice today. Looks like the Cards could be relying on Wydett Williams at safety again after a difficult performance last week. pic.twitter.com/ye8uQKNKPa — Theo Mackie (@theo_mackie) October 8, 2026 The young safety played 64 snaps against the New York Giants in Week 4 after Wingard hurt his knee on first series. For quick a quick background, Williams Jr. was a small school riser starting at Delta State, then to Louisiana-Monroe, and finally to Ole Miss to cap his collegiate career. As an undrafted free agent, Williams Jr. overcame the odds as safety 33 on Dane Brugler’s big board , leaving him without a profile in The Beast . Per FTN Fantasy , with Williams Jr. in the game, the Cardinals ran zone at a 70.6% rate in Week 4, and utilizing him as a single-high safety on 67.6% of dropbacks, which is up from the season rate of 42.7%. Lions wide receiver Jameson Williams is a major deep ball threat due to his speed and has a massive opportunity to blow the game open. It’s a great opportunity to be great. Brad Holmes vs. Monti Ossenfort Following Dan Campbell admitting the team had significant interest in trading for cornerback Joey Porter Jr. as a rental option to bolster the secondary, the focus turns to Brad Holmes and what he may be looking at next. With the Arizona Cardinals starting teh season with a 1-3 record and a new regime looking to rebuild the organization, they are a likely candidate to be sellers at the trade deadline. In our trade candidate outlook article last week , Morgan Cannon and I highlighted two Arizona defensive backs that could be good fits for the Lions and are on expiring contracts. The first option is free safety, Andrew Wingard, who recently suffered a bone bruise in his knee and will be most likely be ruled out against the Lions. Dan Campbell has said he wants his defense to focus on turnovers. Wingard had a good showing in his first game as a Cardinal in Week 1. Andrew Wingard has an INT and a forced fumble in his first game as an Arizona Cardinal. pic.twitter.com/AY1Z8FQvAn — Alex Taylor (@alex_m_taylor22) September 13, 2026 Second is cornerback Garrett Williams, who recently returned in Week 3 from a 2025 season-ending Achilles injury. Slowly, Williams has had an increase in his snap counts from 19 in Week 3 to 33 in Week 4. Williams has experience playing in both the nickel role as well as outside. Versatility is one of his calling cards as a former third-round pick in the 2023 NFL Draft. Garrett Williams (#21) has turned into a standout player for the Cardinals. Love his versatility. https://t.co/mr8Efx0fuH pic.twitter.com/PA0gqG3FuM — Nate Tice (@Nate_Tice) May 22, 2025 Brad Holmes will have an opportunity to sit down with the Cardinals general manager Monti Ossenfort to lay down any foundational discussions for either Williams or Wingard before the November trade deadline. If mediocrity is not acceptable, then this is a great opportunity for Holmes to make this roster great. Bonus matchup Brian Branch vs. (Director of Player Health) Brett Fisher, (Head Trainer) Mike Sundeen, and the medical staff is the final key matchup of the game and whether Branch will get the green light to play in any capacity to knock off some of the rust. We know if it was up to Branch and Sheppard, the defense would be getting its star safety back on the field as soon as possible . “If we were playing tonight, it would be realistic. Like, this dude—it’s like he hadn’t been out. I’m serious. It literally looks like he hasn’t been out. It’s unbelievable. So, it’s just a matter of I’m going to lean on (Director of Player Health) Brett Fisher, (Head Trainer) Mike Sundeen, and our medical staff here. They’ve always done a tremendous job, and whatever they tell me. If that’s 20 plays, if that’s 30, if it’s 50—I want it to be 60—but whatever they tell me, I’m going to lock that, and we’re going to roll.” I have been vocal at just how big of an issue I believe the safety room has been for the Lions given the attrition experienced over the first month. Getting Branch back is extraordinarily important for taking stress off of the other position groups, which I expect to have a positive ripple effect in this unit’s performance moving forward. These are the matchups. These are the opportunities to be great.
author: Anthony Balaj

title: NFL predictions: 4 keys to a Lions victory over the Cardinals in Week 5
summary: The Detroit Lions (2-2) and Arizona Cardinals (1-3) will square off in Week 4, with both teams looking to get back on the winning track. “New week, new opponent, Arizona,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said earlier this week. “These guys are playing hard. (Cardinals Head) Coach (Mike) LaFleur’s doing a really good job with them, […]
full_text: Sep 22, 2024; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) passes in the first half against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Matt Kartozian-Imagn Images | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con The Detroit Lions (2-2) and Arizona Cardinals (1-3) will square off in Week 4, with both teams looking to get back on the winning track. “New week, new opponent, Arizona,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said earlier this week. “These guys are playing hard. (Cardinals Head) Coach (Mike) LaFleur’s doing a really good job with them, man. They’ve been in all these games. […] So look, we’re going to get this team’s best. They’re going to be ready to go. They’re looking for a win, and so are we.” Let’s take a closer look at this matchup and predict how the Lions will earn a victory over the Cardinals in this week’s Honolulu Blueprint. This week’s predictions preview is sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook , who currently have the Lions listed at +2700 to win this year’s Super Bowl and 5.5-point favorites in Week 4 . Cardinals base schemes For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 5 preview: Breaking down the Cardinals’ offensive and defensive schemes . Prediction 1: Jameson Williams catalyst to offensive success When wide receivers coach Scottie Montgomery discussed Jameson Williams’ performance through the first four games of the season, he was openly honest about the receiver’s missed opportunities. Many will view his comments as overly harsh or too critical, but this coaching staff doesn’t pull their punches and players often respond positively to that. “Every target he had in that game should have been a catch,” Montgomery said. “If it hits you in the foot, fingertips, you jump up, and it hits you, you gotta catch it. He understands that part of it. But that is exactly what I’m talking about: You can’t be boom or bust in this league.” Williams, who has been credited with five drops through four games, acknowledged Montgomery’s criticism and agreed that he can be better with his consistency, telling Will Burchfield of 97.1 The Ticket that “if I would grade it myself, it’s probably one of my worst starts to my career.” While Williams failed to catch at least 50 receiving yards in each of the first three games, he hauled in six of his eight targets for 102 yards against the Panthers’ zone-shell defense last week. A bounce-back performance that offensive coordinator Drew Petzing believes could lead to more production. “The first thing I’m going to evaluate is effort, assignment, energy, and intensity. And I think he’s doing a really nice job,” Petzing said of Williams. “He’s bounced back and made some really big plays for us. […] I’m pleased with where he is at, and I’m always going to say, ‘Hey, can you give us more? Can you make more plays? Can you have a bigger role?’ And I think he wants that.” In the past, a zone-shell defense like the Cardinals run would have presented problems for Williams’ vertical style of play, but as he showed last week in Carolina, Williams can do more than stretch the defense. The Cardinals’ Vic Fangio-style secondary (two-high split-safety shells with heavy Cover-3, -4 and -6 looks) can be difficult to throw against. But it’s also a difficult system to run, and if the players don’t execute their assignments correctly, it can get exposed and break down. Williams is exactly the type of player who exposes those flaws in this zone. Look for the Lions to lean on Williams early in this game, giving him an opportunity to stretch the safeties in the zone, make contested plays downfield, and respond to his critics. If he can come through—which players often do when challenged in this manner—he will force the Cardinals’ safeties to expand their coverage zones and open things up underneath for players like Amon-Ra St. Brown, Sam LaPorta, and Jahmyr Gibbs. Prediction 2: Jared Goff picks apart the Cardinals’ zone defense Last week against the Panthers, Jared Goff threw for 412 yards and a score, including a 49-yard catch to Williams and a 57-yarder to Isaac TeSlaa. The Cardinals’ zones are even looser. Against the pass this season, the Cardinals are having a worse statistical season than the Lions’ secondary—and we all know how Detroit fans feel about their performance. Here’s a glance at some statistics to support this statement: Pass defense DVOA: 31st Pass yards allowed per play: 9.1 (32nd) EPA per pass play: 0.29 (30th) Explosive pass allowed: 32nd Pressures forced: 37 (32nd) — for reference, the Lions have 75 (2nd) With the Cardinals’ run defense looking solid (run defense DVOA: 10th), look for the Lions to keep the ball in Goff’s hands, moving away from an even run/pass split, and letting one of the NFL’s top passers (third in passing yards, fifth in passer rating, third in EPA vs. zone, second in PFF passing grade) go to work. Prediction 3: Lions DBs step up to stop the run early Despite having two talented running backs on the roster—third overall pick Jeremiyah Love and Tyler Allgeier—the Cardinals’ rushing output has been average: Rushing DVOA: 13th Rush yards per game: 100.5 (21st) Rush yards per play: 3.9 (21st) EPA per rush: -0.05 (14th) Some of that lack of rushing production is because the Cardinals have trailed in most games and needed to rely on the passing attack, but the true catalyst has been their inability to produce explosive plays on offense. With the Cardinals not pushing the ball downfield, defenses have brought defenders closer to the line of scrimmage, resulting in the fewest explosive plays in the NFL and 29th in runs that gain 10+ yards, with just six on the season. While the Cardinals’ rushing attack isn’t scary on paper, their game film raises some concerns. Arizona is at their best when deploying their outside-zone rushing attack, and because they have the talent to get to the edge, the Lions will need their defensive backs and linebackers to be heavily involved in stopping those stretch plays—an area they’ve struggled with lately. For the Lions to take away the Cardinals’ rushing attack, they’ll need their entire defense—especially the defensive backs on the edge—focused on stopping the run early in this game, and if the Lions’ offense can also put up points, they’ll force Arizona into a situation where they’ll need to throw to keep up. Prediction 4: Lions pass rush wins the game The Lions’ biggest advanatge in this game is arguably Detroit’s pass rush vs.Arizona’s pass protection. If the Lions’ struggling defense can hang their hats on one part of their defense to build around, it should be their pass rush. Through four games, they’re near the top of the NFL in pass rushing production: Pressures forced: 75 (2nd) Pressure rate: 39.3% (8th) Quick pressure rate: 39.3% (1st) Non-blitz pressure rate: 27% (1st) Time to pressure: 2.6 seconds (12th) Sacks: 15 (1st) Sack rate: 7.9% (6th) “We have to feed off of them. And I told those guys, ‘I’m going to lean on y’all.’ Because of the evidence that’s been proven,” Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard said. “These guys are playing at an elite level. […] When you have guys playing like that up front, we should be benefiting, feasting off of things like that.” While the Cardinals offensive line has done a decent job of keeping Jacoby Brissett upright (allowing 53 pressures, 16th in the NFL, and just seven sacks, 10th best), they’ll have to overcome potentially losing two starters this week. Left tackle Paris Johnson (arguably their best OL) was placed on injured reserve after tearing his biceps last game, while right guard Isaiah Adams hasn’t practiced all week after injuring his ankle and is in danger of missing this game. While Brissett has avoided sacks, he hasn’t performed well under pressure. Through four games this season, according to SumerSports, Brissett’s EPA when pressured ranks 29th in the NFL among qualified quarterbacks, and 40th when teams blitz…

title: Detroit Lions vs. Arizona Cardinals preview, prediction: On Paper
summary: The Detroit Lions need a bounce-back win in a big way, and they certainly have an opportunity to do so with the 1-3 Arizona Cardinals on deck. The Cardinals have hung with the 49ers and beat the Chargers in Week 1, but they were dominated by the Seahawks and lost a disappointing game against the […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - SEPTEMBER 22: Aidan Hutchinson #97 of the Detroit Lions looks on against the Arizona Cardinals during the fourth quarter at State Farm Stadium on September 22, 2024 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions need a bounce-back win in a big way, and they certainly have an opportunity to do so with the 1-3 Arizona Cardinals on deck. The Cardinals have hung with the 49ers and beat the Chargers in Week 1, but they were dominated by the Seahawks and lost a disappointing game against the Giants. Where do the real Arizona Cardinals lie, and what does it mean for this week’s Lions matchup? Let’s find out in our Lions vs. Cardinals preview, prediction, and statistical breakdown. It’s On Paper time. Lions pass offense (9th in DVOA) vs. Cardinals pass defense (31st) It hasn’t been as consistent as the Lions want, but Detroit’s passing offense remains a clear top-10 unit, bordering on a top-five unit. Some of their key efficiency metrics: Sixth in passer rating (108.6) 10th in yards per attempt (7.5) Fourth in dropback EPA (0.274) Fifth in dropback success rate (52.2%) Jared Goff is off to a phenomenal start, and he’s helped by a pretty decent pass-blocking unit. Detroit ranks fifth in ESPN’s pass block win rate (57%), seventh in PFF pass blocking grade (69.0), and they have the 10th-lowest pressure rate allowed (32.8%). The only thing that really seems to be holding this unit back is the amount of explosive plays and drops. They have just four passes of 30+ yards through four games, which ranks t-15th in the NFL. Pro-Football-Reference has the Lions with seven drops so far, which ranks t-sixth most. You may think the Lions have the worst pass defense in the league, but the Cardinals have a pretty good case for it. They rank: 31st in passer rating allowed (114.9) 32nd in yards per attempt (9.1) 31st in dropback EPA (0.346) 25th in dropback success rate (49.6%) If you’re a common reader of On Paper, you know that if success rate looks better than every other stat, it’s usually explosive plays that are to blame, and that’s exactly the case here. The Cardinals have given up 14 plays of 20+ yards through the air, tied for ninth most. But with a 25th-ranked success rate, the problems obviously run deeper than that. One major issue is pass rush. They sport a 30.3% pressure rate (29th), yet they opt not to blitz very often (23.8% rate, 23rd). Last week against the Giants, the Cardinals opted to up the blitz rate (30.3%, 12th) and it resulted in a better pressure rate (48.5%, seventh) and four sacks—so don’t be surprised if they choose to send extra pressure at Goff. They also seem to have issues in coverage. They have the fifth-worst team PFF coverage grade (48.2), and the worst offenders appear to be the linebacking corps. Mack Wilson Sr. (49.8) and Jack Gibbens (43.7) have some of the worst coverage grades on the team, meaning the middle of the field could be open for Detroit. Player to watch: Sam LaPorta. Last week, when the Lions had to largely abandon the run game and get consistent yardage over the middle, no one was more reliable than LaPorta. He is now second on the Lions in targets (32) after tallying 13 last week. Advantage: Lions +3.5. This seems like an absolute monster advantage for Detroit, and it’s hard to imagine things going south for this unit. Detroit has weapons to attack every part of the field, and Goff with time is dangerous. When he’s not pressured, Goff has completed 72.2% of his passes, thrown for 7.9 yards per attempt, eight touchdowns and zero interceptions. Arizona’s best shot is to send blitzes, where the Lions have been inconsistent. But Goff still has a 119.1 passer rating (sixth) and +0.28 EPA/dropback (fifth) when blitzed. Lions run offense (4th) vs. Cardinals run defense (10th) The Lions’ run offense is in a weird place where the stats don’t seem to be passing the eye test. The perception is Detroit’s running game has been extremely inconsistent and not there when it needs to be. The advanced statistics, though, still point to this as a top-10 rushing attack, maybe even better. Detroit ranks: 16th in yards per carry (4.2) 17th in EPA (-0.093) Seventh in success rate (44.9%) High success rate, low EPA and YPC means one thing: no explosives. While the Lions do rank tied for ninth in 10+ yard rushes through four games, they only have a single run of 20+ yards (t-23rd). That lack of explosiveness can make your rush totals look pretty low with the sample size so small this year. Some other positive signs: Detroit ranks sixth in adjusted line yards (4.62), fifth in yard before contact per attempt (1.9), 10th in success rate in power situations (75%), and have PFF third-highest run blocking grade. Some bad signs: They have the seventh-highest stuffed rate (19.4%), rank 27th in yards after contact per attempt (2.36), and rank 22nd in run block win rate. So… I don’t know. To me, it still seems like they are on the precipice of breaking out a long run, which will go a long way in upping the YPA, EPA, and yards after contact numbers. But the high percentage of negative plays is legitimately concerning. They’ve also clearly been much worse on the road, which could very well be an offensive line communication issue—although I’m not so sure how loud Arizona is going to be on Sunday. The Cardinals have been similarly inconsistent the run game. Two bad performances against decent rushing attacks, and two decent games against mediocre-to-bad run offense. Overall, they rank: 17th in yards per carry (17th) Third in rush EPA (-0.241) 11th in success rate (38.0%) Without a doubt, the strength of the Cardinals’ defense is how their front four defends the run. Former Lion Roy Lopez is having another fantastic season, sporting PFF’s seventh-highest run defense grade (76.3) among defensive tackles, and EDGE Zaven Collins has the third-best run defense grade (90.6) among defensive ends. The Cardinals do a pretty good job limiting explosive plays (only two 20+ yard rushes allowed) and their stuffed rate (17.0%) is average (14th). They find their success by stacking the box. Their 27.7% stacked rate is eighth highest in the league. What’s also ballooning their EPA is their success in short-yardage situation. They are allowing just a 29% success rate in power scenarios, which is first by a significant amount. The league average is around 65%. Player to watch: Collins vs. Sewell. If you’re into run blocking vs. setting the edge matchups, you literally don’t get better than this. Collins splits his time between both sides, but when he’s opposite Sewell, it’s going to be awesome to watch the two go at it in the run game. Advantage: Draw. I’m fascinated to see how this plays out. It’s a strength vs. strength matchup, even if both teams have been a bit inconsistent week-to-week. If I were the Lions, I’d lean more into the passing game this week, but I know they also want to have more consistency in the run game, and it may make sense to control the ball for longer to keep the defense off the field. Cardinals pass offense (17th) vs. Lions pass defense (28th) The pressure is mounting on Jacoby Brissett after a rough outing against the Giants last week, but the Lions could be the bounceback game he needs. For the season, the Cardinals’ pass offense ranks: 21st in passer rating (83.2) 32nd in yards per attempt (5.4) 22nd in dropback EPA (0.010) 17th in success rate (46.8%) The main complaint about the Cardinals’ passing attack is the toothlessness of it. Brissett is a checkdown machine, averaging just 6.2 air yards per pass (29th). Brissett’s 5.9 deep ball percentage ranks 26 out of 29 qualifying quarterbacks. Brissett has also been extremely ineffective when pressure , as I outlined earlier in the week: -0.32 EPA/dropback vs. blitz (25th out of 29) -0.67 EPA/dropback vs. pressure (25th) Pass protection hasn’t been a huge issues for the Cardinals so far this year, but it could be this week. title: What is the ceiling for the Lions’ OL when Cade Mays returns to the field?
summary: When the Detroit Lions hired Dan Campbell as their head coach and Brad Holmes as the general manager back in 2021, one thing was very clear from the beginning—they wanted to establish an identity with their offensive line. They immediately backed up those words when they made All-Pro tackle Penei Sewell the seventh overall pick […]
full_text: When the Detroit Lions hired Dan Campbell as their head coach and Brad Holmes as the general manager back in 2021, one thing was very clear from the beginning—they wanted to establish an identity with their offensive line. They immediately backed up those words when they made All-Pro tackle Penei Sewell the seventh overall pick in the 2021 NFL Draft. Football is both complicated and simple. If you want to win, you have to be able to control the line of scrimmage. After a down year in 2025 where the offensive line was one of the factors that led to a disappointing 9-8 finish, it was time for a change of the guard. Left tackle Taylor Decker was released by the team along with interior offensive lineman Graham Glasgow. On top of those moves, All-Pro center Frank Ragnow had tried and failed to make a comeback out of retirement. It was time for the organization to lean into the youth, and that is exactly what they did. Now, after spending the first few years as the young guy in the room, Sewell is the most tenured player along the offensive line as well as one of the oldest at nearly 26 years of age. To his right is third-year left guard Christian Mahogany, center Juice Scruggs, second-year right guard Tate Ratledge, and rookie right tackle Blake Miller. And while Scruggs has played well, newly-signed center Cade Mays recovers from a broken wrist suffered in training camp, it’s hard not to wonder what this unit may look like around Week 10 of the 2026 season. That brings us to today’s question of the day. What is the ceiling for the Lions’ offensive line once Mays returns to action? My answer: I think this unit could quickly become a top-five unit in all of football with time on task. Sewell will only get better as he settles back in on the left side; Mahogany has had good moments and bad, but I like the power aspect he brings to the table next to Sewell. On top of that, Scruggs may get the chance to push for that job once Mays returns to center. Ratledge is playing like one of the better guards in the league, and Miller has been steadily improving save for a few mental mistakes here and there. As the season marches on, it’s important to remember that this is a bit of a transitional year for the offensive line. With that said, it’s also an exciting time. If they can continue to grow in their roles and begin to gel as a unit, the Lions’ offense could really begin to hit their stride. What about you? What do you think the ceiling is for the offensive line in 2026? Let us know in the comments below.

title: Packers Injury Report: 7 given statuses vs. Bears
summary: The Green Bay Packers are officially going to be out running back Chris Brooks (and receiver Savion Williams) against the Chicago Bears on Sunday, according to the Packers’ final injury report of the week. Brooks left Week 4 action with an ankle injury and was a non-participant for all three practices this week. The team […]
full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers are officially going to be out running back Chris Brooks (and receiver Savion Williams) against the Chicago Bears on Sunday, according to the Packers’ final injury report of the week. Brooks left Week 4 action with an ankle injury and was a non-participant for all three practices this week. The team already moved up running back Pierre Strong Jr. from the practice squad to the active roster, so it’s almost certain that Green Bay will roll into their divisional matchup with MarShawn Lloyd, Kaleb Johnson and Strong as their three-man backfield. Two players were also listed as doubtful for the game, meaning there’s a good chance they’ll miss Sunday’s action: left guard Aaron Banks (knee/toe) and offensive lineman Jacob Monk (quadricep). Both Banks and Monk were non-participants on Wednesday and Thursday, but were limited participants for Friday’s practice. Thankfully, the Packers have 11 offensive linemen on the 53-man roster, so they can afford to scratch three players at the position and would still have an eight-man unit going into games. Players listed as questionable, true toss-ups, are offensive lineman Jager Burton (back), defensive lineman Anthony Campbell (ankle) and defensive lineman Javon Hargrave (toe). Burton and Campbell were limited participants in practice for most of the week (Burton was only a non-participant on Wednesday), while Hargrave was a full participant until Friday, when he popped up on the injury report and was listed as a limited participant. Like the offensive line, the defensive line is “oversigned,” as the team has seven at the position on the 53-man roster, while the team generally keeps five players up on the 48-man game-day roster. Because Strong and Kristian Welch (backfilling for Edgerrin Cooper at the linebacker position) have already been brought up from the practice squad, don’t expect there to be moves made by the team before kickoff. On the Bears’ end of the injury report, the most notable piece of news was that quarterback Caleb Williams went from a non-participant (hamstring) on Thursday to a limited participant on Friday and was given a questionable status going into Week 5. Rule out are linebacker Keyshaun Eliott (quadricep) and running back Kyle Monangai (thumb/toe). Beyond Williams, three other Chicago players are questionable: cornerback Kyler Gordon (calf), linebacker Noah Sewell (Achilles) and defensive lineman Shemar Turner (knee) — all of whom are on the Bears’ injury lists but have had their practice windows opened up. #Packers RB Chris Brooks (ankle) OUT. They signed RB Pierre Strong Jr. from PS last night. Veteran DL Javon Hargrave now questionable with a toe injury. #Bears RB Kyle Monangai, who rushed for 146 yards and two touchdowns vs. the #Jets is OUT with a toe & thumb injury: pic.twitter.com/meH4TJ4h7f — Mike Clemens (@MikeClemensNFL) October 9, 2026
