title: The “firsts” of Packers’ top performances against the Bears
summary: Normally I write about the best performances against a particular team in the lead-up to that week’s game. But against an opponent as old as the Bears, I think we should dig a little deeper. The Packers have been playing against the Bears for virtually their entire history and have had great performances throughout that […]
full_text: American football player Lynn Dickey, a quarterback for the Green Bay Packers, posing at Lambeau Field Stadium in Green Bay, Wisconsin, August 11th 1981. (Photo by UPI/Bettmann Archive/Getty Images) | Getty Images Normally I write about the best performances against a particular team in the lead-up to that week’s game. But against an opponent as old as the Bears, I think we should dig a little deeper. The Packers have been playing against the Bears for virtually their entire history and have had great performances throughout that history. But who were the first players to hit some noteworthy high-water marks against Chicago? I’m glad you asked. Here are the earliest -recorded big performances by a few of the Packers’ greatest players over the years. First 300-yard passing game – Lynn Dickey, 1983 Given the relatively late adoption of passing relative to running, ti’s not a surprise to see it took a while for the Packers to hit a big number through the air. But, in a 31-28 win in 1983, Lynn Dickey became the first Packers passer to surpass 300 yards in a game against the Bears. Amusingly, 10 years and one day later, Brett Favre became the first Packers player to break 400 yards passing against the Bears — the only time in his Packers career that he’d pass for 400 or more yards. First 100-yard rushing game – Clark Hinkle, 1936 Given how spotty early stats are, there was almost certainly a 100-yard rushing day against the Bears earlier than this, but Clark Hinkle’s 1936 effort is the earliest example from the Pro Football Reference database. Hinkle, considered by early Packers historians to be the greatest player to ever wear the green and gold, needed just 13 carries to crack 100 yards, thanks in part to a 59-yard rushing touchdown in the second quarter. First 100-yard receiving game – Verne Lewellen, 1926 New research recently published by Pro Football Reference is giving us a look at some of the best statistical performers in early Packers history, and you can’t mention that category of player without bringing up Verne Lewellen. A weapon in all three phases of the game, Lewellen caught six passes for 109 yards in a 1926 draw against the Bears. Even Lewellen’s greatness apparently couldn’t solve the deadlock. First sack – Cliff Lewis and Ezra Johnson, 1983 Sacks weren’t an official stat in the NFL until 1982, and according to Pro Football Reference, the Packers didn’t manage any in their two games against the Bears the first season the stat was official. But they made up for lost time in 1983, recording four sacks between Cliff Lewis and Ezra Johnson (one and three apiece, respectively). Johnson technically gets the honor here, as he nabbed quarterback Jim McMahon on the fourth play of the game to set the tone. Incidentally, this was the same game in which Lynn Dickey passed for 300 yards, as mentioned earlier in this piece. First interception – Don Hutson, 1940 Finally, Don Hutson gets the tentative honor of the first on-record interception against the Bears. Given that the Packers and Bears had been playing for around 20 years by this point, it seems probable that someone probably grabbed a pick before this point, but you never know. Maybe Hutson is just the beneficiary of a weird statistical quirk!
author: Jon Meerdink

title: How the Packers defense overwhelmed Jalon Daniels
summary: Last Sunday, the Green Bay Packers defense bounced back after an abysmal performance in week three by tightening up and overwhelming a lifeless Buccaneers offense. They forced two interceptions on backup quarterback Jalon Daniels, making his first NFL start for the injured Baker Mayfield, and held the Bucs offense to 86 non-scrambling rushing yards.  The […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - OCTOBER 4: Xavier McKinney #29 of the Green Bay Packers sacks Jalon Daniels #10 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the game at Raymond James Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last Sunday, the Green Bay Packers defense bounced back after an abysmal performance in week three by tightening up and overwhelming a lifeless Buccaneers offense. They forced two interceptions on backup quarterback Jalon Daniels, making his first NFL start for the injured Baker Mayfield, and held the Bucs offense to 86 non-scrambling rushing yards. The offense sputtered in this game again, but was able to generate 10 points off the two interceptions in the first half. The cost was steep, though: Edgerrin Cooper suffered what is expected to be a season-ending Achilles tear in the third quarter. On the injury, head coach Matt LaFleur said the outlook was “not good” and that he suspects it is season-ending, though testing still has to confirm the tear. McDuffie replaced Cooper and finished with four tackles. Cooper leaves with 30 tackles, three sacks and an interception on the season. Tampa Bay finished with 275 total yards and 19 first downs. and Green Bay sacked rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels three times, hit him seven times, picked him off twice, defended five passes, forced three three-and-outs and made a fourth-down stop. 17 pressures had an overwhelmingly negative impact on Daniels performance. He looked confused and overwhelmed with different looks Jonathan Gannon was throwing at him from the first series of the game. Cooper set the tone early and Gannon called his first pressure to confuse and throw off the young quarterback. Cooper sacked Daniels for no gain on a third-and-2 on Tampa Bay’s opening possession. The defense aligned in an all-out blitz front with eight on the line of scrimmage. This forces the offensive line to pick a slide to one direction and hope the quarterback can mitigate any free rusher with a hot throw. The snap revealed that the Packers would pop out into a 2-deep zone palms pressure. The two zone droppers off the line of scrimmage drop to underneath shallow zones looking to rob anything from the #2 receivers inside. The outside flat defenders take #2 to the flat or take #1 vertical. Evan Williams is the flat dropper to the defense’s right while Brandon Cisse takes the deep half. The deep safety cuts the crosser and the underneath zones close the throwing windows to the underneath routes. Lukas Van Ness came screaming off the edge as Daniels tried to turn out around the edge. The move by Van Ness turned Daniels back inside where Cooper was waiting at the line of scrimmage. On the Bucs’ second possession, Daniels scrambled to the Green Bay 49, and on the next play Evan Williams undercut Emeka Egbuka on an out route for a sideline interception. That set up Matthew Golden’s leaping 2-yard touchdown catch on fourth-and-goal. The interception happened because Daniels failed to recognize what was happening pre-snap. The defense aligned in a single high shell before the snap with man coverage indicators, most likely cover-1 to Daniels. Williams started to creep up toward the slot receiver (“capping the receiver”) which is a pressure indicator, with Brenton Cox covering the slot initially. This should’ve indicated to Daniels that he was going to get a 5th rusher off the edge and that Williams would be there in coverage on the slot. Cox looped inside and pressure got to Daniels, forcing him to short arm the throw and allowing Williams to undercut it as the pass arrived. Late in the second quarter, with Tampa driving for a go-ahead score, Cooper jumped in front of a pass intended for Kameron Johnson and returned it to the Bucs’ 44. That set up Trey Smack’s 58-yard field goal on the final play of the half for a 10–7 lead. On Tampa’s first possession of the second half, with Green Bay up 17–7, Cooper was coming on a third-and-8 blitz from the Bucs’ 37 when he went down without contact. Cooper finished with nine tackles, a sack and an interception in a little over two quarters of work. On the same play, Xavier McKinney sacked Daniels with 8:31 left in the third quarter. The defense was aligned again in an all out blitz front. This time, they sent seven rushers and left four in coverage. McKinney broke free through the B-gap when no one picked him in protection, forcing Daniels to pull the ball down and take a sack. Late in the fourth quarter, one of the game sealing plays was another 6-yard sack by Evan Williams on another two-deep pressure package call by Gannon. The defense rotates late in the presnap with Javon Bullard backing off to the deep half. The shell converts to 2-deep/4-under with the zone droppers coming off the line of scrimmage. The offense also doesn’t really run anything to challenge the coverage with a mirrored smash concept. Daniels really didn’t have time to read the concept anyways. Williams comes screaming off the edge and records the sack almost immediately, setting up the game sealing 4th down stop a couple of plays later, which we’ll cover in the next breakdown article.
author: Rich Madrid

title: Why Edgerrin Cooper’s absence is a big deal
summary: It’s easy to understand that Green Bay Packers off-ball linebacker Edgerrin Cooper was (and still likely is) a budding star, and an incredibly important player for the Packers. You don’t need any fancy numbers or a scout’s eye to pick him out, he’s the kind of player that just looks different. Even among professional athletes, […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - SEPTEMBER 24: Edgerrin Cooper #56 of the Green Bay Packers runs onto the field prior to the game against the Atlanta Falcons at Lambeau Field on September 24, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s easy to understand that Green Bay Packers off-ball linebacker Edgerrin Cooper was (and still likely is) a budding star, and an incredibly important player for the Packers. You don’t need any fancy numbers or a scout’s eye to pick him out, he’s the kind of player that just looks different. Even among professional athletes, he’s faster, lighter on his feet, and changes direction in a way that seems to defy physics. Cooper also plays a position that is often looked down on by analysts as the least “valuable” part of the defense. Like running backs on offense, most teams (not the Packers, mind you) are able to field at least competent running backs without difficulty. The “off ball” linebacker is not directly in control of pressuring the quarterback or covering receivers, and while they are important, they play a secondary support role. The problem with wedging Edgerrin Cooper into this analysis is that the reason you can generally find a competent linebacker is because that other positions CAN serve to cover many of their responsibilities. (Emphasis on can.) Good safeties can reduce the field they are responsible for in pass coverage. Good defensive linemen can create clear lanes for them in run support. Good edge rushers can occupy multiple blockers, leaving them free to shoot up field and bring people down. And in doing so, they can allow a linebacker to play to his strengths. The well-liked veteran Zaire Franklin is this kind of linebacker, and honestly, he’s a great running mate for Cooper. Franklin is smart, he’s generally in the right position, and he’s a sure tackler, but he’s slow and can be exploited in pass defense. To put it simply, for most teams the play of the non-linebackers can allow that team to get away with lesser linebackers. However, with Cooper, the exact opposite is true. Cooper allowed the Packers to get away with lesser players at other every other position AND allowed the good players and stars at other positions to focus on what they do best. Without him, every edge rusher and corner will have to focus more on tasks that they would prefer not to be bothered with. Zaire Franklin will have to cover more than he (or the Packers) would like. Evan Williams and Xavier McKinney will have to worry just a bit more about the space in front of them. Every time a tight end is split out wide, someone will have to make a decision that they previously did not have to make. Green Bay has had an extremely rough few seasons so far losing lynchpins, going back to Micah Parsons. All teams suffer injuries, but few have endured quite so many “domino effect” losses. The Packers spent the last two weeks valiantly attempting to repair their interior offensive line by signing three veterans, only to have another big leak spring on defense. They did not have a ton of depth in the first place, and Cooper is one of the least replaceable players on the team. The Bears will, at least be starting backup quarterback Tyson Bagent, but even so, the Packers face a tall task on defense going forward.

title: Green Bay Packers News: Running back committee remains unsettled
summary: Good luck trying to predict which of the Green Bay Packers’ running backs is going to lead the way on any given week at this point. The trio of MarShawn Lloyd, Kaleb Johnson, and Chris Brooks have struggled mightily so far this season, and although each of them had some high points in last Sunday’s […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - OCTOBER 4: Running back Kaleb Johnson #26 of the Green Bay Packers running for a first down in the third quarter against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Raymond James Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good luck trying to predict which of the Green Bay Packers’ running backs is going to lead the way on any given week at this point. The trio of MarShawn Lloyd, Kaleb Johnson, and Chris Brooks have struggled mightily so far this season, and although each of them had some high points in last Sunday’s win over the Buccaneers, there are plenty of mistakes going around as well. Lloyd can’t seem to read blocks and has a fumbling problem. Johnson’s fumble issues might be even worse. And now Brooks is injured and probably will miss Sunday’s game against the Chicago Bears. Obviously the Packers’ offensive line issues have limited these players’ ability to impact the game to this point, but the players are simply making too many unforced errors to this point. Unfortunately for the Packers, there aren’t many other options available to them; however, they did exercise one of them by calling up Pierre Strong from the practice squad this week. Will Strong help this group bounce back? Who knows, and we’ll start to find out on Sunday afternoon. But if he can simply read blocks reasonably well and hold on to the football, that might be more than enough to be an upgrade over the players who have been carrying the ball to this point. Kaleb Johnson believes he has fixed his fumbling problem | Packersnews.com ($) He had better fix it quickly if he hopes to get any more of a role in this offense. Apparently he believes a change in shoulder pads was part of the problem. Packers don’t know if RB Chris Brooks (ankle) will play vs. Bears | Packers Wire Brooks’ status being uncertain is surely why the team promoted Pierre Strong, Jr. from the practice squad to the 53-man roster on Thursday. Packers’ defense looks to pick up where Edgerrin Cooper left off | Packers.com It’s also going to be linebacker by committee, with Isaiah McDuffie and Ty’Ron Hopper doing the bulk of the work to fill in for the injured star. Jordan Love Excels In This Phase, So Why Aren’t Packers Leaning Into It? | SI.com Love’s passer rating off play-action is 3rd in the NFL — proof that you don’t need a good run game for play-action to work. Isn’t it time to get more of that going early in games? The Packers will need to find a way to score some points on Sunday, but perhaps they can get some regression to the mean from a Bears defense that has been playing unsustainably well in a few specific areas: Beavers destroy sign warning about beavers | Notes from Poland Good! title: Value of Things: By the numbers
summary: The usual course of these things is to look at what the opponents are doing and look at what the Texans are doing and predict what will happen in this week’s game. We have two 0-4 football teams this week so neither team will be good across the board. What i will be doing this […]
full_text: The usual course of these things is to look at what the opponents are doing and look at what the Texans are doing and predict what will happen in this week’s game. We have two 0-4 football teams this week so neither team will be good across the board. What i will be doing this week is looking at what those in the industry lovingly call :self-scouting.“ Self scouting is the most important scouting because it involves what you are actually doing well and who is actually doing the the good and the bad. This week, we are taking a look at the offense and next week we will take a look at the defense. It is one thing to look at your rankings as a team, but now that we are four weeks in, we can take stock in what opponents actually do and how that pertains to what you do. Obviously, the offense has always been more in the crosshairs even if it is not particularly fair in terms of how the early season has gone so far. As per usual, there are some good things and some bad things. Let’s employ the sandwich and start with some positives. What is going right The number one thing here is obviously the performance of C.J. Stroud. He has a 95.7 quarterback rating. If you were simply to give that number to most fans at the beginning of the season they would naturally assume that we were no worse than 2-2 and likely 3-1 going into the Titans game. We should say this without reservation, very little of this 0-4 streak is Stroud’s fault. If Stroud puts these numbers up over a full season it will likely be one of the best quarterback seasons ever for a Texans quarterback. However, this isn’t to say that all has been sunshine and roses for the Texans quarterback. There are some numbers that are not terrific, but one has to wonder how much of that Stroud and how much of that is what is going on beyond Stroud. When looking at Stroud and the passing game there are a few stats we can look at that help explain success and lack of success. Two of those hidden numbers are the percentage of targets of become catches and the success rate (as measured in first downs and predicted first downs). We will look at all of the primary receivers here and see what you notice. Targers Catches Success% Nico Collins 18 14 61.1 Xacier Hutchinson 26 12 42.3 Jared Wayne 12 4 33.3 Keyshon Boutte 13 9 61.5 Jaylin Noels 12 8 58.3 Dalton Schultz 27 21 63.0 Foster Moreau 9 7 55.6 This does not include the backs out of the backfield which has to be considered. Woody Marks and David Montgomery have combined for 14 catches on 16 targets. Their success rate combines for over 50 percent. A number of teams have succeeded historically on a short passing game, but those quarterbacks usually hover around a 70 percent completion percentage where Stroud sits at 61,5. Even if we ignore Stroud for a moment, we can see there are two targets that are dragging down the whole thing. Xavier Hutchinson and Jared Warune have combined for 38 targets and 16 receptions. If you take those out then Stroud is close to that 70 percent. This is where advanced analytics come into play. Hutchinson is on pace to have 50+ catches on the season. At first blish this looks good for a third or fourth wide receiver. The problem is the efficiency is very low. Noel and Boutte are a lot more efficient when looking at the numbers, so the obvious takeaway is that they should be a much more featured part of the offense than Hutchinson and Wayne. All that being said, obviously increased exposure is not a guarantee for success. So, it would appear that having them play more is not the only answer. The other answer comes in a relying on players like Schultz and Moreau in combination with more opportunities for Montgomery and Marks to elevate the short passing attack. That would definitely get Stroud closer to that 70 percent completion percentage and would maximize the passing game in lieu of a failed running attack. Focus on the running game The early going is definitely eye opening when you look at the Texans first four opponents independent of the Texans game. Of the first four opponents, three of them are among the worst rushing defenses in the league. The Cowboys sit as the worst by virtue of the fact that they are one of two teams to play five games. However, the Bills and the Colts are also among the bottom ten teams against the run. Remove the Texans from their schedule and they obviously look worse on a per game basis. Attempts Yards YPA David Montgomery 47 127 2.7 Woody Marks 28 87 3.1 Jet Sweeps 6 36 6.0 Not included in these numbers are the 66 yards that Stroud has gained on nine carries. Obviously, Stroud is not a traditional running threat like some other quarterbacks in the league. I would never advocate for including that as an established part of the offense. However, this gets us to what the Texans have been doing versus what has actually worked. Montgomery has gotten more than half of the team’s carries and he is the least effective. Is that his fault? The Texans are DAL (dead ass last) in the percentage of times a runner is hit at or before the line of scrimmage. Montgomery has taken the bulk of that. They sit at 60 percent and that is six percentage points worse than 31st place. It should be obvious that most if not all of those are happening on traditional running plays. A portion of self-scouting occurs when we admit to what is happening. We could say it is the offensive line’s fault or the running back’s fault, but neither explanation changes what is actually happening. So, what is actually happenng is that the team is less successful on David Montgomery running plays than anything else they are doing. Again, this is not a slight on Montgomery. What it does show is that they are slightly more effective with Marks running the ball and more effective on jet sweeps. I’m not for giving a wide receiver ten carries a game, but some running offenses (most notably the 49ers with Deebo Samuel) have used that tactic to maximum effect. The likely solution here for the short-term is inverting the way you use Marks and Montgomery. Marks should be getting the 10-15 carries where Montgomery should be getting the 5-10. The Texans might also employ more jet sweeps (maybe five a game) to keep the defense on their toes. That would probably maximize the running game to the point where it becomes a plausible threat. Putting it all together The Texans move the ball more through the air than on the ground. That statement alone is not stepping out on a limb. The likely fan response is “well duh.” It seems that leaning into that would be the most elegant solution. It means having more Boutte and Noel on the field than Hutchinson and Wayne. It also would mean utilizing more two tight end formations where Moreau and Schultz can get involved in the passing game. Doing all of that (while also including Marks and Montgomery in the passing game) would get you closer to a 70 percent completion rate and therefore running more efficiently than what is currently happening. This of course brings us to Nick Caley and whether he is capable of recognizing what is actually happening and responding to it intelligently. Smart play callers respond to what is actually happening and not to what they hope will happen. We would all love an offense where the backs get 20-30 carries a game and grind it out on the ground. That is not who the Texans are right now and it will be better in the short term if we simply admit that and react accordingly.

title: Five Good Texans Questions with Possum Holler’ Tribune
summary: We come to that time of year where it is rivalry week in the NFL. Unfortunately, we were not able to catch up with Music City Miracles, but we were able to catch up with one of their local competitors as we reached base with Wedge Fickus of the Possum Holler Tribune. They aren’t quite […]
full_text: We come to that time of year where it is rivalry week in the NFL. Unfortunately, we were not able to catch up with Music City Miracles , but we were able to catch up with one of their local competitors as we reached base with Wedge Fickus of the Possum Holler Tribune. They aren’t quite on the internet yet, but they are making inroads and could possibly launch by the end of the decade. Fickus is the winner of the prestigious Golden Marisupial Award for Journalistic Excellence. We caught him on a good day to ask him five questions about the state of the Titans. Battle Red Blog: How do you feel about Robert Saleh as a head coach so far? Wedge Fickus: That guy can sure coach em’, but he ain’t got the Jimmy and Joes. He’s got himself a good chucker there, but there ain’t no good runners or boys to catch them chucks from the chucker. We keep getting these guys that can coach em’, but we can never find the guys that can actually do something. Give Saleh a nice five seasons and I’m quite sure they will get up to five wins in that amount of time. BRB: You mentioned Cam Ward. Do you think he is one of the elite quarterbacks in the NFL? WF: Dammit boy, stop with your high falutin’ terminology for them players. He’s a chucker. I’m sure you and your fancy numbers will say no, but Ward can chuck that football and he can run it too. I think you fancy city slickers call that a dual threat quarterback. I’ve heard tale he can dance a mean lick and can even belt out a tune, so he’s a quadruple threat in my book. The problem is that there ain’t no one to catch his chucks and we are always playing from behind because we are the Titans. BRB: Are there any new faces we should be concerned about in this matchup? WF: What is this a Nicolas Cage motif man? Ain’t nobody changing faces here in Possum Holler. We go with the face the good lord gave us. Carnell Tate is a good chuck catcher that has already caught 22 balls for over 300 yards in the early going. My fancy countin’ skills tell me that could end up being over 500 yards by Christmas. That would make him the best chuck catcher in Titans history damn near. The rest of the picks were on the interior or defensive side of the pigskin, so we don’t pay much attention to dem boys. We just need more chuck catchers. BRB: Who do Titans fans enjoy beating the most in the division and who do you think wins the AFC South? WF: You boys in bayou country absolutely piss us off with your incessant need to wear the Columbia Blue we earned fair and square. Sure, we didn’t keep the name and sure we don’t really celebrate the history, but those damn colors represent excellence and achievement that you boys will never understand. Think of all the great teams in Titans history. Just think of them dammit. You boys want to keep those damn colors because you had them for 37 years. Even your weak local school kids at UH use those colors. We enjoy beating your ass every chance we get. I don’t care what your fancy records say, we own you down here in Possum Holler. As for dem division, I’d glow with the Glitter Kitties in Jacktown. That chucker they got there has some beautiful hair I’ll tell you what. and that is a team with some chuck catchers and even one that plays a little defense on the side. Who doesn’t love that? BRB: Fanduel has the Texans favored by 7.5 points even though both teams are winless going in. How do you see the game going and are there any prop bets you feel comfortable recommending? WF: Prop bets? We don’t do any of that Hollywood stuff out here. I think you can bet there are some balls on that sideline and maybe a fan to keep players cool. Those are some props you can bet on. As for the game, I am going all in on my boys. The Columbia blue represents an excellence you Houston boys will never understand. I don’t care how many times you have beaten us in the last three years. Ward is going to chuck that ball and he’ll probably run it too and we will take the game 35-31 in a thrilling back and forth battle. The Houston boys will cry all the way home and finally take their rightful place in last place in the division. Oh, my assistant is telling me that prop bets are side bets. You boys have to stop with the fancy terminology. I like these teams over the 37.5 points as neither defense can stop chuckers. We want to thank Wedge for taking the time to talk to us and answer our questions about the Titans. As per usual we want to wish Wedge and the Titans the best of luck this season and we hope that luck begins on Monday. Make sure to look in every waste basket and on every porch for your copy of the Possum Holler Tribune as they hope to be on the world wide web by the year 2030.
author: Scott Barzilla

title: Do the Colts actually have a chance to win in Pittsburgh?
summary: Yes. That’s the answer to whether the Indianapolis Colts can beat the Steelers in Pittsburgh. There is a chance. There is a chance for a lot of things, so that isn’t really saying much though. For the Colts to win in Pittsburgh on Sunday, they will have to turn in a nearly perfect and polar […]
full_text: Nov 2, 2025; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA; Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones (17) runs the ball against the Pittsburgh Steelers during the fourth quarter at Acrisure Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Yes. That’s the answer to whether the Indianapolis Colts can beat the Steelers in Pittsburgh. There is a chance. There is a chance for a lot of things, so that isn’t really saying much though. For the Colts to win in Pittsburgh on Sunday, they will have to turn in a nearly perfect and polar opposite performance from last time. Six turnovers. That’s how many the Colts committed last year. Five of them came at the hands of Daniel Jones. It was a turning point for the high-riding Colts and marked the beginning of the end. They only won one more contest from that point forward. Jonathan Taylor had been the main fuel powering the AFC leading Colts, but in this one, he only got 14 carries for 45 yards. It was a fall from grace that the Colts never recovered from. So, is there a chance the Colts can win on Sunday? Sure thing. The Colts haven’t won in Pittsburgh since 2008. Curt Cignetti, when asked about his team’s chances at Penn State after being told Indiana had never won there said, “this team has never played here”. That seems appropriate here as well. This is a new team. Knock on wood, but is Jones going to commit five turnovers? Is Taylor only going to get 14 touches? Yes, this “team” hasn’t played here, but at the same time, enough players and staff remain from last season to carry the memory. The Colts should be and have to be prepared. Winning this week is huge. A win breaks them out of a tough start to the year at 3-2. Not to look too far ahead, but the schedule starts to open up a bit. A loss won’t sink the Colts, but a win would sure have them sitting pretty. Whatever chance the Colts have to end the drought in Pittsburgh, they must capitalize.

title: 5 Thoughts on the Colts Heading into Week 5
summary: We’re 4 weeks into the season and this Colts team is VERY hard to read. Most people expected a bumpy start. Opening up the year vs. Baltimore, then immediately heading to Arrowhead in primetime is a recipe for a rough couple of weeks. The Colts parlayed their 0-2 start into 2 wins, but none of […]
full_text: London, United Kingdom - October 4: Daniel Jones of Indianapolis Colts in action during the Indianapolis Colts and Washington Commanders match between Indianapolis Colts and Washington Commanders at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on October 4, 2026 in London, United Kingdom. (Photo by Vince Mignott/DeFodi Images/DeFodi via Getty Images) | DeFodi Images via Getty Images We’re 4 weeks into the season and this Colts team is VERY hard to read. Most people expected a bumpy start. Opening up the year vs. Baltimore, then immediately heading to Arrowhead in primetime is a recipe for a rough couple of weeks. The Colts parlayed their 0-2 start into 2 wins, but none of them were particularly decisive. They played a Nico Collinsless Texans team at home and then a Commanders team who was on there 3rd string QB. In both wins, Daniel Jones has had some horrific turnovers and the offense has lacked explosive plays. Yet, they’re 2-2 and still have the best rushing offense by EPA in the league. 1. Daniel Jones Can and Probably Will Play Better I know every time you log onto Twitter, particularly during an NFL game, you are bound to see a lot of emotionally-driven reactions. Want to acknowledge that there is nothing wrong with that! At the end of the day, being a fan isn’t or shouldn’t be that serious. Football is fun and there’s nothing more intense than a NFL game where every win matters and your entire mood for the week is seemingly dictated by a 60 minute game on Sundays. Even reporters, who take immense pride in their objectivity and journalistic integrity, can let the emotional nature of a football game seep into their analysis and coverage. I am no exception either. That being said, often times those takes aren’t rooted in logic. Benching Daniel Jones, even as horrific as he was on Sunday, is not logical. For better or for worse, Carlie Irsay-Gordon publicly put this regime on the hot seat. Paying Daniel Jones $90 million over two years means this staff is choosing to live or die by his performance. I know there’s a contingent of Anthony Richardson diehard supporters within the fanbase, but the staff isn’t going to save there jobs by benching the guy they just paid for the guy they already benched. I have not been excited by how Daniel Jones has played this year, but I also know he has, can, and probably will play better. I don’t believe in “flukes”. If you show you can play at a high level in this league, it means you have that ability within you— it just might take something to unlock it again. In other words, just because Daniel Jones is playing poorly now, doesn’t mean it has to be this way for the rest of the year. The most puzzling thing about Jones play is the turnovers. Brutal picks and fumbles have plagued Daniel for his entire career, but I don’t understand how a player can fumble as much as he has. It was a problem in New York, it was a problem during the tail end of 2025, and it’s still a problem this year. If Daniel Jones isn’t getting strip sacked by Odafe Oweh and Will Anderson Jr., I think we’re a bit more gracious about his play this year, but those are just inexcusable turnovers. 2. To state the Obvious: The Colts are missing Alec Pierce When Alec Pierce got the contract he did, the entire NFL world called it an overpay. Part of the reason the Colts had to back up the brink trunks was twofold. 1) the Colts front office refuses to extend ascending players early to get ahead of the market, and 2) the way the Colts handed the balancing act between the Jones and Pierce contracts seemed to blow up in there face. That being said, schematically the Colts are in a nightmare situation without him. To put the loss of Alec Pierce into context.. Through 4 games, the Colts have had: 43 plays of 10+ yards 14 plays of 20+ yards Both are the 2nd lowest in the Ballard tenure through 4 games. pic.twitter.com/nclICUqsDA — Colts Film Room (@ColtsFilmRoom) October 9, 2026 The Colts are relying on an elite success rate to carry the lack of explosive plays. What made the 2025 offense so efficient, and the whole ethos of Steichen’s offense is to generate explosive plays that flip the field, thus limiting the amount of plays needed to score and limiting the exposure to turnovers, sacks, and negative plays . That’s why they drafted Anthony Richardson, and that’s why Alec Pierce got paid. Without the explosive plays… As a result the Colts are seeing a lot more Cover 3. 24% of plays the Colts faced through 4 games last year were Cover 3. This year? 33% — Colts Film Room (@ColtsFilmRoom) October 9, 2026 3. What Tyler Warren is and what he isn’t Another causality to the loss of Alec Pierce is Tyler Warren. He is still proving to be a really good player, but fantasy owners probably aren’t as excited about his production. That’s because he is a unique player, that also has some limitations He’s not a high volume pass catcher because he can’t run a lot of routes. He’s a straight line athlete that is explosive north and south but he’s not going to separate at the top of a route like Kelce, Bowers, McBride, Loveland, etc. What he gives you is a good blocker with very strong hands and someone who’s extremely physical at the catch point. That makes him great in the red zone, but he’s not gonna run a pivot and gain 15 yards. He hasn’t had the chance to break as many tackles either because it’s one thing to break a tackle in open space where a DB isn’t going to bring you down, but it’s another to try and break one when the coverage is compressed and everyone is nailing down on certain routes because they aren’t threatened deep. Outside of that bizarre drop a couple weeks ago, he’s got incredible hands and has a limited but effective route tree that probably needs to be paired with some sort of run action. He’s not a problem, but he’s probably not going to be the entire solution either. Few Tight Ends are. 4. The Colts Defense has Rebounded, but they need a real test After a truly abysmal start to the year vs. the Chiefs and Ravens, the Colts defense settled back in vs. two offenses that were depleted and had no business dicing the Colts up. The Steelers are a small step in the direction towards giving the Colts a real test, but you have to assume the Colts should be able to limit the damage. This is a unit that is still figuring themselves out, but great defenses never magically become great. There are some issues they have to work through. 5. Marvin Harrison Jr. is a fun story, but a bad idea I was almost sure that the initial speculation that the Colts would trade for Marvin Harrison Jr. was false, but now we’ve gotten more reporting that the Colts are one of the teams interested in the former Ohio State WR. I personally would love the story, but despise the idea. It’s the same fairy tale move this organization has been doing for years. Letting your GM buy at the deadline after publicly putting him on the hot seat year after year is a bad process. I recognize the cost may be insignificant, and the argument for trading him is to acquire a player who gives the Colts the best chance to win while potentially developing into a long-term WR, regardless of Chris Ballard’s job security. But Chris Ballard has whiffed or traded away pieces on this roster, and the answer can’t be to convince yourself it’s ok to just buy in a sellers market to patch up the hole. (You know who’s a better option than trading away assets to get Marvin Harrison Jr.? AD Mitchell.) Heading into Pittsburgh the Colts have a chance to get above .500 and maybe turn some heads. But there’s a long season to go and this team is not in a position to take any opponent likely. Every week will be an absolute dogfight. And if the Colts do in fact make the playoffs, it’s because they scratched and clawed for every single win to get them there. This may not be a talented team, but we’re about to find out if it’s a more mentally tough team.

title: Jaguars vs. Eagles: Staff roundtable and game picks for Week 5
summary: Welcome to Big Cat Country’s staff roundtable! Today, we’re previewing Week 5’s matchup between the Jacksonville Jaguars and Philadelphia Eagles. Question 1: What questions do you still have about the Jaguars, if any, after they beat the Bengals last week? Dillon Appleman: I know the defense made the big stop at the end eventually, but I really need […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - NOVEMBER 3: Jalen Hurts #1 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks to pass the ball against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Lincoln Financial Field on November 3, 2024 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to Big Cat Country’s staff roundtable! Today, we’re previewing Week 5’s matchup between the Jacksonville Jaguars and Philadelphia Eagles. Question 1: What questions do you still have about the Jaguars, if any, after they beat the Bengals last week? Dillon Appleman : I know the defense made the big stop at the end eventually, but I really need to see more execution from that side of the ball in crunch time. In Week 2 against the Broncos, and this past week against the Bengals, both opposing offenses had long, seemingly easy drives down the field when it mattered most late in the game. I would like to see more of a blood-in-the-water style of play in those situations going forward. Travis Holmes : Can this Jacksonville squad handle the weight of expectations? Heading into Jacksonville’s Week 2 game, heaps of praise were heaped upon this Jaguars team as a top AFC Super Bowl contender, only for them to fail to play the game we know they’re capable of the following week. In a week-by-week, matchup-by-matchup league, losses will happen, but Jacksonville clearly didn’t play its style of football against Denver. It was this inconsistency issue that has plagued the team for years. Similarly, Jacksonville is once again the national media’s “Belle of the Ball” this week, with talking heads coming out of every corner of the media sphere to praise this team’s future prospects. Can they tune out the noise and handle today’s business? Gus Logue : Where are the deep passes? Trevor Lawrence has thrown the ball 10+ yards downfield on 43.3% of his attempts — the highest rate in the league, per NFL Pro — but most of that production has come in the intermediate area. He ranks eighth in pass attempts 10-19 yards downfield (37) and just 25th in pass attempts 20+ yards downfield (8). It’s good that Jacksonville’s offense has been lighting up scoreboards without relying on shot plays. But the team does have Brian Thomas Jr., after all. It would be nice to see a couple of deep passes completed against a talented secondary. Henry Zimmer : My big question will be how good the offensive line can be in terms of protecting Trevor Lawrence and keeping the running game going. Overall, the offensive line did OK against a solid Bengals front but the games never get easier as they go. This unit needs to find its footing, find its right five guys. When that happens, this team could be special. Question 2: What’s the key to a Jaguars victory this week? Dillon : It’s a bit simple, but it’s just to win the turnover battle. The Eagles are snakebittin with injuries more than just about any team in the league right now, so really it’ll come down to not gifting a desperate team favorable opportunities via turnovers or mistakes. Clean execution and not forcing anything should lead to a positive outcome. Travis : Ezra Cleveland and Robert Hainsey versus Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, and Moro Ojomo will be the matchup that determines this game’s outcome, in my estimation. Vic Fangio’s defense has struggled to consistently pressure quarterbacks this season when not blitzing, ranking 16th in the NFL with a 31% pressure rate when rushing 4 or less. That’s while playing a defensive scheme specifically built around getting home with four. Jalen Carter has clearly seemed limited as a pass rusher while playing with a cast on his right wrist due to a hairline fracture, in a similar manner to Travon Walker in 2025. However, given Hainsey and Cleveland’s slower start to 2026, Carter is likely still dangerous enough with his power rushes to disrupt the pocket for Trevor. Gus : Winning the explosive-play battle. I don’t expect Vic Fangio to allow Lawrence to paper-cut his defense to death by taking short, efficient passes and checking into runs against light boxes all game long. The Jaguars will need to make a few plays on offense. On defense, they really just need to avoid getting Mossed — because without multiple Pro Bowlers surrounding him, Jalen Hurts just isn’t that good by himself. Henry : This could be another “don’t play with your food” game for Jacksonville. Just go out and win. Your key is to beat a banged-up team that is in free fall. This roster, at least on paper, is better than Cleveland’s but the process is the same. You are supposed to win, so go out and do it for 60 minutes. Question 3: Who will be an X-factor for the Jaguars on Sunday? Dillon : Bhayshul Tuten. Liam Coen and Trevor Lawrence get most of the attention for the Jaguars, but the impact of Bhayshul Tuten this season has been undeniable. He’s third in the league in success rate, as well as missed tackles forced, which has been huge considering the middling performance of the offensive line to this point. I expect Sunday to be a heavy workload for the young back. Travis : An often-overlooked area may come front and center this week. With an extensive Eagles injury report heading into the London matchup, most attention has gone to the starting players who may or may not be available. However, I believe this creates a huge opportunity for Heath Farwell’s special teams unit to be this week’s biggest X-factor. When so many starting-level players have been either traded, placed on injured reserve, or simply injured this week, that forces many practice squad, rotational depth, or recently signed players into increased special teams opportunities. A missed block, missed tackle, missed assignment, or miscommunication in a key situation could be all it takes to bust Sunday’s game wide open for Jacksonville. Gus : Travon Walker. In case you didn’t hear, future Hall of Fame right tackle Lane Johnson announced his retirement after missing last week’s game due to personal reasons. Our friends at Bleeding Green Nation believe third-round rookie Markel Bell will draw his second NFL start over veteran swing tackle (and former Jaguar) Fred Johnson. Walker should be licking his chops to face a young buck following his 1-pressure performance against Amarius Mims. On top of that, it’s no secret that Jalen Hurts is much more efficient when rolling out to his right than his left. Even if Walker doesn’t destroy Bell on every snap, he’s got to contain Hurts. Henry : My X-Factor for Sunday morning is Anthony Campanile. He should be able to feast upon the remnants of this bad Eagles offense. With potentially no DeVonta Smith or Saquon Barkley, this could be a very long afternoon for new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion. Final score prediction? Dillon : Jaguars 27, Eagles 17 Travis : Jaguars 30, Eagles 13 Gus : Jaguars 27, Eagles 13 Henry : Jaguars 35, Eagles 14 What are your Week 5 predictions, Jaguars fans? Let us know in the comments! summary: The Jaguars (3-1) head to London as massive favorites over the Eagles (2-2), and it’s easy to see why. Part of it is how well Jacksonville has been playing. The rest is an Eagles team that has been crippled by injuries, and their Hall of Fame right tackle just announced his retirement. Jacksonville’s report is […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - OCTOBER 04: Eric Murray #29 of the Jacksonville Jaguars is evaluated by medical staff during the third quarter of the game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jaguars (3-1) head to London as massive favorites over the Eagles (2-2), and it’s easy to see why. Part of it is how well Jacksonville has been playing. The rest is an Eagles team that has been crippled by injuries, and their Hall of Fame right tackle just announced his retirement. Jacksonville’s report is lengthy too, but the Eagles’ injury problems are far more of a story. #Jaguars & #Eagles Thursday Injury Report Eric Murray (concussion protocol) upgraded to Limited Quinyon Mitchell upgraded to Full Participant today; Dontayvion Wicks added Thursday with a hamstring pic.twitter.com/WiG2wHe2QV — Mia O'Brien (@MiaOBrienTV) October 8, 2026 Jaguars Injury Report RB LeQuint Allen Jr. – Hip – Full Participant WR Jakobi Meyers – Thumb – Full Participant S Eric Murray – Concussion – Limited (upgraded from DNP Wednesday) CB Montaric Brown – Hamstring – Limited CB Jarrian Jones – Foot – Limited CB Jaylon Jones – Hamstring – Limited CB Jourdan Lewis – Hamstring – Limited DT Davon Hamilton – Foot – Limited OT Anton Harrison – Elbow – Limited DE Josh Hines-Allen – Groin – Limited OT Cole Van Lanen – Knee – Limited It’s a long list, but most of it looks like week-to-week maintenance. Allen and Meyers both getting full practices on Thursday is a good sign for the offense. Two names still carry a risk of missing Sunday: Murray, who was upgraded to limited after sitting out Wednesday but still has to clear the concussion protocol, and Brown, who missed last week’s game with a hamstring injury. Corner is the group to watch, with four of them on the report. That makes Brown’s status the biggest factor for the secondary’s depth in London. Eagles Injury Report RB Saquon Barkley – Hamstring – DNP WR DeVonta Smith – Hamstring – DNP WR Marquise Brown – Ankle – DNP S Marcus Epps – Groin – DNP LB Jonathan Greenard – Ankle – DNP C Drew Kendall – Knee – DNP LB Zack Baun – Concussion – Limited LB Jihaad Campbell – Knee – Limited (upgraded from DNP Wednesday) TE Dallas Goedert – Knee – Limited T Fred Johnson – Knee – Limited WR Dontayvion Wicks – Hamstring – Limited CB Quinyon Mitchell – Knee – Full Participant (upgraded from Limited Wednesday) The Eagles are in rough shape. Barkley and Smith not practicing Thursday is a major blow to the offense, and Marquise Brown sitting out as well thins the receiver room even more. Wicks was limited, so he’s the one pass catcher with a chance to help. Up front, Kendall didn’t practice and Johnson was limited, which adds more concern to an offensive line already hit by the retirement. On defense, Baun, Campbell and Goedert were all limited, but Greenard and Epps sitting out leaves real questions at linebacker and safety. The one bright spot was star corner Quinyon Mitchell, who went from limited to full on Thursday. Eagles Injuries (get ready for a LONG list): Zack Baun (concussion) Marquise Brown (ankle) Dallas Goedert (knee) Fred Johnson (knee) DeVonta Smith (hamstring) Marcus Epps (groin) Lane Johnson (personal) Jordan Davis (calf) Hollywood Brown (ankle) Dallas Goedert (knee) Zack… — SleeperEagles (@SleeperEagles) October 6, 2026 What it means for Sunday Jacksonville should be close to full strength, with Murray and Brown the only real question marks. Philadelphia could be without several of its best players, and with so much of the offense in doubt, the Jaguars’ defense could have a big day. Expect both reports to sharpen with Friday’s final designations. What injury do you have your eye on heading into game day, Jags fans? Download the SB Nation App and drop your thoughts.

title: Kenneth Walker has taken his game to another level with the Chiefs
summary: Witnessing this kind of running back in a Kansas City Chiefs uniform takes me back to my childhood as I watched Priest Holmes, Larry Johnson, and Jamaal Charles. But this time, the running game is paired with arguably the best quarterback in football history. Can we take some time to appreciate just how good running […]
full_text: (Photo by Chris Unger/Getty Images) | Getty Images Witnessing this kind of running back in a Kansas City Chiefs uniform takes me back to my childhood as I watched Priest Holmes, Larry Johnson, and Jamaal Charles. But this time, the running game is paired with arguably the best quarterback in football history. Can we take some time to appreciate just how good running back Kenneth Walker has been? Because this isn’t just a hot start. It’s one of the best four-game stretches to begin a season by a running back in the last two decades. Walker has 537 rushing yards and 621 yards from scrimmage. Both numbers currently lead the NFL. He’s keeping some wildly impressive company. His 537 rushing yards are the most by any player through the first four regular-season games since Arian Foster rushed for 539 yards for the Houston Texans in 2010. The only other running backs in the past 25 years to have more rushing yards at this point in the season than Walker were Jamal Lewis ( Baltimore Ravens ) and Stephen Davis ( Carolina Panthers ), who both did it in 2003. Walker was always known for his big-play ability, but he’s taken it to another level with the Chiefs. He already has six carries of 20+ yards, matching Derrick Henry, Jonathan Taylor and Saquon Barkley’s total 20+ yard runs this season… combined. The only other running backs in the past 15 years with six 20+ yard carries through the first four regular-season games were Derrick Henry (2024), Nick Chubb (2020), Matt Breida (2018), and Kareem Hunt (2017), according to Pro Football Reference . Walker’s 267 rushing yards after first contact are the second-most in the Pro Football Reference database, which has tracked the statistic since 2018 (Leonard Fournette, 278 in 2019 ). We could go on and on, but we don’t need to continue with the stat-off. The point is clear — it’s been a special start to the season for the Chiefs’ prized free-agent addition. He’s been every bit the game-changer the team hoped he’d be. That’s good, because they’ve needed it. And that need is only growing more acute by the day. The Chiefs’ pass protection showed its first signs of weakness over the past couple of games against the Miami Dolphins and Las Vegas Raiders . The Seattle Seahawks loom in a couple of short weeks. It remains to be seen if left tackle Josh Simmons will be available to stop the bleeding. Wideout Tyquan Thornton had been the Chiefs’ most productive wide receiver through the first month of the season, and he’s now expected to miss most, if not all, of the regular season with a brutal ankle dislocation. We’ll see when Rashee Rice is able to return from his hamstring injury, but typically wide receivers don’t immediately return to the field with a soft tissue issue like the one he experienced against the Raiders. All of this points to a heavier workload for Walker in the coming weeks. He’s handled it thus far. His next touch will be his 100th of the season. If that sounds like a lot, that’s because it is. From 2021-2025, only five other players had as many touches through their first four games of the regular season as Walker’s had this season: Derrick Henry, Joe Mixon, Saquon Barkley, and Christian McCaffrey. Those are all legitimate workhorse backs. Walker has never finished with more than 260 touches in an individual season. Can he hold up to that kind of workload? He better. This is not the first time head coach Andy Reid has leaned heavily on a running back. He did so with Kareem Hunt in 2017 during his rookie year when Hunt finished that year with 325 touches and led the league in rushing. Brian Westbrook finished his 2007 season for the Eagles with nearly 370 touches in 15 games while leading the league in yards from scrimmage. It’s true Reid has not traditionally been a coach who leans heavily into the running game, but he’s more than happy to keep the running back involved both on the ground and through the air when his team needs it and when the back’s talents demand the ball. That certainly fits the Chiefs’ current situation. I would be surprised if the Chiefs don’t add reinforcements to the passing game eventually. Health will help, and an outside addition or two feel inevitable. In the meantime, this will likely remain the Kenneth Walker show. It’s been a heck of a watch so far. I hope it can continue.
author: Brandon Kiley

title: The Chiefs are reportedly one of ‘several’ teams interested in Justin Watson
summary: It was a big blow to the Kansas City Chiefs’ offense when wide receiver Tyquan Thornton dislocated his ankle against the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 4. He could recover in time for the postseason, but the team still has 13 regular-season games to play well against a much tougher slate of opponents. So it […]
full_text: (Photo by Justin K. Aller/Getty Images) | Getty Images It was a big blow to the Kansas City Chiefs ’ offense when wide receiver Tyquan Thornton dislocated his ankle against the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 4. He could recover in time for the postseason, but the team still has 13 regular-season games to play well against a much tougher slate of opponents. So it shouldn’t be surprising if the team looks for a way to replace Thornton’s downfield role in the offense. Before Thornton was plugged into the offense in 2025, wide receiver Justin Watson manned an impactful spot in Kansas City as a deep-ball threat. It sounds like the Chiefs may be interested in turning back the clock to Thornton’s predecessor. The Chiefs are among several teams interested in WR Justin Watson, per source. Watson played for Kansas City from 2022-24 and is a three-time Super Bowl champion, having beaten the Chiefs with the Bucs before being part of their back-to-back title teams. — Pete Sweeney (@pgsween) October 9, 2026 According to good friend of the site Pete Sweeney of The Kansas City Star , the Chiefs are “among several teams” interested in signing Watson, who is currently a free agent after the Houston Texans released him this preseason. In 2025, Watson signed with Houston as a free agent after Thornton impressed on the Chiefs’ practice squad through the end of the 2024 season. He appeared in only two games for the Texans last season before going to the Reserve/Injured list with a calf injury; he returned for the Texans’ regular-season finale and played on special teams in the playoffs. In Kansas City, Watson caught 64 passes for 1,064 yards and seven touchdowns; 56 of his 64 completions resulted in a first down or touchdown. Over his last two seasons with the Chiefs, Watson accumulated 694 yards and three touchdowns on 35 catches on passes thrown 10 or more yards downfield, according to Pro Football Focus . Watson may not be the only reunion in Kansas City’s receiving corps, but he may provide the field-stretching dynamic Thornton built his role on. Watson has limits that were evident once Thornton stepped into a similar position and excelled further, but the familiarity with the offense — along with the downfield chemistry with quarterback Patrick Mahomes — could be enticing for a midseason addition.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Flashback Friday: The last time the Chiefs were undefeated at the bye
summary: This weekend, the Kansas City Chiefs and the Carolina Panthers will have an off-day while the rest of the NFL plays Week 5. It’s the first week the league schedule includes a bye. Two years ago, the Chiefs were in a similar position: after a Week 5 win over the New Orleans Saints on “Monday […]
full_text: (Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images This weekend, the Kansas City Chiefs and the Carolina Panthers will have an off-day while the rest of the NFL plays Week 5. It’s the first week the league schedule includes a bye. Two years ago, the Chiefs were in a similar position: after a Week 5 win over the New Orleans Saints on “Monday Night Football,” Kansas City entered an early bye week undefeated (5-0) with crucial conference wins over the Baltimore Ravens and Cincinnati Bengals as well as a road victory against the Los Angeles Chargers . In that road win over the Chargers, the Chiefs suffered a crucial injury to the receiving corps: second-year wideout Rashee Rice tore his ACL while trying to make a tackle after an interception. The start of the 2024 season sounds eerily similar to this year’s. The offense will need to move forward without one of its top receivers, Tyquan Thornton, but it has the benefit of a lead in the standings, with wins over the Denver Broncos and Las Vegas Raiders . In 2024, the Chiefs continued the hot streak into Week 11: Kansas City won four straight games after the Week 6 bye before falling to the Buffalo Bills on the road. That featured a road trip to face a contending NFC West team (the San Francisco 49ers ) and a division rival (the Raiders). Can the 2026 Chiefs stay undefeated through this year’s road trip to Buffalo? It would also require surviving a West Coast trip, this time against the Seattle Seahawks and Broncos. The biggest difference between this season’s team and the squad that was attempting to finish off a three-peat is the offense. In the first five games of 2024, the Chiefs’ highest-scoring output was 27 points. Through Week 5, the season-high rushing total was 149, in a game where starting running back Isiah Pacheco broke a bone in his leg. This year, the Chiefs have scored 30 or more points in three of their four games, and running back Kenneth Walker has surpassed 148 rushing yards twice on his own. The offense will need to keep finding ways to score despite the significant injury. In 2024, that meant trading for All-Pro wide receiver DeAndre Hopkins. He scored two touchdowns in his second game in Kansas City, but he didn’t make a big-time impact on the field through the team’s AFC championship run that year. General manager Brett Veach made that move when the team was 6-0. He doesn’t like wasting opportunities to win Super Bowls when quarterback Patrick Mahomes is at the helm. The receiver position could use a similar boost, but it remains to be seen whether the younger pass catchers will step up in Thornton’s place. Regardless, this year’s Chiefs need to finish stronger than the 2024 team did. The wheels fell off against the Philadelphia Eagles in Super Bowl LIX, and a major factor was an injury at left tackle. This year, the team has made it work with rookie Kahlil Benson on the left side, but the health of last year’s first-round pick, Josh Simmons, could be key to avoiding a disappointing end to the season in Kansas City.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: 3 things that must improve about the Chiefs after the bye week
summary: There’s reason to feel confident the Kansas City Chiefs can build on their 4-0 start and return to postseason glory. They’ve had a strong start to the season, but the team needs to address a few areas over the bye week to stay atop the AFC standings. Here are the three things the Chiefs most […]
full_text: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images There’s reason to feel confident the Kansas City Chiefs can build on their 4-0 start and return to postseason glory. They’ve had a strong start to the season, but the team needs to address a few areas over the bye week to stay atop the AFC standings. Here are the three things the Chiefs most need to improve on for the rest of the campaign: 1. Third-down defense This season, the Chiefs allow 37% of third-down conversions, ranking 13th in the NFL. The Chiefs’ pressure rate is middle of the pack (24%), but on third down, they rank 25th (40%). The team has only one third-down sack this year: defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah’s strip sack of Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix in Week 1. The pass rush is the clearest path to getting off the field more often. Defensive tackle Chris Jones needs to be more disruptive on pass downs, because defensive ends George Karlaftis and rookie R Mason Thomas seem to be muddying the pocket from the edge at a good rate. 2. True pass protection The Chiefs’ offense has operated well by leaning on the run game and its effect on the defense with play action from under center. It’s been refreshing to see, but Kansas City still needs to give quarterback Patrick Mahomes time to operate on straight dropbacks. Pass protection composite ratings pic.twitter.com/WMwOxhrJ70 — Computer Cowboy (@benbbaldwin) October 6, 2026 So far this season, the pass blocking has been subpar in true pass sets. Rookie left tackle Kahlil Benson has allowed six pressures (three quarterback hits) over 48 true pass sets, according to Pro Football Focus . That means the Chiefs drop back into a traditional pass play an average of only 12 times per game. As opponents get tougher, Mahomes will need to win games by throwing the ball when the defense knows he is. The return of left tackle Josh Simmons (back) — regardless of how the right tackle position is handled — feels like the only path to significant improvement here. 3. Playmaking from pass catchers We probably aren’t making a big enough deal of wide receiver Tyquan Thornton likely missing the entire regular season with a dislocated ankle. He’s been the pass-catching group’s biggest playmaker so far, but that says little given how well this team’s pass offense has performed this year. Whether the run game opens it up or Mahomes puts passes on the money, the receivers haven’t been asked to do much more than execute the play so far this year. Without Thornton (and No. 1 target Rashee Rice (hamstring) in the short term, potentially), the offense desperately needs receivers like Xavier Worthy, Jalen Royals and rookie Cyrus Allen to step up and make plays themselves. Whether it’s Royals’ run-after-catch ability or Allen’s route running, the offense needs to use these players to their strengths while Worthy likely sees an increase in overall target share. The former first-round pick needs to look the part moving forward. That said, the pass-catching group’s playmaking may be impossible to elevate without a trade or free-agent signing. The NFL trade deadline is November 10, between Weeks 9 and 10 of the season. Look for general manager Brett Veach to make a move as he has in previous years, whether it was wide receiver Kadarius Toney in 2022 or DeAndre Hopkins in 2024.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Chiefs News: Mansoor Delane named a top-5 rookie in the NFL

The latest Kansas City Chiefs news NFL defensive rookie rankings at quarter mark of 2026 season: Sonny Styles or Arvell Reese at No. 1? | NFL.com No. 4: Mansoor Delane KC | CB DRAFTED: Round 1, No. 6 overall After Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson relocated to the Rams in March, the Chiefs aggressively pounced on Delane in April. Jumping up the draft board from No. 9 to No. 6, Kansas City selected the cornerback to immediately start opposite second-year pro Nohl Williams. That’s a tall task for a rookie in any defense, but it’s particularly challenging in Steve Spagnuolo’s scheme, given how much press-man coverage the vaunted DC likes to employ. Not a problem for this silky-smooth technician, who has played man at one of the highest rates in the league — 53.3%, per Next Gen Stats — yielding just a 68.2 passer rating against in the coverage, with an interception and three pass breakups over 14 targets. Kansas City Chiefs Quarter-Season Awards | Athlon Sports Defensive MVP: Drue Tranquill It’s hard to find a winner for this award. The Chiefs defense has been up-and-down this season, with no huge standout individual performances. With that being said, Tranquill is a solid choice for this award four games in. The veteran linebacker has done a little bit of everything for Steve Spagnuolo’s defense. He’s taken on a bigger role with Leo Chenal gone and played well. Tranquill has 29 total tackles, five tackles for loss, and two passes defended. He’s a key cog for this Chiefs defense. Chiefs at the bye: Updated playoff odds, best rookie, breakout player | The Athletic Key player who needs to improve: Chris Jones Jones’ salary-cap number this season is nearly $45 million. That’s top-of-market money for a defensive tackle ( by roughly $15 million, according to Over the Cap ), and for that price, the Chiefs should be expecting top-end production from their star. They’re not getting it … yet. Jones has no sacks through four games, but perhaps more worrying, per PFF, he’s tied for 50th in the NFL with 11 QB pressures. Chiefs bye-week awards: The top players on the defense and special teams | The Kansas City Star Top defensive player: Mansoor Delane Votes: Mansoor Delane (3), George Karlaftis (2) Rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane made an instant impact in the NFL when he intercepted a pass from Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix on the third play of the season. Unfortunately, Delane aggravated a shoulder injury on that play and was unable to return to action in that game, the season opener at Arrowhead. He also missed the Chiefs’ second game but played in wins over the Dolphins and Raiders. 5 Chiefs Players Under Pressure Coming Out of the Bye | Heavy Sports Kansas City Chiefs Players Under Pressure Coming Out of Bye Week: Defense S Alohi Gilman Gilman is off to a struggling start to his Chiefs career. It’s only been four games, so perhaps he just needs more time to settle in. Hopefully that happens soon, because opposing quarterbacks have strongly attacked the deep middle portion of the field this season. Gilman ranks 81st out of 93 safeties with a poor 45.2 grade from Pro Football Focus. He has 17 total tackles so far, and not a single pass defensed. With Chamarri Conner now back from injury, perhaps Gilman will be used more as a box safety. Revamped defense plus Kenneth Walker III: How the Chiefs re-established themselves as a Super Bowl contender | CBS Sports Kansas City is on pace for 259 pressures, according to TruMedia, which would be the team’s highest total in a decade. Last season, it generated a higher team pressure rate (39.2%), but that effort required more blitzes. Steve Spagnuolo’s defense is impacting the opposing quarterback without sending five-plus rushers as often, which takes some pressure off an entirely revamped secondary. The problem thus far has been finishing plays. Despite the uptick in pressure, Kansas City has just four sacks on the year, tied for the second-lowest in the NFL. Around the NFL Cowboys’ Prescott irked by stadium worker’s callout after loss | ESPN As Dak Prescott walked down a long hallway to the locker room after the Dallas Cowboys’ 24-16 loss to the previously winless Tampa Bay Buccaneers, he heard someone yell, “Embarrassing.” It was a third-party contractor positioned just outside the players’ exit from the AT&T Stadium field. “When he said it, I just happened to look at him, and at that point, he looked away,” Prescott said. “And when I turned my head back, he said something else. And so that’s the part that, just as a man or as just a person, feel free to speak your mind — just speak it. Don’t cower away from the reaction that you’re going to get. Bucky Irving and rookie QB Jalon Daniels help Bucs beat sloppy Cowboys 24-16 | NBC Sports Bucky Irving ran for a career-high 165 yards, including a 72-yard run to set up the touchdown that put Tampa Bay ahead for good, while scoring twice himself, and the Buccaneers beat the Dallas Cowboys 24-16 on Thursday night for their first win of the season. Jalon Daniels threw a TD pass to Irving in the first half while directing a turnover-free offense amid several Dallas miscues in just the second start for the undrafted rookie. Daniels, who was 19 of 25 for 189 yards, is filling in for Baker Mayfield, who’s expected to be sidelined at least one more game with a dislocated thumb on his throwing hand. Through four weeks of the season, zero kickoff return touchdowns | Pro Football Talk That continues a downward trend in kickoff return touchdowns that began before the 2024 adoption of the “dynamic kickoff” and hasn’t changed under the new rules, which have encouraged more returns but haven’t resulted in more big plays. There were only six kickoff return touchdowns all of last season, and seven in 2024. In 2023, the last season of the old kickoff rules, there were only four touchdown returns. Grueling months of rehab led to the Chiefs’ opening salvo against the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football.” Fans were nervous; Mahomes had fully participated in training camp but hadn’t seen any live reps in the preseason. Everyone held their breath when, on the first drive of the game, Mahomes didn’t just drop back to pass in the red zone—but began to actually run with the football. Mahomes scored a rushing touchdown, not once, but twice (the first score called back due to penalty) for the first touchdown of the Chiefs’ season. full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 27: Dorian Williams #42 of the Buffalo Bills attempts to tackle Quentin Johnston #1 of the Los Angeles Chargers after a six-yard reception during the first quarter of the game at Highmark Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chargers are going to be down even more starters on both sides of the ball in their Week Five matchup with the Broncos. After missing last week’s game in Seattle, safety Derwin James will miss his second consecutive game, leading the way for another Tony Jefferson start in his place. Right tackle Joe Alt is also among the group who will sit this week, leaving the door open for rookie Travis Burke to earn his first NFL start. The other five players who are not suiting up this week are wide receiver Quentin Johnston, rookie receiver Brenen Thompson, offensive guard Kayode Awosika, cornerback Donte Jackson, and guard Trevor Penning. Without Johnston and Thompson, the Chargers will look towards a limited Ladd McConkey, Tre’ Harris, Derius Davis, and Marquez Valdez-Scantling to shoulder the receiving load. Tight end Charlie Kolar could also make his return to the lineup this week and is listed as questionable, which could go a ways in alleviating the pressure on the receiver room. game status for week 5 vs DEN QUESTIONABLE — Charlie Kolar, Scott Matlock, Ladd McConkey, Branson Taylor, Rodney Shelley DOUBTFUL — Trey Lance OUT — Quentin Johnston, Brenen Thompson, Joe Alt, Kayode Awosika, Donte Jackson, Derwin James, Trevor Penning — Los Angeles Chargers (@chargers) October 9, 2026 Joining Kolar and McConkey as questionable this week are fullback Scott Matlock, offensive guard Branson Taylor, and cornerback Rodney Shelley. The return of Taylor up front could be huge for the Bolts. If he does not play, they would most likely be forced start four rookies at left tackle, left guard, center, and right tackle this week. Taylor returning to start at left guard would at least provide a veteran (well, second year) presence between Slaughter and presumed starter Logan Taylor on Justin Herbert’s blindside.

title: NFL predictions: Chargers face long odds vs. Broncos in Week 5
summary: The Los Angeles Chargers are facing off against the Denver Broncos in Week 5 at SoFi Stadium hoping to grab their first win of the season. The Chargers have dropped their first four games and have been one of the more disappointing teams in the league. Nothing more would get them back on track with […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - JANUARY 04: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos scrambles for a first down in the first quarter against the Los Angeles Chargers at Empower Field At Mile High on January 04, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by C. Morgan Engel/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Los Angeles Chargers are facing off against the Denver Broncos in Week 5 at SoFi Stadium hoping to grab their first win of the season. The Chargers have dropped their first four games and have been one of the more disappointing teams in the league. Nothing more would get them back on track with a statement win in Week 5 against the defending AFC West champions. Per FanDuel Sportsbook , the Chargers are an underdog by 3.5 points. Let’s take a look at some predictions for the game. Over/Under: 42.5 The Chargers’ offense has struggled out of the gate, managing no more than 16 points in any of their first three games. The team had its best offensive showing last week against the Seattle Seahawks, with 23 points, but two of those scores came late in the fourth quarter, in what appeared to be garbage time. The offense needs to make a statement at home against a division rival, but the Broncos have one of the better defenses in the AFC. Given how they have performed this season, as well as how the Broncos have performed on offense, posting an average of 18.5 points per game, there’s a good chance the under hits. Prediction: Under Chargers +3.5 FanDuel is giving the Chargers 3.5 points to start the game. Given the fact that they have not won any of their first four games, this is not much of a surprise. Home underdogs are 9-13 this season, suggesting that there’s reason for them to not be favored against the Broncos. That being said, the Chargers are hungry for a win, and it wouldn’t surprise me if they won outright. We’ll go ahead and take the Chargers despite them being 3.5-point dogs. Prediction: Chargers +3.5 Final Score The Chargers are in desperate need of a win, but nothing will come easily in the divisional matchup, especially against a team like the Broncos, who also need to make a push after starting out the season 2-2. I could see the game going either way, but there is a very good chance it will come down to the final possession. Given where the Broncos and Chargers are, I’ll take Denver by a field goal.
