title: 5 questions and answers about Patriots vs. Raiders
summary: You know what they say: revenge is a dish best served during the 1 p.m. window of a mid-October regular season game. The New England Patriots will get some chance for pay-back on Sunday against the Las Vegas Raiders, after they spoiled Mike Vrabel’s first game with the organization last fall. Of course, these are […]
full_text: You know what they say: revenge is a dish best served during the 1 p.m. window of a mid-October regular season game. The New England Patriots will get some chance for pay-back on Sunday against the Las Vegas Raiders, after they spoiled Mike Vrabel’s first game with the organization last fall. Of course, these are not the same Raiders that left Foxborough with a 20-13 victory in hand in 2025. So, in order to find out more about the Patriots’ opponent, we spoke with Matt Holder of Pats Pulpit’s sister site Silver and Black Pride , the SB Nation community for all things Raiders. What effect has Klint Kubiak had on the Raiders’ organization and offense early in his tenure? I write a weekly NFL Power Rankings roundup column , and the big theme after the hard-fought battle with the Chiefs is that Kubiak is clearly building something special in Las Vegas. He’s come in and immediately changed the culture and has managed to get buy-in from the players. The team is doing a lot of little things like wide receivers run blocking, all defenders pursuing the football, playing through the whistle, etc. That seems pretty simple, but it wasn’t happening with the previous regimes. On top of that, Kubiak has brought over his creative offensive scheme and has helped defensive coordinator Rob Leonard install a variation of Mike Macdonald’s defense. Granted, Leonard and Macdonald did work together for a year in Baltimore, so Leonard gets credit for that too. But my overall point is the Raiders finally have good systems on both sides of the ball and a well-coached team for the first time in a long time. Let’s be honest, the Raiders’ roster is not very talented and has plenty of glaring holes. That’s why this season was viewed as year one of a rebuild heading into the campaign. However, the Raiders find themselves at 3-1 and just went toe-to-toe with a team that’s one of the betting favorites to represent the AFC in the Super Bowl, six months after having the No. 1 pick in the draft. That’s a culture change and a big feather in Kubiak’s cap. How is Brock Bowers being used under Kubiak? Should the Patriots treat him like a WR1? They aren’t the same type of player, so this isn’t a one-for-one comparison, but Kubiak is using Bowers similarly to what he did with Jaxon Smith-Njigba in Seattle last year. The 2025 Offensive Player of the Year would line up all over the Seahawks’ offense so that he could get favorable matchups. We haven’t seen Bowers deployed quite as diversely as JSN was a year ago, but he’s also only played in two games under Kubiak so far and is constantly at different alignments. It’s funny, despite being labeled as a “tight end”, the “ football robot from heaven ” has only been in-line on 12.6% of his passsnaps, per Pro Football Focus . It’s kind of like how Sean Payton used to use Jimmy Graham, where Graham was split out wide so much that he tried to get wide receiver money when the Saints put the franchise tag on him back in 2014. Because of that, and the fact that the Raiders don’t have a ton of talent at receiver, opposing defenses kind of have to give Bowers the WR1 treatment. He’s such a unique player/athlete for his position that he’ll beat safeties and linebackers all day if you treat him like a traditional tight end. The Broncos started the trend when the 2024 first-round pick was a rookie. Denver got tired of him beating their safeties and just put Patrick Surtain II on Bowers. That worked because Surtain is one of the best corners in the league and helped neutralize Bowers. So, if Gonzalez is playing on Sunday, I think the Patriots have to put their best on the Raiders’ best. Ashton Jeanty is immensely talented, but his stats this season aren’t reflecting that. Where’s the disconnect? There are a few factors going on. First, Jeanty doesn’t seem to be 100% right now. He suffered a sprained ankle at the end of training camp and hasn’t missed any gametime, but I think he aggravated it in Week 3 against the Saints. The CBS broadcast team said he got his ankle taped or re-taped mid-game, and Jeanty didn’t have the same explosiveness on his jump cuts we’ve seen before. I get the sense that he’s healthy enough to play but isn’t at full capacity at the moment. Second, the offensive line has improved but still isn’t very good right now. Like last year, the second-year back is still facing a good amount of defenders in the backfield. For example, Next Gen Stats has 234 of his 264 rushing yards (88.6%) coming after contact. Also, he’s currently facing the fourth-highest percentage of stacked boxes (32.1%, and it was the second-most heading into Week 4) because defenses have been daring Kirk Cousins to beat them deep. Cousins has played well enough to suggest that trend will slow down, but that’s been the primary game plan for the Raiders’ offense so far. On a similar note, Kubiak mentioned that he feels like there is a tell in the running game, and my podcast/YouTube co-host broke down how that might be tied to how the Raiders are using motion when they run the ball . The Chiefs were rotating a safety in the box just about every time they saw someone motion across the formation, which contributes to the heavy boxes mentioned above. As good as Kubiak’s scheme has been, there’s still room for improvement, and I’m glad that he seems to have caught on to it early rather than continuing to do the same thing and expecting different results. Also, the Seahawks’ rushing attack got off to a slow start last year, as Vincent Bonsignore of the California Post noted: The early returns in Seattle last season were hardly overwhelming, either. With Kubiak in his first and only year as offensive coordinator, the Seahawks averaged just 3.7 yards per carry through their first eight games, finishing below 100 rushing yards four times. Over their final 12 games, including the Super Bowl, they surpassed 100 yards 10 times and averaged 4.5 yards per carry. This provides more hope that the Raiders and Jeanty will improve down the line. What did the Raiders do to slow down Patrick Mahomes, and how much of that plan could translate against Drake Maye? I’m going to contradict myself a bit here, but the way Leonard slowed down Mahomes was similar to how Mahomes was able to generate explosive plays. The Raiders were able to get pressure by running simulated pressures, creeper blitzes or rushing five defenders. Essentially giving the offense confusing looks to set up one-on-one opportunities for guys like Maxx Crosby and Malcolm Koonce while still having enough coverage defenders to avoid giving up the big play. That’s been Leonard’s formula all year, regardless of the opponent. However, he got in trouble last week when he dialed up the heat too much by calling Cover 0. Vegas ran Cover 0 three times against Mahomes, resulting in a 41-yard catch, a two-yard touchdown and a 55-yard completion to increase the Chiefs’ probability by over 50% (h/t Ryan Paganetti on X/Twitter ). Las Vegas has the highest rate of Cover 0 usage (9.6%) in the NFL through the first four weeks of the season, according to Fantasy Points Data , and it was obvious on film that the Chiefs were ready for it. So, I think Leonard has to get away from sending the house, but I’d still expect him to scheme up pressure against Maye. I know Maye did much better under pressure last week, but his numbers against pressure in the first three weeks were pretty bad. Expect the Raiders to test whether the 2025 MVP runner-up has turned the corner or if the Bills game was more of a fluke. Who are some under-the-radar Raiders that Patriots fans should know about entering this game? Koonce is the first guy who comes to mind. Crosby, deservedly, gets a lot of attention, but Koonce is also having a great year, and they have nearly identical pass-rush win rates so far this season (19.8% for Crosby and 18.9% for Koonce, per PFF ). Also, fifth-round corner Hezekiah Masses isn’t the stickiest in coverage and has had a few rookie moments this…

title: Patriots cornerback depth chart, updated ahead of Raiders game
summary: The New England Patriots ruled out six players for their upcoming Week 5 game against the Las Vegas Raiders, and four of them are members of their cornerback group. Starters Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis will miss the contest due to respective shoulder and neck injuries, as will backups Karon Prunty and Channing Canada, who […]
full_text: The New England Patriots ruled out six players for their upcoming Week 5 game against the Las Vegas Raiders, and four of them are members of their cornerback group. Starters Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis will miss the contest due to respective shoulder and neck injuries, as will backups Karon Prunty and Channing Canada, who are both dealing with hamstring issues. Needless to say, this leaves the team quite thin at the position heading into a game against one of the most productive passing offenses in the NFL so far this season. Let’s therefore reset the depth chart ahead of Sunday’s meeting with Kirk Cousins and the Raiders offense. 53-man roster: Christian Gonzalez (0) , Carlton Davis III (7) , Marcus Jones (25 | PR), Charles Woods (22), Channing Canada (29) , Karon Prunty (21) Practice squad: Kindle Vildor (28), Al’zillion Hamilton (26) As of Friday afternoon, the Patriots have only four healthy cornerbacks available between their roster and practice squad. On the 53-man team, Marcus Jones and Charles Woods are the only options left, and naturally expected to see considerable playing time on Sunday. That said, even they are not at a 100%. Woods, who got banged up during last week’s win over the Buffalo Bills, is also listed on the injury report: he is questionable with a shoulder injury. Considering this, both of Kindle Vildor and recent addition Al’zillion Hamilton getting elevated from the practice squad on Saturday seems like a foregone conclusion. In addition, the team has also started experimenting with safety Jaylen Reed as more of a nickel option in practice; he too could factor into the mix come Sunday. As things currently stand, however, the starting trio at cornerback will likely consist of Jones, Woods and Vildor.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Patriots vs. Raiders Friday injury report: Christian Gonzalez, Carlton Davis III among six ruled out
summary: The New England Patriots will be down six members of the active roster against the Las Vegas Raiders, including Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis III. Both perimeter starters have been ruled out for Sunday’s matchup along with fullback Reggie Gilliam, wide receiver Mack Hollins and fellow cornerbacks Karon Prunty and Channing Canada. “We got six […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - SEPTEMBER 9: Christian Gonzalez #0 of the New England Patriots celebrates after a play during an NFL football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on September 9, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots will be down six members of the active roster against the Las Vegas Raiders, including Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis III. Both perimeter starters have been ruled out for Sunday’s matchup along with fullback Reggie Gilliam, wide receiver Mack Hollins and fellow cornerbacks Karon Prunty and Channing Canada. “We got six guys out. We’re going to make some roster moves. We got to have 48 for the game,” head coach Mike Vrabel shared during his final press conference of the week. Here’s the rest of the game designations leading up to the 1 p.m. ET kickoff at Gillette Stadium. OUT Patriots FB Reggie Gilliam (ankle, knee) WR Mack Hollins (calf) CB Christian Gonzalez (shoulder) CB Carlton Davis III (neck) CB Karon Prunty (hamstring) CB Channing Canada (hamstring) Raiders WR Jalen Nailor (concussion) WR Dont’e Thornton (hamstring — IR return) G Trey Zuhn (knee) Headlining the season-high six ruled out, Gonzalez has missed six consecutive practices dating back to the end of September. The extended All-Pro will now miss a second game due to a shoulder injury. And across from No. 0, Davis stayed sidelined throughout preparations due to a neck injury after playing all 59 defensive snaps last Sunday against the Buffalo Bills. What became a 29-26 AFC East upset at Highmark Stadium also did not include Canada after the undrafted rookie was downgraded on the eve of the 1 p.m. ET kickoff with hamstring injury. And now, the scarce cornerback depth chart will also be without its fifth-round pick in Prunty because of a hamstring issue of his own. Veterans at fullback and wide receiver won’t be on hand in Foxborough, either. Gilliam has seen 58 downs on offense and 39 downs on special teams during his inaugural Patriots campaign. The lead blocker began the week as a limited participant due to knee and ankle ailments before becoming a fifth absence on Thursday. As for Hollins, he sustained a non-contact calf injury after halftime Orchard Park and did not return despite being announced as questionable. A non-participant in practice since then, the 33-year-old wideout currently ranks atop an A.J. Brown-less passing game in targets, catches and yards. QUESTIONABLE Patriots RB Rhamondre Stevenson (knee) OT Morgan Moses (foot) DT Christian Barmore (shoulder) LB Dre’Mont Jones (shoulder) LB Christian Elliss (chest) CB Charles Woods (shoulder) S Craig Woodson (shoulder) Raiders RB Ashton Jeanty (ankle, foot) While there’s uncertainty in Raiders’ backfield, Stevenson is also “not out as of yet,” per his head coach, after practicing in a limited capacity throughout the week for the Patriots. The downhill running back hobbled off with a knee injury on the final drive last Sunday after totaling 47 rushing yards, 27 receiving yards, one touchdown as well as a two-point conversion. He’s among seven questionable entering the weekend. As is Barmore. The defensive tackle had been a scratch for the divisional matchup because of a shoulder ailment, yet climbed back to full participation on Friday while the rest of the New England’s 50-50 group remained partial participants. The Patriots currently carry one open spot on the 53-man roster after promoting safety and back-to-back standard elevation Mike Brown. It’ll soon be going to Brenden Schooler, who moves forward without a game status. The 2025 special teams captain had his 21-day practice window open last month and is eligible for activation after spending the initial four games on the non-football injury list . “Yeah, I imagine Schooler will be ready to go,” Vrabel said.

title: ‘Dominant force’ Maxx Crosby the latest test for Patriots O-line
summary: Had the offseason gone as planned, the New England Patriots would not be going up against Maxx Crosby this Sunday. Instead, the Las Vegas Raiders star would be playing for the Baltimore Ravens this weekend. However, Baltimore famously backed out of the deal after Crosby failed his physical, retaining two first-round draft picks while seeing […]
full_text: Had the offseason gone as planned, the New England Patriots would not be going up against Maxx Crosby this Sunday. Instead, the Las Vegas Raiders star would be playing for the Baltimore Ravens this weekend. However, Baltimore famously backed out of the deal after Crosby failed his physical, retaining two first-round draft picks while seeing the 29-year-old go back to Las Vegas. Seven months later, he continues to play his typical high-volume role along the Raiders edge as if nothing had happened. For the Patriots, that is not exactly good news. Crosby, after all, continues to be a problem for opposing offensive lines. “It’s a guy that you have to pay attention to until the whistle blows, and a little bit after,” said starting right tackle Morgan Moses. “He’s always around. He’s a max-effort guy, that’s what he does. It’s hats off to him, what he’s been able to do in his career in this league so far. He’s a dominant force so we have to be able to have our details, our technique and our fundamentals, and know where he’s at all the time, and obviously limit him to the ball.” Through four games this season, Crosby and the Raiders defense have been among the most disruptive forces in football. The team as a whole ranks second in the NFL in quarterback pressure rate (35.6%), with Crosby checking in at No. 4 with 25 total pressures including a pair of sacks. He also forced fumble and registered a recovery. Long story short, he is looking every bit the player he has in the past — including last year, when he had a sack and season-best seven total disruptions in a 20-13 Raiders win in Foxborough. Naturally, the Patriots know the importance of slowing him down. “He’s a great player. We have to try our best to stop him,” said running back TreVeyon Henderson. “We know it’s not going to be easy, so we all have to help each other out to do a good job stopping him.” Based on alignment charting, that job will mostly fall on Moses and the right side of New England’s line. Crosby has lined up there for 176 of his 222 defensive snaps this season (79.3%). However, as Mike Vrabel pointed out, the Patriots need to be on high-alert at all times. “Maxx will go wherever he wants to go, and he will do whatever he wants to do, and it’s worked out really, really well,” the Patriots’ head coach said. “I have a lot of respect for Maxx Crosby as a person and also as a player. So, we’ll have to know where he is on every single play.” Vrabel in general has been impressed with Las Vegas’ ability to force offenses into mistakes under a first-year coaching staff led by Klint Kubiak and defensive coordinator Rob Leonard. “Guys have come from different places, and they’ve really put together a cohesive group,” he said. “[Adam] Butler was there, [Jeremy] Chinn was there, Maxx was there, [Malcolm] Koonce was there. But they’ve been able to supplement that with the guys off the football with [Nakobe] Dean and [Quay] Walker, and obviously continue to add guys inside, and then also [Kwity] Paye. So, they’ve really come together and gelled well together, and we will have to know where Maxx is, certainly, to start every play.”

title: Patriots preparing for mental challenge against Raiders QB Kirk Cousins
summary: Kirk Cousins has never been known as the most athletically-imposing quarterback in football. And yet, he has found success through his 15-year career in the NFL. Whether it was Washington, Minnesota or Atlanta, he continued to play his style of football and keep himself. Nothing flashing, but consistently performing at a steady level. It’s the […]
full_text: Kirk Cousins has never been known as the most athletically-imposing quarterback in football. And yet, he has found success through his 15-year career in the NFL. Whether it was Washington, Minnesota or Atlanta, he continued to play his style of football and keep himself. Nothing flashing, but consistently performing at a steady level. It’s the same thing he has brought to the Las Vegas Raiders as well after arriving this offseason. And it also is what the New England Patriots will go up against this week. “Processing information, getting the ball out, getting the ball where it needs to go, giving it to their playmakers,” defensive tackle Milton Williams said when asked to describe Cousins’ game. Doing all those things from the get-go in Las Vegas, Cousins has played some of the best football of his career even at age 38. Working under first-year head coach Klint Kubiak, he has completed 93 of 144 passes for a 64.6% hit rate, 1,026 yards, a league-leading 11 touchdowns and just four interceptions. He also has taken only five sacks and ranks ninth among quarterbacks with 0.214 expected points added per play (for comparison, Drake Maye ranks 16th at 0.049). “He’s an amazing veteran quarterback,” said linebacker Christian Elliss. “He knows how to run an offense well. Kubiak knows how to use his brains well. Obviously, he’s extremely smart and he diagnoses defenses well.” “They have a lot of chemistry,” added defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr. “Obviously, Klint and Kirk being in Minnesota together, they definitely know each other well. You can tell that from Week 1 there wasn’t really any slow growth. They hit it. They hit the field running. They’re doing a great job with their big skill and they’re dialing up some good plays to their skill.” Tops among that skill options is tight end Brock Bowers, who has caught 16 of Cousins’ passes for 202 yards and a pair of touchdowns. The Patriots are making him a priority this week, but they also know that they need to be able to impact the quarteback himself. “For us it’s about trying to affect him in any way we can,” said Elliss, “and we’ll go from there.”

title: Patriots mailbag: Will injuries force an addition at wide receiver?
summary: The New England Patriots are looking to build off of their big win against the Buffalo Bills, and now return home for a matchup against the surprising 3-1 Las Vegas Raiders. So, let’s get into this week’s #PostPulpit Mailbag. Hey Brian. Do you think there’s a move made at wide receiver if the team gets […]
full_text: The New England Patriots are looking to build off of their big win against the Buffalo Bills, and now return home for a matchup against the surprising 3-1 Las Vegas Raiders. So, let’s get into this week’s #PostPulpit Mailbag. Hey Brian. Do you think there’s a move made at wide receiver if the team gets grim news on Hollins, or do you think they just elevate one of the practice squad guys? – Pat in Agawam With Hollins’ injury not considered long term and the return of A.J. Brown looming, I don’t think an outside addition is needed. If they believed otherwise, that addition would have been in the building early this week. The Patriots can continue to primarily run Romeo Doubs at the X, Efton Chism at the Z in place of Mack Hollins, and DeMario Douglas in the slot with Kyle Williams working in at multiple spots as well. That should be enough to get by in the mean time, with Cameron Dorner or Kyle Dixon potential practice squad elevation options if spots are available. Via chats with other Pulpiteers, I’m curious, what’s up with Kyle Williams lack of “production?” Is he seeing the field? Is he being used primarily as a “Sacrificial X” WR to clear out safety help and open the field for others? Is he doing his job in respects beyond catching the ball?—running good routes, blocking etc. Or, does he just suck? I believe Vrabel and McD have said in the past that doing your job doesn’t always mean you are the guy who gets targeted with the ball, and I’m wondering if that might be the case with Kyle. – Maye The Force Be With You Is there a future for our WR Williams ? With now Chism emerging, Doubs starting to catch and Douglas established in the slot we can imagine Brown and Hollins will come back so Williams could be the odd man Non active on game day …. – 7i165 The effort is not an issue for Kyle Williams. He’s running hard routes, blocking in the run, and continuing to earn praise from the coaching staff behind the scenes. His role simply leads to volatile production, as he’s mainly playing outside in a sacrificial X role, where he’s often running clear-out routes. I did think his third-down catch against Pittsburgh over the middle of the field was a big play, as he fought through contact to convert. At the same time, it’s been disappointing that Drake Maye has not been able to get him the football on two specific instances when he won deep along the outside: the blood-fumble play and a second-down incompletion late against Buffalo. The skill set is still valuable in this wide receiver room, and I would still be in favor of Williams working at different positions and running a more diverse route tree like he did in college. But with the veterans ahead of him, those opportunities simply haven’t presented themselves. He should get more of them this Sunday, however. Why did it take so long to get around to Efton Chism? All we’ve been hearing about is how good this guy is how hard he plays he could become the next Julian Edelman,who wasn’t used much his first couple of years.. he needs to be out there going forward. What’s your take? – PatriotsWay We’re not comparing him to Julian Edelman or any other former Patriots slot receiver, but frequent readers here know we’ve been a fan of Chism since before the draft. While he’s dominated virtually every practice we’ve watched since his arrival, he was an undrafted free agent joining a depth chart that included veterans such as Stefon Diggs, Mack Hollins, and DeMario Douglas. Like Williams, Chism needed an opportunity. He got one late last season and then again Sunday, and he impressed both times. Now, we’d expect to see more of him moving forward. The Right Guard position continues to be a mess. Brown was bad against Buffalo. I believe between Lomu, Bryant, and Crownover one of those could be a better RG than they have on the roster. Will those guys get a shot at that position or does the team view them strictly as Tackles. – Elderly Lothario Ben Brown will be “slated to start at right guard” this week, according to Mike Vrabel. Brown did allow three pressures, failing to pickup a stunt and got pushed back on the strip sack (in part due to an uncalled hands to the face penalty) but was certainly not a train wreck in his first meaningful NFL reps at right guard. I’d continue to roll with Brown. Mike Vrabel has not ruled out Lomu potentially factoring into he mix at some point, but the rookie appears to be behind newly signed Matt Pryor and Walter Rouse at the position. Moses shocked me by having a pretty good pass protection grade but his run blockjng grade is horrible. Do you think he gets replaced at some point by Lomu? – XGhost-PepperX It was definitely a bounce back game for Moses in Buffalo, who allowed one tackle for loss in the run game and just one pressure while drawing the most matchups against Gregory Rousseau. The veteran is battling through a painful foot injury, but don’t think the team has any immediate plans to pull the plug for Caleb Lomu, who did not look ready in a limited sample size against the Jaguars. When is our 2025 Sack Leader Harold Landry expected to make his return? Getting him back as a Pass Rusher and Run Stuffer will help this Defense. – For Pats Sake I haven’t had any expectations for Harold Landry this season after what he played through last season. Anything they get from him would be a bonus in my book, and I’m not sure how impactful he would even be following that knee injury. Considering that the Pats no longer have a 2028 1st round pick, would you target the OL again in the next draft or look at other potentially weak areas like TE, LB? – Arschloch Certainly can never have enough offensive lineman, but with two straight first-round picks invested in Will Campbell and Caleb Lomu I would not use another first on an offensive tackle. I’m also largely against using that capital on an interior offensive lineman. I would still look at some position in the defensive front seven. That’s all for this week’s #PostPulpit mailbag. If you have questions you’d liked to be answered next week, submit them online in our weekly submission post on the Feed. Make sure to follow @iambrianhines and @PatsPulpit as well.

full_text: Last year’s meeting between the New England Patriots and the Las Vegas Raiders at Gillette Stadium was a wet affair. There is a chance this week’s game between the two clubs is as well, but it does not seem particularly likely. According to NFL Weather , there is a “slight chance of rain showers” throughout the contest on Sunday. That chance, however, has been calculated at a minuscule 2%. More likely, the game will be played under consistent cloud cover and with temperatures in the low 60s; wind should not be a major factor despite gusts of up to 15 mph being possible. The National Weather Service shares a similar projection. According to its models, Sunday will be “mostly cloudy, with a high near 64” and rain showers only expected to happen after 7 p.m. ET. Long story short, as far as October football is concerned those are pretty standard conditions that should not negatively impact the game. For the Patriots, who have struggled with ball security and will be going up against the league leaders in takeaways this week, this can be seen as positive news. The Week 5 game between the Patriots and Raiders at Foxborough’s Gillette Stadium is scheduled for Sunday, Oct. 11 at 1 p.m. ET.

title: Patriots offense looking for consistency after finding its stride in Buffalo
summary: The New England Patriots offense took a major step forward last Sunday in Buffalo. The unit looked different, scoring a season-high 29 points as the four touchdowns it scored doubled the amount they previously had through the first three weeks. According to offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels, however, not much changed. “I just think staying consistent. […]
full_text: The New England Patriots offense took a major step forward last Sunday in Buffalo. The unit looked different, scoring a season-high 29 points as the four touchdowns it scored doubled the amount they previously had through the first three weeks. According to offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels, however, not much changed. “I just think staying consistent. I know this is hard to believe, but we didn’t really do a whole lot different from week one to two to three to four,” McDaniels said. “We knew we hadn’t played our best brand of football that we could play. And again, I keep saying this, it’s about the group. The group has to play well in order for us to play well as an offense, and believe it or not, we didn’t, that was far from perfect also, so there was much to improve on that we’re going to work hard to try to make better and hopefully we can do that.” Entering the week last in motion rate and 29th in play-action rate, the Patriots increased both in Buffalo. That included running motion on 75.3% of their plays, their highest rate in a single game since Week 15, 2023. But McDaniels noted that it’s not simply about playing fast. The Patriots have to play fast and execute to see results. The results were there for Drake Maye, who played his best game of the season. Maye threw for a season-high 269 yards and three touchdowns while adding 54 yards on the ground. “I think his approach being consistent with the things we’re trying to improve on for himself, but also the group as a whole,” McDaniels said. “There are just so many areas where we can do better and make better decisions, use better techniques and fundamentals and produce more offense. And so hopefully we’ll see that again Sunday.” Maye and the Patriots offense will hope to keep building on that performance Sunday against the Las Vegas Raiders. It’s the next step toward reaching their full potential as a unit. “I think we’re just starting up the mountain,” Maye said. “I think you would like to think that, and we have to go and prove that, but it’s a race for us to improve, knowing that you have to improve throughout the season and throughout the year for these teams. These teams, once you get closer to the end, are going to be at their best at the end, and I think that’s one of the things that you strive to do throughout the year. “Knowing that, you would like to say everybody – especially on offense – you’d like to say that the first three weeks weren’t what we wanted to put out there. You have to try to build off last week, knowing that it’s not just going to do it for you. You have to put the work in and the focus, and hopefully continue to catch a trend and catch a stride.”
author: Brian Hines

title: Our defense vs. their offense: Minnesota Vikings
summary: The challenge for the Saints continues this week as they are set to host the undefeated Minnesota Vikings. The Vikings come into New Orleans 4-0, and while they feature offensive players with elite talent, this Vikings offense has yet to hit its stride. Through four games this season, the Vikings currently rank 31st in total […]
full_text: The challenge for the Saints continues this week as they are set to host the undefeated Minnesota Vikings. The Vikings come into New Orleans 4-0, and while they feature offensive players with elite talent, this Vikings offense has yet to hit its stride. Through four games this season, the Vikings currently rank 31st in total offense, averaging 262.8 yards per game. That stat would be understandable had the Vikings lost Justin Jefferson to an injury for the entire start of the season or had they not added veteran QB and former first-round draft pick Kyler Murray. But Murray was acquired this offseason, and Jefferson has only missed one game so far, which was this past Sunday. This matchup presents the Saints with a really valuable opportunity. After getting bullied by the Falcons on Monday night in the Dome, they have a chance to regain their confidence. The Vikings currently average only 156 passing yards per game, which ranks dead last in the league. They are 16th in rushing, averaging 106.8 yards per game, and 18th in scoring at 21.5 points per game. This is a game where the Saints need to come out and keep the lid on this offense. Do not be the defense that this team uses to get itself right. The Vikings still have elite talent on this offense, including notable players who have already had career-defining moments in the NFL. They just have not figured out how to put the pieces together right now. The biggest area of concern for the Vikings is along their offensive line. Injuries have been a major cause for concern and are one of the primary reasons why their offense has been stagnant. This week, the Vikings will most likely be coming into the Dome without the starting left side of their offensive line. Left tackle Christian Darrisaw is currently in the concussion protocol. He was injured last week against Miami, as was Donovan Jackson, who tore his meniscus and required season-ending surgery. This presents the Saints defense with a chance to establish its pass rush and do something it has not been very good at throughout the season: stop the run. The Vikings are already struggling to run the ball, and now they will have to play this game with half of their starting offensive line on the sidelines. Minnesota has allowed 13 sacks through four games this season. That amount of pressure is one of the reasons the passing game is out of sync. Right now, the leading receiver for the Vikings is TE T.J. Hockenson. Hockenson has 22 receptions for 195 yards and one TD. He is followed by LSU legend Justin Jefferson, who has only 13 receptions so far for 179 yards and two TDs. The Saints have had issues covering tight ends and elite wide receivers this season. The Vikings are bringing a really good tight end and one of, if not the best, receivers in the league. The Saints will need to keep the Vikings off schedule. Force them into third-and-long situations, and do not bail them out. The Vikings have been plagued by pre-snap penalties this season, creating longer down-and-distance situations to overcome. Right now, their offense is playing not to lose games. They are not a threat to go out and take a game away, but they have the talent to become that kind of problem if they are able to put everything together. This team is 4-0 and has not played a complete game yet. A matchup like this will be a get-right game for one of these units. The Saints offense versus the Vikings defense is a matchup of strength against strength. This game will come down to whichever team can get more out of its weakest unit than its opponent gets out of theirs.

title: A look back at the history between the Saints and Vikings
summary: In Week 5, the New Orleans Saints will host the undefeated Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, Oct. 11, at the Caesars Superdome. These two teams first faced one another way back on Oct. 13, 1968, when New Orleans defeated Minnesota 20-17 in Tulane Stadium. Sunday’s matchup will mark the 38th meeting between the two, including the […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS - JANUARY 24: Kicker Garrett Hartley #5 of the New Orleans Saints successfully kicks a 40-yard game-winning field goal in overtime from the hold of Mark Brunell #11 against the Minnesota Vikings during the NFC Championship Game at the Louisiana Superdome on January 24, 2010 in New Orleans, Louisiana. The Saints won 31-28. (Photo by Jed Jacobsohn/Getty Images) | Getty Images In Week 5, the New Orleans Saints will host the undefeated Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, Oct. 11, at the Caesars Superdome. These two teams first faced one another way back on Oct. 13, 1968, when New Orleans defeated Minnesota 20-17 in Tulane Stadium. Sunday’s matchup will mark the 38th meeting between the two, including the postseason. The Saints and Vikings have met five times in the playoffs, with perhaps their most memorable meeting coming on Jan. 24, 2010, in the NFC Championship game at the Superdome. In a thrilling overtime battle, New Orleans defeated Minnesota 31-28 on Garrett Hartley’s 40-yard field goal, sending the Saints to Miami for Super Bowl XLIV, where they would go on to capture the franchise’s first Super Bowl championship. The two teams have continued to produce memorable postseason moments, including their meeting in the 2017 NFC Divisional round, which ended with the famous “Minneapolis Miracle,” when Vikings wide receiver Stefon Diggs scored on a 61-yard touchdown reception as time expired. The Saints enter this matchup with a 1-3 record, looking to rebound from their embarrassing loss on Monday Night Football to the Atlanta Falcons. A victory over an undefeated Minnesota team would provide a significant boost for New Orleans as they look to gain back some ground with fans and in the NFC standings. Meanwhile, Minnesota enters the matchup with a perfect 4-0 record and will look to keep their unbeaten streak alive. The Vikings have gotten off to a strong start this season and will present another challenge for a Saints team hoping to turn its season around. Sunday’s matchup will also be a special occasion for the Saints organization and its fans, as legendary quarterback Drew Brees will be inducted into the team’s Ring of Honor. During his 15 seasons in New Orleans, Brees became the franchise’s all-time leader in passing yards and touchdown passes while earning 12 Pro Bowl selections with the Saints and becoming one of the most beloved figures in franchise history. In a fitting tribute, Brees will also be in the broadcast booth for Sunday’s matchup, serving as FOX’s color analyst. Kickoff is set for noon CT, and the game will be broadcast on FOX, with Adam Amin (play-by-play), Drew Brees (color analyst) and Kristina Pink (sideline reporter) on the call.

title: Key matchups: Saints vs. Vikings
summary: The New Orleans Saints need to get back on track, but it won’t come easy facing the 4-0 Minnesota Vikings with the best defense in the NFL. On paper, this game is a surefire loss for the Saints, but there are holes and advantages the Saints can capitalize on to come out of Sunday with […]
full_text: The New Orleans Saints need to get back on track, but it won’t come easy facing the 4-0 Minnesota Vikings with the best defense in the NFL. On paper, this game is a surefire loss for the Saints, but there are holes and advantages the Saints can capitalize on to come out of Sunday with a 2-3 record. Kellen Moore vs. Brian Flores There is no talking about this Vikings team without talking about their defense. And while we could highlight their pass rush alone, I think the better key matchup to highlight for Sunday is Kellen Moore vs. Brian Flores. Since the season has started, we have been waiting for Moore to prove why he deserves to be a head coach. He ended 2025 on a good note, but the Saints’ Week 4 struggles are a reflection of their Week 1 struggles, showing a lack of growth. Well, here’s your chance, Kellen Moore. You are facing your direct opposite. Flores is the best defensive play caller in the league, and truthfully probably deserves another chance at being a head coach. His pass rush is the fiercest in the league, and he blitzes at a 76% rate. On the other side, the Saints are one of the worst teams in the NFL against he blitz. The real major key matchup on Sunday won’t be how the Saints’ offensive line can handle the Vikings’ pass rush, but how Moore can scheme around it. Saints run defense vs. RB Aaron Jones Look, I’m not here to defend the Saints’ run defense, but facing the league’s top three running backs through the first four weeks of the season is brutal. With that being Said, New Orleans has one of the worst defenses in the league and will now face off against Aaron Jones, who is having a career resurgence with the Vikings. While the Saints have the third-worst run defense in the NFL, they’ll be facing a Minnesota offense that is middle of the pack in terms of running the ball, ranking 17th in rushing offense. When New Orleans faced a rushing offense similar to the Vikings’, against the Las Vegas Raiders, they held their own, allowing the Las Vegas Raiders to rush for 113 yards on 27 carries. The run defense in New Orleans is bad; don’t get me wrong. But it’s possible that how bad their run defense is could be skewed by the talent they’ve faced early in the season. Still, Jones is not a running back to overlook, and the potential absence of Kaden Ellis is sure to leave a hole in the defense. Saints rushing offense vs. Vikings run defense Shough has thrown 180 passes through four games this season, averaging 45 attempts per game. At this rate, the second-year quarterback’s arm may fall off at the end of the season. The best way to counter the team’s excessive passing is to run the football. Establishing the run would also calm down the pass rush, relieving Shough from the major pressure he’s faced all season. The Vikings run defense is one of the better units in the league, ranking seventh, while the Saints have the sixth-worst rushing offense. Headlined by Alvin Kamara, the rushing offense for New Orleans lacks talent. Kamara isn’t the running back he used to be, but he can still be effective with a limited number of touches each game. The loss of Travis Etienne will prove to be huge, and now it’s up to Moore to scheme the run properly and set his quarterback up for success.

title: Former Saints, Bears Coach and NFL Legend Mike Ditka Dies at 86
summary: The NFL has lost another legend. Pro Football Hall of Famer Mike Ditka has died at the age of 86. One of the most recognizable figures in professional football, Ditka built a remarkable career spanning decades as both a player and head coach. Known for his fiery personality, toughness and passion for the game, Ditka […]
full_text: Mike Ditka, Head Coach for the New Orleans Saints looking on from the sideline during the American Football Conference pre season game against the Oakland Raiders on 16th August 1997 at Oakland-Alameda County Coliseum, Oakland, California, United States. The Oakland Raiders won the game 18 - 16. (Photo by Otto Greule Jr/Allsport/Getty Images) | Getty Images The NFL has lost another legend. Pro Football Hall of Famer Mike Ditka has died at the age of 86. One of the most recognizable figures in professional football, Ditka built a remarkable career spanning decades as both a player and head coach. Known for his fiery personality, toughness and passion for the game, Ditka became synonymous with the Chicago Bears before later taking over as head coach of the New Orleans Saints. Ditka’s greatest coaching achievement came during the 1985 season, when he led the Bears to a dominant 15-1 regular-season record and a victory over the New England Patriots in Super Bowl XX. Chicago’s legendary defense and Ditka’s larger-than-life personality helped make that team one of the most memorable in NFL history. Before his coaching career, Ditka established himself as one of the league’s premier tight ends. Selected in the first round (fifth overall) by the Bears in the 1961 NFL Draft, he played 12 seasons with Chicago, the Philadelphia Eagles and the Dallas Cowboys. Ditka served as head coach of the Bears for 11 seasons (1982-92) before returning to the sidelines in 1997 when the Saints hired him to lead the franchise. His arrival in New Orleans generated excitement among fans hoping the Hall of Famer could bring the same championship success he had achieved in Chicago. However, Ditka’s three seasons with the Saints were far less successful. New Orleans finished 6-10 in both 1997 and 1998 before falling to 3-13 in 1999. He compiled a 15-33 record and failed to lead the franchise to a playoff appearance. Following the disappointing 1999 season, Ditka and the Saints parted ways, ending his NFL coaching career. Despite his struggles in New Orleans, Ditka’s overall accomplishments remained significant. He finished his 14-year head coaching career with a 121-95 regular-season record, including 106 victories with Chicago. Ditka was one of the few figures in NFL history to win championships as a player, assistant coach and head coach. In 1986, Ditka was enshrined into the College Football Hall of Fame and in 1988, he made history as the first tight end inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Affectionately known as “Iron Mike,” Ditka was a legendary figure both on the field and on the sidelines, leaving behind a lasting legacy in NFL history.

title: Interview with the Enemy: Minnesota Vikings
summary: This week, the New Orleans Saints will face the Minnesota Vikings in Week 5 of the 2026 regular season. To break it down, Christopher Gates of Daily Norseman joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup. NJ: Through the first four games, while the Vikings remain undefeated, the offense has struggled to consistently move the ball downfield and […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - NOVEMBER 12: Chris Olave #12 of the New Orleans Saints catches a touchdown pass against the Minnesota Vikings during the third quarter at U.S. Bank Stadium on November 12, 2023 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images This week, the New Orleans Saints will face the Minnesota Vikings in Week 5 of the 2026 regular season. To break it down, Christopher Gates of Daily Norseman joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup. NJ: Through the first four games, while the Vikings remain undefeated, the offense has struggled to consistently move the ball downfield and put the ball in the endzone. What has been the cause of this for Minnesota? CG: A lot of it has been the play at the quarterback position. For the most part, the offensive line has held up relatively well, and the running game has done its job through the first few weeks of the year, but the quarterback play has been mostly bad for the first four games. Whether it’s been Carson Wentz or Kyler Murray, the passing game just hasn’t gotten going. Sure, Justin Jefferson missed most of the Tampa Bay game and all of the Miami game with an ankle injury, but there’s still enough talent at the skill positions without him for this team to be able to move the ball through the air without him. We saw a few flashes at the end of the Dolphins’ game on Sunday, but we’ll have to see if that carries over into this Sunday’s game or not. NJ: Who are some notable names who will be sidelined for the Vikings on Sunday against the Saints? Is there a particular area in which New Orleans could exploit? CG: Jefferson’s status is still in question for Sunday, although he’s stated that the plan is for him to play in front of the fans in his native Louisiana for the first time. His only other trip to the Superdome came in the COVID year, his rookie season, when there were limited fans in attendance, so I’m sure he’d love nothing more than to be out there on Sunday. He was limited in Wednesday’s first practice, so we’ll see how he progresses this week. Wide receiver Jordan Addison didn’t practice on Wednesday with a hamstring issue, but that’s being described as minor and doesn’t sound like it’s going to prevent him from playing this week. Left tackle Christian Darrisaw is currently in concussion protocol after having to leave the game against the Dolphins and didn’t practice on Wednesday, so he’s definitely in doubt, and left guard Donovan Jackson is done for the year after tearing his meniscus on Sunday. That means the entire left side of the offensive line could be down for the Vikings, which I’m sure the Saints would definitely try to take advantage of. The offensive line has been pretty solid for the Vikings this year, but having to replace both of the guys on your quarterback’s blind side could prove problematic. NJ: With J.J. McCarthy officially out of the picture in Minnesota, has Kyler Murray shown he can be the answer at quarterback? What have been some of his strengths and weaknesses so far? CG: I’ve gone on record several times saying that I’ve never been particularly impressed with Murray, going back to when he was in Arizona. He’s played about 8 1/2 quarters of football for the Vikings so far this season and has been pretty bad for about 7 1/2 of them. I mean, Carson Wentz hasn’t been great either, but you don’t expect Carson Wentz to be great. Murray has shown some mobility, even though the Vikings don’t seem to be all that willing to exploit that mobility with rollouts or anything like that. He did come alive in the fourth quarter against Miami, and there’s a lot of hope that he can carry that over to this Sunday. As far as being the long-term answer, I don’t know if I’d be willing to give him what seems to be the standard rate for quarterbacks in this league now to be the guy for the next 3-4 years. His contract has a no-tag clause in it, so the Vikings might end up with him on a more modest deal, but I honestly just wish they could find a guy in the Draft who could be their answer for the next 10-12 years so that we wouldn’t have to play the “What are we doing at quarterback?” game every year. NJ: Who is one Vikings player you think Saints fans should keep an eye on Sunday—someone who may not receive much national attention but could have a strong performance? CG: Defensive lineman Jalen Redmond probably still isn’t getting the level of recognition that he should outside of Minnesota, but Saints fans will almost certainly know who he is by the time Sunday’s game is over. There are more recognizable names on the Vikings’ defense that get a lot of attention, but Redmond is the guy doing the dirty work on the inside who makes it possible for a lot of those guys to go around making plays. He can get pressure on the quarterback from the interior and is a force against the run as well. The interior of the Saints’ offensive line is going to have their work cut out for them trying to slow down #61 all afternoon. NJ: According to FanDuel Sportsbook , the Vikings (-130) are currently 1.5-point favorites over the Saints (+110) in Sunday’s matchup; what is your final score prediction and how do you see the game playing out? CG: The only bet I think you can take for sure in this one is to hammer the under, which is currently sitting at 42.5. I know the Saints have allowed the most points in the NFL through the first four weeks, but the Vikings aren’t exactly scoring points at a breakneck pace or anything. I think that the Minnesota defense is going to make things difficult for young Tyler Shough, and while they may get a few points on the board, the Vikings. . .as they’ve done for much of the early part of this season. . .will do just enough to escape with a win. Call it 17-13, Vikings. Thank you again to Christopher Gates for joining us to preview this week’s matchup! You can check out the rest of his work here .

title: Our offense vs. their defense: Minnesota Vikings
summary: After the first month of NFL football, the New Orleans Saints hold one of the best offenses in the league. Despite their 1-3 record, New Orleans has had a premier offense across the league, but will face the NFL’s best defensive play-caller, Brian Flores. After four weeks, the Saints are tied with the 10th-best scoring […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - OCTOBER 05: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints celebrates a touchdown against the Atlanta Falcons during the second quarter of the game at Caesars Superdome on October 05, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images) | Getty Images After the first month of NFL football, the New Orleans Saints hold one of the best offenses in the league. Despite their 1-3 record, New Orleans has had a premier offense across the league, but will face the NFL’s best defensive play-caller, Brian Flores. After four weeks, the Saints are tied with the 10th-best scoring offense, averaging 26.3 points per game. The Vikings defense, on the other hand, has allowed the fewest points, allowing just 12.8 points per game to opposing offenses. It’s no doubt this is the week New Orleans tries to establish the run, holding the sixth-worst rushing offense in the league and averaging just 88.5 rushing yards per game. Minnesota’s defense is known for its exotic pass-rushing looks, blitzing the quarterback over 70% of the time. Establishing the run will force the Vikings to ease up on the pass rush, but so far this season, teams haven’t found success in the run game. Minnesota has the seventh-best run defense in the NFL, allowing just 94.5 rushing yards per game. But it’s likely New Orleans won’t find success in the run game. Running back Travis Etienne Jr. is on the injured reserve after suffering a hamstring injury, and Alvin Kamara was a non-participant in Wednesday’s walk-through with a back injury. With these injuries, the Saints are likely to lean on their passing offense, which ranks as one of the best in the NFL. New Orleans is averaging 278.5 passing yards per game, which ranks fourth in the league. Quarterback Tyler Shough is set to face the most fierce pass rush he has so far this season, even despite the brutal loss to the Atlanta Falcons. Shough is currently third in the NFL in passing yards with 1,203 and tied second in touchdowns. He’ll likely lean on his WR1, Chris Olave, who is second in the NFL in receiving yards with 491. The Saints are in desperate need of getting back to winning games, but facing this Minnesota defense may be their hardest task so far this season. Over the last three weeks of the season, the Vikings are allowing opposing offenses to score just 9.6 points per game, and aren’t looking to budge against a New Orleans offense that starts slow week in and week out. But while this is the best defense the Saints will see so far this season, the opposite is true for the Vikings. They haven’t seen an offense as successful as New Orleans this season. While they did face the Chicago Bears in Week 2, it wasn’t without heavy rain and an eventual injury to quarterback Caleb Williams. Will the Saints find a way to get back on track against the 4-0 Vikings and their fierce defense?

title: Saints vs. Vikings Predictions: One, Two Win for Drew!
summary: The 1-3 New Orleans Saints return to Caesars Superdome on Sunday looking to get back in the win column against the undefeated Minnesota Vikings. However, the action on the field won’t be the only storyline, as Saints legend Drew Brees will be inducted into the Ring of Honor during a special halftime ceremony. Coming off […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - OCTOBER 17: Former New Orleans Saints quarterback Drew Brees speaks during halftime of an NFL Football game between the Denver Broncos and the New Orleans Saints at Caesars Superdome on October 17, 2024 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 1-3 New Orleans Saints return to Caesars Superdome on Sunday looking to get back in the win column against the undefeated Minnesota Vikings. However, the action on the field won’t be the only storyline, as Saints legend Drew Brees will be inducted into the Ring of Honor during a special halftime ceremony. Coming off a disappointing 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons on Monday Night Football, New Orleans faces a quick turnaround against one of the NFL’s hottest teams. The Vikings enter Sunday’s matchup led by a defense that has allowed just 12.8 points per game, the fewest in the league. Minnesota has also been effective at forcing turnovers, boasting a plus-five turnover differential. For the Saints, Tyler Shough has been one of the bright spots this season, throwing for 1,203 yards, nine touchdowns and three interceptions through four games. However, Shough is dealing with some soreness in his non-throwing hand following Monday’s loss, but Kellen Moore said it’s not expected to be an issue. Defensively, the Saints must find a way to limit the Vikings offensive opportunities while improving against the run. New Orleans is allowing 147.8 rushing yards per game, ranking near the bottom of the league. While the Saints hope to turn their season around, Sunday’s matchup will also provide an opportunity to celebrate one of the greatest players in franchise history. Brees, who was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame earlier this year, will become the ninth member of the Saints Ring of Honor. During his 15 seasons in New Orleans, Brees transformed the franchise, leading the Saints to their first Super Bowl championship during the 2009 season. However, Brees won’t just be attending Sunday’s game. He will also be calling the action for FOX alongside play-by-play announcer Adam Amin and sideline reporter Kristina Pink. His return adds another layer of significance to a matchup already carrying plenty of importance for New Orleans. When Brees returns to receive one of the franchise’s highest honors, the Saints will once again have additional motivation to deliver a memorable performance in front of their home crowd. As Drew Brees famously said during his team chant for the Saints dream season in 2009: When I say 1, you say 2. When I say win, you say for you… 1! 2! Win! For you! When I say 3, you say 4. When I say win, you say some more… 3! 4! Win! Some more! When I say 5, you say 6. When I say win, you say for kicks… 5! 6! Win! For kicks! When I say 7, you say 8. When I say win, you say it’s great… 7! 8! Win! It’s great! When I say 9, you say 10. When I say win, you say again… 9! 10! Win! Again! Win Again! Win Again! Win Again! Win Again! Prediction: Saints 34 – Vikings 31 So I’m being optimistic on this one because I know on paper that this Saints team is better than their 1-3 record. But a bad mix of some penalties, injuries and poor play calling is a recipe for disaster, however, it’s one that is somewhat fixable. So, let’s hope some of Drew’s magic can rub off in the golden dome and get the Saints back in the win column. Because like he used to say, it’s time to… Win Again, Win Again, Win Again! title: Giants at Commanders: Jayden Daniels, Malik Nabers to play
summary: The 3-1 New York Giants and the 1-3 Washington Commanders both received good news, and bad news, on the injury front as they prepare for a rainy showdown in Week 5. The story of the week is on the Washington Commanders’ sideline. Third-year quarterback Jayden Daniels is making his return from the dislocated left elbow […]
full_text: The 3-1 New York Giants and the 1-3 Washington Commanders both received good news, and bad news, on the injury front as they prepare for a rainy showdown in Week 5. The story of the week is on the Washington Commanders’ sideline. Third-year quarterback Jayden Daniels is making his return from the dislocated left elbow that endangered his season. This is the same elbow that he injured twice last year (dislocated in Week 9, sprained in Week 14) and ultimately cost him seven games. Daniels opted to forego surgery and return to the field, though it remains to be seen how the injury will impact Daniels’ game. Daniels won’t have one of his top receivers in Stefon Diggs (hamstring), who has been ruled out of the game. Wide receiver Terry McLaurin was a limited participant in practice but his game status has yet to be determined. On the Giants’ side of things, the bad news is that the team will be without defe nsive lineman Chauncey Golston , who suffered a neck injury in the Giants’ win over the Arizona Cardinals, and safety Jason Pinnock who suffered a concussion in the same game. The absence of Golston will likely mean the debut of returning Giant Jihad Ward , who was a favorite of former Giants’ (and Baltimore Ravens) defensive coordinator Wink Martindale. The news is that Giants will have five of their best players available. Left tackle Andrew Thomas (groin), wide receiver Malik Nabers (knee), tight end Isaiah Likely (knee/groin), tight end Chris Manhertz (shoulder), and running back Cam Skattebo (shoulder) are all expected to play. Thomas has been managing his injury through decreased practice reps, while Nabers is still working his way back from ACL and meniscus surgery. It will be interesting to see if the shoulder injury limits Skattebo’s physical running style, or if the Giants shift more of the load to Najee Harris , Tyrone Tracy , or Devin Singletary . The Giants have no players with a listed game status beyon Pinnock and Golston. title: Giants-Commanders matchup: Can the Giants contain QB Jayden Daniels?
summary: The New York Giants travel down I-95 this weekend to take on the Washington Commanders. The Giants are carrying a 3-1 record and are currently in sole possession of first place in the division, while the Commanders are 1-3 and in last place. Despite that, the Commanders are 3.5-point favorites over the Giants at home. […]
full_text: ﻿The New York Giants defense | Getty Images The New York Giants travel down I-95 this weekend to take on the Washington Commanders. The Giants are carrying a 3-1 record and are currently in sole possession of first place in the division, while the Commanders are 1-3 and in last place. Despite that, the Commanders are 3.5-point favorites over the Giants at home. Both of these teams are already beat up and have lost core players to injury. However, one significant difference is that Jayden Daniels decided to forego surgery on his dislocated elbow in order to return this season, while Jaxson Dart had to have season-ending surgery on his knee. Daniels is back and practicing fully, and is almost certain to get the start against the Giants. The Commanders are counting on Daniels to turn their season around and get them in the divisional hunt. The Giants, meanwhile, are looking to build on the momentum of one of the most exciting defensive performances we’ve seen in some time. The defensive turnaround Rarely do we get to see an in-game turnaround like we saw from the Giants’ defense against the Cardinals’ offense. The Cardinals’ first two drives were difficult to watch from the Giants’ perspective. Then the second quarter hit and it was as though a switch had been flipped, and while the same players were on the field, the Giants’ play was very different. The actual schematic differences were somewhat subtle, but they had a profound impact. The Giants used man coverage rules on the first two drives, but then switched to much more Cover 1 with press man coverage in the second quarter. The look was similar, however the rules are different and the secondary played more aggressively. Likewise, Wilson began using more A and B-gap pressures. While he continued to walk Tremaine Edmunds and Arvell Reese up to the line, there was an effective blitz disguise that dropped the walk player back into coverage while the other blitzed from the second level. That isn’t a common path for NFL defenses, but the Giants’ speed made it possible. Likewise, the defensive front played less to eat blocks, or stack and shed them, and more to penetrate into the backfield. That helped disrupt the Cardinals’ off-tackle runs before they could develop. Washington’s offense with Jayden Daniels This is yet another game in which the Giants’ defense doesn’t have much tape to go on. The Commanders have played four games so far, which does give the Giants a fair amount of tape on the general shape of new OC David Blough. There are enough similarities between Jayden Daniels and Marcus Mariota that the tape with Mariota at starting quarterback is still useful for the Giants. However, it still isn’t quite the same as tape of Daniels. He’s his own man, with his own strengths, weaknesses, preferences, and tendencies. And unfortunately for the Giants, there are only 109 snaps worth of tape on Daniels in Blough’s offense. That’s not nothing, but it’s also not a ton to go on. Going back to Week 1 against the Philadelphia Eagles, there were some notable trends. First and foremost, the Commanders primarily played out of the shotgun, using zone blocking schemes in more condensed formations. Outside zone seemed to be their bread and butter, with a sprinkling of inside zone and misdirection eye-candy to spice things up. We should expect a steady diet of outside zone runs from Washington as they test the perimeter of the Giants’ defense after the Cardinals’ early success there. Washington hasn’t run the ball particularly well this year, averaging 4.2 yards per carry and scoring just 1 touchdown on the ground. Bill Crosky-Merritt is their most frequent runner, carrying the ball 56 times so far, but he’s also only averaging 2.8 yards per attempt. The quarterback run game is much more dangerous, with Daniels averaging 8.3 yards per attempt on 12 rushes. Against the Eagles, Daniels scrambled three times for 29 yards, while his two designed runs only totaled 2 yards. It’s worth noting that both of those plays were read-option runs and they came in the Red Zone, so that’s something of which the Giants will need to be alert. Washington’s passing game was primarily in the short-to-intermediate area of the field. That’s likely due to a couple factors. First and foremost is the nature of Vic Fangio’s defense in Philadelphia limiting vertical passing. Likewise, the Commanders need to account for the loss of left tackle Laremy Tunsil to injury. 2024 third-round pick Brandon Coleman has moved from left guard to left tackle, and has allowed a team-high 14 pressures (sixth-most in the NFL). Coleman is an obvious target for the Giants’ pass rush, and the Commanders will likely try to help him with double-teams, chips, and quick passes. We don’t know the status of receivers Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs as of this writing. Neither of them practiced to start the week and both are dealing with hamstring injuries and could miss the game. Their absence would leave rookie Antonio Williams and Dyami Brown was Daniels’ top targets in the passing game. Williams is both quick and fast, as well as a natural catcher of the ball and a threat to pick up yards after the catch. That said, he’s a bit undersized at 5-foot-11, 187 pounds, and it wouldn’t be a surprise to see the Commanders try to get him matched up on Dru Phillips or a safety. If McLaurin and Diggs are both out, we’ll likely see Daniels distribute the ball to Williams as the primary option, followed by tight end Chig Okonkwo and backs Rachaad White and Crosky-Merritt (both of whom are dealing with injuries as well). If Washington’s two veteran receivers don’t play, we might see quite a bit of Deonte Banks covering Okonkwo after his success against Trey McBride last week. The big confounding factor in all of this is that we don’t know precisely what wrinkles Blough has in store with Daniels at quarterback. Just how much of their offense is, as yet, unseen — and how the Giants respond — will be one of the major pivot-points in this game. How to play a Daniels-led offense? This is, of course, the question facing the Giants this week. We saw just how much faster and just plain better the Giants played in the final three quarters against the Cardinals. Playing press-man coverage, mixing pressure looks, and attacking the offense ignited the Giants’ defense and allowed them to smother a talented Cardinals’ offense. The X-factor in all this is Daniels and his legs. Daniels is a talented passer, but his mobility is what maximizes his arm talent. The question the Giants will have to answer is just how mobile Daniels will be. Playing pressure defense and attacking gaps creates opportunities for mobile quarterbacks. Missed or evaded tackle attempts are opportunities to scramble and extend plays, or pick up yards on the ground. Likewise, man coverage plays to the Giants’ strengths in the secondary, however that also takes eyes out of the backfield and makes the secondary slower to react to quarterback runs. The answer has traditionally been to spy the quarterback, and that’s a viable route for the Giants. The duo of Tremaine Edmunds and Arvell Reese are among the longest and most athletic linebacker duos in the NFL. They can cover a lot of ground, and are secure tackles when they arrive. That could make them effective counters against Daniels on the ground. Taking things a step further, Wilson could make use of simulated pressures. Walking Reese, Edmunds, or both, up to the A or B-gaps to show pressure before backing them off into coverage will help to muddy Daniels’ reads and confuse their battered offensive line’s protection calls. Likewise, a Fire Zone blitz that sends a fifth rusher but creates a layered defense behind the pressure could give the Giants the ability to use their athletic rushers without compromising their ability to cover behind it. Mixing simulated pressures, smart blitzes, and Green Dog (ie: a blitzer only rushing if a running back stays in to pass protect)…
