title: Giants-Commanders matchup: When the Giants have the football
summary: The 3-1 Giants travel to Washington to play the 1-3 Commanders, who will receive starting quarterback Jayden Daniels back. The 2024 Rookie of the Year is returning from a dislocated left elbow. Washington is favored by three-and-a-half points, and the Over/Under is set at 43.5 points. The Commanders are returning from London, where the Indianapolis […]
full_text: Malik Nabers | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The 3-1 Giants travel to Washington to play the 1-3 Commanders, who will receive starting quarterback Jayden Daniels back. The 2024 Rookie of the Year is returning from a dislocated left elbow. Washington is favored by three-and-a-half points, and the Over/Under is set at 43.5 points. The Commanders are returning from London, where the Indianapolis Colts defeated them 30-13; Washington had to play rookie third-stringer Athan Kaliakmanis at quarterback after Marcus Mariota suffered a knee injury in the first half. Washington has won the last four matchups against the Giants. New York leads the series 108-75-5. Team statistics (And a persepctive on the Giants’ pass rush) The Commanders surrender the third-most points ( 122 ) and the 15th-most yards allowed ( 1,344 ). They allow the eighth-most passing yards (970) and are tied for the most passing touchdowns surrendered, with 11. Dan Quinn’s unit, coached by first-year defensive coordinator Daronte Jones, has the sixth-best run defense in the league per yard allowed; they allowed 374 yards through four games, for 4 yards per carry. Quinn’s team has the fewest penalties accepted this year — they have only 19 penalties against them. They are third in blitz rate, with a 36.8% blitz rate and sixth in pressure percentage . The Giants have been a topic of discussion in pressure and sacks this season, since they rank last in both through four games. Here are some thoughts on that: The Giants are last in sacks (3) and last in pressure% (22%)…but how do we effectively qualify how good the Giants’ pass rush is when every offensive game plan was constructed to mitigate it? Quick passes. Get the football out fast. Don’t hold onto the ball. Avoid… — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) October 7, 2026 Defensive personnel As for the Commanders, they’ve been pressuring opposing quarterbacks. Odafe Oweh and Darone Payne both had four pressures against Daniel Jones and the Colts. Oweh and Payne lead the team with 12 pressures, and K’Lavon Chaisson has 11. Javon Kinlaw, Charles Omenihu, and Dorance Armstrong each have six pressures, while star rookie linebacker Sonny Styles has five with a sack. Washington has a solid front that lacks star-power names other than Daron Payne. Kinlaw and Omenihu play alongside Payne, with Tim Settle and Shy Tuttle as rotational defensive linemen. Oweh and Chaisson are the primary edge rushers, with long-time Quinn favorite Dorance Armstrong as the third rusher. Rookie Joshua Josephs has also played 53 snaps over four games. Linebacker Frankie Luvu has four pressures on the year, but he missed Weeks 2 and 3. Luvu plays a hybrid linebacker/edge role; he returned in Week 4 against the Colts. Second-year sixth-round pick Kain Medrano, out of UCLA, has played in Luvu’s absence, and he recorded an important interception in Washington’s impressive Week 3 win over Seattle. Sonny Styles is the fulcrum of the defense and is playing quality football. Sonny Styles has been a PROBLEM for some of the NFL’s most dangerous RB’s. Styles has recorded 3 STOPS against both Jonathan Taylor and Saquon Barkley. The Commanders rookie LB is already one of the BEST run-stoppers in the NFL 😳😈 pic.twitter.com/qWDO9mzRLZ — Rookie Watch (@RookieWatxh) October 5, 2026 Arvell Reese’s former teammate is a good football player that the Giants’ offense must account for on Sunday. Off-season signing Leo Chenal suffered a neck fracture in Week 3 and is out. Washington likes to use three-safety sets. A three-safety defense against the heavier Giants’ offense could struggle against the run. Safety Percy Butler played 19 of his 32 snaps on Sunday. While Quan Martin and Jeremy Reaves played 59 and 53, respectively. Safety Nick Cross was out the last two weeks; early optimism suggests he may play on Sunday. The cornerback position is manned by Rasul Douglas and Amik Robertson. Mike Sainristil struggled early in the season and was benched. The former second-round pick played just five snaps against the Colts. 2025 second-round pick Tre Amos is on the I.R. with a fractured fibula. Fabian Moreau played 26 snaps against the Colts. Washington’s corner room is being held down by journeymen. The matchup With Jameis Winston as the listed starter, the Giants are using a heavier personnel package ( more than 11 ) at a 62% rate, with 27% of that being 22 personnel, meaning two tight ends, a running back, and Patrick Ricard at full-back. Of the 62%, only 12% is 12 personnel. The Giants are a beefy team that wants to establish the run. This will lead to more base looks from Washington, which removes a nickel and puts Tim Settle on the line of scrimmage between Daron Payne and an edge defender. The Colts ran 11% at a high 47% rate and 12 personnel at a rate of 42%. The Giants will be a different challenge for the Commanders, but can New York effectively establish the run against Washington? The Colts ran well against Washington’s nickel looks; Jonathan Taylor averaged 4.8 yards per carry, and Seth McGowan averaged 5.2 yards per carry. The Giants, though, have struggled to run the football. They averaged 3.1 yards per carry against the Cardinals, and the running backs averaged 3.9 yards per carry against the Titans — both wins. New York should look to keep the run defense honest with misdirections, counters, or jet sweeps, as they did in Week 3 with Darnell Mooney, which resulted in a nine-yard gain. Getting to that early, against an aggressive defense like Washington, could work for a chunk gain; or perhaps a few drives in after showing jet-motion from 12 personnel. New York used EMPTY 13 personnel to spread the defense out and create mismatches for the No. 3 ( innermost) receiver against zone coverage. New York scored two touchdowns in the red zone this way on Sunday, and it was refreshing to see the success of the strategy for the run-heavy team with a second-string quarterback who has struggled in the red zone. The Commanders have more athletic ability at their second level than the Cardinals, though. The Giants will likely go to these looks, but it may not be as successful as it was in Week 4. Malik Nabers should remain the focal point of the passing attack, and his usage should expand across the formation. Malachi Fields is an asset on the outside in a winnable matchup when up against Robertson, who is 5’8. Robertson starts on the right side and has been Quinn’s best cornerback, but the size difference is noteworthy. Robertson is aggressive by the line of scrimmage; New York could look for a double-move or fake screen to bait a mistake and create explosive plays off the top. New York can look to their matchups when facing man coverage, specifically Fields, Isaiah Likely, and Malik Nabers. Far-hash throws are another thing the Giants could use to attack Quinn if the veteran coach opts for Cover-6 looks that leave the deep curl/flat vacated to the field. I would love it if the Giants leaned on Cam Skattebo a bit more in this game. Najee Harris and Skattebo essentially split time and touches until the former fumbled. Then there’s Tyrone Tracy Jr. The Giants should keep using him in the package between the 10-25 yard line on the opponent’s side of the field. New York tried to run RB-Corner routes out of shotgun against Cover 3; it’s a look they used in the preseason with Tracy too. Isaiah Likely’s usage should remain — keep using him in the short/intermediate parts of the field as an easy target with high-YAC upside. Final thoughts The Commanders are a respectable team who, much like the Giants, are bitten by the injury bug. A divisional road win is incredibly valuable. The Giants’ offense must play mistake-free football. Winston must operate with better discernment and play poised in the pocket, while the backs need to hold onto the football. It won’t be easy, but I have the Giants winning, 20-16.
author: Nick Falato

title: Arvell Reese vs. Sonny Styles: Which rookie linebacker has been, will be, better?
summary: Arvell Reese of the New York Giants is the reigning NFL Rookie of the Week. He leads the NFL with 26 solo tackles in four games. He is the second choice behind Jacob Rodriguez of the Miami Dolphins in ESPN’s current Defensive Rookie of the Year odds. Everything about the 21-year-old Reese screams star in […]
full_text: Arvell Reese | Getty Images Arvell Reese of the New York Giants is the reigning NFL Rookie of the Week. He leads the NFL with 26 solo tackles in four games. He is the second choice behind Jacob Rodriguez of the Miami Dolphins in ESPN’s current Defensive Rookie of the Year odds . Everything about the 21-year-old Reese screams star in the making, if he isn’t already. Reese says he wants to be a “game-changer” and “dominant player.” News flash, Arvell! You’re already there. Maybe the Giants should send flowers to the New York Jets, Arizona Cardinals, and Tennessee Titans — the three teams who picked ahead of the Giants at No. 5 in the 2026 NFL Draft — for leaving Reese available to them. In an alternate world, though, the Giants could have Washington Commanders inside linebacker Sonny Styles playing next to Tremaine Edmunds. Head coach John Harbaugh said after Round 1 of the draft that GM Joe Schoen “ran about a zillion mocks” and getting Reese was a scenario that “didn’t come up. This was one one that was really anticipated.” It was Styles, Reese’s Ohio State teammate and an athletic freak just learning the linebacker position after starting his collegiate career as a safety, who was the consensus choice for the Giants with the fifth pick. The way Styles has played thus far, it looks like both could be difference-making stars for years to come. What the stats say Player Tackles TFL INT PD FF Times Blitzed Pressures Missed tackles Passer rating PFF grade PFSN Impact Score Reese 34 (27 solo) 3 1 4 0 10 2 2.90% 79.3 77.1 (5th overall) 86.6 (4th) Styles 20 (11 solo) 2 1 2 1 19 5 16.70% 35.4 76.9 (6th) 79.2 (21st) What the experts say To get some perspective on both players with them meeting as opponents for the first time on Sunday, I turned to a variety of analysts for thoughts on both players. Below, their thoughts. Cole VanWeichen, Land Grant Holy Land (SB Nation’s Ohio State site) “In my opinion both have looked like top 10 picks so far, but Reese has been the one who’s really jumped off the screen. His game against Arizona was the kind of performance that makes you sit up. He was everywhere, breaking up passes, coming down with an interception and flying to the football. What I love is that he looks completely comfortable already. He plays fast, he plays with confidence, and the Giants are trusting him to do a little bit of everything, which is exactly how Ohio State used him. “Styles has been a bit quieter, but I’m not worried. He’s still a converted safety learning the finer points of playing linebacker, and the high-level flashes are already there. He’s already forced a fumble and picked a pass off. Once the game slows down for him, I think he’s going to be a really good player for a long time. “The biggest surprise for me has been how quickly Reese has become an every down guy. 2025 was his first full season as a starter in Columbus, and there were real questions about whether he was more of an edge rusher or an off-ball linebacker. So far the answer looks like he can be both. “At Ohio State, it’s honestly close. Styles was the heartbeat of that defense, but Reese’s 2025 season was special, and I always thought he had the higher ceiling. If I had to choose, I’d lean Reese as the better single season, Styles as the better career (kind of cheating). “As for the Giants, I think they made the right call. It’s early, and I fully expect both guys to be long time starters, but Reese is already playing like a Defensive Rookie of the Year candidate. Washington getting Styles two picks later looks like great value too, and this might be one of those rare cases where both teams got it right.” Nick Baumgardner (draft analyst, The Athletic) “I think both Reese and Styles are playing really well right now, improving with each week. Styles is probably a tick ahead as a coverage defender right now and while he’s been slightly more productive as a pass rusher, it’s important to remember a few things. The Giants started Reese, a younger player, at a position (stack LB) where he was sort of part-time last season. He’s needed a bit more time to adjust there as Styles is simply playing the spot he had in college. “Long-term, I still think Reese is going to be the more impactful front-seven defender. Styles, however, has an elite coverage ceiling. We’ve already seen a bit of that from Dan Quinn and the Commanders. And, remember: Styles used to be a safety in college. That piece is more natural for him. Whereas rushing the passer and stopping the run is where Reese will ultimately thrive.” Justin Melo (Draft on SI) I gave Melo three questions about Reese and Styles. Here they are, with his answers. Can you assess the play of each thus far? Has one been better than the other? “Both Arvell Reese and Sonny Styles have looked like potential Defensive Rookie of the Year winners. We’d give the slight edge to Reese, who is showcasing the same playmaking versatility that made him so dominant at Ohio State. Were the Giants right to take Reese over Styles? “The Giants should feel vindicated in their decision to take Reese over Styles.” Long-term, which guy would you rather have? “Reese’s versatility makes him the better long-term asset. He can play off-ball LB, and has also shown the capability to rush off the edge. There’s so much a creative defensive coordinator can do with Arvell Reese.” Andrew York (SB Nation’s Hogs Haven ) This is specifically about Styles. “Sonny Styles has been amazing and already looks like he’ll be a star on defense for many years to come. At first in the preseason, he seemed a bit hesitant and afraid to trust his first read, but quickly improved his reaction time and his tremendous athletic measurables have really shown up. He’s been a very strong tackler showing sideline-to-sideline speed and can limit runs anywhere on the field. He’s also shown to be very good in coverage, like this play where he ran step-for-step with Seahawks RB Jadarian Price to break up a pass. He’s also shown to be a dangerous blitzer, like in this play where he ran straight through Saquon Barkley to sack Jalen Hurts. He’s good at everything you’d want a LB to do and hasn’t shown any obvious weaknesses. “In addition to his presence in games, I’ve also been impressed by how he carries and presents himself off the field. He seems very humble, serious, hard-working, and simply eager to be a good teammate and improve himself. He has a mindset that I think will age extremely well in the NFL. He actually reminds me of how Bobby Wagner spoke and acted when he was here, though without Wagner’s aura of accomplishment.” A little something extra As a bonus, here is something Bill Barnwell of ESPN wrote this week in making Reese his current favorite for Defensive Rookie of the Year: Reese is a very scary player. He has been on the field for over 99% of the defensive snaps for the Giants, opening the year in what has primarily been an off-ball linebacker role while leading the league in solo tackles (27). With Brian Burns suffering a season-ending torn ACL, though, the Giants moved Reese onto the line of scrimmage more often against the Cardinals in Week 4, with their first-round pick playing more than 46% of his defensive snaps as an edge defender, up from 34% over the first three weeks. The operative phrase with Reese is going to be “stuffing the stat sheet,” and we’re already getting there. Against the Cardinals, Reese recorded his third tackle for loss of the season, batted down a pass and caught an interception off a deflection at the line of scrimmage. Another Reese pressure on a blitz from the second level hit Jacoby Brissett as he threw and produced a pick by Greg Newsome II on an underthrown ball. Reese isn’t the Micah Parsons-esque pass rusher Giants fans might have hoped they were landing when he fell to the fifth pick of this year’s draft, but New York probably doesn’t beat Arizona on Sunday without him being the best player on the field. Final thoughts It looks like both teams…

title: Giants’ center Bryan Hudson ‘ready to take advantage of every rep that I get’
summary: Sometimes, an unheralded NFL player just needs to be in the right place at the right time to get — and capitalize on — an opportunity. For New York Giants center Bryan Hudson this might be that right-place, right-time opportunity. After going undrafted in 2024, Hudson bounced from the Detroit Lions to the New England […]
full_text: Bryan Hudson | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Sometimes, an unheralded NFL player just needs to be in the right place at the right time to get — and capitalize on — an opportunity. For New York Giants center Bryan Hudson this might be that right-place, right-time opportunity. After going undrafted in 2024, Hudson bounced from the Detroit Lions to the New England Patriots to the Giants. He sat on the Giants’ practice for half of the 2024 season and all of 2025, playing in two games for a grand total of just three offensive snaps in 2025. Hudson, 25, looked ticketed for a return to the Giants’ practice squad this season, but as the summer wore on he surpasses Lucas Patrick and earned a roster spot at the Giants’ backup center. “It’s definitely been quite the journey, from right out of college, from my first two years, but, it all happens for a reason,” Hudson said during a quiet moment at his locker on Wednesday. “And, you know, I’m very grateful that, the good Lord has put me on the path that he has, that everything that has happened and will happen happens for a reason, even though maybe at the time it may not be what I would like or what I thought would happen for like my first two years in the NFL. “But, I’m just thankful for the perspective that the Lord has given me about just being able to stay the course and trust him and just be able to be ready to take advantage of every rep that I get and be able to be ready whenever my number is called for the team.” Hudson got his first chance to start in Week 4 against the Arizona Cardinals, with the Giants using John Michael Schmitz’s absence from practice for a couple of days due to the birth of a child as an opening to get him on the field. He did not waste it. Hudson did not surrender a sack or pressure against the Cardinals, and his 73.8 Pro Football Focus grade was sixth-best among centers. His 82.7 Pro Football and Sports Network Impact score was best among Giants’ offensive linemen and 17th among 167 offensive linemen graded in Week 4. “I felt really good,” Hudson said. “Very thankful for the opportunity and just to be able to step up in the role that my team needs me in for the week. I’m just really thankful for that. “It felt really good to be out there. It was a lot of fun to be out there playing with those guys. A lot of stuff to clean up as a unit and personally, but I feel like it was a good, solid start.” Offensive coordinator Matt Nagy agreed. “Just came in and just did really, really well in the run game and in the pass game,” Nagy said. “It’s something that we knew and saw going back to training camp. He’s always done a great job with us, so we were not surprised the way he played. We just got to keep that going. We needed that.” Head coach John Harbaugh has been non-committal about whether Hudson would start Sunday against the Washington Commanders, or if Schmitz would return to that role. Based on what we’re hearing and seeing from Giants practice this week, though, Hudson could be in line to start again. In an odd twist, Patrick is now the starting center for Washington. “He one-thousand percent helped me a ton on and off the field, really,” Hudson said of Patrick. “I think, especially with him being early in his career in a similar position as I am and have been, he was able to give me really, really good perspective and really, really good advice and guidance about just how to go about things, how to take steps towards making a team, and just getting better at the center position from his experience. He was a tremendous help to me.” Hudson smiled when I told him that Giants fans really don’t know him, following that by asking what he would like to tell them about the kind of player he is. “Just the kind of player that I’ve always tried to be is, for one, especially being at the center position, just well-prepared, a guy that’s smart and able to communicate and get everybody on the same page consistently, just kind of stay pretty level-headed in all situations, not get too high or too low at that position I think is important, so I feel like I am that,” he said. “And at the end of the day, just a physical football player. “At the offensive line position, that’s one of the key things and something that I think we all bring to the table, everybody in this room, and me personally, just somebody that’s smart, physical, and going to be consistent all the time.” If he can be that, and consistently play the way he did in Week 4 against the Cardinals, Giants fans will be very happy to have him.
author: Ed Valentine

title: NY Giants news: Dennard Wilson on Tae Banks, Arvell Reese named Rookie of the Week
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know about as rhe Giants will meet the Washington Commanders this weekend. Giants standout says ‘bad things’ are coming for Commanders QB Jayden Daniels | NJ.com Abdul Carter is well aware that he has just one sack through four games this season […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know about as rhe Giants will meet the Washington Commanders this weekend. Giants standout says ‘bad things’ are coming for Commanders QB Jayden Daniels | NJ.com Abdul Carter is well aware that he has just one sack through four games this season — and five through his first 21 NFL games. He also doesn’t really care because he knows how he is impacting quarterbacks with his consistent pressure. “I do think sacks are overrated,” the Giants outside linebacker told NJ.com. “Obviously, it looks the best — getting to the quarterback and getting that negative play. But at the same time, when you hit a quarterback, they feel it. They don’t want to get hit. It forces them to make quick decisions, and they might throw a turnover. ESPN Insider praises Carter, Reese Arvell Reese and Abdul Carter look like legit superstars to me. pic.twitter.com/F02wFnXaVT — Mina Kimes (@minakimes) October 8, 2026 Giants’ Malik Nabers reminds Matt Nagy of Travis Kelce in all the right ways | New York Post “I was around a very similar player talent-wise and person-wise in Travis Kelce,” Nagy said before Thursday’s practice. “He was a guy who wanted the ball a lot, and he had great ways on how to let you know how to do it.” Head coach John Harbaugh actually relayed through the headset that Nabers wanted more targets, as seen on NFL Films. “I do really like it as long as it’s done the right way,” Nagy said. “Malik is without a doubt one of the most talented players – not just receivers – I’ve ever been around. On top of that, he’s probably one of the most competitive. You morph those together and you have somebody that sometimes that may happen. Don’t ever take that away from a player. You are crazy if you take that away from somebody. Don’t ever try to not get him the football.” Highest-graded rookie of the Week: LB Arvell Reese, New York Giants | PFF.com When he wasn’t causing havoc at the line of scrimmage, Reese still made an impact in the passing game. Four of his five tackles resulting in a defensive stop came in coverage, where he looked anything but a rookie, decisively chasing down receivers after the catch. Against the run, Reese looked confident taking on blocks. Along with his tackle resulting in a defensive stop, he recorded multiple wins in the run game where he didn’t make the tackle but still impacted the play. J.J. McCarthy gets high marks from Matt Nagy Matt Nagy says that J.J. McCarthy has been an "A+" when it comes to learning the Giants' offense pic.twitter.com/7F5Vga7VKv — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) October 8, 2026 2026 NFL quarter-season awards: MVP picks, top rookies, OPOY, DPOY, best coaches | ESPN.com Defensive Rookie of the Year. 1. Arvell Reese, LB/Edge, New York Giants. Reeseis a very scary player. He has been on the field for over 99% of the defensive snaps for the Giants, opening the year in what has primarily been an off-ball linebacker role while leading the league in solo tackles (27). With Brian Burns suffering a season-ending torn ACL, though, the Giants moved Reese onto the line of scrimmage more often against the Cardinals in Week 4, with their first-round pick playing more than 46% of his defensive snaps as an edge defender, up from 34% over the first three weeks. The operative phrase with Reese is going to be “stuffing the stat sheet,” and we’re already getting there. Against the Cardinals, Reese recorded his third tackle for loss of the season, batted down a pass and caught an interception off a deflection at the line of scrimmage. Another Reese pressure on a blitz from the second level hit Jacoby Brissett as he threw and produced a pick by Greg Newsome II on an underthrown ball. Reese isn’t the Micah Parsons-esque pass rusher Giants fans might have hoped they were landing when he fell to the fifth pick of this year’s draft, but New York probably doesn’t beat Arizona on Sunday without him being the best player on the field. McCarthy compared to what it would be with Jaxson Dart. Dart’s season-ending knee injury could also have residual effects on the franchise beyond this season. title: Scouting Jets linebacker Trevin Wallace
summary: The Jets recently acquired former Panthers linebacker Trevin Wallace, who has already been active a few times due to injuries at linebacker. Today, we break Wallace down in detail. The 23-year old Wallace is listed at 6’1” and 237 pounds and was a third round pick out of Kentucky in 2024. He has started 20 […]
full_text: CANTON, OHIO - AUGUST 06: Trevin Wallace #32 of the Carolina Panthers looks on during the first quarter of the 2026 Pro Football Hall of Fame Game against the Arizona Cardinals at Tom Benson Hall Of Fame Stadium on August 06, 2026 in Canton, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images The Jets recently acquired former Panthers linebacker Trevin Wallace, who has already been active a few times due to injuries at linebacker. Today, we break Wallace down in detail. The 23-year old Wallace is listed at 6’1” and 237 pounds and was a third round pick out of Kentucky in 2024. He has started 20 games in his NFL career, racking up 125 tackles, seven tackles for loss, four pass breakups and three sacks. Background Wallace was a four-star recruit coming out of high school and headed to Kentucky where he saw action in 12 games as a true freshman, albeit with just one start. He had 32 tackles, four tackles for loss and two sacks. His role increased in 2022 as he started six of 12 games and racked up 54 tackles, 5.5 tackles for loss, 2.5 sacks and two interceptions. In 2023, he became a full-time starter and had 80 tackles, 8.5 tackles for loss and 5.5 sacks. Having decided to enter the 2024 NFL draft, Wallace attended the scouting combine and was eventually drafted by the Carolina Panthers with the 72nd overall pick. The Panthers had planned to bring Wallace along slowly as a rookie but injuries forced him into a bigger role than they intended, exposing his rawness at times. In 13 appearances, he made eight starts and had 64 tackles and two forced fumbles. In 2025, he started in all 12 of his appearances and had 61 tackles, five tackles for loss, four pass breakups and two sacks. This year, Wallace was competing for a starting role during training camp but then was relegated to backup after the Panthers signed Bobby Okereke. This led to him being waived after preseason. The Jets claimed Wallace off waivers after final cuts, but initially opted to leave him as a healthy scratch as they had just four active off-ball linebackers in week one and then elevated Troy Reeder over him in week two. He’s been active for the past two games, albeit only seeing action on special teams. Let’s move onto some more in-depth analysis of what Wallace brings to the table, based on in-depth research and film study. Measurables/Athleticism Wallace isn’t very tall but has adequate size and length for the linebacker position. He is a former track athlete and impressed with his workout numbers at the combine as he ran a 4.50 in the 40-yard dash and posted excellent explosiveness numbers. At his pro day, he showcased good strength with 20 bench press reps. Usage Wallace showcased athleticism and versatility in high school as he saw time as a wide receiver, running back and even at quarterback on offense. At the collegiate and NFL levels, he has been employed as an off-ball linebacker and didn’t match up in the slot or out wide, or creep up to the edge, very often. Run defense As a run defender, Wallace’s strengths lie more in pursuit going sideline-to-sideline than plugging gaps between the tackles. According to analysis site Pro Football Focus, his run defense grades improved during his college career but have been poor at the NFL level. Coverage skills Wallace’s athletic ability can be an asset in coverage and his numbers haven’t been too bad. He showed some playmaking ability with three interceptions in his college career and four pass breakups last season. However, he can be flat-footed in coverage and his route recognition is lacking at times. At the NFL level he has given up three plays of longer than 30 yards and four touchdowns in his first two seasons. Tackling Wallace has been a relatively productive tackler and his tackle efficiency numbers are acceptable although he does miss tackles from time to time. He closes and hits strongly and with good technique, and can stop a runner in his tracks. He forced two fumbles in his college career and has already forced two at the NFL level as well. Blitzing Wallace has a good knack for blitzing, as evidenced by his 10 sacks in three seasons in college, which included 5.5 in his final season. He has three in two seasons at the NFL level. He also had one in preseason this year. His pressure rates have been solid too, but nothing spectacular, although he shows good timing both on pass rushes and run blitzes. Special teams Wallace has already seen action on special teams with the Jets and was credited with one tackle in his first two appearances. He also made a couple of good contributions to force return men to redirect in the Bears game. He has some good experience on all units apart from the placekicking unit, although he didn’t play special teams because he was a full-time starter last year. His production at the NFL level hasn’t been anything special with just two tackles and one penalty for holding so far but he’s shown some promise here and there. He had five special teams tackles and one penalty in college but did have one major highlight when he returned a blocked field goal for a touchdown. He actually returned some kicks and punts in high school. Physicality As noted, Wallace is not at his best between the tackles and can struggle to get off blocks, so he’s at his best when kept clean. He hasn’t had any defensive penalties at the NFL level and only had two in his college career. Instincts/Intelligence Wallace was very raw when he first made it to the NFL and has had some issues with play recognition and getting caught up in traffic. He can also be susceptible to play fakes and misdirection. However, he has also made some instinctive plays during his career, including recovering to break up this trick play against the Jets. His football IQ has been praised and he was even called upon to wear the headset and the green dot during his rookie season, making him the second-youngest player in the NFL to be doing that at the time. He also took over these duties within his second season, which initially led to a major improvement in the Panthers defense and a couple of wins, which teammates and coaches said he was a key factor in. Amusingly, other players said they struggled with him relaying calls initially because of his thick southern accent, but he was able to overcome this by using his “business voice”. Even so, they took those duties away from him in preseason and he suggested he prefers that because it means he can focus more on what he is doing. Attitude Wallace is a mature player with a good work ethic and a team-first attitude. He was a team captain at Kentucky. As noted, his on-field discipline is solid with just four penalties in his NFL and college careers combined, two of which were on special teams. Injuries Wallace’s first two seasons at the NFL level were disrupted by shoulder issues. He was placed on injured reserve at the end of his rookie season, missing the last four games, and then missed multiple games in his second season before returning and then re-aggravating the injury. At that stage, the Panthers opted to shut him down so he could get season-ending surgery. He had wanted to play through it, though. Rehab from the shoulder surgery also limited Wallace during the following spring. In college, Wallace missed the 2022 opener and one 2023 game due to undisclosed injuries. He was also limited to just four appearances in his junior year of high school due to injuries. Scheme Fit It seems most likely that Wallace would back up Jamien Sherwood on the Jets’ current depth chart. While he does have some experience of playing Demario Davis’ position, this role would probably be better suited to Reeder, given their respective skill-sets. For now, though, both will just be available for special teams. He was a teammate of current Jets quarterback Will Levis at Kentucky. Conclusions When Wallace was acquired, the assumption was that a young former third round pick would have some…

full_text: Aug 21, 2026; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA; New York Jets wide receiver Adonai Mitchell (15) warms up before the game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Where the hell is Adonai Mitchell? Seriously, have you seen him? His family must be worried sick! We definitely saw him through the first two weeks of the season, but he has been MIA since. ESPN’s Rich Cimini said on the “Jets Collective” podcast that he heard Mitchell’s finger is “broken.” Head coach Aaron Glenn denied that. We’ve got a good old-fashioned western standoff. “Well, the Jets have been pretty tight-lipped on this one, but clearly it’s not your run-of-the-mill sprained finger. I mean, if it were a sprained finger or something of that nature, he would have been out there taped up. We all saw the giant cast on his hand,” Cimini explained. “It would not shock me if we find out that he had surgery. I have not seen him at all in the locker room. Usually you see a guy you know wandering through the locker room. I haven’t seen AD Mitchell in a couple of weeks since that injury.” Glenn said AD Mitchell’s finger got caught in a jersey. I’m not a doctor or anything, but did it get amputated? Caught in a meat slicer? Did he slam it in a car door? I mean, good lord! He hasn’t practiced in the first two practices ahead of the Cleveland Browns game, which means he’s likely out another week. However, next week the door opens. title: Eagles roster news: Carson Steele and Jake Majors promoted from the practice squad
summary: The Philadelphia Eagles officially announced four transactions on Friday afternoon. Here’s an overview: Let’s sort through this news on a player-by-player basis. JAKE MAJORS Of the two practice squad promotions, Majors is the more significant one because he’s expected to start at center on Sunday. With Cam Jurgens traded away and Drew Kendall out due […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 22: Carson Steele #34 of the Philadelphia Eagles jumps over Eric Butler #30 of the New England Patriots to score a touchdown during the second half of the preseason game between the Philadelphia Eagles and the New England Patriots at Gillette Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Maddie Meyer/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Philadelphia Eagles officially announced four transactions on Friday afternoon. Here’s an overview: C Jake Majors and RB Carson Steele were signed from the practice squad to the active roster. QB Andy Dalton was released. DT Uar Bernard was placed on the practice squad injured list. Let’s sort through this news on a player-by-player basis. JAKE MAJORS Of the two practice squad promotions, Majors is the more significant one because he’s expected to start at center on Sunday. With Cam Jurgens traded away and Drew Kendall out due to a knee injury, Majors is the Eagles’ third-string option at the pivot. Majors, who entered the NFL last year as an undrafted rookie free agent, will be making his NFL regular season debut on Sunday. He played better in the preseason than he did in training camp practices this summer, which isn’t really saying much. CARSON STEELE Steele was a rare fun player to watch during the Eagles’ preseason games. The running back/fullback hybrid led the team in receiving this summer with 14 receptions for 136 yards and two touchdowns. There were multiple plays where he hurdled defenders to pick up extra yardage. There was some concern another team might claim Steele on waivers after the Eagles cut him … but that didn’t happen. He instead signed to the Eagles’ practice squad, where he’s been since getting this call up. Steele figures to be RB3 behind Will Shipley and Dameon Pierce (who was also called up from the practice squad earleir this week) in Week 5 with Saquon Barkley ruled out and Tank Bigsby on injured reserve. Most of his action will probably come on special teams. ANDY DALTON According to NFL insider Mike Garafolo, the Eagles have interest in bringing Dalton back on the practice squad. Why? No. Dalton, who turns 39 later this month, just isn’t good at this point in his career. It never made sense for the Eagles to keep him as their QB2. Kudos to them for finally waking up and cutting him. But the team wasted reps while splitting them between Dalton and Tanner McKee this summer. They could’ve gone to one player to actually prepare them to be QB2. That should’ve taken a higher priority than trying to potentially flip one of Dalton or McKee for a meager trade return. Anyway, at least he’s gone for now. UAR BERNARD Bernard apparently got hurt in practice. He’ll miss some time. Putting him on this list doesn’t free up a practice squad spot since he was already not counting against the limit with his international exemption.

title: Eagles-Jaguars Final Injury Report: Saquon Barkley, DeVonta Smith among players ruled out
summary: The Philadelphia Eagles issued their third and final official injury report of the week on Friday in advance of their Week 5 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars in London. The Eagles ruled five players OUT: Saquon Barkley, DeVonta Smith, Drew Kendall, Marcus Epps, and Hollywood Brown. Barkley missed practice all week due to a hamstring […]
full_text: Feb 9, 2025; New Orleans, LA, USA; Philadelphia Eagles wide receiver DeVonta Smith (6) celebrates a touchdown with running back Saquon Barkley (26) against the Kansas City Chiefs during Super Bowl LIX at Ceasars Superdome. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Philadelphia Eagles issued their third and final official injury report of the week on Friday in advance of their Week 5 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars in London. The Eagles ruled five players OUT: Saquon Barkley, DeVonta Smith, Drew Kendall, Marcus Epps, and Hollywood Brown. Barkley missed practice all week due to a hamstring injury. With Barkley out and Tank Bigsby on injured reserve, the Eagles are down to three healthy running backs on the active roster: Will Shipley, Dameon Pierce, and Carson Steele. Pierce and Steele were called up from the practice squad this week. Both players offered some intrigue in the summer, so, it’ll be interesting to see if they can pop in regular season action. Of course, the Eagles’ offensive line situation might not really make that possible for them. Smith is missing his second game in a row due to a hamstring injury. With Smith and Brown out, the Eagles are down to five wide receivers: Dontayvion Wicks, Darius Cooper, Makai Lemon, Elijah Moore, and Britain Covey. Wicks is going to suit up despite suffering a hamstring injury on Thursday that had him limited in practice over the past two days. Cooper saw more snaps and targets than Lemon did in Week 4; it’ll be interesting to see if that’s the case again in London. Moore might see some occasional snaps on offense (as long as he can figure out what he’s supposed to be doing this time). Covey will probably be limited to punt return duty. Kendall’s absence means the Eagles will be down to their third-string center option. The Eagles called up Jake Majors from the practice squad to start in the pivot. Majors is a 2025 undrafted rookie free agent signing who has never played in an NFL regular season game. He also didn’t look very good in training camp this summer. Yikes. Epps is missing his second straight game. The Eagles will start Andrew Mukuba and Cooper DeJean at safety in base packages with DeJean moving to the slot and Michael Carter II entering the game on the back end of the defense in nickel scenarios. The Eagles ruled one player QUESTIONABLE: Jonathan Greenard. Greenard’s status is curious since he did not practice this week. Players who don’t practice rarely play in games. But he’s a veteran and maybe he’ll be able to contribute in a limited capacity. Spoke to Jonathan Greenard who didn’t practice all week with an ankle injury suffered in the Rams game. He told me he’s day-to-day and woke up feeling a lot better this morning. More so dealing with the mental frustrations of dealing with another injury and not allowing himself… — Ashlyn Sullivan (@ashlynrsullivan) October 9, 2026 Players notably listed without a game status : Jalen Hurts, Dontayvion Wicks, Dallas Goedert, Quinyon Mitchell, Zack Baun , Jihaad Campbell, Fred Johnson, E.J. Jenkins, and A.J. Epenesa. Hurts is a new addition to the report. He was a full participant in Friday’s practice but he’s listed with a calf injury. Something to keep an eye on. As previously noted, Wicks is set to play despite being less than 100%. Speaking during a Friday morning press conference, Nick Sirianni praised Wicks’ toughness. Goedert is officially back in action after missing the Eagles’ last two games. His return is certainly a positive for an undermanned offense. Look for Hurts to target him often. Will be interesting to see how the Eagles split snaps among Goedert, Zach Ertz (assuming he’s temporarily elevated from the practice squad), Johnny Mundt, and E.J. Jenkins. Speaking of Jenkins, he’s also a new addition to the report with a toe injury but he fully participated in Friday’s practice. Mitchell is ready to play after suffering a knee injury in Week 4. He was full go on Thursday and Friday. Good news for the defense. Baun is also back in action after missing Week 4 due to a concussion. He’s been cleared to play. Campbell missed some practice time this week due to a knee injury but he’s ready to suit up. We’ll see if the Eagles decrease his playing time at all while looking to get Jeremiah Trotter Jr. more involved. Vic Fangio said that much is a possibility. Johnson is back after missing multiple games. He figures to serve as the swing tackle behind Jordan Mailata and Markel Bell. He could also factor in at guard in a pinch. Epenesa is a new addition to the report with a back injury. He was limited on Friday but he’s not going to be held out due to injury. title: Lane Johnson’s championship roots began in Groveton, Texas, carving an all-time Eagles’ great
summary: Lane Johnson had a way of making everyone around him feel welcome. He has always been that way. Piled under a mountain of pads, the hulking, 6-foot-6, 335-pound perennial Eagles’ All-Pro right tackle was an anomaly since high school, part superhero, part ballerina with the way his nimble feet were able to move his massive […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 26: Lane Johnson #65 of the Philadelphia Eagles reacts after a touchdown run against the Washington Commanders during the third quarter in the NFC Championship Game at Lincoln Financial Field on January 26, 2025 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Lane Johnson had a way of making everyone around him feel welcome. He has always been that way. Piled under a mountain of pads, the hulking, 6-foot-6, 335-pound perennial Eagles’ All-Pro right tackle was an anomaly since high school, part superhero, part ballerina with the way his nimble feet were able to move his massive frame and spring out on edge rushers. He had that patented right backfire mule kick that he borrowed from Jason Peters and perfected it. He will no doubt one day be inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame for being a two-time, first-team and three-time second-team All-Pro selection, earning six Pro Bowls, winning six NFC East titles, and two Super Bowls. Five years from now, Canton, Ohio, will be covered in midnight green when Johnson gets inducted, a city paying homage to a true hero on and off the field. The fourth overall pick in the 2013 NFL Draft changed the tenor of this franchise as a parting gift from former Eagles’ coach Chip Kelly. In his 14 NFL seasons, Johnson was the cornerstone of a team that had only three losing seasons (7-9 in 2015 and 2016, and 4-11-1 in 2020). The Eagles won 66% of the time, going 122-63-1 when he played. They were 18-30 when he didn’t. His brilliance first began to shine in the dusty, sun-bitten back trail of Groveton, Texas. It seemed odd at the time that this rangy, gangly kid was surrounded by a troupe of bobbing smaller runners coming around the turn of the track. But there he was, Johnson, all feet, and churning arms, and pumping fists, standing head-and-shoulders above everyone else running the 400-meter dash. Then it was off to the field events to throw the shot put. There really wasn’t anything the tall kid from tiny Groveton High School couldn’t do. Including perfect dead-on voice impersonations. Johnson could throw the shot 50 feet and run the quarter in 49 seconds. Then go into Frank Caliendo mode and imitate his teammates and coaches. Everything with Johnson seemed to come late. He was 17 when he graduated from Groveton, a Class A school at the time located in a rural community. He was 6-foot-6 then, but he weighed 215 pounds with aspirations of playing quarterback at a major Division I level. “Lane graduated at 17 years old and he really didn’t start growing until he got out of high school,” said Kevin Parker, Groveton’s defensive coordinator who was also Johnson’s high school basketball coach. “It’s crazy what happened. He probably put on 40 pounds between the time he graduated and the fall of the next year. He began growing pretty rapidly from that point on.” Johnson’s dream was to play quarterback, but his high school coaches projected him as a tight end, if he was going to play major college football. No one was looking at Johnson as a quarterback. “Of course, Lane outgrew that position, too, once he got to Oklahoma, but he could probably still play tight end, he was phenomenal,” Parker said. “I was his basketball coach at Groveton. Lane was a good basketball player, too. We’re not very good in basketball, but we were a lot better when Lane was here. He really did everything for us, he played inside and outside. He could bring the ball up the floor. “Lane was so athletic, he used to run the quarter for us—and throw the shot put. That’s a pretty rare combination. I’m not surprised by Lane’s success through the years. There’s a great story with Lane recently. About 15 years ago, we had a linebacker here in Groveton that was a really good player. He was about 235 pounds and can run. He and Lane were really good friends. Lane was working out with him and they were picking at each other one day. The linebacker kid was saying how he could outrun Lane.” So, Parker brought them out to a track and Johnson raced the smaller—perceived faster—kid. Imagine a mini-locomotive and you have an idea of Johnson coming at you. “They literally ran five or six 40-yard dashes and the linebacker kid couldn’t touch Lane, I mean can’t even get close to him, that’s when we started to realize Lane could be really, really be something,” Parker recalled. “Lane was probably 285 pounds at that point.” Anyone around Johnson had to watch themselves though. No one was waterproof to Johnson’s impersonation wrath. One time at Oklahoma, Johnson was taped doing impressions of teammates. He needed a little time, but when he got someone down, he nailed them. His Sooner teammates kept pestering Johnson to mimic then-Sooners’ coach Bob Stoops. Johnson kept saying no. When he finally relented, he nailed Stoops’ thick Southern draw perfectly—and about that same time Stoops walked into the Oklahoma meeting room greeted by everyone erupting in laughter. It was typical Johnson. What was revealed through time, however, was not everything was a continuous riot around Johnson. The smiles and laughter hid something deeper, something he kept away from others, buried in places that only he knew. Five years ago, Johnson went public about his battles with depression and anxiety. He missed three games during the 2021 season stating it was because of a “personal matter.” He then released a statement on social media explaining why: “I would like to thank everyone for their understanding and support over the last two weeks. I appreciate the positive notes and messages as I’ve worked hard to restore my personal life. Depression and anxiety are things I’ve dealt with for a long time and have kept hidden from my friends and family. If you’re reading this and struggling, please know that you are not alone. I am excited to rejoin my teammates and coaches. I’m grateful for the entire Eagles community and look forward to continuing to play in front of [the] best fans in the world.” In many ways, it was typical Johnson, thinking about others before himself and how his message may be able to break some of the barriers that still stand when it comes to mental illness. “There are a lot of former players who are suffering, some who used to play here that I know of,” he said. “I’m not going to give any names, but they’re in pretty damn bad shape. You hate to see your old warriors — they haven’t really had a chance to live life. They’ve been playing football their whole life, and now they get out and they’re suffering. They have bad anxiety or depression. It affects their wives. It affects their children. I think there’s a lot of work that can be done in a good way, but they just need to understand the voices of the past players.” His current personal matters outweigh anything on a football field, and knowing Johnson, he was going to face them without interference. He retired without regrets from a hardboiled fanbase that came to love and appreciate a one-time gangly kid who used to run around a track to the laughter of anyone who watched. After 14 years in the NFL, Lane Johnson will pedal his fast feet to the Hall of Fame, when hopefully one day he could sit back and enjoy the good times and indelible memories of winning he provided a championship-starved city.

title: Andy Dalton released: Eagles reportedly cut veteran quarterback
summary: The Philadelphia Eagles have several roster moves to make after an interesting week, and one of those moves is reportedly releasing quarterback Andy Dalton just days ahead of the London game. Although, NFL insider Mike Garafolo reports that the move doesn’t mean an end to the QB in Philly, but the team needed the roster […]
full_text: Photo by Isaiah Vazquez/Getty Images | Getty Images The Philadelphia Eagles have several roster moves to make after an interesting week, and one of those moves is reportedly releasing quarterback Andy Dalton just days ahead of the London game. Although, NFL insider Mike Garafolo reports that the move doesn’t mean an end to the QB in Philly, but the team needed the roster spot and he could return to the practice squad — as a veteran, he isn’t subject to the waiver wire. This doesn’t close the door on Andy Dalton’s tenure with the #Eagles . They have a lot of injuries and needed his spot. Could still return, even via a practice-squad spot, a source informed says. https://t.co/ctgvUMlUDk — Mike Garafolo (@MikeGarafolo) October 9, 2026 Trading for Dalton was always a bit of a questionable move, and the Eagles probably mishandled the backup QB competition throughout the summer and training camp. After splitting reps between Dalton and Tanner McKee, the Eagles went with Dalton as QB2 for three weeks — until he threw an interception (with his one and only pass as an Eagle) against the Bears when Jalen Hurts was being evaluated for concussion . Dalton was probably a nice addition to the meeting room, with his various experience, but ultimately, the Eagles turned back to McKee for their Week 4 game against the Rams , and with other roster needs, had to evaluate keeping four quarterbacks. The team will now move forward with McKee and rookie Cole Payton behind Hurts, and will still have some other moves to make to restock their 53-man roster.

title: Eagles News: It’s Willie Lampkin time
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! Really excited to see how Willie Lampkin fares in his first NFL start. Despite his unconventional frame, he might be a pretty good player? Lampkin was the 11th-highest graded interior offensive lineman by Pro Football Focus during the 2025 preseason. He […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Willie Lampkin #61 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on against the Washington Commanders during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! Really excited to see how Willie Lampkin fares in his first NFL start. Despite his unconventional frame, he might be a pretty good player? Lampkin was the 11th-highest graded interior offensive lineman by Pro Football Focus during the 2025 preseason. He was sixth-highest in the 2026 preseason. Lampkin stood out in a good way during training camp practices and he drew unprompted praise from Lane Johnson in a conversation the former Eagles right tackle had with some reporters off to the side with no microphones or cameras after a joint training camp practice with the Patriots. Let’s see what he’s got! Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Willie Lampkin to make NFL history Sunday in first career start – NBCSP There’s never been an NFL offensive lineman built like Willie Lampkin. There’s about to be. Lampkin stands 5-foot-11, 290 pounds. And when he made his NFL debut playing four special teams snaps in the Eagles’ opener vs. the Commanders, he became the heaviest offensive lineman in NFL history under six feet. That’s a distinction previously held by Terry Long, who was 5-11, 272, and played in 105 games for the Steelers from 1984 through 1991. Now, for at least one week, Lampkin will be a starter. With Landon Dickerson not eligible to come off Injured Reserve until next week and Cam Jurgens now a Baltimore Raven, Lampkin will play regular-season offensive line snaps for the first time in his career. It may be at guard and it may be at center. Lampkin and Drew Kendall are both natural centers who got reps at guard this summer, but one of them will have to start at left guard. Most likely it will be Lampkin because you would think they wouldn’t want to move a 24-year-old Kendall to guard when he’s just starting to play well at center. Although it’s easier to hide a 5-11 guy at center than guard. So we’ll see. Either way, Lampkin on Sunday will become the Eagles’ shortest offensive line starter in 69 years, since 5-11 Abe Gibron started 12 games at left guard in 1957. There’s almost a foot between Markel Bell and Willie Lampkin. But they’ve become ‘brothers’ as O-Line careers take off. – Inquirer When the two players first met, over the summer, they realized they shared a resilient spirit. Before long, they were inseparable; “always together” at the practice facility and at the stadium, in Lampkin’s telling. “He’s like my brother, man,” the guard said of Bell. “He’s like a humble beast.” Like any brothers would, they began to engage in some good-natured ribbing, mostly about the ACC rivalry between UNC and Miami. They never faced each other, but Lampkin will never let Bell forget about the Tar Heels’ 41-31 win over the Hurricanes in October of 2023. “I always tell him that we beat them,” Lampkin said. “I got my dub over Miami.” He also gave Bell a nickname (which appears to have been borrowed from reality TV personality Alexis Radcliff). “I call him ‘Big ‘Kel not the Little One,’” Lampkin said. “He hates when I say that. I’ve heard it online and I always just say it to him. I don’t even know, I just heard it. I always be like, ‘Big ‘Kel not the Little One.’” Added Bell: “He just be trollin’, he just be trollin’. I laugh and I tell him to get out of my face.” Eagles-Jaguars Game Preview: 5 questions and answers with the Week 5 enemy – BGN 1 – The Jags are 16-5 in the Liam Coen era. What’s he done to turn this team around since Super Bowl LII champion Doug Pederson was fired? … When Coen was hired, the thought in Jacksonville was, “He seems to have the goods as a playcaller. But can he also be a culture-setter?” 18 months later, the answer is a resounding yes. Look no further than Jacksonville’s latest victory: a gritty five-point win in Cincinnati. The Bengals may not be juggernauts, but the last time the Jaguars played at their stadium (Week 2 last season), Jake Browning led a stunning second-half comeback to steal the dub. “Winning ain’t easy in this league,” Coen told the locker room after getting redemption this past week. “Do we have to clean sh t up? Absolutely. But guess what? Our culture prevailed. Our f cking toughness prevailed … The last time we were in this locker room, in a similar type situation, it wasn’t a great feeling, right? Talk about growth. Talk about us as a unit, us as an organization, what the f*ck we’re building. That’s what I’m proud of.” Jaguars vs. Eagles: Matchup History Through the Decades – Big Cat Country The Jacksonville Jaguars begin their London stretch this week against the Philadelphia Eagles. The two teams have played each other eight times, and the Eagles currently lead the series 5-3. The Jags are technically the home team this week, so let’s look at Philadelphia being defeated in Jacksonville throughout the decades. Eagles-Jaguars preview: 5 things to watch – PhillyVoice If there’s a weakness on this Jaguars team, it’s probably their offensive line. It’s just kind of an average group. But, they’re (mostly) healthy, so at least there’s that. The only injury they have is to starting RG Patrick Mekari, who has been on injured reserve all season so far. The Eagles’ defensive line has been disappointing this season. One way the Eagles can win this game is if the pass rush makes a few big plays and creates turnovers. I just don’t see it. My guess? The Jags run a conservative offense on Sunday, take what the Eagles give them, and let their talented defense shut down the Eagles’ woeful offense. NFL Week 5 preview: Picks, predictions, schedule, betting odds, fantasy tips – ESPN Bold prediction: The Jaguars will win by two touchdowns. Philadelphia is 2-2 and ranks 27th in EPA per play on offense and 25th on defense. That is rough. And in three of those games, the Eagles had the now-retired Johnson, too. We can and should think about these teams dramatically differently now than when the season began (for the Jaguars, this is a good thing!). […] Why you should watch this game: You can play a game called “how many Eagles players do I recognize?” as they take the field without Johnson (retired), TE Dallas Goedert (knee), WR DeVonta Smith (hamstring) and RB Saquon Barkley (hamstring) — and now Jurgens is a Raven! If Willie Lampkin gets the start on the now sparse offensive line, as expected, he’ll be the shortest Eagles offensive lineman (5-foot-11) to start in over 60 years. Eagles trading Cam Jurgens fully accelerates a mid-season rebuild on the offensive line | Five Thoughts – PHLY Eagles Final thought, written a few hours removed from all the commotion of the day: The Eagles find themselves fully in a transition on the offensive line now. They’ve made bets, at least in the short-term, that some combination of Lampkin, Kendall, and Bell can be part of a rebuilt group tasked with replacing one of the best collections of offensive-line talent the NFL has seen in recent memory. And they’ve made that bet having just split with one of the league’s best talent developers at the position in Jeff Stoutland. It’s fair to ask whether Roseman has done enough replenishing the offensive line for this sudden rebuild given the shaky ground Johnson, Dickerson, and Jurgens were on even entering this year’s training camp. As I said on our show Tuesday before the Jurgens trade, it’s hard to argue with any individual pick Roseman has made in each of the last few drafts, but the cumulative affect of missing out on the offensive line prospects at the latter stages of the first and second rounds over the years has now shown up. The best argument by my estimation would be in favor of taking former Arizona State tackle…

title: Steelers CB Jalen Ramsey says there is a disconnect with players and coaches
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers’ defense has struggled over the last two weeks after a strong start in Weeks 1 and 2. full_text: (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers’ defense has struggled over the last two weeks after a strong start in Weeks 1 and 2. Since Week 3, the Steelers rank 29th in EPA per play, and they have allowed 54 points. Teams have also been able to get the ball out quickly against the Steelers, as they have allowed the fourth-quickest time to throw over that span. When speaking to the media on Friday about new cornerbacks Sean Murphy-Bunting and Terell Smith, cornerback Jalen Ramsey hinted at some issues between the coaching staff and the players. “The coaches have to put [new secondary members] out there with us so we can all get on the same page,” Ramsey said via Ashley Wenskoski . “There’s a little bit of a disconnect here right now, just with what we want to do on the field and how we play as a team and together as a secondary vs. just throwing a playbook in their hands and the coaches saying ‘This is how it has to look.‘ That’s not how football works.” Ramsey continued by saying the best teams he’s been part of have been player-led. “I think Aaron said it the other day in his press conference – the best teams that I’ve been on in my career are player-led teams,” Ramsey said. “We’re the ones on the field, we’re the ones that see and feel how the game is going and the flow of the game. When we can all be on the same page, it usually brings some success. Instead of just some guys going with the flow of the game, some guys going off of experience, and some guys having a playbook stuck in their locker and have to learn by the book things that offenses nowadays in 2026 don’t give you by the book drawn up formations.” Ramsey is one of the most proven veterans on the Steelers’ roster as a multiple-time All-Pro and Super Bowl winner. His words don’t exactly hide there being a separation of feelings on the players’ side of things compared to the coaching staff, and it will be something to monitor if that unit continues to struggle. title: Seahawks-49ers game designations: Leonard Williams, Ty Okada cleared to play
summary: Ahead of the Seattle Seahawks’ most important game of the young 2026 season, the team got some welcome good news about defensive lineman Leonard Williams. The veteran anchor of the Seahawks’ front, who was battling an ankle injury he suffered last week, has no game designation for Week 5, meaning Williams is good to go […]
full_text: Ahead of the Seattle Seahawks’ most important game of the young 2026 season, the team got some welcome good news about defensive lineman Leonard Williams. The veteran anchor of the Seahawks’ front, who was battling an ankle injury he suffered last week, has no game designation for Week 5, meaning Williams is good to go against the rival San Francisco 49ers. The lack of a designation is a tad bit surprising considering Williams was limited in practice on Wednesday and was held out completely on Thursday . Yet that might have been a precaution to get Williams extra rest, as the Seahawks have a short week after playing the 49ers. Williams and the return of safety Ty Okada, who also did not have an injury designation, will be a massive boost for the Seahawks defense that is hoping to slow an undefeated 49ers offense. Seattle also got positive news on special teamer Irv Charles, who had his designation changed from out to questionable on Friday. He would have to be placed on the 53-man roster in order to play. On the more negative side of the news, the Seahawks will be without running back Zach Charbonnet, and fellow back George Holani is questionable with rib and ankle injuries. Seattle will need to lean on Emmanuel Wilson and newly acquired Robert Henry Jr. to tote the ball against San Francisco. Cornerback Julian Neal and linebacker Chazz Surratt were also ruled out. Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald said Neal, a key depth piece, was hurt during practice. The injury to Neal will leave the Seahawks short in the secondary and could mean an elevation of cornerback Trevon Diggs for the second week in a row. After a week of worrying, the Seahawks appear to have staved off the serious injury bug for another week. Seattle will showdown with their NFC West rivals at 1:25 p.m. on FOX. title: The third-down blitzing of the Seahawks offense will continue until morale improves
summary: The Seattle Seahawks third-down offense is bad. It’s hardly a new development given most of the Russell Wilson and Geno Smith seasons, but it’s been a struggle for Seattle to convert on third down to start the 2026 season. Entering Week 5, the Seahawks rank 31st in third-down conversion rate at 31.1%, way off the […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks third-down offense is bad. It’s hardly a new development given most of the Russell Wilson and Geno Smith seasons, but it’s been a struggle for Seattle to convert on third down to start the 2026 season. Entering Week 5, the Seahawks rank 31st in third-down conversion rate at 31.1%, way off the pace of last season’s 39.8% rate (16th in the NFL). A couple of common themes have emerged with Seattle’s current struggles that: Seattle is in third-and-long way too often New year, new offensive coordinator, mostly familiar results. When filtering out QB kneels, Seattle’s average distance to go on third down is 7.9 yards, which is tied with the Tennessee Titans, Los Angeles Chargers, and Tampa Bay Buccaneers for fourth-longest distance in the NFL. Take a look at where the San Francisco 49ers are, by the way. It is a low probability to convert longer down and distances, and the Seahawks have really made life difficult for themselves when they do get to a third down. Seattle’s early down offense invites third-and-long The Seahawks rank 25th on early-down rush attempts (per SumerSports ) yet run it at the fifth-highest rate in the NFL. Seattle’s pass rate on 2nd and 7+ is just 52.5%, second-lowest in the league. So they’re essentially wasting downs more often than not. At the moment, the Seahawks do not have the type of offense that can control a game through the run. They are a much better passing team on early downs yet adopt a run-first mentality. Pre-snap penalties have also hurt the Seahawks, with multiple drives derailed by false starts. The Seahawks already have nine false starts on offense this season, halfway to matching their 2025 total (playoffs included). You can’t have drive-killing penalties on offense and drive-extenders on defense, which Seattle has had in abundance to start the year. Opposing defenses are blitzing the Seahawks at a comically high rate This is from NFL Pro /Next Gen Stats: Seattle’s passing offense has been blitzed on third downs at a higher rate than any other team, and it’s not even remotely close. It’s pure sicko mode to have nearly 60 percent of your dropbacks blitzed on any down, let alone the money down. But the difference between the Seahawks getting blitzed excessively on early downs and late downs is all about personnel. When the Seahawks play early downs, they are overwhelmingly an under center offense in 12, 13, or 21 personnel. They’re carrying at least an extra tight end and/or Brady Russell more than 60 percent of the time when it’s first or second down. Once it hits third down, the Seahawks are in 11 personnel at an 80 percent clip , which is actually not high compared to the rest of the NFL. Say goodbye to your extra protection, goodbye to play-action in hopes of freezing the defense for a split second, hello to an obvious passing situation. It’s early days, but the results have not been good for Sam Darnold. When he’s put in unfavorable spots and the Seahawks can’t resort to play-action from heavy personnel and condensed splits, the operation is not very clean. Sam Darnold vs. 3rd down blitz from 11 personnel this season: 3/8 for 29 yards and 2 sacks (1 of which was injurious), 1 successful 3rd down conversion. Every single one of these plays is at least 3rd and 5. The bulk of Seattle's 11 personnel pass plays are 3rd and long. pic.twitter.com/jxclCRRcYW — Mookie Alexander (@mookiealexander) October 6, 2026 One of the few under center looks Seattle managed on a 3rd and short was a touchdown to Tory Horton. Why? Sam Darnold checked into a pass from a run look. But you won’t get those opportunities too often when it’s 3rd and long. Tory Horton with his first TD of the season 🏈 @LACvsSEA on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/5UiWYapoiy — NFL (@NFL) October 4, 2026 The blitzing won’t stop unless the Seahawks can get out of constant third-and-long situations, and/or the offense can actually punish these blitzes in some form. Neither is happening right now, and it’s part of why the Seahawks offense has been worse than the three straight games of 30+ points suggests. Of their 13 touchdown drives, only four have involved multiple third-down conversions. When they’re cooking on early downs, they’re in great shape. When they aren’t, there’s trouble ahead that the Seahawks have yet to solve.

title: Why the Seahawks signing Terrion Arnold for one year was never about 2026
summary: Through the first four weeks of the season the Seattle Seahawks have battled a number of injuries in the secondary, and many fans had hoped that the recent hearing in the ongoing legal case of Terrion Arnold might shed some light on when Arnold might be able to contribute. Obviously, no such light was shed, […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 30: Terrion Arnold #0 of the Detroit Lions breaks up a pass during an NFL football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Ford Field on September 30, 2024 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Through the first four weeks of the season the Seattle Seahawks have battled a number of injuries in the secondary, and many fans had hoped that the recent hearing in the ongoing legal case of Terrion Arnold might shed some light on when Arnold might be able to contribute. Obviously, no such light was shed, and with the next court date for Arnold scheduled for December 15, it seems likely that no update is coming soon. This has some fans inquiring as to why the Seahawks even bothered to sign Arnold to a one-year contract, because at the present the likelihood of any on-field contributions during the 2026 season seem minimal. Specifically, the December 15 court date comes just ahead of Week 15, so even if a trial date is set at that hearing, it seems almost impossible for any conclusion to the matter to come before the end of the season, meaning Arnold will remain on the Commissioner’s Exempt List, will continue to get paid and his current contract will expire without ever having set foot on the field for Seattle. With that being the case, some have started to ask what the point is for Seattle to keep Arnold on the roster and continue to pay him $59,722 each week to not practice and not play, when there seems very little possibility for him to contribute in 2026. The answer to that question requires a deep dive into the collective bargaining agreement to understand that Seattle signing Arnold to a one-year contract was likely never about 2026, and was more so about 2027 and beyond. That, of course, seems paradoxical because the one year contract Arnold signed only covers 2026, so he’s not under contract for 2027, and therefore to understand the machination behind why, it’s necessary to turn to some light reading in the form of the collective bargaining agreement. To jump right to the point, it is Article 8, Section 1(a) that is relevant to Arnold’s situation, and that portion of the CBA reads: (Author’s Note: Bolding added for emphasis of the relevant portion of the legalese) Section 1. Accrued Seasons Calculation: (a) For the purposes of calculating Accrued Seasons under this Agreement, a player shall receive one Accrued Season for each season during which he was on, or should have been on, full pay status for a total of six or more regular season games (which shall include any games encompassed in any injury settlement, injury grievance settlement orinjury grievance award), but which, irrespective of the player’s pay status, shall not include games for which the player was on: (i) the Exempt Commissioner Permission List , (ii) the Reserve PUP List as a result of a nonfootball injury, or (iii) a Club’s Practice Squad. The reason Section 1(a)(i) is bolded is, obviously, because of the simple fact that Arnold is on the Exempt List, which means he is not earning credit towards an accrued season. That means that assuming he stays on the Exempt List through at least the December 15 court date, it will be impossible for him to earn an accrued season in 2026, which in turn means that upon the expiration of his contract at the end of the league year in March, he will have the exact same number of accrued seasons as he has now, which is two. The fact that Arnold has two accrued seasons is laid out in the above screengrab from OverTheCap.com , and it’s relevant for a very important reason. That reason is that players whose contracts have expired and who have earned only two accrued seasons are exclusive rights free agents. Exclusive rights free agents, of course, have next to zero bargaining power when it comes to negotiating because their options are to play for the ERFA contract tender the team extends or to sit at home on the couch. Thus, while the Seahawks and Arnold only agreed to a one-year contract, assuming he does not see any game action this year, the team will have the ability to bring him back again in 2027 on a league minimum contract for $1.12M. Of course, at that point it comes down to where things stand with the legal case. If he is found guilty and given a long prison sentence, the Seahawks are out the $1.075M they paid him this season and can move on. If, however, the legal matter is resolved in his favor when the charges get dropped or he is found not guilty, then Seattle will have paid a 24-year old former first round pick $2.195M for a season of on field performance, which is a value that seems to fall right in John Schneider’s wheelhouse. From there is where things get interesting because as noted on social media during training camp, a one-year deal for a player with two accrued seasons isn’t really a one-year deal. A contract for a player with only two accrued seasons is effectively a two year deal, with the second year an option at the price of the RFA tag. https://t.co/3urWrMVrFZ — John P Gilbert (@JohnPGilbertNFL) August 14, 2026 Basically, assuming Arnold doesn’t play for the Seahawks in 2026 and things somehow work out in his favor during the offseason, his only option for 2027 will be to sign for whatever ERFA tender Seattle extends. Then in 2028 he’d be a restricted free agent. Restricted free agents, of course, also have limited ability to move around in free agency and very rarely sign offer sheets with other teams, making it very likely Arnold could be retained for 2028 on an original round tender for little more than $4M. Putting all of those pieces together, it would work out to two seasons of a former first round talent for a total price tag of $6M-$7M, which could potentially prove to be a huge value. Of course, it’s all predicated on Arnold being able to play because he’s not on the Exempt List or in prison, so it’s all speculative until a resolution is reached on the legal matter. However, for those who may have worried about the fact that it appears his contract may expire before he’s able to do anything on the field for the Seahawks, at this point the expiration of his contract in March will be almost irrelevant because with only two accrued seasons the only way he will be able to hit unrestricted free agency upon the expiration of his contract is if the Seahawks opt not to extend an ERFA tender. Summing it all up, Arnold might not currently be under contract past 2026, but because of the CBA he’s under team control for the foreseeable future.
