title: NFL predictions: Jaxon Smith-Njigba will dominate for Seahawks vs. 49ers
summary: The Seattle Seahawks scraped by the Los Angeles Chargers with a narrow 7-point win last week and now turn to their toughest test of the season. Their NFC West rival, the San Francisco 49ers, will come to town this week in what looks to be a narrow contest, with FanDuel Sportsbook listing the Seahawks as […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks scraped by the Los Angeles Chargers with a narrow 7-point win last week and now turn to their toughest test of the season. Their NFC West rival, the San Francisco 49ers, will come to town this week in what looks to be a narrow contest, with FanDuel Sportsbook listing the Seahawks as three-point favorites. Let’s take a look at what it will take for the Seahawks to reassert their divisional dominance on Sunday. 1. Seattle will reestablish the JSN I’m well aware it’s a little comical to suggest that Seahawks’ star wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba will have a “bounce back” game after he posted 76 yards on five catches last week. However, the statistical performance was below the extremely high standard he has set in 2026, and the offense felt it. That should change this week as I guarantee Sam Darnold and offensive coordinator Brian Fleury will have their minds set on getting JSN the ball more, especially considering how he dominated the 49ers last season, totaling 227 yards and a touchdown. Not to mention the 49ers are dealing with several secondary injuries, making Smith-Njigba a prime target for an impressive day. Prediction: Smith-Njigba goes for 100 and two touchdowns. 2. Rashid Shaheed will be a factor in the backfield Seattle debuted a Deebo Samuel-esque package against the Chargers, welcoming speedy wideout Rashid Shaheed to the backfield and using him like a running back. Shaheed scored on a toss against Los Angeles and looked like the explosive player Seattle paid him to be. With the Seahawks seemingly signing any running back they can get their hands on, expect to see Shaheed used more in key moments to generate explosives against a stout 49ers run defense that is holding teams to under 100 rushing yards per game. Prediction: Shaheed goes for 50+ rushing yards. 3. Seahawks will cover -3 San Francisco, and especially quarterback Brock Purdy, have struggled against Mike Macdonald-led defenses for the last three years. The Seahawks defense held them to nine points, no touchdowns, in their last two meetings, and while nobody should expect that level of dominance on Sunday, it shouldn’t be far off. The 49ers are fresh off a battle with the Denver Broncos, who were missing several key players on defense, and only managed 24 points. Seattle will have to play more disciplined football than last week, but they should get the job done. Prediction: Seahawks cover the three-point spread. 4. Game finishes with under 47.5 points While Seattle should cover, this should be an old-fashioned rock fight, much like what these two teams put together in Week 18 of last season. Both of these offenses are battling through significant injuries and have not gotten off to the hottest starts. They will be forced to lean on their defenses and special teams to get this one done, which should result in a low-scoring and stressful game. Prediction: Seahawks escape with a 21-17 victory, total points 38 . Closing thoughts The Seahawks have been a frustrating team to watch in 2026, and that’s an unfortunate trend that should continue into this heated rivalry contest. While my confidence in the Dark Side defense is relatively high, as long as they can fix their penalty bug from last week, as they’ve looked the part through the first four games. Much depends on the health of Leonard Williams, however, Macdonald has earned enough trust for me to believe in his group. Meanwhile, Seahawks’ offense has yet to face a defense as solid as San Francisco’s. Seattle will need a better performance from Darnold, especially in the turnover category, as this run game will likely struggle to get past Fred Warner. This game will likely come down to the fourth quarter, so make sure to have your blood pressure medication of choice on hand Sunday at 1:25 p.m PT. Will any of these predictions come true? title: Seahawks vs. 49ers, Week 5 preview: The keys to Seattle beating San Francisco once again
summary: The 3-1 Seattle Seahawks head into Sunday looking to hand the 4-0 San Francisco 49ers their first loss of the season. San Francisco has looked like one of the league’s best teams through the first month, while Seattle has started to establish an identity built around an aggressive defense and an offense that has shown […]
full_text: The 3-1 Seattle Seahawks head into Sunday looking to hand the 4-0 San Francisco 49ers their first loss of the season. San Francisco has looked like one of the league’s best teams through the first month, while Seattle has started to establish an identity built around an aggressive defense and an offense that has shown flashes of efficiency. This is an important game for Seattle beyond the standings. A win would prevent the 49ers from creating early separation in the division, give the Seahawks a head-to-head advantage and provide a significant boost heading into a more difficult portion of the schedule. Seattle has already beaten the Patriots and Cardinals, lost to Washington and handled an 0-4 Chargers team in Week 4. Beating San Francisco would be a different kind of statement. Close the cracks in the run defense Seattle’s run defense remains one of the biggest areas to watch, and the tape shows a potential weakness opponents can attack: the space between the interior defensive linemen and the edges. Again, the Chargers attack the same space. Mills gets moved by the double team and driven into Jones, opening the lane. Seattle needs an answer before this becomes a trend. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-10-07T15:56:55.121Z That is exactly the kind of space Kyle Shanahan wants to create. Outside zone remains the foundation of San Francisco’s rushing attack, and Christian McCaffrey is playing at an extremely high level. Through four games, McCaffrey has carried the ball 50 times for 218 yards and four touchdowns while adding 16 catches for 122 yards. The important part for Seattle isn’t simply stopping McCaffrey at the line of scrimmage. It is preventing him from turning small creases into five-, eight- or 15-yard gains. When the 49ers can consistently run the football, Shanahan gets to open up the entire playbook. Motion becomes more dangerous. Play-action becomes more convincing. The defense has to hesitate before attacking the quarterback. And that is where San Francisco can really hurt Seattle. Shanahan will also have to adjust without Kyle Juszczyk, whose injury removes one of the most versatile pieces of the 49ers’ formation and motion game. Juszczyk isn’t just a traditional fullback. San Francisco frequently uses him in pre-snap motion to create leverage and manipulate defensive assignments before the snap. The concept is simple but difficult to defend: Juszczyk can move across the formation before the snap, forcing the defense to communicate and adjust, then enter the play with momentum as a blocker. Instead of identifying where the defense is lined up, the motion can create a better blocking angle and put an extra body into the run fit. Shanahan has been doing this for years, so losing Juszczyk won’t suddenly make the concept disappear. The 49ers will find other ways to recreate it. Seattle has to make those adjustments matter. Pressure Brock Purdy and finish the play One of the biggest lessons from Seattle’s previous games is that pressure alone isn’t enough. Marcus Mariota showed how quickly a quarterback can neutralize the pass rush when he consistently gets the ball out on time. Washington’s quick passing game limited Seattle’s opportunities to get home, even though the Seahawks were able to generate pressure. San Francisco can use the same blueprint. Brock Purdy is also much more dangerous once a play breaks down. He has the ability to escape the pocket, extend plays and pick up yards with his legs. Through four games, Purdy has already rushed 20 times for 122 yards and a touchdown. Seattle has already seen quarterbacks hurt its defense with their legs this season. Drake Maye rushed seven times for 47 yards in Week 1, while Justin Herbert ran six times for 40 yards in Week 4. The Seahawks cannot allow Purdy to turn third-and-long into a scramble drill. More importantly, pressure has to become sacks. Hits are nice. Hurries are useful. But against an offense as efficient as San Francisco’s, allowing Purdy to escape pressure and still complete the play is almost as damaging as not pressuring him at all. Seattle needs to collapse the pocket, maintain rush-lane discipline and finish. The challenge is tough once 49ers dit not allow a sack yet. Don’t let Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel, and George Kittle dictate the game San Francisco’s receiving corps has added another dimension with Mike Evans. Evans gives Purdy a legitimate back-shoulder and contested-catch option, particularly in situations where the quarterback needs a reliable safety valve outside the numbers. Through four games, Evans has 17 receptions for 213 yards and two touchdowns. That creates an interesting matchup for Seattle’s secondary, especially if Evans is consistently targeted against smaller defensive backs. Josh Jobe could see some of those snaps, and the size difference is something San Francisco can attempt to exploit. Maybe Trevon Diggs can be elevated again , especially as Nehemiah Pritchett seems to be dealing with an injury. Then there is Deebo Samuel. This version of Deebo looks much closer to the player San Francisco originally fell in love with than the version we have seen at times in recent seasons. Through four games, Samuel has 14 receptions for 185 yards and three touchdowns while also rushing seven times for 74 yards. That versatility changes the math for the defense. Deebo can line up outside, move into the slot, take a handoff, catch a screen and turn a routine touch into a chunk play. Seattle’s tackling discipline will be critical because the first defender often isn’t the one who ends the play. And then there is George Kittle. Fresh off an Achilles injury, Kittle has 16 catches for 244 yards and four touchdowns through four games, averaging more than 15 yards per reception. His impact isn’t limited to the passing game. Kittle’s ability as a blocker gives Shanahan another way to manipulate the front, especially when Seattle is trying to defend outside-zone concepts. Seattle cannot allow Kittle to become both a sixth offensive lineman and a vertical receiving threat on the same afternoon. There is no room for mistakes If there is one thing Seattle cannot repeat from the Chargers game, it is the penalty problem. Seattle committed 14 penalties for 150 yards against Los Angeles, and the Chargers committed 16 penalties for 130 yards. What should have been a comfortable Seattle victory became a game that remained alive until the final drive. That cannot happen against San Francisco. The 49ers are too efficient, and their offense is too good at turning extended drives into points. Giving Shanahan free first downs or putting the defense in disadvantageous situations is an invitation to disaster. Turnovers are another obvious concern. Seattle has already seen how costly they can be after the loss to Washington. Sam Darnold also struggled against the Chargers, throwing for 168 yards with two touchdowns and an interception. Against the 49ers, a three-turnover game probably isn’t survivable. Seattle doesn’t need Darnold to throw for 350 yards. It needs him to protect the football, take the throws that are there and avoid giving San Francisco short fields. The margin for error is going to be small. Brian Fleury needs to make the run game show up This might be the most important offensive question for Seattle. Brian Fleury has done a good job getting the passing game moving, but the Seahawks still haven’t found that consistent rhythm on the ground that can make the entire offense more difficult to defend. Through four games, Seattle has rushed for 441 yards at 3.9 yards per carry. 49ers defense vs. Duo runs this season (per @NextGenStats ) 39 carries, 162 yards (4.2 YPC), 48.7% SR, 20.5% 1D% https://t.co/ZOcIsh1Z6V pic.twitter.com/JfNJFfZ9Ri — Nate Tice (@Nate_Tice) September 28, 2026 The 49ers, meanwhile, have already shown that their defense can be vulnerable to teams willing to run directly at them and attack the edges. That is the good news. The bad news is that…

full_text: SEATTLE, WA - DECEMBER 29: Jacob Hollister #48 of the Seattle Seahawks makes a reception but is stopped just short of the goal line by Fred Warner #54 and Dre Greenlaw #57 of the San Francisco 49ers during the game at CenturyLink Field on December 29, 2019 in Seattle, Washington. The 49ers defeated the Seahawks 26-21. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images 49ers star DE Nick Bosa eyeing Week 6 return vs. Commanders after calf injury “But the fact that I’m already feeling like I could go out on Monday night and definitely not wait,” Bosa said. “Definitely Atlanta, possibly next week. Probably.” Bosa said he was initially concerned the calf injury could be a long-term situation. “I’ve never had a calf, so I didn’t really know,” he said. “They told me they’re pretty finicky sometimes, calves. But, actually, I checked with my brother (Joey), who had one last year in OTAs. He said three weeks, and he never even noticed it (after that).” Nick Bosa said he has been during two-a-day running sessions and his normal lifts in the weight room. He said he felt as if he turned the corner with his recovery within the past few days. “I’m feeling better and better,” he said.” 49ers DT Sebastian Valdez worked in the shadows as a rookie, but his coaches were watching (paywall) “(Sebastian) Valdez is No. 1 for me; he has been for the last two years,” Puni, the San Francisco 49ers right guard, said recently. “He just does a great job at giving the right look. And he matches the right intensity that you should have for practice.” Added left guard Connor Colby: “You know his effort is always going to be there. Especially the padded practice (on Thursday) — it helps out a lot. It gives you an opportunity to work on things you need to correct.” Until two weeks ago, Valdez’s de facto job title was Guy Who Preps the Starters. As a defensive tackle on the 49ers’ practice squad and scout team, his role was to line up in the three-technique and mimic how the upcoming opponent would play the run, the pass, etc., so that offensive linemen such as Puni, Colby and center Jake Brendel were well prepared on Sunday. He was essentially a sparring partner for the interior offensive line.” Mykel Williams to make season debut in 49ers-Seahawks; Upton Stout questionable “Williams is listed as questionable, but coach Kyle Shanahan confirmed on Friday that he will be back for the 49ers.” Five 49ers to watch as Kyle Shanahan, offense try to solve Seahawks in Week 5 “Green had a good training camp and has gotten off to the best start of his three-year NFL career. In four games, he has surrendered only 12 receptions for 101 yards and no touchdowns. He had an interception of Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford in the season opener. Green faces a stiff task on Sunday, as Seattle quarterback Sam Darnold will look to target Jaxon Smith-Njigba early and often. Smith-Njigba might be the best receiver in the game today. He already has 32 receptions for 481 yards and six touchdowns.” 49ers vs. Seahawks: The Standard’s 5 fast predictions (paywall) “Kawakami: Seahawks 20, 49ers 17. The 49ers are fully capable of winning at Lumen Field and have, in fact, done it several times in the Shanahan/Purdy era. But they have to be at their absolute best — and usually need Bosa doing Bosa stuff to close it. They won’t have Bosa plus a few others in this one. The 49ers will probably get two more shots against the Seahawks this season. Presumably with Bosa in those games.” 49ers-Seahawks preview: Giddy up (paywall) “But against Seattle, I think Brock Purdy is going to need to take some of the dicier shots he’s turned down at times this season. The boundary, not the middle of the field, is the better place to beat the Seattle secondary….There have been some opportunities (like on this B gap release to Deebo on a corner route) where Purdy turned it down. Seattle condenses windows and runs a lot of Cover-6 and Cover-8 instead of this Cover-2 look, but they can be vulnerable to vertical stretch to the boundary. These also require time, of which Seattle usually offers little….Now, Seattle’s dominant against under center runs. But they can be vulnerable against counter because it funnels the ball away from where Seattle usually attacks….The Seahawks’ center-right guard pairing is the place to direct pressure. And you HAVE to get pressure against Darnold. He’s been abysmal when you speed him up.” 5 matchups to watch in 49ers-Seahawks: The 1 player Brock Purdy should avoid “He’s one of the best linear athletes in the NFL. You have to make him flip his hips. You can’t let Emmanwori run in a straight line. Put him in conflict, whether with high-low concepts, or isolate him on George Kittle or Christian McCaffrey by giving them two-way go’s. Despite all the plays he can make, Emmanwori is not a player the 49ers should shy away from…..If you’re the Niners, as good as Williams is (8th-most quick pressures in the league, so pretty good!), you have to trust Puni. He’s been great all season. Last week was the first time Puni had a blown block in pass protection. Connor Colby came close a couple of times in the first three weeks, but Zach Allen got the best of him in Week 4. He had three blown blocks in pass protection. Murphy is the final boss in the Allen hierarchy. I’d like to see Colby be aggressive and use jump sets against Murphy. Colby has the prototypical farmer-boy frame from Iowa, but don’t let that fool you into thinking he’s a subpar athlete. Against Murphy, I’d like to see Colby be the aggressor, rely on some of that quickness and strength before Murphy can initiate his move. That could go a long way in how the offense can attack.”
author: Yinon Raviv

title: Nick Bosa ‘pretty darn likely’ to return to the 49ers in Week 6
summary: The San Francisco 49ers’ final injury report is out. Here’s who will miss Week 5 against the Seattle Seahawks: FB Kyle Juszczyk (knee)S Marques Sigle (ankle)DL James Thompson (ankle)DL Nick Bosa Here are the players who are listed as questionable: CB Upton Stout (shoulder)DE Mykel Williams (knee) Kyle Shanahan said the plan is to activate […]
full_text: (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers’ final injury report is out. Here’s who will miss Week 5 against the Seattle Seahawks: FB Kyle Juszczyk (knee) S Marques Sigle (ankle) DL James Thompson (ankle) DL Nick Bosa Here are the players who are listed as questionable: CB Upton Stout (shoulder) DE Mykel Williams (knee) Kyle Shanahan said the plan is to activate Mykel Williams from the PUP list on Saturday. When asked how he’s looked, Shanahan said, “He’s lost weight in a good way. I don’t know if he’s lost weight, but he’s leaner. He’s had a good two weeks. He was good last week, and this week’s been even better. Ready to get back out there on the field.” Kyle’s update, 2:44 pm PT: The Athletic’s Matt Barrows tweeted that Bosa says he’s made a lot of progress recently with his calf injury and thinks he’ll be able to play Week 7 in Atlanta, perhaps even in Week 6 versus Washington. Nick Bosa is “pretty darn likely” to return in Week 6 against the Washington Commanders on Monday Night Football, per Matt Maiocco . Whether it’s next week or the week after, it sounds like Bosa will return before the 49ers bye week in Week 8. Shanahan wouldn’t say exactly how much Williams would play. “When he’s out there, he’ll be a full-go. We rotate our guys. Understand it’s his first game. We gotta see how it goes.” That means wide receiver Mike Evans (ribs) isn’t on the injury report after missing Thursday’s practice, suggesting the team likely gave him a day off to manage the injury. Stout did not practice on Friday. But Shanahan also said no when asked if Stout had a setback on Thursday. That explains why his availability is in question. The Seahawks ruled out the following players: RB Zach Charbonnet (knee) CB Julian Neal (hamstring) LB Chazz Surratt) Charbonnet has not played this season. Seattle has not run the ball well. They are 29th in EPA per rush and 20th in rushing success rate. Losing your right guard doesn’t help. Neither does your first-round running back. George Holani was more snaps than price this season. He was limited all week with multiple injury designations: Ribs, knee. That leaves Emanuel Wilson, a former Packers restricted free agent. Green Bay let him walk. He’s been boom-or-bust with Seattle so far. Wilson’s had 20.8% of his runs result in a gain of zero or negative. Their line is only providing 0.77 yards before contact for Wilson. Defensive tackle Leonard Williams (ankle) practiced in full, as did safety Ty Okada (hamstring), who seems poised to make his season debut.

title: Which personnel splits have been the most successful for the 49ers in 2026?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers offense has been very successful heading into Sunday’s monster matchup with the Seattle Seahawks. Brock Purdy is playing the best football of his career, Kyle Shanahan has made timely play calls, and the 49ers offensive line has performed as a top-five unit. Even with injuries to Mike Evans, who is fighting […]
full_text: (Photo by Lachlan Cunningham/Getty Images) The San Francisco 49ers offense has been very successful heading into Sunday’s monster matchup with the Seattle Seahawks. Brock Purdy is playing the best football of his career, Kyle Shanahan has made timely play calls, and the 49ers offensive line has performed as a top-five unit. Even with injuries to Mike Evans, who is fighting through bumps and bruises, and the losses of Demarcus Robinson, De’Zhaun Stribling, and Ricky Pearsall, the 49ers offense has kept trucking. Which personnel groupings have been the most effective for the 49ers in 2026? According to Football Insights , the 49ers are tied for first in the NFL with the Baltimore Ravens with an EPA of 0.25 from heavy personnel packages (two or fewer WRs). The 68% rate is the second-highest rate for two receivers or fewer, behind the Las Vegas Raiders, and the 49ers have a 59.7% success rate and a 14.4% explosive play rate. Now, with three or more receivers on the field, the 49ers lead the league with a 0.33 EPA. Again, the 49ers don’t use three or more receivers much, with the second-lowest rate of 32%. The success rate of 58.1% is the best in the NFL, and the explosive play rate of 16.7% is good for the third-highest in the league. A deeper look shows the 49ers have three of the top EPA performances in the top 12 of any personnel grouping. With 72 plays from 11 personnel (5th in the NFL), the 49ers sport a total EPA of 23.90 and a 0.49 EPA/pass. The league average for passing from this grouping is 56.19% and an average EPA of -0.03. The 49ers are at a 68.06% pass rate. Out of 12 personnel, the 49ers rank tenth in the NFL with a total EPA of 14.15 and a play rate of 14.91% (34 plays out of 228). That is good for second amongst all teams out of 12 personnel. The league average usage is 21.87%, and EPA is -0.01. The offense has positive EPA/pass and rush with 0.80 and 0.03, respectively. The 49ers follow up with the 11th-best EPA performance, and it comes from 21 personnel. This grouping is by far their most utilized at 40.79% (93 out of 228 plays). The 49ers are the number one offense from 21, with a total EPA of 13.39. The league average is a lowly 6.73% with an EPA of -0.06. The 49ers pass 38.71% of the time and have an EPA/pass of 0.18 and an EPA/rush of 0.12. The 49ers offense has been efficient and explosive so far. Sunday will be the biggest test of the season and a chance to show the offense can take down top-flight defenses.
author: Jason Aponte

title: 49ers release Ogbo Okoronkwo
summary: The San Francisco 49ers announced they released Ogbo Okoronkwo. He appeared in all four games and has the second-most snaps of any edge rusher this season. Okoronkwo hasn’t lit up the stat sheet, but he managed 10 pressures with an 11.8% pass-rush win rate. But he’s only played 33 run snaps this year. This move […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers announced they released Ogbo Okoronkwo. He appeared in all four games and has the second-most snaps of any edge rusher this season. Okoronkwo hasn’t lit up the stat sheet, but he managed 10 pressures with an 11.8% pass-rush win rate. But he’s only played 33 run snaps this year. This move is the 49ers telling us they need a run defender. Hello, Mykel Williams. The 49ers just created a roster spot to activate Williams from the PUP list. That move will likely be announced on Saturday. Raheem Morris has done a fantastic job using his personnel to hide the lack of edge options. We’ve seen plenty of 5-man fronts that include three defensive tackles and Jaden Dugger. The other edge rusher on the roster that Morris seems to trust as a run defender is Khalid Kareem. He’s played 100 snaps, 43 of them against the run. That may not change much, as Keion White and Romello Height have primarily been pass-rush first layers. The same was true last week for Matt Judon. It might also signal that Williams could play more than 20-30 snaps. We’ll see if the 49ers bring back Okoronkwo to the practice squad. If Nick Bosa is close to returning, there won’t be a need to bring back Okoronkwo.
author: Kyle Posey

title: 5 matchups to watch in 49ers-Seahawks: The 1 player Brock Purdy should avoid
summary: Since it’s such a big game, we’ll flip the script and talk about the players on the other side of the ball. Some matchups in this game the San Francisco 49ers have to win. There are a couple of players they should avoid. Here are five Seattle Seahawks to watch in Week 5. LB Nick […]
full_text: (Photo by Alika Jenner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Since it’s such a big game, we’ll flip the script and talk about the players on the other side of the ball. Some matchups in this game the San Francisco 49ers have to win. There are a couple of players they should avoid. Here are five Seattle Seahawks to watch in Week 5. LB Nick Emmanwori This is a linebacker. This is a pass rusher. This is not a safety. He’s more Bruce Irvin than Kam Chancellor. Seattle can play nickel against heavy personnel groupings because of Emmanwori. To me, it’s base. They ran dime personnel (6+ defensive backs) at a season-high 27.9% of the time. That’s nickel. Emmanwori had been playing a little less than half of the snaps up until last week, when he was on the field for more than 77% of the snaps. He played on the line of scrimmage or in the box on 73.6% of his snaps. He rushed the passer eight times and had four pressures. He’s one of the best linear athletes in the NFL. You have to make him flip his hips. You can’t let Emmanwori run in a straight line. Put him in conflict, whether with high-low concepts, or isolate him on George Kittle or Christian McCaffrey by giving them two-way go’s. Despite all the plays he can make, Emmanwori is not a player the 49ers should shy away from. RG Beau Stephens The 49ers must win this matchup. Stephens was one of my draft crushes. The rookie is currently in a time-share with Christian Haynes after Seattle placed starter Anthony Bradford on the injured reserve. Haynes has out-snapped Stephens 112-76, but I found it interesting that Seattle played Stephens last week while running the clock out to end the game. Stephens has a 5.2% blown-block rate. Haynes is at 1.8%. Historically, the league average has been right around 2.7%. Stephens whiffed a couple of times in the run game last week. He’s also allowed a team-high 8.1% pressure rate. Keion White has been a terror rushing over guards. White has a pressure rate over 17% as a 3-technique. His quickness off the snap should make a difference. It’s also a great opportunity for Mykel Williams to get his feet wet. Stephens arm length is in the first percentile. Morris would be wise to hunt matchups and get Stephens into 1-on-1 situations. S Julian Love It looks like the Seahawks may get Ty Okada back, which means they’ll have both starting safeties. One player to steer clear of is Julian Love. In my opinion, he’s one of the best, if not the best, safeties in the NFL. He can do it all. Love isn’t your traditional. Mike MacDonald has no issue blitzing him. He had a couple of unblocked pressures last week. He’s the kind of playmaker who’ll bait quarterbacks into thinking he’s going one direction, or that a route down the middle is wide open, only to appear out of nowhere and snag an interception. You think you’re looking him off, but you’re playing right into Love’s hands. He will miss a tackle here and there, but he times MacDonald’s run blitzes well and is just as comfortable in the open field. Love doesn’t get the recognition that Devon Witherspoon does. He’s just as big of a star. Be careful, Brock. TE A.J. Barner Brian Fleury has used play-action on over 37% of Sam Darnold’s dropbacks. While he has a high completion percentage (69.2%), he’s thrown a pair of interceptions and been sacked twice, which is why there’s a -0.193 EPA per play. The success rate is good at 53.6%. It’s comical that no player has been targeted more than 15 times other than Jaxon Smith-Njigba. Tight end A.J. Barner has more targets than JSN with Darnold under center on play-action. It’s only one more target, but it’s also happened on three fewer routes. Barner has six targets on Darnold’s 22 play-action dropbacks. If you’re the 49ers, you’re welcoming targets to Barner. Any play where the ball isn’t going to No. 11 should be considered a win. Barner caught a 32-yard screen pass against Washington, but the Commanders missed multiple tackles. Outside of a screen, Barner is rarely Darnold’s first read. If he’s getting the ball, it’s likely because the first two options were covered. Barner dropped a would-be first-down target on 3rd and 5 last week. Remember, Fleury has been coaching George Kittle for years. Seattle ran the screen where you pump one direction, then the other, and hit the tight end down the middle. They picked up 12 yards on it last week. Barner isn’t mentioned here because he’s a threat, but on play-action and in the red zone, he’ll get opportunities. DT Byron Murphy Hard-hitting analysis here. “Look out for one of the best defensive tackles in the game.” This is matchup-based. Unfortunately, it could be a long day for the former Hawkeye offensive linemen. On 3rd and 4 last week, Seattle put a wide-9 defensive end to Murphy’s side and used Leonard Williams to occupy the center. That left Murphy 1-on-1 with the right guard. Murphy beat the guard in under a second and sacked the quarterback. Last year, Murphy generated a league-high 33 pressures when aligned inside the guard. He’s picking up where he left off. He’s 29th in pressure rate, but that doesn’t account for how often Murphy gets double-teamed. Leonard Williams will spend a lot of time going against Dominick Puni. If you’re the Niners, as good as Williams is (8th-most quick pressures in the league, so pretty good!), you have to trust Puni. He’s been great all season. Last week was the first time Puni had a blown block in pass protection. Connor Colby came close a couple of times in the first three weeks, but Zach Allen got the best of him in Week 4. He had three blown blocks in pass protection. Murphy is the final boss in the Allen hierarchy. I’d like to see Colby be aggressive and use jump sets against Murphy. Colby has the prototypical farmer-boy frame from Iowa, but don’t let that fool you into thinking he’s a subpar athlete. Against Murphy, I’d like to see Colby be the aggressor, rely on some of that quickness and strength before Murphy can initiate his move. That could go a long way in how the offense can attack.
author: Kyle Posey

title: 5 takeaways from coordinators: Mykel Williams gives the 49ers ‘a lot of juice’
summary: San Francisco 49ers coordinators Raheem Morris and Klay Kubiak spoke to the media ahead of their Week 5 showdown with the Seattle Seahawks. We’ve already highlighted why the Niners are unlikely to shadow Jaxon Smith-Njigba. Here are some of the other newsworthy items from their pressers. Raheem Morris is ready to see Mykel Williams “Just […]
full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images San Francisco 49ers coordinators Raheem Morris and Klay Kubiak spoke to the media ahead of their Week 5 showdown with the Seattle Seahawks. We’ve already highlighted why the Niners are unlikely to shadow Jaxon Smith-Njigba . Here are some of the other newsworthy items from their pressers. Raheem Morris is ready to see Mykel Williams “Just the energy. His ability to show that he wants to get out there and play. It’s been almost a year, as he said to multiple people. He’s just excited, and I don’t blame him. I’m excited to see him as well. This will be my first time seeing him this week and getting a chance to watch him go out there and play. He’s big, he gives us a lot of energy, gives a lot of juice, and we’ll see where he is by the end of this week and see what happens, but I’m excited about it.” Mykel said Nick Bosa helped him with his rehab. Judging by the videos from practice on Thursday and this photo from last season, desserts have been off the menu for Williams: Looks like a completely different person https://t.co/pfF8IyJrDE pic.twitter.com/yqgTUzhkWF — Kyle Posey (@KP_Show) October 8, 2026 What kind of impact or how much will he play? That’s to be determined. Here’s Morris on that topic: “Really hard question for me. I wasn’t around when he was able to play last year. Obviously, I knew him through the draft process and know what type of player he is, so I’m really excited to see him come out there and, first and foremost, do the really important things we ask our ends to do: set edges. I’m really fired up to see him go out there and have a chance to be able to affect the passer. So those two things that he was brought here to do are the things that I’m most fired up to see, and nobody’s more fired up than him, obviously.” Does he start? Maybe a better question is, why wouldn’t he start? But you also have to acknowledge that Williams didn’t have OTAs or the preseason. He’s had less than a handful of practices under his belt. Expecting Williams to be anywhere close to the shape he needs to play 40 snaps feels like a stretch. Why the 49ers are putting such an emphasis on limiting the big play defensively The 49ers have allowed an explosive play rate of 2.3%. That’s a smidge behind the Rams and slightly ahead of the Seahawks. The best division in football is making opposing offenses earn it. Morris explained why there’s such an emphasis on it: “A lot of it is really if you’re able to limit those plays, those explosive plays, that keeps the score down. If you can keep the score down, that gives your offense a chance to win every single game. That gives your team the opportunity to go out there and play how you planned all week. We’ve been able to limit the explosions to be able to play the way we want to play, to be able to dictate the terms. Fortunately or unfortunately, now we’ve got to go out there and continue to do those things however that works. We’ve got the guys to be able to do it. They’ve got the mental stamina to be able to survive throughout the practice, to be able to make the mistakes in practice, to be able to correct those things, take it to the grass and make those things come to life. Those are things that are all helping us.” Eventually, your opponent will make a mistake. Last week was a good example. Denver had multiple third-down penalties, putting them behind the sticks. If you make an offense earn it over 10, 11, or 12+ plays, a run stop, incompletion, or some kind of mistake tends to end the drive. That’s what the 49ers are banking on, and why they go out of their way to keep everything in front of them. Protecting Dre Greenlaw from injury? Some have speculated that the 49ers are limiting Greenlaw’s snap counts to keep him healthy for the season. Morris was asked whether that’s been the case this season: “It’s hard to say manage when you’re talking about Dre. It’s just really doing whatever it is to win football games. He comes out at times. We’ve had packages where he’s out. We have packages that he’s in. He’s in most of them. He’s not the green dot, so we can be able to switch those guys in and out of rotation. You do it a lot with linemen. People kind of get wigged out when you do it with the defensive back or you do it with a linebacker. But, realistically, that’s going to become the norm because people want to play fast. How fast can you play for 50 snaps as opposed to 80? If you go play 89 snaps, you’re not going to get the same Dre we got the next week. If that was the case, we wouldn’t have got what we got last week. To get what we got last week, we keep hunting. Whatever the best formula is for that to happen, I think it’s what we’re going to do.” Based on when Greenlaw comes off the field, Morris seems to have more faith in Garret Wallow in specific sub-packages and obvious passing situations. Greenlaw came off the field on second-and-long last week. We’ve seen him leave the field in two-minute situations or when Morris knows the offense will throw the ball. Brock Purdy finding the balance between aggression and patience Brock Purdy has been afforded the seventh-most time to be pressured in the NFL, with having the eighth-most time to throw. He can get a little antsy in the pocket, occasionally leaving clean ones when he doesn’t have to. Purdy’s aggressiveness hasn’t wavered. Kubiak explained how to coach a quarterback to be aggressive while maintaining his patience, and whether those traits work against each other in some ways: “You’d like to say the quarterback should always have that mentality. I think we’ve never really had a problem with [QB] Brock [Purdy] in terms of being aggressive. We’re going to call plays where we’re hoping to get big plays and get explosives. And if Brock sees it right and he’s feeling confident, he’s going to let it rip. But you have to understand what you’re going against. You have to understand that there’s a nature to the defense you’re playing where there is a bend-but-don’t-break mentality for them where you got to be disciplined. Good quarterbacks got to find a way to balance those things out. When you look at teams who’ve had success against Seattle these past couple years, it’s guys like [Los Angeles Rams QB Matthew] Stafford. And when Brock’s played good against them, it’s that. You get your shots when they’re there. You make the throw, but you’re patient when it’s not there, and you keep playing. So, Brock knows that. And it’s just a big part of this game. It’s part of every week, but especially going against these guys.” As buttoned up as Seattle is defensively, you can’t shy away from pushing the ball downfield. You have to make them cover and keep every player honest. The 49ers couldn’t last season because they didn’t have the players. Mike Evans and George Kittle change a lot of how the Niners can attack the Seahawks. Improved team speed should keep the 49ers honest Kubiak was asked whether he felt the offense was better equipped to attack Seattle this year, and if now they could get Seattle’s safeties to creep up: “It’s a good question. I think the nature of their scheme, they never want their safeties playing that aggressive at the line of scrimmage. Just the way they play their corners, it’s the way they play their front. It’s really hard to kind of to get those guys out of that, but there is a time and a place where if you can run the ball and you can stay on the field, eventually, hopefully you get more people to commit to the box. And that’s our goal every week, really, honestly. I think when you look around the league, teams want to play shell until you force them not to. And, these guys, that’s why they’re a good defense – they can defend the run with their corners, with their two-shell defense. And so our goal is to, like every week, run the ball consistently, stay on the field, stay out of obvious passing situations so that we can try to get the defense to tee off a little bit and we can hopefully take…
author: Kyle Posey

title: The 49ers are running into the stingiest defense in the NFL
summary: The San Francisco 49ers are looking for a perfect first leg against the NFC West with a win on Sunday in the Pacific Northwest against the Seattle Seahawks. After defeating the Rams and Arizona, the 49ers sit atop the NFC West, but the 3-1 Seahawks are within shouting distance, and an early division lead is […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers are looking for a perfect first leg against the NFC West with a win on Sunday in the Pacific Northwest against the Seattle Seahawks. After defeating the Rams and Arizona, the 49ers sit atop the NFC West, but the 3-1 Seahawks are within shouting distance, and an early division lead is on the line. A win would give San Francisco the tiebreaker over all three NFC West foes in the early goings and a two-game lead in the win column. But Seattle was a tricky game (twice) in the ladder half of 2025 for the 49ers, and Sunday could be the same with Seattle getting Sam Darnold back a couple of weeks ago. And while Darnold will lead the Seattle offense, the main attraction of the Seahawks is that defense. Let’s take a closer look at the Seattle defense with this week’s numbers to know: 246.8 Yards per game. The Seahawks defense allows 246.8 yards per game, the best in the league. The Denver Broncos defense was just a Week 4 appetizer for the Week 5 main course: Mike Macdonald’s elite Seattle defense. Entering Week 5, only two defenses have allowed fewer than 1,000 yards. After Sunday, the 49ers will have played both of those teams. The 49ers offense put up 379 yards in Week 1 against the Los Angeles Rams, the current season-high against Los Angeles, but since then, the Rams have allowed 611 in three games, bringing their season total to 990 yards allowed. Only one team has allowed fewer yards: the Seahawks. While the 49ers offense has gained more than 300 yards in all four games this season, Seattle has allowed more than 300 yards once, last week when the Los Angeles Chargers gained 301. And just as the 49ers’ ability to gain yards has led to the second-highest point output through four weeks (122), Seattle’s ability to hold offenses has kept teams to the fifth-fewest points (73). In simpler terms, Sunday will be an immovable object versus an unstoppable force. Now, where will the 49ers find the firepower against Seattle’s defense? Mike Evans is banged up, and unlike Week 1, the 49ers will be without Demarcus Robinson and De’Zhaun Stribling. The receiver injuries will be familiar, though, as the position group was hurt last season when Seattle dominated the 49ers offense in Week 17 and the playoffs. 1 Touchdowns. The Seattle defense has allowed one rushing touchdown this season, the second-fewest allowed in the league. While the passing game has been responsible for 11 of the 49ers’ 16 touchdowns this season, Christian McCaffrey on the ground remains the biggest scoring threat on the 49ers’ offense, especially inside the red zone. Seattle’s defense has been susceptible to the run this season, allowing 100+ rushing yards in two of its four games. But because Seattle is so good everywhere else on defense, that slight issue against the run hasn’t hurt much. But this game might be decided by how often the 49ers offense can get into the red zone. Seattle has allowed the second-fewest red zone entries with nine through four games. Despite the few entries, Seattle has allowed five touchdowns, a 66.7 touchdown rate tied for the tenth-highest. Only one of those red zone touchdowns has come on the ground. And that’s where McCaffrey comes into play. All 27 of his rushing touchdowns have come inside the red zone , and all four of his rushing touchdowns in 2026 were one-yard scores. It’s safe to say that Seattle’s defense won’t face a red zone weapon like McCaffrey outside the two games against the 49ers. It’s tough to move the ball against Seattle’s defense, and it’s especially hard to score on the ground. McCaffrey could be the answer to that threat. 7-3 Record. The 49ers are 7-3 (including playoffs) against the Seahawks under Brock Purdy. If Purdy can continue his current form against this Seattle defense, it would be a statement game we look back on to solidify an MVP case at the end of the season. Purdy did have his struggles against the Seahawks in 2025, averaging 181.3 passing yards in three games against Seattle, in a season where he averaged 240 yards per game. Even after success in his first try against Macdonald’s version of the Seahawks when Purdy threw for three touchdowns leading a 49ers win, all three of Purdy’s losses to the Seahawks have come under Macdonald’s tenure. But that doesn’t mean Purdy hasn’t had success against Macdonald. Purdy has led the 49ers to two wins against Seattle and has looked good in both. The first being the aforementioned three-touchdown game from Purdy, picking up a win in Week 6 of the 2024 season, but he also led the game-winning drive in Week 1 last season, capping off a two-touchdown day. Purdy’s dominance of the Seahawks was more of a Pete Carroll thing than it was a Macdonald. And while the Seahawks’ head coach has had Purdy’s number dating back to Christmas Day 2023, Purdy has had his fair share of success as well. Sunday, however, Macdonald and the Seahawks defense will have to face Purdy in the middle of one of the best stretches of his career.
author: Andrew Pasquini

title: Why the 49ers likely won’t shadow Jaxon Smith Njigba
summary: The San Francisco 49ers have quite the challenge ahead of them this week, as they’ll have to find a way to cover Seattle Seahawks star receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who is off to a torrid pace this season with 32 catches for 481 yards and six touchdowns through four games. Regardless of quarterback, Smith-Njigba has produced, […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - JANUARY 17: Deommodore Lenoir #2 of the San Francisco 49ers defends against Jaxon Smith-Njigba #11 of the Seattle Seahawks during the second half of an NFL divisional playoff football game at Lumen Field on January 17, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers have quite the challenge ahead of them this week, as they’ll have to find a way to cover Seattle Seahawks star receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who is off to a torrid pace this season with 32 catches for 481 yards and six touchdowns through four games. Regardless of quarterback, Smith-Njigba has produced, and the 49ers will have to find a way to mitigate the defense. Interestingly, they’ve been among the league’s best though at limiting explosives, which is exactly what the Seahawks will try to accomplish when funneling passes to their star receiver. In years past, when Charvarius Ward was on the team, he could be a corner that the 49ers used to shadow elite outside receivers. Deommodore Lenoir has asked for that assignment as well. But San Francisco has elected not to do so. Why has that been the case, and why will that likely continue on Sunday? “There’s always things you can do and that’s always something that’s definitely within the system. But, those guys nowadays are a little bit different,” defensive coordinator Raheem Morris said when asked on Thursday. “Back in the day when you shadowed somebody, you moved, the other people didn’t move. That was back when Marvin Harrison played on one side and Reggie Wayne played on one side and they just sat there. But as you see in today’s game, there’s a bunch of different things that happen, moving parts. People move, they move inside, they move outside, they move into the backfield, particularly these guys and how they game plan. That’s not always the best thing for the team at times. “[Lenoir] will be matched up with [Smith-Njigba] a bunch. He will match up a little bit. They cannot stay away from each other, but we won’t do necessarily the shadow thing where you follow him inside, you follow him outside. There’s things we have to do, how we play our game, that won’t be able to pinpoint that all the time, but there will definitely be moments that they’ll get a chance to get together. I don’t know if that’s a nice answer of saying no, but it’s just one of those things of it’s just not the same as it used to be.” One of Smith-Njigba’s biggest assets is the way he wins regardless of placement on the field, and the Seahawks do a good job drawing him targets by aligning him all over the place. That’s a key reason why the 49ers can’t regularly assign a corner to shadow. “It’s a bunch of different things [why shadowing isn’t ideal],” Morris continued. “You have these corners, whether it be Patrick Surtain or whether it was Jalen Ramsey or whether it’s DMo. Those receivers are all over the place. As you see our guys moving around all over the place, there’s not just a stationary X anymore, a stationary Z. It just doesn’t work that way. There’s definitely times you can. There’s definitely got-to-have-it moments you can match those things up. It’s definitely dictated by the call at times like some of those things give things away. These quarterbacks nowadays are too smart to just go out there and determine things and dictate things before the snap. You want to be able to sort it out a little bit as they’re taking the snap, taking their drop, going through their process, if that makes sense.” The 49ers will have to devise a gameplan to limit the star wideout’s targets, and they’ve done a great job of limiting explosives so far. But Smith-Njigba will be their biggest challenge yet, and the 49ers will also be on the road in a big rivalry game on Sunday.

summary: After looking at some Seahawks tape, some thoughts:  The offensive line seems not as good as I thought they’d be.  The defense, while still being super disruptive, is missing more tackles.  Otherwise, they’re still pretty nasty. full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images After looking at some Seahawks tape, some thoughts: The offensive line seems not as good as I thought they’d be. The defense, while still being super disruptive, is missing more tackles. Otherwise, they’re still pretty nasty. If Bosa was playing, I’d be more confident that the 49ers could disrupt Sam Darnold enough to stay in it and prove my prediction wrong. It’s still possible, especially if Mykel plays and shows us more in the pass-rush. Faithful, take 49ers game day wherever you go! Stay connected to the action and share every reaction with fellow 49ers fans on the SB Nation app. Join the live game-day chat Browse with fewer ads Seamlessly jump between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . That said, I am confident that Kittle, McCaffrey, and a half-healthy Evans (with a sprinkling of Deebo and Kaelon) are enough to make plays against this defense. Especially if they get the ball in space. The 49ers offensive line gets a great chance to show that their improvement is for real, especially in the run game. That’s where they really struggled in the playoff loss last year. How to solve Seahawks’ defense? 49ers’ Kyle Shanahan has admitted he’s not one to ask (paywall) “After his motions, shifts and other eye candy didn’t fool the Seahawks, Shanahan resorted to trickery to try to gain yards in the divisional playoffs. A double-reverse pass gained one yard. A 4th-and-1 option pitch from fullback Kyle Juszczyk to running back Christian McCaffrey lost three yards. “They’re never out of position,” left guard Dominick Puni said. “They always know where each other is going to be. You can see it on film. They’re always just attached.” In February, as an analyst, Shanahan explained what made Seattle’s defense so special. The Seahawks prevent explosive passing plays by playing their two safeties deep, which usually exposes a team’s run defense. However, Seattle can still stuff opponents’ rushing attacks in its nickel defense, using an extra defensive back, and with their safeties residing in Spokane.” 49ers guard Connor Colby shows speed on George Kittle’s long touchdown “I wouldn’t say I was necessarily gaining on him,” Colby said of his sprint alongside Hufanga. “I was just trying to make a block, but then I realized once I got up there, anything I did probably would have been a penalty. So I figured, I’d just let George run.” …. “The guy’s definitely an athlete,” 49ers center Jake Brendel said. “He might not look it with his hair and his style, but, I mean, there’s definitely a reason the front office and the coaches liked him. He can run. He can run wide zone. He’s a good player.” Williams rejected the label of “sneaky athletic” to describe Colby. “I wouldn’t say that,” Williams said. “I think he’s just athletic. The mullet makes it worse. But if you work closely with him and see him, you know he’s an athlete, for sure.” 49ers DE Romello Height inspired by Patrick Willis to play through broken hand (paywall) “I was going off adrenaline,” Height said of his second-half performance in the 49ers’ 35-13 win. “I felt pain, but it didn’t matter at that point. I wanted to play for my brothers, and I wanted to finish the deal.” After further evaluation postgame, doctors determined Height’s hand would require surgery. He had a procedure Sept. 22 that kept him out of the 49ers’ subsequent contest against the Cardinals, before making his return in Week 4 against the Denver Broncos, starting and playing 37 snaps. Protecting his hand was a club — a club so hard that when Height gave fellow rookie Jaden Dugger a fist bump, he questioned how Height was even playing. Beneath his club was “a lot” of protective padding, Height said, giving the cast so much bulk that it could only be compared to a boxing glove.: 49ers’ Kyle Shanahan delivers positive Mykel Williams and Nick Bosa updates “It’s been good,” Shanahan said. “It’s been his second week back, so he had a good week last week—even better this week. So, should be good to go for Sunday.” Raheem Morris, Klay Kubiak, Brock Purdy share updates ahead of 49ers-Seahawks “A technical quarterbacking question. Your non-throwing arm. What’s the role of the non-throwing arm in throwing and is that something that you’ve ever felt like you needed to adjust or tweak or anything like that? “That’s a good question. I don’t know to be honest. I think as I’ve gone throughout my life as a thrower and looking at my mechanics and things, that is something that I’ve looked at. How should the opposite arm be? Should it be tight, like you could have your thumb hold your collar of your shirt and stuff and have it tight, but then other guys are out wide. I don’t know. It’s something that I look at every once in a while, but I don’t think it drastically changes my throwing mechanics and stuff. There’s other things that I’d look at rather than that, but it is a good point. A lot of people do look at it, so it’s a good question.” John Lynch on the 49ers ahead of the trade deadline: ‘I think you’re always in active mode’ “49ers general manager John Lynch was asked about the deadline on KNBR. He said, “I think you’re always in active mode.” Josh Sweat plays in the division, but names like Khalil Mack, Will McDonald, Danielle Hunter, Josh Uche, Kayvon Thibodeaux, and any other pass rusher with a pulse will be linked to the Niners over the next month. Lynch continued, “I always say, I think our history speaks to the fact that we will not hesitate to improve this team if we can, and we’ve done that on a number of occasions. So we’re doing our jobs, and real proud of the way our team’s playing.”

title: Notes and stats from the Buccaneers 24-16 win over the Cowboys
summary: – The Tampa Bay Buccaneers defeated the Dallas Cowboys, 24-16, on Thursday Night Football. With the win Buccaneers General Manager Jason Licht earned the 100th win of his career in Tampa Bay, including playoffs, becoming the first general manager in franchise history to reach the 100-win milestone.  – Head Coach Todd Bowles picked up his 37th career win as Buccaneers head coach, […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - OCTOBER 8: Jalon Daniels #10 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers celebrates during the second half against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on October 8, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Ron Jenkins/Getty Images) | Getty Images – The Tampa Bay Buccaneers defeated the Dallas Cowboys, 24-16, on Thursday Night Football . With the win Buccaneers General Manager Jason Licht earned the 100 th win of his career in Tampa Bay, including playoffs, becoming the first general manager in franchise history to reach the 100-win milestone. – Head Coach Todd Bowles picked up his 37 th career win as Buccaneers head coach, including playoffs, surpassing Bruce Arians for the fourth-most total wins by a head coach in team history. – Rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels , in just his second career start, completed 19-of-25 passes for 189 yards and one touchdown, earning a 110.2 passer rating and picking up his first career win. He became just the third undrafted rookie quarterback since 1950 to win in primetime in either their first or second career start joining Devlin Hodges (110/13/19) and Tom Greene (9/17/60), and just the fifth undrafted rookie quarterback in the common draft era to do so in any start. He became just the ninth undrafted rookie quarterback to lead his team to 400+ total yards of offense in a game and the first since Tommy DeVito (12/11/23). He is also the first undrafted rookie quarterback to ever defeat the Dallas Cowboys. – On the offense’s opening possession, Daniels led the Buccaneers on a 15-play, 73-yard drive that took 10:58 off the clock. It marks the Buccaneers’ longest drive by elapsed time since 11/4/07 vs. Arizona (11:59) and marks the team’s longest scoring drive since Pro Football Reference data is available dating back to 2001. Per team records, the touchdown drive was the second-longest scoring drive in team history, trailing only a 10:59 drive vs. New Orleans on 9/18/94. The team’s eight first downs on the opening drive matched its most on a single drive since at least 2001. – Daniels went a perfect 8-for-8 passing on the drive. Daniels is 1-of-2 undrafted rookie quarterbacks since 1991 – and the first since 2013 – to earn a 100.0% completion percentage in a single quarter, while completing seven-or-more passes (also Matt McGloin, third quarter, 12/15/13 vs. Kansas City). He is the only undrafted rookie quarterback since 1967 to complete his first eight passes of a game. – Bucky Irving took 21 carries for a career-best 165 yards and one rushing touchdown, adding two receptions for 10 yards and one receiving touchdown. It marked the first time in Irving’s career that he has had a rushing touchdown and a receiving touchdown in a single game. His 175 yards from scrimmage marked the third-most of his career. Irving’s 72-yard run on the day is the longest of his NFL career. – Thursday’s game marked Irving’s fourth career 100-yard rushing performance and also helped him surpass the 2,000-yard rushing milestone for his career. He is the 13 th player in franchise history to reach 2,000 career rushing yards for Tampa Bay. Irving reached 2,000 career rushing yards in his 32nd career NFL game, tying Warrick Dunn for the fourth-fewest games to reach that milestone in franchise history, trailing only Doug Martin (25), Cadillac Williams (29) and Errict Rhett (29). – Irving’s 165 rushing yards were the most by a player vs. Dallas in a Cowboys home game since 2012 (Bryce Brown, 169, with Philadelphia). – Emeka Egbuka contributed six receptions for 38 yards, in addition to tallying the first rushing touchdown of his NFL career on a 14-yard run. – Tez Johnson hauled in a career-long 64-yard reception, which also marked a career-long completion for Daniels . – As a team Tampa Bay finished with 419 total net yards of offense, including 241 yards on the ground. The 419 total yards of offense marked the most for Tampa Bay since 10/5/25 at Seattle (426), while the team’s 241 rushing yards were the most in a game since 10/13/24 at New Orleans. Tampa Bay’s 6.2 yards per rush attempt on Thursday set a new season high and secured the team’s highest average in a single game since its 7.9 yards per rush on 10/13/24 at New Orleans. It’s also the fourth-highest average in team history among games in which Tampa Bay rushed 35+ times. – The Buccaneers recorded 24 first downs – the team’s most in any game this season and its most since 12/11/25 vs. Atlanta. – Tampa Bay’s defense won the turnover battle, 3-0. It marked the Buccaneers’ first three-takeaway game since Week 18 of the 2025 season. – Alex Anzalone sealed the game with his first interception for Tampa Bay, and the fifth interception of his NFL career. Since he entered the league in 2017, Anzalone is 1-of-6 linebackers with 600+ tackles, 35+ passes defensed, 12.0+ sacks and five-or-more interceptions, alongside Jordan Hicks, Deion Jones, Eric Kendricks, Roquan Smith and Bobby Wagner. – Yaya Diaby recorded his first career interception on a Dak Prescott pass that was deflected by both OLB David Walker and S Tykee Smith . – Jacob Parrish recorded a career-best four passes defensed, marking his third career game with multiple passes defensed. Parrish’s seven passes defensed on the season are tied for the most in the NFL this season and he is 1-of-5 players in 2026 to post a game with four-or-more passes defensed. Parrish also led the team in tackles, with nine, matching his career high (10/5/25 at Seattle). – Zyon McCollum recorded two passes defensed, marking his 10 th career game with multiple passes defensed. McCollum’s six passes defensed on the season are tied for the fifth-most in the NFL this season. – Tampa Bay’s secondary held Cowboys wide receiver CeeDee Lamb to just two receptions for nine yards. It marked the fourth-lowest receiving yards total and tied for his fourth-fewest receptions of any game of his NFL career. – Tampa Bay held the Cowboys to just 16 points on Thursday – the lowest scoring output by Dallas since 9/21/25 at Chicago. Additionally, the Cowboys totaled just 50 rush yards in the game – the team’s lowest rushing total since 10/12/25 at Carolina. The Buccaneers are the first team to hold Dallas to 16-or-fewer points and 50-or-fewer rushing yards in a single game since the New Orleans Saints on 9/29/19. – With seven tackles in Thursday’s contest, Josiah Trotter surpassed Lavonte David (33 in 2012) for the second-most and Kendell Beckwith Jr. (36 in 2017) for the most tackles by a Buccaneers player through their first four career games since at least 2000. – DB Keionte Scott amassed a career high seven tackles, including one for loss, adding one pass defensed. – On special teams, Miles Killebrew forced a fumble on a kickoff return that was recovered by Kevin Knowles . It marked the second career forced fumble for Killebrew and the second career fumble recovery for Knowles. (Courtesy of the Buccaneers Communications Department .)

It’s not a huge surprise that the Titans are 0-4, but a lot of people thought the Texans were going to be Super Bowl contenders this season. That feels like a long shot at 0-4. It would be virtually impossible at 0-5. On paper, the Texans are a much better team. Their defensive front is one of the best in the league. The Titans offensive line has played much better this year, but they have not faced a front like this to this point. This will be a really good test for that unit. I’d love to call an upset here, but I just don’t see it. The Titans are going to get the Texans’ best shot with their season on the line. Cam Ward played better last week than the week before, but he is going to be under more pressure this week. We have seen that when he feels pressure, he has the tendency to revert to some bad habits that create inconsistent play. Look for the Texans to get at least 4 sacks of Ward in this one. On defense, the key to stopping the Texans is stopping Nico Collins. The Texans average over 30 points per game when Collins plays and under 12 points per game when he doesn’t. full_text: The Commanders waived sixth-round running back Kaytron Allen on Thursday, and then GM Adam Peters and head coach Dan Quinn spent some of their Friday public appearances saying they liked him and hoped to sign him the practice squad . That won’t be possible. The Miami Dolphins claimed him off waivers, the Dolphins announced on Friday afternoon. The Dolphins have a super high spot on the NFL waiver wire order, which is now based on the reverse order of the league standings. Miami is 0-4. The Dolphins also recently lost running back De’Von Achane to a torn ACL , so the claim makes sense. Allen endeared himself to fans with his tough rushing style, Penn State highlights, engaging personality and the fact he prefers the nickname “Fatman.” During his brief time in Washington, Allen had 12 rushes for 41 yards in four regular-season games . The Commanders faced a logjam at running back and real needs at other positions, creating the gamble of waiving Allen while trying to get him to the practice squad. That attempt was unsuccessful. The Commanders have Bill Croskey-Merritt and Rachaad White available. They also signed veteran Austin Ekeler last week and have Jeremy McNichols nearing a return off injured reserve. title: Tyler’s Take — Adam Peters is on a bad trajectory as Washington’s general manager
summary: Adam Peters’ hire as general manager of the Washington Commanders was met with much fanfare. He cut his teeth as a scout with the Patriots and Broncos, who both won the Lombardi Trophy while he was there, and learned as an executive under John Lynch in San Francisco. Fans felt that owner Josh Harris had […]
full_text: Adam Peters’ hire as general manager of the Washington Commanders was met with much fanfare. He cut his teeth as a scout with the Patriots and Broncos, who both won the Lombardi Trophy while he was there, and learned as an executive under John Lynch in San Francisco. Fans felt that owner Josh Harris had landed a true football mind. Fast-forward two-and-a-half years and many are questioning Adam Peters’ philosophy here in the Nation’s Capital, and for good reason. Settling on Dan Quinn Make no mistake about it. Dan Quinn was not Adam Peters’ first choice. That honor would go to one Ben Johnson. Quinn wasn’t Peters’ second choice. That would have been Mike Macdonald, who went to Seattle instead. I don’t even know if Quinn was third on the list. Point is, we ended up with him and now he’s one of the top coaches on the hot seat after just two full seasons. “Settling” on Dan Quinn may have turned out to be a really bad look for Peters’ first hire as general manager. After a rather lucky 2024, Quinn has come back down to planet Earth and has settled into his expected routine as a head coach — one of mediocrity. There is a severe lack of development with players Quinn and his staff have been handed, and some of those players have barely been able to even see the field. Those who have seemed to have regressed or been hit by the injury bug. And since the injury bug has been brought up, I think it’s fair to question Dan’s “back to play” protocol as being a bit TOO cautious. Unless there is some miraculous turnaround over the next three quarters of Washington’s season, Quinn may have exhausted his final shot at being a successful NFL head coach — and much of the blame can be pinned on Peters for making the underwhelming hire. Missing badly on draft picks Adam Peters believes in building through the draft and supplementing through free agency. Although many point to him trading away draft picks for an aging and injured Marcus Lattimore and Pro Bowl left tackle Laremy Tunsil, his bread and butter is still the draft. Well, what if your draft picks aren’t that good? 2024: Let’s not confuse anything here. With the exception of what many viewed as a “can’t miss” prospect in Jayden Daniels, who fell into Peters’ lap at pick No. 2 overall , the 2024 draft has been a disappointment. QB Jayden Daniels – great pick. Needs to stay on the field. DL Johnny Newton – currently on IR, but has done nothing to date beside one game against Dallas’ reserves in 2025. CB Mike Sandristil – has essentially been benched for a street free agent. TE Ben Sinnott – career 17 receptions, 148 yards and two touchdowns. Currently, Brandon Coleman has as many receptions and more receiving yards in 2026. WR Luke McCaffrey – has been inactive for three of Washington’s four games in 2026. LB Jordan Magee – on IR yet again… LB Dominique Hampton – no longer with the team. EDGE Javontae Jean-Baptiste – back-up EDGE. 2025: It’s still very early to grade the 2025 draft class, but… OL Josh Conerly – starting right tackle who is improving. CB Trey Amos – current injury concerns. WR/KR Jaylin Lane – currently on IR. Mainly a special teams contributor. LB Kain Medrano – backup linebacker. RB Bill Croskey-Merritt – starting running back who looks to have regressed from 2025. 2026: Although Peters’ 2026 draft class is looking promising, it’s way too early to judge the class. However, Washington did just waive their rookie sixth-round running back Kaytron “Fatman” Allen on Thursday and, per ESPN’s Adam Schefter , he was claimed off waivers by the Miami Dolphins. Trading away draft picks This one is two-fold. DB Marshon Lattimore: 2025 third-, fourth-, and sixth-round picks (Washington received a fifth-round pick from New Orleans). The move for an aging, declining and injured Marshon Lattimore was a whiff. And look, it happens. I will give Peters credit for seeing a need and making a move to fill that need, however this was a poorly calculated decision moving on a player who was on the decline and battling injury. OL Laremy Tunsil: 2025 third- and seventh-round picks, plus 2026 second- and fourth-round picks (Washington received a 2025 fourth-round pick). I loved the trade for Laremy Tunsil. He’s been a stalwart in the league and has shown no signs of decline. It was unfortunate he got injured in training camp, but there were no injury red flags with him like there were with Lattimore. WR Deebo Samuel: Although not as costly as the previously mentioned, Peters gave up a 2025 fifth-round pick for the aging 49ers former star. It wasn’t a bad move; it wasn’t a great move. It was just MEH. And, by the way, Samuels leaves a $12.4M dead cap hit for 2026. AARP Adam (2025 offseason) I joked about Adam Peters being “AARP Adam” in the 2025 offseason due to his propensity for signing aging veterans on one-year deals – or did I… Re-Signings LB Bobby Wagner – major liability against outside runs and in coverage. TE Zach Ertz – got injured and finished season on IR. TE John Bates – quality blocking TE. WR Noah Brown – played in four games before being placed on IR. RB Jeremy McNichols – tough runner, but not a difference maker. QB Josh Johnson – started two games (out of necessity). WR Chris Moore (futures contract) – wound up starting five games. Unrestricted free agents DB Will Harris – cut this summer after one year of a two-year deal. DL Eddie Goldman – older, big-bodied interior presence who did nothing. CB Jonathan Jones – injured; came back and forced into starting duties because of other injuries. DL Deatrich Wise – injured in second game of season. put on IR. EDGE Jacob Martin – started 14 games and recorded 5.5 sacks. EDGE Von Miller – led the team with nine sacks. Street free agents EDGE Preston Smith – recorded half a sack over 13 games. WR Robbie Chosen – played in three games and caught five passes. Make no mistake – Washington had cap room to spend some money on young, ascending players. Instead, Peters chose to hand Quinn the bingo room at the local VFW! A MASSIVE oversight by the “smartest man in the room” that backfired. The current mess at center Scott Bair wrote this about Peters’ plan at center heading into the 2026 season: Commanders general manager Adam Peters had a plan for the center position entering the 2026 campaign. It obviously wasn’t good enough. We’ve seen that play out painfully over the course of this summer, with presumptive starter Nick Allegretti out most of training camp with a calf strain. Allegretti suffered the injury during Washington’s first training camp practice, way back on July 29 . He returned on Aug. 18, following nearly three weeks on the shelf. Allegretti aggravated the issue a day later and hasn’t returned since. Because of Adam’s mismanagement at center, Jayden Daniels took snaps most of the offseason from Julian Good-Jones and rookie Matt Gulbin. When training camp ended, and regular season game preparation began, Nick Allegretti finally returned to practice and took over starting center responsibilities. The “Allegretti Experiment” lasted just two weeks. After Sam Cosmi was ruled out for a concussion, Allegretti slid over to right guard and street free agent Lucas Patrick slid in at center. Surprisingly, Washington won their first game of the season against Seattle despite Allegretti getting absolutely abused at guard. Patrick, maybe not so surprisingly, looked good at center. Last week against the struggling Colts, Quinn decided to make a change at right guard, giving rookie Matt Gulbin the start while “wonder boy” rode the bench. Gulbin played so poorly in that game that fans were calling for Allegretti to be put back in at the half – something that never happened. Now, you may want to pin the blame on Dan Quinn for having confidence that Allegretti could hold down the center position, but I put this one squarely on Adam Peters for his offseason mismanagement of the position. title: Commanders vs. Giants Friday injury report: Stefon Diggs out, Jayden Daniels will play
summary: Commanders receiver Stefon Diggs (hamstring) has been ruled out of Sunday’s game against the New York Giants, head coach Dan Quinn said in his Friday press conference. That’s a big blow, considering Diggs has been Washington’s leading receiver to this point. Fingers are crossed for better news on Terry McLaurin, who was able to practice […]
full_text: Commanders receiver Stefon Diggs (hamstring) has been ruled out of Sunday’s game against the New York Giants, head coach Dan Quinn said in his Friday press conference . That’s a big blow, considering Diggs has been Washington’s leading receiver to this point. Fingers are crossed for better news on Terry McLaurin , who was able to practice on Friday and for the first time this week. Quinn said he looked good in the workout. The Commanders formally listed McLaurin as questionable Friday afternoon on the team’s official injury report. The veteran suffered a hamstring injury in the last practice before Washington played the Colts in London, which kept him from playing that Week 4 game . The Commanders also ruled safety Nick Cross (illness) out after not receiving a medical clearance to play. Adding to that trouble, safeties Percy Butler (hamstring) and Tyler Owens (hamstring) are out of this game. Down three active safeties, Washington must elevate one to get through the game — they just added Darren Hall to the practice squad — where Quan Martin and Jeremy Reaves will play a ton. Defensive end Charles Omenihu (groin/ankle) is also out, which is a big blow to the defensive front. He has been integral to some generally solid run defense. Quarterback Marcus Mariota was ruled out earlier, so that was no shock. Quinn delivered some good (yet expected) news for the Commanders, saying that quarterback Jayden Daniels (elbow), right guard Sam Cosmi (concussion) and running back Rachaad White (shoulder) will play against the Giants in a crucial Week 5 matchup. The Commanders opened 21-day practice windows for cornerback Trey Amos, defensive lineman Deatrich Wise and running back Jeremy McNichols and designated them questionable — that’s fairly common — but would have to add them to the active roster before playing. Was hospitalized for internal injuries in Dallas after the game. S Tyler Owens – Has a hamstring issue Questionable WR Terry McLaurin – Has a hamstring strain suffered in Friday practice in London CB Trey Amos – Returning from an ankle injury; still on IR RB Jeremy McNichols – Returning from a quad strain; still on IR DL Deatrich Wise Jr. – Just returning from a torn quad; still on PUP
