title: NFL Week 5 betting guide: Analysis, best bets, TD predictions for Sunday
summary: Our experts dive into the odds and player props for Week 5 and offer their betting tips and favorite plays.
full_text:
Value is value, no matter where -- or how -- you find it. And that's what we'll aim to do each week in this space: finding betting value.

 Ben Solak, Seth Walder and Matt Bowen bring different perspectives into how they approach sports betting. Solak leans on his expertise in player evaluation and the X's and O's to find edges, while Walder relies on statistical models to pick out plus-expected value bets, focusing mainly on defense. Bowen, a former NFL safety, predicts positive matchups and game winners from tape study and his understanding of the league. Also included are fantasy projection creator Mike Clay's top predicted anytime TD scorers for Week 5.

 From spreads and money lines to totals and defensive player props, a good price might be found anywhere. Results will be tracked throughout the season, with flat one-unit wagers for each listed bet. With that, let's dive into our best bets, the top game to bet, favorite defensive props to play and the top predicted TD scorers.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 Jump to: 
 Bowen's Game of the Week 
 Solak's plays  | Walder's props 
 Clay's TD projections 

 

 

 Bowen's Game of the Week 

 Indianapolis Colts at Pittsburgh Steelers (-2.5, 44.5) 
1 p.m. ET on CBS, Acrisure Stadium, Pittsburgh

 

 We need to have a bounce-back week here after betting on the Bills last Sunday. So, let's pivot to a rested Pittsburgh team that played Thursday night in Week 4 at home against an Indianapolis team straight off a London trip. We'll look at both sides of the ball, then hit some props from this game and across the league in Week 5.

 

 When the Steelers have the ball: Running back Jaylen Warren has seen his usage (and production) elevate over the past two games. During this stretch (against Cincinnati and Cleveland) Warren has averaged 6.5 yards per carry, 21 touches and 151 scrimmage yards. He's also playing fast on the tape, and there's a lot of outside zone here, with Warren finding daylight. Plus, he's getting the ball on swings, screens and checkdowns. This is a good matchup for Warren against a Colts defense giving up 131 rushing yards per game (28th in the league). I expect a volume day for the Steelers' lead back.

 The Colts' defensive numbers in the pass game point to a Pittsburgh edge as well, as the Colts are giving up 261.3 yards per game through the air and are pressuring the QB at a rate of only 28.3% (29th in the league). But can the Steelers protect and give Aaron Rodgers time and a clean pocket? Rodgers has three touchdown passes and six completions of 15 or more air yards in each of his past two games, but he has been sacked seven times during that stretch and a total of 13 times on the season (tied for most in the league). Rodgers' declining mobility also plays a role, but he needs the pocket to throw vertically to  DK Metcalf  and work the play-action pass game in Mike McCarthy's offense.

 When the Colts have the ball: This offense runs through Jonathan Taylor . The Colts' running back ranks fifth in the NFL at 88.3 rushing yards per game, and his 86 carries are the third most through four games. He's a volume back with home run ability. Taylor has 12 rushes of 10 or more yards this season, and he gets a Steelers defense that is giving up 4.3 YPC (20th). I'd expect a run-heavy approach from the Colts to start this one, but the Steelers should counter with more single-high coverages, spinning down from their split-safety shells to get numbers in the front.

 Look for quarterback Daniel Jones to lean on play-action throws that mirror the run game. Jones ranks fifth in play-action attempts this season, and the Colts will look to open intermediate windows against a Steelers defense that plays heavy zone coverage (75.4% of coverage snaps). And without wide receiver Alec Pierce (IR/heel), there is a missing vertical element for the Colts, as Jones' 5.7 YPA ranks 28th. Josh Downs and Keenan Allen need to uncover and make themselves available to the QB in this one, and I would like to see tight end Tyler Warren featured more on seams and corner routes to create chunk plays.

 Picks: Steelers -2.5 (-118), Under 44.5 (-118)

 Prop bets: Jonathan Taylor rushing + receiving yards OVER 105.5 (-114) 

 I'll trust the anticipated volume for Taylor, who has had at least 21 touches in all four games played this season, producing at least 110 total yards in two. With the rushing totals and targets on screens and check downs, Taylor should hit the over.

 Jaylen Warren rushing yards OVER 62.5 (-112) 

 Warren has rushed for at least 93 yards in two straight games, with 17 carries in each. Take Warren's recent run on production in a matchup versus a Colts defense allowing 4.8 YPC (sixth highest in the league).

 

 Now, let's get to some other bets I like ...

 Christian Watson anytime TD (+195) 

 Watson has scored at least one touchdown in three of four games played, and he has four end zone targets on the season. Plus, we know Watson can separate over the top. I like the matchup here for the Packers' receiver against the Bears' cornerbacks, and Matt LaFleur can also scheme zone-beaters for Watson.

 San Francisco 49ers at Seattle Seahawks total points UNDER 45.5 (-105) 

 In the two games these clubs played last season, the totals hit 30 and 16. Mike Macdonald has the scheme (and personnel) to limit the 49ers' offense. I'd take the under in this one.

 Three-team parlay (+638) 

 Jacksonville Jaguars -7.5 vs. Philadelphia Eagles 
 Cleveland Browns +1.5 at New York Jets 
 Las Vegas Raiders +3.5 at New England Patriots 

 The Jaguars might be the best team in football, and they get an Eagles squad that is going through major in-season transitions on the offensive line. Plus, Philly will be without Saquon Barkley and DeVonta Smith .

 Cleveland also is playing good ball. Todd Monken's offense can take vertical shots in the pass game, and the downhill rushing attack is a foundational approach with Quinshon Judkins . The Browns can run the ball against a Jets defense that just gave up 232 yards on the ground to the Bears in Week 4.

 Let's finish this parlay with the Raiders getting points on the road in New England. Las Vegas features a top-10 passing defense, and quarterback Kirk Cousins is an easy fit in Klint Kubiak's schemed-up system. The Raiders need more here from Ashton Jeanty and the run game, but I like them to cover.

 

 

 
 Solak's plays 
 

 Washington Commanders -3.5 vs. New York Giants 

 The 1-3 Commanders welcome Jayden Daniels back to the starting lineup with the 3-1 New York Giants -- who still have Jameis Winston starting at quarterback -- coming to town. The Giants' 2-0 run with Winston has been extremely unimpressive. They beat the Titans 12-7 on a rainy and windy day in MetLife Staduim thanks to a game-sealing end zone pick from Jevon Holland . They beat the Cardinals 36-24 thanks to a 98-yard pick-six by Deonte Banks on fourth-and-goal. With a little bit better red zone execution from two of the league's worst starting quarterbacks, the Giants are 1-3.

 

 As it is, the Giants are 27th in EPA per drive and in success rate during Winston's two starts, and they draw a plucky Commanders defense that can bring out the worst of Winston by blitzing heavily (second only to the Vikings in blitz rate) and forcing turnovers. Star receiver Malik Nabers  sat out Wednesday's practice because of a sore knee, and if he is at all limited, the Giants' lack of pass-catching depth makes it challenging to move the ball with any consistency.

 Washington is enduring a slew of its own injuries. Receivers  Terry McLaurin  and Stefon Diggs were both absent from Wednesday's practice, and their top two running backs ( Rachaad White and Jacory Croskey-Merritt ), two tight ends ( Chig Okonkwo and Ben Sinnott ), and both starting linebackers ( Sonny Styles and Frankie Luvu ) were all limited. title: Why the Raiders' running game has struggled, and what's next for Ashton Jeanty
summary: The Raiders have made offensive strides ... except for the running game. What's next for Las Vegas and Ashton Jeanty?
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev. -- The Las Vegas Raiders opened their Week 4 matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs with plenty of momentum. Four plays in, and they already were on the scoreboard when quarterback Kirk Cousins threw a 27-yard touchdown pass to tight end Ian Thomas .

 The Raiders tried to replicate that success on their second drive, but were unsuccessful.

 

 With 2:17 to go in the first quarter and the game tied at seven, Cousins completed a 15-yard pass to tight end Michael Mayer , then coach Klint Kubiak turned to the run game to keep the chains moving, but they didn't. Rookie running back Mike Washington Jr . was stopped for a one-yard attempt before Chiefs rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane wrapped up running back Ashton Jeanty for no gain. On third-and-9, Cousins threw an incomplete pass, which forced the Raiders to punt.

 In the Raiders' 30-27 loss to the Chiefs last Sunday, they went toe-to-toe with a team that has won nine of the past 10 AFC West titles. But the Raiders' upset attempt failed because of more than a questionable fourth-down decision from Kubiak or Dareke Young's kick return fumble. For the third straight week, Las Vegas failed to establish a consistent run game, totaling 72 yards.

 The Raiders have made significant offensive strides; they rank eighth in the league in points per game (28.7) and Cousins has thrown a league-high 11 touchdowns. However, their rushing attack has been a problem. Entering the season, the Raiders' run game was meant to be their biggest strength. Instead, their production has mirrored last year when they ranked last in nearly every rushing metric.

 Multiple factors have contributed to Las Vegas' faulty rushing attack, from playcalling to Jeanty, their top running back and 2025 first-round pick, playing through an ankle injury. Jeanty was a limited participant in Thursday's practice due to an ankle and foot injury. If the Raiders want to show their strong first month wasn't a fluke, they will need to improve their rushing numbers, starting Sunday afternoon against the New England Patriots ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ).

 "I think we've just got to be better. Simple as that," Jeanty said. "Make the plays that are out there. ... It starts with us. Starts with me. Got to break tackles and make bigger plays when they're available."

 
 

 FIXING THE RUN game was a big part of the Raiders' preparation ahead of the season. In the past three seasons, Las Vegas ranked last in rushing yards per game (82.7) and yards per attempt (3.6).

 This year was meant to be a different story. Jeanty was entering Year 2 and more experienced. Kubiak brought in a proven outside zone run scheme. The Raiders signed center Tyler Linderbaum , who is one of the better run blockers at his position. And Washington showed throughout training camp that he could be capable of being a reliable second option in the backfield.

 The Raiders didn't have issues running the rock in Week 1's victory over the Miami Dolphins . They totaled 137 rushing yards, with Jeanty recording 102 yards on 23 attempts. Since then, Las Vegas's numbers have declined.

 In the past three weeks, the team has ranked 32nd in yards per attempt (three), 28th in yards per game (80.7), 30th in rushing first downs (11) and tied for 26th in attempts for 10-plus yards (four).

 

 "Going back to that first game [against Miami], just as a whole unit, we played better," Kubiak said. "We were more efficient running the football, and that's something we got to get back to. So, it's something that we're diligent about."

 Jeanty, who was expected to make a jump in Year 2, has struggled as well. He rushed for 58 yards against the Chiefs. He has been held to under 60 rushing yards in five of his past 10 games dating back to his rookie season.

 Through four games, Jeanty has a rush success rate of 35.9% and a rush EPA of minus-23.2. Now, Jeanty's inconsistent production is not all on him. He has been playing through an ankle injury , which he suffered near the end of training camp.

 He said after the loss to Kansas City that the injury hasn't nagged him, but he expects to be 100% healthy real soon.

 "I'm going to continue to keep getting better and stronger," Jeanty said.

 Yes, Jeanty has to improve his vision and take advantage of open lanes whenever they appear. At the same time, the run blocking has to be cleaned up. Against Kansas City, Jeanty was stopped for no gain or a loss of yards on six attempts. Meanwhile, Washington had three of his nine attempts result in zero or fewer yards.

 Las Vegas is 30th in yards before first contact per attempt (1.34), and has the most carries for zero or negative yards (29).

 "You want to hit a home run every single time, but it's not going to happen," Linderbaum said. "It's how many times can we get to second-and-6 [and] second-and-5. That's the challenge. ... At the end of the day, that falls on the [offensive] line."

 
 

 AFTER THE RAIDERS' first loss of the season, Kubiak said they need to find answers for their inconsistent rushing attack. Kubiak is more than capable of finding those answers.

 When Kubiak was the offensive coordinator for the Seattle Seahawks last season, the run game started slow before finding a groove and becoming instrumental in their Super Bowl LX victory over New England.

 They averaged 3.6 rushing yards per attempt and had a success rate of 37.4% from Weeks 1-4. From Week 5 to the end of the season, the Seahawks averaged 4.3 yards per attempt, a success rate of 41.6% and recorded 14 rushing touchdowns.

 In Las Vegas, Kubiak admitted that he needs to scheme up better plays to get the run game flowing. There were times against the Chiefs when the Raiders' pre-snap motion forced a defender to move over a gap, freeing them up to stop the run.

 

 Raiders frequently face stacked boxes (eight or more defenders at the line of scrimmage), which has also been a challenge. Las Vegas has faced stacked boxes on 30.3% of its run plays -- the fourth-highest percentage.

 The reasons behind opponents loading up the box are respect for Jeanty and the Raiders utilizing heavy personnel groupings at a high volume. With Kubiak using multiple tight end and running back formations, it requires the opposing defense to bring more defenders to the line of scrimmage.

 Las Vegas has seen success in the passing game when using heavy personnel groupings. But that success hasn't translated to the run game. The Raiders are tied with the Buffalo Bills for the most carries against stacked boxes (nine per game). However, they are 14th in yards per carry (2.3) and 26th in success rate (27.8%).

 "It just becomes a little bit of the math of how many players are down inside the tight end box, and do we have angles, do we have numbers or don't we? And it changes play to play," Cousins said. "... Teams are always going to be in that cat-and-mouse game a little bit of how you're trying to defend or how you're trying to attack the defense."

 The Raiders still believe the run game can be the identity of the offense despite their early struggles to find consistency. Once they gain more momentum in their rushing attack, they will be even more dangerous on play-action plays.

 Las Vegas knows it has the right players and coaches in the building to improve its run production. As a whole, they are confident that things will turn around, and hope that shift comes against the Patriots.

 "We got a great opportunity to go out there and do great things," Jeanty said.

title: How Saints can regroup, fix slow starts ahead of matchup with unbeaten Vikings
summary: New Orleans had a tough Week 4 loss to Atlanta, which also highlighted key deficiencies the Saints need to correct.
full_text:
METAIRIE, La. -- The bitterness of the New Orleans Saints ' 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons on Monday night will linger throughout a shortened week. 

 That's exactly how Saints defensive end Chase Young wants it with the 4-0  Minnesota Vikings up next on Sunday ( 1 p.m. ET, Fox ).

 "You should be upset," Young said Wednesday. "We didn't play to our standard, but the positive is seeing everybody come in today, how they're dealing with it. And that's what you want to see: dudes who have a sour taste in their mouth, dudes who are mad about it. I hope you mad. You get punched in your mouth, hopefully you ain't smiling."

 Young said he was pleased with the response of his teammates this week as they figure out how to regroup on both sides of the ball before Sunday. While Young will be facing an offense that ranks 18th in scoring, the Saints' offense will go up against the NFL's best scoring defense and top pass rush. 

 "They're undefeated, so that kind of speaks to the defense that they've had," tight end Juwan Johnson  said. "[They] bring a large amount of exotic blitzes, exotic looks. You're going to get a lot of shell looks, you're going to get a bunch of different shell looks. The biggest part is just exploiting just the gaps in their defense ... just playing our ball. We know how to play. 
 
"We just need to execute better."

 

 The Saints (1-3) will be underdogs against a Vikings squad that Saints wideout Chris Olave said is "one of the best teams in the NFL." Olave noted in an interview with French media this week that the Vikings have a lot of stunts and blitzes that can be difficult to face.

 "We're just going to have to put our best foot forward," he said. 
 
"They're 4-0, we're 1-3. On paper it's a lopsided matchup, but at the end of the day we still have to go out there and play for 60 minutes."

 Early mistakes doomed the Saints against the Falcons. The Saints allowed 205 yards on the ground after letting Bijan Robinson run 59 yards for a touchdown three plays into the game. The Saints rushed for only 50 yards as a team. 

 That rushing output and the team's slow starts have gone hand in hand. The Saints have the third-fewest first-quarter points this season (six), compared with 39 in the fourth quarter, which is tied for the most in the league with the Buffalo Bills and Denver Broncos . 

 The Saints have rushed for more than 100 yards only once this season. 

 "To be transparent, it's obvious that we've struggled running," Johnson said. "And I think we've been pretty good in the offseason just being dialed in on our keys and running the ball and it hasn't shown, but I think whenever we, and when we do well at running the ball, we're going to see an explosive amount of big plays just from our offense."

 Part of the lack of run game comes from falling behind early, which has forced the Saints to pass more. Defensively, they've given up 32 points per game, last in the league, a difficult combination for offensive balance. 

 Saints quarterback Tyler Shough has already attempted 180 passes this season, which is the second most in franchise history through four games behind Drew Brees' 191 attempts through four games in 2012. Brees had to throw often in those games (the Saints started 0-4) to try to keep pace due to a defense that still holds the record for most yards allowed in a season. 

 The current Saints know they have to eliminate mistakes they can no longer afford with such a small margin for error.

 "In the NFL, you can't live in that world where they know you're going to throw it every single time," Shough said. "And I don't have a problem doing that, but it's just tougher. 
 
"You can't have turnovers early in the game, and then we've got to be able to go down there and score. Three-and-outs, stuff like that. It's going to happen sometimes but ... limit those mistakes."

 

 So how do they fix the slow starts issue that dates to last season? Johnson said he doesn't think the Saints need to "turn practice over" or make huge adjustments. 

 "That's what people do when you have no answers, but we do have answers to the things that we do need to do. Again, we're only four games in. This is essentially this season's first quarter," Johnson said. "We know what we need to work on, and we're going to do exactly that."

 The Saints will make adjustments, though. Shough said the team put an emphasis on starting faster this week and made small changes, such as tweaking the practice schedule to try to build momentum quicker. 

 "More than anything, as players, we just have to do a better job of executing faster earlier. I think what we've done in the past and what we did last year, I think what we're going to start doing, is just have a compete period at the beginning of practice instead of the end," Shough said. "And that way you're immediately going right into it, and that's something that you can work on."

 Shough said there's no magic fix, pointing out that the team started better against the Las Vegas Raiders (the Saints scored a touchdown in the first quarter but missed the point-after attempt), then fell apart in the fourth quarter with turnovers. 

 "It's kind of a double-edged sword there," Shough said. "And more than anything, it kind of comes down to relentless execution."

title: Arvell Reese an easy call at ILB for Giants
summary: Most of the league projected rookie Reese as an outside linebacker, but the Giants saw him as an inside linebacker -- and it's working.
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- New York Giants rookie linebacker Arvell Reese just finished dominating an NFL game last Sunday. His stat sheet was filled with solo tackles, an interception, a forced interception and passes defended against the Arizona Cardinals .

 The greatest linebacker of all time, Lawrence Taylor, had said at halftime after being part of a celebration for the 40th anniversary of the 1986 Super Bowl team that Reese was "playing great." That might be the ultimate validation for a linebacker playing for the New York Football Giants in the swamps of East Rutherford.

 But although Reese was flattered by the compliment, he wasn't fully content.

 "Oh man, that means a lot," Reese said. "With a guy like that in the building, him setting the standard for how that position is supposed to be played back in the day, it definitely means a lot to play a decent game like that."

 Decent?! If that's decent, the Giants should look forward to seeing what good or even great translates to on the field.

 Reese, the fifth overall pick out of Ohio State in the 2026 NFL draft, said he left some plays out there in the 36-24 win over the Cardinals. 

 Yet he had nine tackles, a tackle for a loss, three passes defended, an interception and a pressure that forced another interception. It earned him NFC Rookie of the Week honors for Week 4.

 The Giants deserve some credit for Reese's early success -- some consider him the favorite for Defensive Rookie of the Year. Most of the league projected Reese as an outside linebacker coming out of Ohio State, but the Giants saw him as an inside linebacker.

 Why?

 "I would answer it this way -- that's what he played. So, it was easy," Giants coach John Harbaugh said. "You watched him on tape and he played it really well. And I could see where they might have said, 'Well, he's young, he hasn't played a lot, he's 20 years old,' and all that, but he played it really well at Ohio State against the best teams in the country in a pretty complicated defensive system that they have over there. So, yeah, it was, to me, the evidence was right there."

 

 Reese said at the NFL scouting combine in March that he was telling teams he's "an outside linebacker/edge." He played 238 snaps as an inside (off-ball) linebacker and 356 as an outside linebacker in his final season at Ohio State.

 The reality is that he would have adjusted either way. Fellow inside linebacker Tremaine Edmunds sees him as a rare athlete with the skills to excel at both.

 Reese told ESPN this week he recalls only two teams telling him he would be an inside linebacker at the NFL level: the Giants and Minnesota Vikings .

 "Everyone else pretty much said 'he's an edge guy,'" Reese said.

 The uncertainty about his position was the primary question about the defensive standout in the leadup to the draft and likely the top factor in him slipping to the Giants with the fifth pick. Two NFL defensive assistants even told ESPN they weren't sure Reese had a full-time position at this level. 

 The Giants saw it differently. Outside linebacker/edge was never in consideration for their 3-4 defensive scheme, which employs two starting outside and inside linebackers. They wanted Reese's size and physicality in the middle of their defense as a weakside linebacker.

 "It was easy. When you evaluate talent, and I think that Harbaugh did an outstanding job of this, [inside linebackers coach] Frank Bush did an outstanding job of this, when you watched him play at Ohio State, when he was off the ball, he made a huge impact," Giants defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson said. "He can read. He can dissect. He's just a natural linebacker."

 Reese is proving it at the professional level. He is first in the NFL with 26 solo tackles through four games while playing 99% of the Giants' defensive snaps. His physicality and ability to knock back blockers has been an asset in the run game.

 Reese said he has always been a physical player. He sought out hits as a running back when he was growing up. He didn't transition to linebacker until he was in his early teens.

 

 "I was just so raw at running back. I loved it," Reese said. "My brother used to play football. So when I was 3, I was running on the field and playing and all that type of stuff. Tackling them at practice and stuff. I was 3. He was about 7. I was 3 or 4 years old. It has always been in me to run through the bigger ones." 

 This is the kind of attitude that appeals to Harbaugh, who admitted after the draft to being sold on Reese after seeing him in person at the Ohio State pro day. Harbaugh craves big, fast and physical players. Reese fits that bill.

 The young and impressionable Reese (6-4, 243) and the cagey veteran Edmunds (6-4, 251) have been a capable combination this season. Edmunds, a nine-year veteran, has been impressed because it's not often a player with edge rusher skills can also succeed at inside linebacker in the NFL.

 "It's not easy to come play standup 'backer because your job in the passing game is the major difference. You have to go back in coverage, cover receivers, cover tight ends, running backs," Edmunds said. "That's probably the major difference. It's definitely not an easy thing to do. Take my hat off to him."

 While Reese has had his ups and downs in pass coverage, the Giants are still happy with the early returns. And they have no regrets about where they have him in their defense.

 "When we saw him, there was no question from day one that he was a linebacker, and that's how we always viewed him. And you're starting to see it," Wilson said. "Game 4 of his rookie year, you see the maturation already. You see the impact that he's had on his defense. He's a guy that just loves football. He's tenacious about it. He doesn't want to be wrong. He's had some plays that he wished he had back, but he doesn't make those mistakes again.

 "And when you see him, he is a force of nature when he's on the football field, and we expect him to keep getting better and better."

title: Can the Seahawks' defense again silence the 49ers' hot offense Sunday?
summary: Seattle's defense stole the show the past two times these teams met. But the 49ers and Brock Purdy are on a roll heading into Week 5.
full_text:
RENTON, Wash. -- It took Mike Macdonald several weeks to rewatch the Seattle Seahawks ' 29-13 victory in Super Bowl LX. It was partly because of his packed schedule and partly because of his perfectionist ways. The head coach and defensive playcaller knew that even though his unit had dominated the New England Patriots , it had also made miscues that would eat at him once he saw them on film.

 Macdonald had no such hang-ups about either of Seattle's two January victories over the San Francisco 49ers , a pair of defensive masterpieces in which the Seahawks held their divisional rivals out of the end zone -- first in Week 18, then again in the divisional round of the playoffs.

 That was then.

 The 49ers (4-0) and their offense are rolling heading into an NFC West clash with the Seahawks (3-1) on Sunday at Lumen Field. San Francisco ranks second in points per game (30.5), Brock Purdy leads the league in Total QBR (89.2), and the quarterback has a few playmakers who weren't on the team nine months ago.

 "None of what happened last year matters," linebacker Ernest Jones IV said. "It's a new year, new season. They've got a hell of a group. They've put together four good games, won every one of them. Just like we have a new team, they've got a new team. They're doing some different things. We've just got to go out there and do our job."

 In the first of two defensive performances that even Macdonald might have considered perfect, the Seahawks held Kyle Shanahan's team to 173 total yards in last year's regular-season finale, a winner-take-all affair in which the NFC West and No. 1 seed were on the line. Seattle intercepted one of Purdy's passes, forced two more turnovers on downs and limited Christian McCaffrey to 23 yards on eight carries in a 13-3 victory at Levi's Stadium.

 When the Seahawks hosted the 49ers after their first-round bye, it was more of the same. Macdonald's top-ranked scoring defense allowed only 236 yards, generated three takeaways to go along with three more turnovers on downs, and bottled up McCaffrey again (35 rushing yards on 11 attempts) in a 41-6 rout .

 

 While appearing on NBC's pregame coverage of Super Bowl LX, Shanahan said self-deprecatingly that his "expert opinion" on the Seahawks might not be worth much given that his offense couldn't generate a touchdown against them during the past two times they met.

 "We tackled really well. We limited extra yardage. I thought we rushed the quarterback with discipline and married the coverage," Macdonald recalled this week. "That's what it takes to play really good football, in general. But the guys played hard, played physical, played well situationally."

 Said safety Julian Love : "I think we communicated really well. I think these guys do a lot of stuff pre-snap, motions, shifts, crazy alignment-type things. For the most part, we have a good feel of our communication versus them. And then just man for man, understanding who you're lined up against. I think we match up well with them just body for body. I think that's our biggest advantage compared to any other team."

 But the matchup is a bit different this time.

 Cornerback Riq Woolen and safety Coby Bryant , who missed the Week 18 game, are two starters gone from the Seahawks' defense. That unit, which is allowing the fifth-fewest points (18.3) this season, will have defensive tackle Leonard Williams on Sunday despite an ankle injury that sidelined him for the end of their win last week over the Los Angeles Chargers .

 

 The 49ers, meanwhile, brought back Deebo Samuel Sr . this summer after adding another veteran receiver in Mike Evans . They also didn't have tight end George Kittle in the divisional round game last season after he tore his Achilles a week earlier.

 That trio has accounted for nine of Purdy's 11 touchdown passes, a figure that is tied for the league lead. He's completing nearly 70% of his passes, has thrown only one interception and has yet to be sacked.

 "He's playing really good," Jones said, "getting the ball out really decisive, making the throws, not putting the ball in jeopardy. ... He's playing really smart, and then he's out there extending plays with his legs. He's doing it all right now, playing at a high level. We've got to go execute. We have to play at a high level because they are."

 The 49ers won't have fullback Kyle Juszczyk . Though that is a significant loss given how much their offense relies on two-back sets -- they've led the NFL by a wide margin in percentage of snaps out of 21 personnel (two running backs, one tight end) under Shanahan -- it also creates a question for Macdonald of how San Francisco will adjust. Juszczyk has missed just seven games since entering the NFL in 2013.

 "Kyle's been extremely durable over the years, so there's not a lot of things you can go to and see how they actually did it with the people that are on their current roster," Macdonald said. "Shoutout to him for being able to play all those games. I don't think they're going to end up in 11 personnel [one running back, one tight end] all game. I don't think that's how they want to operate. We'll have a plan for 11, but we're anticipating multiple tight end people out there, and we'll have to adjust throughout the game to test how we think they're going to play it."

 

 There might be one more subplot to this game.

 As if those two January losses didn't leave a bad enough taste in the 49ers' mouths, they might be extra motivated after having watched the Seahawks win the Super Bowl at Levi's Stadium, then celebrate in their locker room?

 "They might feel a certain way," Love said. "I think regardless of what happened last year, we don't like them, they don't like us, straight up. They might not like us a little bit more because of what happened at the end of last season, but it is what it is. You know, it's going to be a fistfight against a division opponent. That's all of them. We don't like anybody in our division."

title: Fantasy football buzz: Expect Bears' Swift to retain RB1 role with Monangai out
summary: D'Andre Swift will be the Bears' RB1 with Kyle Monangai out, with Roschon Johnson potentially getting work.
full_text:
Everything that happens in the NFL has additional context when viewed from a fantasy football perspective. From position battles to injuries and so much more, the news cycle will constantly affect player values.

 Our fantasy football buzz file, with contributions from our ESPN fantasy writers and our NFL Nation reporters, aims to provide fantasy managers with the intel they need as news breaks around the league.

 

 Oct. 9: What's next for Bears backfield with Monangai out? 

 By Courtney Cronin, NFL Nation 

 Ball security has been the focal point for Chicago Bears running back  D'Andre Swift  in the wake of two lost fumbles in three games. "That ain't me," Swift said , a sentiment coach Ben Johnson shares even after characterizing Swift's fumble Sunday against the New York Jets as "egregious."

 

 There isn't much doubt that Swift will still be RB1 against the Green Bay Packers , however, particularly with Kyle Monangai ruled out of Sunday's game because of a turf toe injury. That means Roschon Johnson is next in line to split the run-game workload.

 As the Bears aim to solve their red zone issues after going 4-for-13 since Week 1 (excluding kneel-downs), Johnson could be "part of the solution" to Chicago's goal-to-go struggles, given that he used to fulfill the short-yardage role prior to Ben Johnson's arrival. In 2024, Johnson had a career-high six rushing touchdowns, all of which came from inside the 10-yard line.

 Oct. 9: Chase, Higgins practice, Bengals won't tip hand on availability 
 

 By Ben Baby, NFL Nation 

 Cincinnati Bengals wide receivers  Ja'Marr Chase  (concussion) and Tee Higgins (groin/neck) are officially questionable for Sunday's game against the Miami Dolphins . Both players were full participants at Friday's practice. While that is Cincinnati's lightest day of the week, it was the first time each player was a full-go at practice.

 Bengals coach Zac Taylor didn't want to give any indication for their status on Sunday. Rookie Colbie Young (knee) is officially questionable as well. That means Dohnte Meyers could receive a sizable workload on Sunday. He had seven catches on nine targets for 82 yards in Week 4's loss to the Jaguars.

 Oct. 9: Bucky Irving puts up 31.5 points on TNF 
 

 By Adam Rank 

 Not even the Cowboys could have seen this coming from Bucky Irving . 

 There are a lot of people who walk around trying to pretend like they saw the twist coming in "The Sixth Sense," "Fight Club" or maybe even "Meet the Parents." That seems more plausible than people who will claim they saw the Bucky Irving game coming. Impossible. I won't believe it. This Tampa Bay Buccaneers team was baaaad . Irving had scored just over six fantasy points in the previous game. Sean Tucker was stealing touchdowns. The Buccaneers were starting an undrafted quarterback.

 But, it's the Dallas Cowboys . In primetime. Perhaps we should have seen it coming?

 The point is, what's done is done. Most of us likely still played Irving because there is a lack of available inventory at running back. Like walking into a Spirit Halloween in late October and trying to find a "Youth the Brat" costume. You can't do it.

 So, the question of the day is, is Irving back? I don't want to be that guy in this situation, considering we're feeling so good about how well Irving played. Nobody wants to be that guy. But ...

 The Buccaneers play the Pittsburgh Steelers in Week 6. Not a great matchup. But then they face the Carolina Panthers (amazing), Atlanta Falcons (not bad) and Chicago Bears (tough). It could be a frustrating exercise guessing where Irving pops in certain matchups and underperforms in others. Kenny Gainwell is still a factor in the passing game. Tucker had more snaps this week than last. Irving is a good RB2 option moving forward.

 Here are some other notes from Thursday night: 
 

 
 The Cowboys allowed 241 rushing yards. Let's take a quick scan at the opponents looming on the horizon for Dallas: Green Bay Packers , Philadelphia Eagles ( Will Shipley ?) and Arizona Cardinals are the next three. Make your plans now for the Jeremiyah Love game. 
 George Pickens finally had the game many hoped for after being selected at the end of the second and early third round this summer. Pickens excelled while CeeDee Lamb battled through a quad injury. Lamb left the game in the fourth quarter. Pickens will shine if Lamb is going to miss time over the next few weeks. Ryan Flournoy is the rare receiver insurance policy. I nearly dropped him in a league this week, but thankfully I didn't follow through. 
 I'm sure you saw the clip of the stadium employee who said it was "embarrassing" when Dak Prescott walked down the tunnel after the game. I'm sorry, was Dak the one who set the ball to Alex Anzalone like he was Karch Kiraly? Embarrassing is a bit strong. But it is another mid performance for Prescott, who has two top-12 outings this season. I mean, he's currently No. 1 this week . Odds are it doesn't hold. And based on recent findings, he's going to end up outside of the top 12 again. The next four weeks should be good, however. 
 

 Oct. 8: Sean Payton is not a cure-all for Broncos' fantasy woes 
 

 By Tristan H. Cockcroft 

 It'd be understandable if fantasy managers of Denver Broncos players are giddy with excitement following the news that head coach Sean Payton is taking back playcalling duties from offensive coordinator Davis Webb.

 These Broncos, who finished 10th in yards and 14th in scoring last season, have seen those rankings dip to 27th in either category in 2026. Bo Nix is only the No. 20 quarterback in terms of fantasy scoring, and much ballyhooed offseason acquisition Jaylen Waddle is 33th among wide receivers. And don't get any of us started on Courtland Sutton or the top two running backs, J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey .

 But here's the reality of the situation: Playcalling changes don't always lend immediate, dramatic results, and this season's returns thus far might be as much of an indication of Nix's raw talent than it is the playcalling.

 

 Sure, under Webb's direction, the Broncos' offense has been more conservative, forcing Nix to rely much more on dump-offs and screens. And perhaps Payton, who coaxed decently productive seasons from the 26-year-old quarterback in 2024 and 2025, will open things up more, raising Nix's ceiling for softer matchups and getting the ball to Waddle with more space to make things happen after the catch.

 To the latter point, Waddle's average depth of target is down more than 2 yards this season, and he's on pace for 51 targets within 5 yards of, or behind, the line of scrimmage, which would be easily his most since his rookie season in 2021. I'd love to see him targeted more in the deep game, raising his ceiling into the mid-to-high range of fantasy WR2s, but it's hardly a guarantee that this coaching move will make it happen. Waddle is slightly more attractive as a trade target -- and this speaks to those of you off to slow starts in need of shaking things up with higher-upside moves -- but I'm not making rash adjustments to my valuations.

 As is, it hasn't been the easiest of schedules for Payton's Broncos (@KC, JAX, LAR, @SF), and things do ease up with matchups against the  Los Angeles Chargers (Week 5) and Arizona Cardinals (Week 7) upcoming. Denver's second-half schedule is better than the first as well. That's as much of an actionable on the trade front for Broncos players, but it's also not something that should dramatically swing the arrow upward.

 Oct. 8: Week 5 stats to know 
 by Michael F. Florio 

 

 
 David Montgomery has posted career lows in yards per carry, forced missed tackles rate, explosive run rate, yards before and after contact per carry, average speed and success rate. Simply put, outside of the three TDs in Week 1, it's been rough for Monty. Wait for his next big game, which could be this week against the Tennessee Titans , and then look to trade him.
